text: As I noted a year ago, my new strategy for keeping animal pests away from my melons is to put a plastic bucket over each one, with a brick on top. A 1-2 gallon bucket is about right. Time to get out the buckets. I used to battle raccoons and possums regularly for these melons. I often knew when a melon was ripe, because I'd come out and there was a big bite taken out of it. Canteloupes are especially risky in this regard because they SMELL ripe. They self-invite pilfering. Of course, the melons themselves don't need sunlight, so putting a bucket over them works fine. It does make for a bit of work, though, because near maturity every day or so you have to uncover them to check for slip. It also helps reduce the threat of rot because the canteloupes don't get wet.

I've had that kitchen ... that identical kitchen!  And it was the best one I've ever had.  I love a small U with a "back cabinet run". Here's what I'd do, if I were in your shoes: - The cabinets appear to be in good condition.  If that's true, I'd have them painted.  This will give you the fresh new look that you desire.  If you start taking out cabinets, you'll end up needing to make changes with the floor ... and suddenly you'll have spent much more than would be wise for a house of this size. - You actually have drawers! Remember that the countertops should coordinate with the floor. - Your floor looks to be in good condition. - I would not remove that back wall of cabinets ... not in a million years.  That's a ton of storage, and I wouldn't give it up! - But I would consider having a cabinet maker alter that cabinet wall a bit ... I'd have someone "cut down" that tall pantry cabinet on the right /make it into a standard cabinet + upper.  The point:  This would about double your "back wall" countertop ... and this would allow you to get the coffee pot, the toaster and whatever else out of your main cooking area.  This "away space" would give you a spot for a cookie jar, a fruit basket or whatever else.  This would cost real money, but it would make a big difference in the usability of your main space. - While we're talking about that wall, the space above the refrigerator is not attractive.  Could a cabinet maker create an above-fridge cabinet for you?  Don't worry about it not matching ... not if you're going to paint the cabinets.  If not, could you find a couple baskets to make that space look more "intentional"? - While the cabinet maker's working, how about having him add some triangular shelves to the upper cabinets that edge the breakfast nook?  That'd allow you to show off some pretty pitchers and a little plant. - While we're talking about plants, some greenery improves every room.  Perhaps some hanging plants by the table-window? - I'd replace the refrigerator with a counter-depth model.  This one seems to stick out /impede the traffic pattern. - You have a lot of clutter on the countertops ... what could go away?  Could you place a magnetic knife strip UNDER the cabinets /hide your knives?  Could you dedicate the top drawer by the stove to the kitchen implements currently standing in that bit of crockery? - I see your trash can is over by the table.  Could you go with a shorter trash can under the sink? - You definitely need a curtain over the sink and a related curtain over the table's window. - I would not give up the window over the sink.  No way. - I see a glimpse of your lighting in the "upshot" from the TV room, and I'm underwhelmed.  Replacing these no-personality pot-lights with pendants will be easy /fairly inexpensive.  It's an opportunity to bring in color and style.  I'd like to see lights added over the peninsula too. - I see you have soffits over the cabinets ... that's not ideal, but I wouldn't replace the cabinets just to be rid of them, especially since they probably contain electrical or ductwork, and that would cost big money to change.  I'd paint them ... maybe hang some deocrative plates or whatever else. - Your husband wants to open the cabinet space /open into the living room ... what if you just open a pass-through between the two rooms?  It would allow you to talk between rooms, and it could create a lovely spot for setting out snacks on game day or parties.  Depending upon what your living room is like, you might even place a stool or two in the living room so they could "see through" to the kitchen.  This might reduce your upper cabinet. There are multiple types of septic systems and not all are "big concrete boxes". Many are just large plastic or fiberglass cisterns and any added weight has the potential to damage their successful operation. In most cases, one is instructed to keep the tanks and drain field free of any above ground obstacles other than planting a lawn or other low growing, shallow rooted plantings. Before you embark on this project, check with your septic system and the company that monitors it to ensure that this is an acceptable practice. Replacing a damaged septic tank or drain field is an expensive proposition....easily more expensive than installing a deck or patio by a significant factor!

An at-grade patio (not deck) should be based on your walk-out basement spaces, access from inside and from the decks, and the greater yard layout. With a patio you can't really cover the tank inconspicuously, so it would be better to avoid it. If you extend the deck(s), then you can have it (somewhat) over the tank because there is plenty of room under the deck to access it (height restrictions would need an access through the deck). You can even reconfigure the deck(s) to have a patio under the deck depending on what's going on with the house. In any case, you do not want the patio, or deck supports, to encroach on the leach field.

Hiya Yes long narrow gardens can be quite a challenge and overwhelming at first sight. A couple of comments and suggestions that might help. Firstly, to divide a garden up into rooms you don't necessarily want to have complete screenings across the garden as this really hides the rest of the garden from view. It is much better to have areas of planting coming out into the space and use items of hard landscaping like paths to add the suggestion of rooms. I attach a photo where this has been done very well. Each circular area feels like a room, but is partly visible from elsewhere in the garden. This creates journeys and half-seem focal points that add interest and mystery to the garden as a whole and draw you out to explore it. Within each room there are also hidden quiet spots. Secondly, the best place to hide the circular covers is in one of the beds that come out into the lawn, or even just in the lawn itself, particularly if it is just beside a bed. With all the other distractions going on, you will not notice them nearly as much, if at all. Planting wise, I would not plant a big tree near the sewerage system, but most shrubs would be fine, as would a small tree like an Acer or an Amelanchier. Both are lovely trees. The final option would be to hire a local garden designer to do this planning for you, or even just pay them for a 'design consultation'. A number of designers will charge you an hourly rate to walk around your plot and make high-level suggestions and ideas for you to implement yourself. Good luck with your design.

The conventional wisdom is to choose a neutral that "works" with everything and that leaves your options for other colors wide open. For me there are some neutrals that work okay with most everything, but they may not be the best with the colors you love or in some cases they may not even be okay. My favorite colors wine reds and purples.  Those neutrals that they say work with everything usually greige (gray/beige with green undertones)   The neutrals with pink or violet undertones (taupe or violet gray) are the ones that most people steer you away from, but that look great with my colors. My sister loves olive greens and golds and orange reds - classic fall colors. - Greige is great in her home. My sister in law loves cornflower blues and peach.  Greige looks muddy with her pastels, a light, clear cream or a light gray both work well. I am in my 60s and I can remember when we struggled with picking colors for our first homes and buying things through the years that were the popular colors of the day.  At some point we all landed on the colors for in our home that are actually the same color families that look good on us.   I am a winter  (dark hair, ivory skin tone) and look good in bright, clear colors, Susie is a fall, (brown hair, olive skin tone) and looks great in muted greens that make me look like I died a week ago.   Lisa has blond hair and blue eyes and skin that tans as soon as she walks out the door.  Spring pastels look beautiful on her.    We all ended up filling our homes with the colors that make our hearts sing, and apparently we are vain and the colors that made us feel like a 10 when we were young make our hearts sing. So what are your favorite colors?  What colors make you feel like a 10 and what is the best neutral background for those color?   What neutral color do you want surrounding you when you sit on your sofa in your favorite outfit while entertaining your friends?

Not a cast iron top like the Bluestar's.  On the other hand, there have been so many reports of the Bluestar ovens being problematic.  Doors sticking, broiler being spotty, wiring loose, and so many others.  The only way I'd buy Bluestar is to get its rangetop with another brand's wall ovens separately, and then I'd be ecstatic.  But that is not what you asked for.  I am just addressing the rec for a Bluestar. Regarding the earlier rec for a Monogram, I would want to be certain that a Monogram range today is still as good as the Monograms of 5 years ago which were solid. The pendant light fixture is one made of a combination of vintage and reproduction lamp parts, and I'll tell you my technique for creating this look.  First I do usually look for an original vintage pendant, and Etsy.com is a good source for these, in addition to your local antique or flea markets and good salvage shops.  For over the sink I like to use a 2 1/2" fitter glass shade, like the one pictured here.  At the very least you should be able to find a vintage shade and use it as the basis for your design, if you can't find a whole fixture in good enough shape. The other elements of the pendant can be ordered and assembled from antiquelampsupply.com, and your local hardware store or electrical supply.  I prefer brass components, but you can choose what you like.  You need the fitter piece  - the bottom of the fixture that has three screws usually to hold the glass shade in place, and has the socket for the light bulb.  Then you need the canopy -- the piece that sits next to the ceiling and hides the crossbar, or other lighting mount which holds the weight of the pendant and covers the electrical connection.  In between you need matching chain through which you will thread your electrical wire from  the ceiling down to the socket. If you're handy you can make the whole thing yourself.  If not - just take it to your lamp repair shop or your handyman, and have them put it together for you.  Remember to leave a bit of extra wire (and chain) to make it long enough; better too long than too short -- it can always be shortened!  I like to see my pendant in front of the window - or whatever the backdrop is behind your sink.  Remember to allow clearance for any windows that open INTO the room -- they may hit the light otherwise. Good luck with the restoration of your home -- it sounds wonderful! All best, Julia juliachasmandesign.com   Here's another example with a shade sourced on Etsy! It's from France.  More photos from this projects and my others in my Houzz site.

Hi! You could achieve a lot of what you've mentioned with a relatively small rear single storey extension. It depends on how space efficient the design is. Is the downstairs bedroom and ensuite necessary to accommodate mobility and access needs? You don't need a double storey extension, unless you want to make changes to the first floor. There are limits to the amount you can build within permitted development. Maximum of 50% of the land that forms the plot, and 4m for a detached house. You can also apply for extended permitted development which allows up to 8m for a detached house. There are other restrictions to heights and materials with permitted development. If you do work that requires planning permission there is planning legislation to be complied with but there is no specific limit to the size or form you can build. The species that is considered invasive here is Clematis orientalis. I suggest you NOT seal and close the opening. In my area, when a gas burning appliance is in a closed interior closet, the building code requires two holes that reach outside air- one in or near the ceiling (so that a leak of lighter than air natural gas can escape) and one in or at the floor, for combustion air for the appliance to use.  I have two such closets with these holes, the bottom holes are open to crawl spaces underneath and the upper hole, one goes to the outside and the other goes to the attic, as is shown in the photo. If you're feeling cold air outside the closet, the best strategy is to put weatherstripping around the door frame (as if it were an outside door) and a threshold at the bottom of the door, to seal the gap.

I will answer some of these questions as an Invisacook owner of over a year. Cookware: The pot and pan set MUST MUST MUST BE 5-PLY or 7-ply (or test a really realy good 3-ply maybe with copper core?) stainless for optimum performance. 3-ply mid-class brands definitely do not perform as fast or as good, and depending on the brand, as evenly dispersed in heating.  At first I had a "middle-cheap" highly reviewed induction cookware set, terrible.  I ditched that stepping up to Caraway, and that performs well enough, but still not a top performer.  So plan on an extra 500-1000 for a really good cookware set, in addition to your cooktop cost. Cast iron does work but the 5-ply stainless seems to distribute heat around the pan better than cast iron (which seams counterintuitive to me).  I do have a knock-off enameled cast iron set I love, but I mostly reserve it for baking.  For the cooktop I do use it for things like chili and a huge pot of pasta sauce for example.  The cast iron throws off more heat, and I believe more heat is wasted into the room, is part of the issue.  Invisacook says something about that too. Tests mentioned above by others, I believe, do not mention exactly which type  and make and brand of pot used.  Temperature of ingoing water, ambient temperature, type of pot, if lid is used, type of porcelain and thickness and quality of porcelain, if the appliance is already warmed up, if power boost is used, if it is wired to 240v, all and more will all affect results in tests.  More on test below, but first here is a bit of results using less than ideal pans: TEST results of pans NOT recommended for illustration and learning, different mid-quality brands: ALL TESTS ARE AT AMBIENT TEMPERATURE OF 68F / 20C ALL TESTS ARE WITH WATER TEMPERATURE OF ABOUT 50F / 10C All but one test is with no lid, as lid will speed up performance markedly First enameled cast iron: Taking my 8 inch wide "knock-off (copy) Le Crueset" enameled cast iron frying pan cold, NO lid, using one cup by volume  (quarter liter) , time to simmer was a minute -- yes a single minute -- and boiling in a minute and about 15 seconds. Taking my 10 inch wide "Le Crueset copy" enameled cast iron sauce pan, cold, NO lid, using 4 cups by volume water (just shy of one liter), water reached simmer in about 5 minutes and boiling in about 7 minutes. This time is vastly reduced with a lid. Caraway (expensive) and inexpensive cookware (Carote): Trying a CARAWAY saucepan, 3 quarts (under 3 liters), cold, WITH LID because no lid is painfully slow!!! 4 cups by volume water (just shy of one liter), time to reach simmer was over 15 minutes (!!!) and boiling about 17.5 minutes.=( Note that this single pan costs well over $100 !!!  This is NOT a cheap pan! Yet it performs horribly. My lower-grade inexpensive induction cookware set I had at the start performed even worse. -- that was a Carote set, took over a half hour for the same amount of water and the same size pan as this Caraway test.   I got rid of those right away.  I did not realize then that the highest end cookware really does make a huge difference. I have a 3-ply stainless 12 inch frying pan that performs fast like the enameled cast iron, but again has the center hot spot and outer cold spots, rendering it fairly useless at that size. I NOTE THAT IN MY BOILING TEST in my "not recommended" enameled cast iron that I can see the ring on the bottom of the pan of bubbles hugging the pan surface, the subsurface bubbles, that is LESS than the diameter of the pan. In other words, I can view the BURNER RING working through the pan, evidence that the heat is NOT distributing around the pan's bottom surface but is instead distributing through the WATER itself.  THAT IS WHY THE CAST IRON IS NOT RECOMMENDED AND 5-PLY or better IS RECOMMENDED.  So with pots of soup or pasta water and so on, these pans are fine.  But if you want to fry an egg or a steak or a veggie patty, you will have cold spots in the pan. THIS IS WHY I SAY 5-PLY or better stainless IS A MUST, at least with pan simmer or frying where even heat by the pan itself is crucial.  It will distribute the heat across the pan cooking surface and allow pan searing and frying or even simmering. I though about ordering the 5-ply copper core Invisacook set itself, because there are risers attached to the bottom that do 2 things:  they are the points of heat distribution, ensuring that the heat is distributed FULLY AROUND the pan's cooking surface, and also the built in risers keep the counter cool thus nothing dripping over will slighly cook onto the surface requiring scrubbing, and thus no mats needed.  But this set ONLY comes in nonstick, and I am trying to stay away from nonstick.  Even if it does not leach into my food, it leaches into our water supply at both manufacturing and disposal, and nonstick does not last a lifetime. Ultimately I have decided on mostly Demeyer brand 5 and 7-ply, with a couple of other makes for various needs. Use of pads: You can cook on your counter without the pads and the counter does not get so hot in those spots that it would burn you.  It gets very warm, or decently hot like a sidewalk, but if a child touched it after moving the hot pan it will not burn.   It gets as hot as heat "bleeding" from the pot lets it get, so it also depends on the type of pan/pot. I have tried other silicone protective mats and they do work for counter protection.  But the Invisacook mats are designed to keep heat from "throwing itself downward" into your counter surface, further protecting your counter from long term heat exposure.  Of course porcelain can in fact take heat, it is a very high fired heat making process, and is much more vitrified than other ceramics from the super high kiln temperatures. I do in fact use their mats mainly because the hot pot bottom would itself slightly cook spillover into the surface requiring scrubbing.  I find my biggest incentive to use the mats is that I don't have to scrub the counter afterwards.  I am not sure it adds to heat conservation INSIDE the pot / pan or not, I cannot tell the difference regarding that.  I intend to run a test soon though. Burner Size and Power Boost: I have the 4-burner square.  Note that the 4-burner square has 2 larger burners and 2 smaller burners.  Note what type of unit you are considering to consider the amount of power reaching each burner.  There is also the power boost function, for liquid in the pan, not for heating for an oil fry.  So it says to only use it for water, but I find it helps also for starting big pots of broth for soup and so on.  I think it is meant to warn against too much food particulate matter in the pot when on power boost so that it does not burn on the bottom. Replacement: You absolutely can replace the unit without damaging your countertop.  And you absolutely can later cut out the counter in place to place inside a conventional cooktop, but you would need an expert counter/ porcelain tile person to do that, using specific blades and saws since they would not be using their wet saw for that.  It would take a bit to do it but could absolutely be done. Granite as a countertop option Yes indeed you can use granite WITH CAVEATS (keep reading).  I had in fact chosen a very specific slab of granite to install.  I chose it to blend with my soapstone counters that surround my cooking island, and it was understated and beautifully charcoal without much patter, just beautiful.  The counter stone place said that we should test it because if it has high iron, the heat will instead veer off into the counter surrounding the burners more than the pot, that it would not provide enough conductivity into the pot.  SOME GRANITE HAS TOO MUCH IRON CONTENT to be effective.  So we planned a test. They cut a small square of the slab, and milled it to the correct thickness (thinness).  I brought down a pot (a cheap one, my first terrible set).  They set the slab on top of the unit.  We poured in the water.  And just a few minutes later, it was a rolling boil, so fast!!  I was so happy, it worked fantastically well, almost indiscernible from a regular cooktop!! I walked away to the office to complete the purchase of the slab and waited for the staff.  About 15 minutes later, one of the crew came running in saying to come look at the slab, hurry!  So I did, as did the owner guy who had set up the test.  The slab piece had a fine crack developing.... from releasing water content! SOME GRANITE HAS REMAINING "INVISIBLE" WATER CONTENT THAT NEEDS EXPRESSING OUTWARD, OR TIME WITH LOW HEAT TO DRY IT OUT, or the slab will crack. So the summary on granite is:  It could possibly perform better than porcelain, but the slab must be cut for a test-piece, milled, hooked up to 240V and tested, to see if there is high iron content (or figure another way to test for iron?).  And then one must wait perhaps 30 minutes to see if the slab-piece cracks.  Or find granite slabs stored in a hot dry zone. Power Must be 240v, you must upgrade if necessary.  Must be on its own breaker, so make sure you have breaker space, or you have to upgrade that as well.    I would NOT choose the 110v version unless you were outfitting a small au pair suite or something and really did not want the added power there and do not mind the added time for cooking (versus not having cooking as an option for the space).  In other words I would only choose 110v if it was a choice of no cooking at all versus that, but then i would probably just choose a portable induction unit unless you were outfitting for more luxury. Power control I cut out a decent amount of the backside of a shallow top drawer about 30 inches wide, that is directly under the unit.  I mounted the control panel in that drawer, centered in the front of the drawer with a wood frame built around it to secure it into place and keep it from traveling around the drawer.    The edges of that frame happen to fall in line with the center line of the burners, and so it is super easy for me to find the burner location by glancing at the corner of that frame and running a mental line straight up onto the counter, and centering my pot on that line, either about 4 inches inward (wherever you mount it, you will adjust), or another pot width beyond that for the rear burners. The drawer gets warm so I do not keep anything else in that drawer but you could keep hot pads in there. Then I have large drawers under the control panel drawer, for pots and pans. Exhaust Fan I recommend a ceiling flush mount fan.  I have the Victory Sunset and absolutely love it.  We have enough windows that I don't have to use it often, but in the winter it is heaven to have such a great fan.  It works really fast, and is mounted at over 9 feet high, or about 6 feet above the surface of the counter. Ease of counter switch to serving and other uses I LOVE this aspect of the Invisacook.  I have a smallish to middle size house (for America, probably average for much of country-not-city-Europe) and need every surface.  My remodel made things work much much better, but when 10-20 people visit for a large meal, I absolutely need my island to convert to buffet serve.  And it is so easy to do that!  As things are plated, the counter is quickly wiped without waiting, the silicone pad is dropped in the drawer below, and the conversion to service area is in .motion.  Once the service line begins no one can tell it was just a cooktop.  It is fully a serving island, pots and pans in the sink out of the way. Also grocery loads can just pile all over the island, no wobbly parts from sitting on burners where they should not be anyway.  And occasionally other projects can take place easily on the counter surface. Porcelain choice I would probably go with whom they suggest, or run a test of different porcelain possibilites (as I suggest you do with the granite) so see if there is a difference in performance.  I don't know enough about porcelain qualities to advise on that but suspect there could be minor differences from cheap to quality porcelains. ___ Ok, I hope this helps someone.  This is all I wish I knew ahead of time.  Good luck to all searching.

If I had that assortment of pots available. I'd probably stick the herbs in the one gallon pots. A couple seven gallon pots each for tomatoes, okra, and maybe three for peppers. Depends on how you treat your plants, but you will need to tend 7 gallon pots pretty heavily for those plants. You might be able to get away with twinning your peppers since they are bananas, they can solo down to a three gallon. Your tomatoes and okra for sure one per pot, and make sure that tomato is a dwarf or determinate variety. I wouldn't suggest trying an indeterminate variety in a seven gallon pot, those tend to need ten gallons plus for a successful plant. I haven't grown okra, so don't know it's container habits. Succession plant your peas, leeks, chard, and choy in the rest of the seven gallon pots. 4-6 pots for peas, do a couple plantings so that as some pots are going flush, the other pots are starting to really go- by the time the first pots are running out of steam, the second set should be flushing in. 3 pots for leeks- use square foot method planting, transplant into the pots about two weeks apart. Technically one is supposed to be able to pack up to 18 in a pot that size, but I think you probably want to cut that back by half and do 9 per pot so they are easier to take care of. You can stagger out harvesting, and you may get a few more leeks than you are used to. But I figure doing a four staggered plantings between two pots might be a bit fussy for you right now. If you do cut and come again on your chard and choy, you can do 3-4 pots of those and keep them on a rotation of one being harvested, one or two recovering, and one about ready to harvest. Depending on the variety of choy you choose to grow, many of them are quick growing and you may prefer to succession plant that instead. And they can take up different space- I have winter choi in bins outside and a green bok choy in the garden outside and the winter choi takes up more space. On the other hand I'm groing Hedou Tiny indoors to harvesting in the little 1-1/2" cell trays that come 72 to a flat. They are tiny:) I'm harvesting radishes right now grown the same way too. Not mentioned by the OP is flowers. I suggest adding some in. Pretty and helps attract pollenators. I'm fond of nasturiums for being wholly edible, pretty, and attactive to pollenators. Marigolds and zinnias are usually popular too. Some of your herbs can add to that too, like your basil going to bloom is lovely for the good critters of the garden. Something that might be helpful to use are ollas. They really can help keep even interior soil moisture in containers. Don't feed in ollas, only use water in them. If you can work in composting, do so. While a large bin or tumbler is out for you, you might be able to set up a small worm composting bin. If you feel like you can be fussy, try looking up bokashi. There are also little composting machines now, but I don't know much about them.

Hi - do yourself a huge favour. Forget  ‘undertones’. Forget ‘only certain colours work for specific points of the compass.’ You can have colours from *EVERY* Hue Family for every point of the compass. The secret? Finding the best partnership of Value (lightness) + Chroma (degree of colour) to fit with the quality of light you have available. More colourful colours do better  in lower light settings, than more neutral colours. Their extra kick of Chroma is what helps bust through any tendency to gloom. So more colourful greens are what you are after. Also more dimly lit spaces do well with light + colourful, dark + colourful or just dark colours. Leave the mid Value near neutrals for more moderately lit spaces. You can compare the Value + Chroma of greens for free, via The Land of Color, Color DNA Table. Some examples for you to consider? F&B Bancha. BM Mountain Lane PPG Mountain Forest But they still need viewing in situ. Paint chips or painted samples. Your northern light quality is specific and likely different to someone elses. So it’s always worth testing/viewing your shortlist. You can find greens from different Hue Families too. (again see the Color DNA Table) Yellow Green-Yellow Green Blue-Green Which Family of greens are you most drawn to? Which work better with your fixed finishes? Colours from this zone have the capacity to shift and appear more blueish in certain imbalanced lighting.  They aren’t blue & don’t have blue ‘undertones.’ If they shift in your room and appear that way, try greens from a different Hue Family. This colour shift occurs more in muted greens and you after something more colourful. But at least you know what to look out for when testing. #shifthappens #green #north #south #east #west

@Fern - Bubbles in veneer can be repaired.  The repair is annoying and time consuming but it is permanent.  However, the pictured veneer is checking and checking can't be fixed.  It can sometimes be hidden but it is never going to be fixed. Anyone who works with unsized veneer long enough will have a failure, there are dozens of reasons it could have failed and there is no way anyone on this board can tell you why.  The only way to prevent failure is to glue size the veneer and that is a time consuming, space consuming, and annoying process that few cabinet shops would bother with. It sucks that this happened, and your cabinetmaker may have never had this failure before.  Checking and bubbling often just suddenly appear with no real change in the veneering process and can disappear just as fast, but they can also hang around until you find and correct the cause.  I find it difficult to believe that cabinetmakers are stumped by a checking and bubbling veneer.  It is something they should be aware of. Your cabinetmaker can't fix this, it is going to have to be replaced.  It is the danger of not glue sizing veneers and, while it certainly makes a lot of financial sense not to do so, every once in a while it will bite you in the rear.  Your cabinetmaker is 100% on the hook if s/he purchased the materials.  I can't imagine the cabinetmaker even requiring you to get an attorney as this is such a straight up loser.  No one in their right mind would try to defend a checked veneer as anything other than a manufacturer defect.

I suspect the issue is related to a 2-pronged issue, an overly water-retentive grow medium and watering intervals too short. Too much water = an insufficient amount of oxygen in the grow medium, which limits Ca(lcium) uptake. The plant cannot move Calcium from place to place within the plant, like it can nitrogen, phosphorous, potassium, and magnesium, Ca must be present in the nutrient stream at all times if cells are to form normally. A deficiency of Ca causes cells walls to be weak or to form incompletely. This results in the dissolution of the cells and imperfectly formed tissue, thus the holes and tears inside of the leaf margins nearer to the mid-vein of the leaf. The spoiled foliage at leaf margins are also likely the result of too much water in the grow medium, inhibiting efficient movement of water to the plant's most distal parts - leaf margins and/ or leaf tips. That is what I suspect, but you didn't answer the question re fertilizer. If you haven't been fertilizing, the plant will rob any/ all of the mobile nutrients listed above from existing foliage to use as the building blocks for new leaves as they occur. This process is called resorption, and it is the first step in the process of shedding leaves. My suggestion is to get to a place where you can be sure watering intervals are appropriate; and, if you aren't fertilizing regularly, let's start a discussion about how to put a plan in place that ensures the plant's nutritional needs are met while giving you full control. In conventional container culture, the grow medium should be all about structure, it's ability to retain that structure for the intervals between full repots, and it's ability to hold volumes of air and water the plant is able to deal with. Nutrition is not the soil's job, that responsibility should be shouldered by the grower. I'll watch for your comments and additional input. Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Al

Don't you agree with those who say that you don't fertilize in winter because the plant slows down its growth? If you're asking about the statement "Plants shouldn't be fertilized in winter because growth slows", I'd have to disagree because it's too broad. If you were to say "temperate deciduous trees shouldn't be fertilized in winter" I could agree, but conifers and broadleaf evergreens don't go dormant, nor do houseplants. Plants use nutrients as the building blocks to create growth, but they also use nutrients for metabolic processes and to produce chemicals that allow them to keep their systems orderly and defend themselves. Houseplants slow somewhat to significantly in climes greater than 15* or so degrees latitude due to a decrease in light levels/ intensity, but they don't STOP growing. Even if the above ground organs of a houseplant seem to have stopped growing, they haven't. Even if they did stop, the roots would still be active and growing. When houseplants grow, in order to support NORMAL growth, it's essential to have all nutrients normally absorbed by the root pathway, in the medium and available for uptake at all times. Watering and plant usage are 2 ways nutrients are depleted from the grow medium. If a grower is watering correctly, so the grow medium is being flushed with each watering, the nutrient load after 3-5 waterings will have been largely or almost entirely depleted. At that point, the plant NEEDS fertilizer and should be fertilized. If it's neglected, growth will become abnormal, the plants systems and metabolic processes will move toward disorder, and the plant's ability to defend itself will be diminished. This topic can't be discussed w/o mentioning watering practices. Plants also use less water in the winter because low light slows them down. This can create the dilemma - 'should I water in small sips to avoid over-watering, or water correctly and risk the medium remaining saturated for extended periods and thereby jeopardizing root function, or worse, root function and health?' The dilemma above is where the advice to never fertilize houseplants in winter comes from, along with the assumption the grower will be using a water-retentive medium. The reasoning goes, "It's better to water in sips and stave off depressed root function or root diseases than to water correctly and take the risk. That, is choosing the lesser of 2 evils, which is still an evil. The correct course is, choose neither horn of that dilemma. Make sure you use a grow medium that allows you to water correctly w/o your plants paying an 'over-watering tax' (poor root function/ health). A medium that forces the grower to water in small sips w/o ever flushing the medium ensures the salts from tapwater and fertilizer solutions will collect and build in the soil. This limits water and nutrient uptake and leads to a LOT of spoiled/ damaged foliage. It also causes the ratio of nutrients in the medium to become badly skewed - especially so if the ratio of the fertilizer being used is far from the ratio at which the plant actually takes up nutrients. 3:1:2 RATIO fertilizers like 24-8-16, 12-4-8, and Foliage-Pro 9-3-6 are good choices with the FP 9-3-6 being the superior of that triad by far. If we have a warehouse to hold materials for building cars, but we have to order an equal measure (number) of steering wheels, tires, and headlights, how long will it be before the warehouse is so full of steering wheels and headlights there is no room for tires? That's what happens to fertilizer ratios when we don't flush the soil of even minor accumulations regularly. Finally, it makes much more sense to tie the frequency with which we fertilize to the frequency with which we water - as opposed to the calendar. Flushing the soil is necessary if we are to maximize vitality, but it depletes the nutrient load. You can fertilize in winter at about the same frequency as in summer, perhaps a little less. When you water, drop a marble/ button, or other object in the pot to keep track of how many times you've watered. Fertilize about every 4th watering in summer and every 5th in winter. IT WILL NOT HARM YOUR PLANT to have an appropriate level of fertility in the medium at all times, even during winter. Your plants will appreciate your consideration. Obviously this is meaningless because the frequency with which it is  watered must be considered. I touched on this above, not realizing you would ask the question. You are correct. In Italian forums, people often recommend  using halved doses and at long intervals, regardless of the fertilizer  (e.g. every 2 months). Instead, I watered with the dose indicated by the  manufacturer (12 ml in 2 liters of water) every 3 waterings. Since I  read some of your posts, I've been watering every time but adding just 2  ml to 2 litres of water. What do you think? There is plenty of credible evidence that plants do best when nutrients are in the soil solution at a specific concentration. This means half doses or doubled intervals are always going to ensure a fertility level lower than optimum if you are watering appropriately. If you're not flushing the grow medium, it turns the whole nutritional supplementation program pretty much into a hit or miss crap shoot. Plants don't vary nearly as much in the ratio at which they take up nutrients, which is why 3:1:2 ratios are a good choice. They come very close to supplying about 6x as much N as P and 3/5 as much K as N ...... and that is approximately how the macro nutrients are taken up as a function of N. Plants DO, however, vary significantly in the o/a amount of nutrients they take up and what the ideal level of nutrients (TDS/ EC) in the soil might be. That (ideal concentration) varies by plant and I don't even try to pay attention to it. If I was in the business of bringing nursery/ greenhouse crops to market, I definitely would because I would have to; but, as much as I love growing plants and working hard to keep them healthy, that's a bridge too far for me as a hobby grower. I do know anyone can predictably grow a wide variety of plants and keep them ALL very healthy by nothing more than getting a few simple basics right. I struggled just like everyone else likely did. For me, the transformational point came when I got to a place where I no longer had to battle the grow media I was using for control over my plants vitality. Get the soil right and watering/fertilizing becomes monkey-easy. Then, all there is to worry about is the right light and things like temperature and other influences governed by common sense. Growing things is different for everyone, and we all order our priorities differently, then we make compromises that mesh with our priorities. Al

Advance is not a cabinet coating, and is well under the durability of a true professional cabinet finish. Advance is a trim paint. It is popular with the DIY painting crowd because it is friendlier to the brush and roll skills of beginners who do not own sprayers, or want to deal with respirators and other professional risk mitigation PPE.  It has a really long open time, so self levels extremely well. That helps produce a nice smooth finish, without someone having a lot of experience in applying paint. That long open time has a price, in that it can have a lot of dust and debris in the finish if you do not have a clean work area. It also has a 30 day plus cure time, to reach full hardness, so requires gentle use until that hardness is reached. Dark colors can take longer than 30 days for cures. Professional cabinet coatings are often dry within an hour, and cured in 6. Many shops also use infrared cure systems to speed up even that quick drying time. Professional cabinet coatings, especially catalyzed or hardener activated ones,  are harder, more chemical resistant, and provide greater long term durability than homeowner grade trim paints. That is why that is why the pros use them! CV, or conversion varnish is a multi part catalyzed system that is riskier to everyone involved that the newer waterborne 2K (2 part) European derived opaque polyurethane coatings like Milesi, Renner, Envirolak, Ilva, Centurion, etc etc. Those have some risks as well, but far less than the old solvent based products. There are no zero risks, and if a homeowner is interested in professional coatings, I always suggest them being applied by the professionals who have the safety equipment and ventilation to do so. If an advanced skills homeowner wants to use pro coatings, they need to also have all of the pro equipment to do so. With at least 40 hours of practice in that properly fit respirator.  They also need to look at the pictures of injection injuries from paint sprayers before ever firing up their sprayer. Safety doing any of this work is a very serious thing. All cabinet coatings are a system of coatings. Not just the final finish coat. It all starts with a clean dry surface that gets sanded. And sanded. And sanded. With the correct sanding schedule for the type of wood, and the type of finish. Both those variables come into that sanding schedule. But, the sanding is whst makes the biggest difference in the final appearance, over any type of finish chosen. The sanding shows through. You have to do the work underneath the coating, for a good result. You can’t make up for poor prep work with an expensive coating over the top.

Ignoring the downdraft's inherent issue with capturing cooking plumes that have upward momentum, typically down-draft ventilation apertures (both hole in the countertop and pop-up) are area constrained (compare with relevant hood entry apertures) so more rated CFM may not actually achieve much once a velocity in the opening in the 1000 to 2000 ft/min range is achieved.  Corresponding CFM can be calculated from the apparent area, although in most cases I've seen, the area equivalent is itself over-valuing the non-linear effects of a multiplicity of small apertures. In any case, most down-draft assemblies are sold as part of a system that includes a blower that the manufacturer believes is suitable.  Such blowers may be designed for higher pressure loss.  I haven't investigated this topic in detail because downdraft schemes are functionally the wrong approach. If you want to do-it-yourself, you will need to evaluate the pressure loss vs. flow rate of the aperture assembly, throw in some more for ducting and imperfect make-up air, and hunt through the fan curves of candidate blowers to find a suitable blower. Just don't expect a downdraft to capture uprising hot oil/grease laden cooking plumes.  At best the pop-up type can deviate low momentum steam plumes, so maybe plumes from simmering bacon or poaching fish on a back burner can be partly captured.  A large ceiling register scheme, in spite of its capture limitations due to plume spreading and draft-caused deviation, should be better at both plume capture and room air clearing.

Gas + Downdraft = distorted flames or flames being extinguished.  Neither are good! Ranges/cooktops/rangetops in islands are usually a bad idea (unless the island is very long and very deep). Downdrafts are close to useless if you cook on the front burners or on the back burners if you use a pot or pan taller than about half the height of the the downdraft (assuming a telescoping downdraft). I strongly recommend finding a way to put the cooktop on the perimeter against a wall. Regardless of location, overhead venting is so much better than downdrafts. Note:  When our range/cooktop/rangetop is on an island (or peninsula or in front of a pass-through), venting is even more important as there are more and stronger air currents, so the hood needs to be stronger & larger than when against a wall. (And, yes, experience talking.  We rented a place for a week with a gas range + downdraft in a peninsula -- what a nightmare!  Supposedly, it was one of the better ones.)

Is your staple up system heating both floors?  If so, I would recommend adding sound isolation clips to the downstairs ceiling and ensure everything is sealed then call it a day. There are a lot of good resources out there for soundproofing information.  I suggest looking at some of the home theater boards as they have collected a wealth of great information.  I would not use any type of resilient underlayment system as they generally work by converting sound energy to heat energy and tend to not be conductive to either.  There are some soundproofing materials with decent thermal conductivity, but they cost too expensive to be practical in a home. There are basically four principles to dampening sound... (1) Sealing, (2) Mass, (3) decoupling, and (4) resilient layers.  With a staple up hydronic system, sealing and decoupling are likely your best options.  Adding mass (thermal mass) can also be effective but your system is going to less responsive if possibly more efficient and I believe that one of the benefits of the staple up systems is their responsiveness. There are other options to add mass that is thermally conductive, e.g. fiber cement (hardieboard), either as a subfloor or an isolated thermal mass between the joists, but they are probably not worth it.  Sealing, drywall isolation clips, and two layers of drywall you will get a lot of deadening. ETA: I am not an expert on this... I did a gut remodel including a master bath and your contract seems odd in terms of not having a final budget before you started - at least for those items that are controlled by the GC and not finishes selected by the homeowner. When I remodeled, the costs were a combination - some stuff like rough plumbing or tile installation etc. was a line item based on the "costs" plus the GC's agreed upon markup. I had no interest in knowing what he paid his workers or for the materials used but it appeared as a line item as a cost. Other stuff I selected such as the tile, the marble, the fixtures and these were paid by me and were noted as an item to be supplied by me. The GC had been supplied with specifications by my designer so that he knew what kind of materials would be used in terms of impacting the costs. Along the way there were changes that resulted in more expenses - some where because I had decided I wanted to upgrade - for example the shower doors were a line item supplied by GC according to specifications but I decided I wanted Showerguard so that was an additional expense. Other examples were unexpected like needing a new electrical panel because of greater electrical needs for kitchen appliances and of course I paid for those as well since they were outside the scope of the original electrical specifications and scope.

A cost plus contract puts the cost control onus on the homeowner, and their design professional much more than on the contractor. The project’s good faith estimate relies on the cost parameters established by all of the preliminary design work to create the Scope of Work and Materials List, and then the labor estimating work of the chosen contractor referencing the design work. Whether your plumbing fixtures for the bath are 3K or 13K for the totals, if the manufacturer discontinued them before you can order, you still have an idea of the pricing that you should try to account for when researching replacements. You may not account for the extra design hours for the designer who has to now regroup for an appropriate replacement, but this is why a contingency amount in the budget  is important. The bigger unknowns in remodels has more often been the Scope of Work changes, due to hidden conditions. Older homes are notorious for the cast iron waste pipe disintegrating when touched. Or a main joist having been cut be a previous plumber and now needing structural reinforcement. Those are understandable changes and price increases. From your description,  I’m having trouble understanding if your cost overruns are from the product end, or the work end. Or both. Any why? Were the original labor quotes from so long ago that the costs have gone up that much? I can understand some of that. Electrical raw materials have risen hugely. Many subs won’t even guarantee a quote to be held past 14 days!

"...375 Max Blower CFM-rated hood..."  Actual flow likely only 200 CFM with correct ducting and lossless MUA.  Rated means blower operating hanging in free air without any pressure losses, particularly those of the mesh filters. Only fume hoods used for grinding and welding develop enough flow (and noise) to suck vapors to them for removal; cooking ventilation that anyone could stand depends on the hood's capture area intercepting the rising and expanding cooking plumes.  In canopy hoods, that is the boundary area at the bottom.  On this decorative hood, it might be the mesh areas.  These are not overlapping the potential cooking plumes that the cooktop below can generate, depending on pan sizes, and no means of retaining plume components that reflect from the sheet metal are present. Likely the installer was depending on house leakage for MUA.  This requires a pressure drop between outside and inside, and this drop reduces blower performance. At a minimum, the installation instructions should be reviewed to determine correct ducting.

...soon the code will require to have laminated glass in all residential and commercial applications. Many places this is already happening, railing systems are required to be laminated rather than tempered. Per the why part of your question, laminated and tempered are both considered to be safety glass but for different reasons. Tempered glass is considered safe because it breaks into tiny, relatively not-sharp cubes when broken (think car side or back windows) while laminated stays attached to a vinyl interlayer when its broken (think car windshield) so there is no broken glass all over the floor and no opening for someone to fall through in the railing system. Simply put, while both products are safety glass, laminated is safer than tempered in most applications, including railings, which is why codes are changing to require laminated glass in those applications.

You could look this up on line, but here goes... Today's poinsettias are about as close to the wild ones as is modern sweet corn and maize. The original wild poinsettia grows as a large multi-stemmed DECIDUOUS shrub that blooms in late fall/early winter with small greenish yellow flowers and large colorful long lasting red bracts. In the past, growers struggled to get the plants in full color AND with green foliage for Christmas, no mean feat. Most planted a fern with the points, to hide the bare stems as the plants naturally lost their foliage, usually by New Years, but sometimes sooner. The other problem is that points are short day plants, they bloom as the days get shorter, much like mums. They require days with more dark hours than light hours. Any light, even from artificial sources, will delay blooming. All this changed when the Eckes of Encinitas CA began to work toward what we know as the modern poinsettia. Today's plants are compact, stay mostly evergreen, and the bracts hold color til you get tired of them. They still are short day plants however, so if one wishes to 'rebloom' their plants for another Christmas they must be protected from ALL light over 12 hours daily for at least 8 weeks. Commercial growers typically cover their plants with 100% black shade cloth for the required period of bud set, then natural light. If your bracts are showing color by Thanksgiving, you're good to go. As far as culture in the house, good light, an east, west, or south window and temps in the 60-80F range suits them. Water so the soil stays evenly moist but not soggy. The medium growers use today drains very well, so be sure to make holes in the bottom of the foil the plants come in, and don't allow pots to stand in water in a cachepot or saucer. And no ice cubes, please!

For those interested in a few ”pro” suggestions, here you go!  To keep your plant pretty for as long as possible, it needs to be located where the temperatures are coolish and the sunlight plentiful.  Avoid direct drafts from an open door or heating vents.  Remove the plant from the foil pot cover as it should never sit in accumulated water.  As said above, water thoroughly but infrequently.  No plants should be given tiny sips to the surface as the means of watering. After the new year, allow your plant to go dormant naturally by reducing watering greatly.  The leaves should begin to fall off and you can pretty much ignore it for a couple of months, watering just enough to keep it alive.  In March or April, cut the stems back to 6 inches, place the plant in a sunny location and resume watering. The first few times, take the pot to the sink and submerge it in tepid water until no more bubbles are visible, allow to drain fully and return it to its sunny location. Commence with your normal fertilization routine, starting with conservative doses at first. I suggest that the new emergent growth be pinched to promote branching; that and plenty of sunlight will prevent stretching. In mid September, you MUST provide artificially short days for thirteen or fourteen UNINTERRUPTED hours of total darkness.  But you can’t put it into a dark dungeon and forget about it!   uninterrupted for fourteen hours of darkness, followed by ten hours of bright sunlight for normal happy growing.  Reduce or eliminate fertilization at this time and be watchful about watering frequency.  Your poinsettia is now shifting into flowering gear. Greenhouse growers use shades and black shade cloth, set on timers.  We can cover the plant with a box, take it to a closet for the night,  pull the blinds in a darkened, unused room for the magic ten hours.  Once it begins to flower, you can allow it to be a normal part of your household, keeping in mind that they do best in a bright location.  The brachts should turn red as the flowering stage continues.  If they don’t,  it’s because you have done something wrong, usually with the light duration.  Or, as in the case of a careless student greenhouse manager at Va. Tech, the nights were interrupted in the big poinsettia greenhouse (full of Hort Club fundraiser poinsettias grown by that year’s propagation classes) by turning on the lights when he walked through to get to where the night blooming cereus were getting ready to burst open and he wanted pictures. Your questions: a) You have added 1000sf, of which I'm sure required excavation and grading, and will be checked. Whether an inspector reviews around the existing house is unknown, but it is all connected and should be reviewed by you and your contractor regardless of inspection. b) Yes, min 6" exposed concrete foundation wall between stucco and grade; if you have impervious hardscape, then 2" gap to allow the use of untreated wood siding/sheathing/framing. c) Grade slope at foundation is 6" in the first 10' (5%) away from house, impervious surfaces 2% slope away from house. Contractor suggestions: a) Piping downspouts is always a good practice. However, proposing to end those in a drywell may not be the best solution. If your soil does not drain well (and will be saturated during a storm event), then the drywell cannot disperse it's water into the surrounding soil. If you have freezing the drywell is useless for 3-6months of the year. If you have leaves, debris, and asphalt shingles a stone drywell will clog up over time. b) Adding hardscape just to try and address a negative grade issue is useless and makes it harder to fix in the future. Water can still flow towards the house on top of a hardscape. Water can still flow towards the house under a hardscape. When you have a flat lot, or even lot that slopes downhill toward your house, you provide surface swales at minimum 10' away from your house to direct water around it.

@Alex [Zone 6a Lithuania.] You're probably on the right track, but more info is required from the OP to confirm. In all likelihood, the issue is soil related and involves a high TDS/EC (salt) level. Root function limitations from lack of oxygen or root disease is almost certainly a part of the issue The soil looks like compacted sand. Residual deposits in the collection saucer bears witness to water being allowed to sit in the collection saucer until it evaporates. If true, a steady increase in TDS/ salts is assured unless the grower is using R/O water or some form of deionized water. I addressed how to deal with a nutritional issue in a temporal fashion, but if the grower wants to put the best foot forward, he would do well to make sure the grow medium is structurally sound and he can water to beyond the point of total soil saturation (so at least 20% of the total volume of water applied at any given watering session exits the drain hole) without concern that root function or health are negatively affected by excess water retention and an inadequate volume of air for extended intervals. I agree this is not something a change in fertilizer can fix, and it's not a magnesium deficiency in the sense that magnesium can be identified as the single most limiting factor, nor do leaves present as being deficient in Mg - not even close. If there are multiple deficiencies (probable), improvement can come only by supplying the nutrient most lacking (see Liebig's Law). Not yet mentioned is the fact that Mg is one of the mobile nutrients, and as such any deficiency would be more conspicuous in older foliage as the plant robs older leaves of their Mg content to use as building blocks for new leaves coming on line. This is not the case. As noted, this is one of those times where the best thing the grower can do is address the basics. * Make sure the plant is in an appropriate soil * Make sure the planting can tolerate the soil being flushed w/o sacrificing root function or health * Make sure watering intervals are appropriate and the plant is watered on an 'as needed' basis as opposed to on a schedule * Make sure water quality is appropriate * Make sure the plant is fertilized regularly with an appropriate fertilizer * Make sure root temperatures are reliably below 90*F/ 32*C (if watering properly and using a pot with gas permeable walls, root temps should remain 10-15* F below ambient temps) Al

You have two basic methods to meet R20 for walls: insulate between studs with a single R value; or insulate between studs with a lower R-value but make up for it with an additional continuous layer of added R-value. Your builder uses a standard of R15+R5 (R13+R5 is Climate 5 code) for the latter method compliance, and with that allows use of cheaper 2x4 framing. Most builders choose the former method and frame with 2x6, which meets an R20 with fiberglass batts. If you were to go to the expense of spray foam, 3" thick (your builder is stating closed cell at 7.0/inch R-value) would meet R20 code just between the stud spaces, so you would not need the extra R5 exterior insulation or any of it's extra detailing and work. Design of a wall assembly needs to consider both the thermal performance and drying potential. I agree that a continuous layer of rigid foam insulation on the exterior of the sheathing enhances performance of a wall assembly designed for climate zone 5.  Properly installed and with seams taped, it's a great air barrier, a great secondary drainage plan, and it will limit the potential for condensation in the wall cavity.   That said, continuous foam insulation on the exterior will limit drying of the wall assembly to the interior side only.  Sandwiching the sheathing between a continuous layer of rigid foam and 2" of closed cell foam will further inhibit drying to the interior side which could cause problems.  If you're going to insulate with foam, I'd keep it on one side of the sheathing.  If you're able to get the code-required R-value with exterior foam and cellulose insulation in the cavity, that would be my recommendation.

I have a number of books about Clematis and almost all of them have a section devoted to propagation techniques.   So you might  get yourself a few clematis books...they are wonderful to  look through.   I have some in my car where I can read if I'm waiting on someone,  or  take to a dr. appointment.    Some beautiful books can be had on ebay at great prices...usually under five dollars including shipping. Most of these books  say to take semi-ripe cuttings.   I have taken many cuttings myself and  currently have about   20+  tiny clematis plants coming along which were rooted last summer and fall.   I  agree with most books on the semi-ripe part.   You know how clematis stems become brown as they age?   Well,   I take cuttings when they're  not quite brown.   You don't want them too soft either.   The cuttings I take are pretty small...I cut just below a node and then  above the node and  trim any leaves to about two leaves.   I scrape  lightly  through the  outer " bark"  for about 1/2",  put  rooting hormone powder on them and bury the node in pure sand with  the leaves sticking out above the sand.   Keep moist ,  put in  dappled light or am sun and leave them alone  for a couple of months.  In hot weather I use a misting system. If you root some and  leave them outside in winter,   know that in spring  it can take some time for some varieties to show new growth.   So don't assume they're dead .   Just wait awhile  to see if new growth pokes out.   I  really like  being able to root them because it takes some of the anxiety out of  planting .   If a plant doesn't make it in one spot a backup plant might make it in another.  It seems the most vigorous clems are the easiest to root...Polish Spirit and Triternata rubromarginata root  readily for example.

The best houses have separation, such as closets, between bedrooms and between bedrooms and public rooms. The best houses do not have roofs that are overly large, and dominate the exterior of the house. The best houses do not have stick on exterior materials only on the front façade. during the 21 months my husband was terminally ill, i ate enough to barely stay alive.    then during the year after he died,  i became a rack of bones.     that first year and to be honest, the next 2-3 years are especially emotionally difficult because it takes that long (at least it did for me) to realize that this was my "new normal" and i hated every minute of it.    i had zero appetite and many days, just the smell of food made me nauseous. it was only after my sister-in-law dragged me, kicking and screaming, to my doctor's office where i could barely speak the words that would convey my grief.     not only had i lost the love of my life, during that first year i also lost both of our dogs, my last living connections to him.    i was beyond depressed, i walled myself off from all social contacts and barely even spoke to family.   reluctantly, i agreed to begin taking an antidepressant and i cannot even tell you how much it helped.   i slowly began to see light at the end of the tunnel and realized that my depression was only causing me more grief.    that was 15 years ago, i took it up until 2 years ago.    while i still have days when i travel down the proverbial rabbit hole, i am much better able to grip at the edge and claw my way back out before i fall completely down into the darkness. if you haven't already, i would urge you to talk to your doctor about the possibility of taking something that can help you cope.    it doesn't have to be forever, you might get by just fine after stopping in a few months, maybe a little longer.    i had no concept that taking a simple little pill every day could improve my outlook and drive away the thoughts i had of driving off the bridge on my way to work but it did help me so so so much! i'm deeply sorry for your loss.    another widow once told me, we have to go through grief, we cannot go around it.    wishing you comfort and please know, you are not alone.  💞

We used to keep plastic storage on a lazy susan, and it was a pain in the neck. When we remodeled our kitchen, we specified a drawer for that purpose, and it was game changing! Our current house doesn't have a lot of drawer space, so we have storage containers (plastic and glass) in upper cabinets. I find it much more efficient to use the lazy susan for canisters of dry goods.

Here's mine, staggered shelves with an after-market turntable that I added to the bottom floor of the cabinet. I keep the bulk of my storage containers in an upper cabinet over the prep area, with the lids stacked vertically to one side like books on a bookshelf. I use Pyrex instead of plastic and I have to admit that I have to nest the Pyrex to conserve space, which is a pain, but necessary in my small kitchen. As you can see, my lazy Susan holds so much stuff, but it's not stuff I have to reach for constantly, whereas my storage containers are used multiple times per day, and so it makes sense for me to keep those items handy in an upper cabinet over my prep area.

I agree (as a lawyer) to look at the contract, but at the end of the day your contractor shouldn't be pressuring you to use his preferred vendor on something like a counter.  (I could see the contractor being insistent on using a preferred sub if he'd have to work with them on an ongoing basis or for a critical part of the job like framing or foundations, but counters are a pretty self-contained job.) Ask him for a reason why he can't work with your preferred vendor.  Tell him that if he really will not work with them, you will handle this part of the job yourself.  If he gets aggressive or continues to pressure you hard, that would set off alarm bells for me.  No one wants to change contractors in the middle of a job, but I'd be questioning what else is going here.  My spidey senses tingling, particularly since there is an insurer paying.

Hello, violetsnapdragon, There are all kinds of compost, depending on the materials added and the circumstances of their decomposition, and how it was processed. However, I was using seeds I had saved and apparently, my saved seeds were carrying some of the Damping-Off organisms. So I began watering my seed-starting pots with a solution containing one or more sterilizing ingredients. So, spending money on a sterile starting mix is not always enough. There is a lot to unpick in this and you have lots of choices, which ones suit you best will depend on many factors including financial. For example - how much of a structural alteration to make, and which period features to protect. You've already started to make decisions around this, for example with the tiles in the hall, which is excellent. You could for example remove the chimney breast which splits the space in two between what would probably have been the original kitchen and morning room or laundry/scullery. This chimney continues up through the whole house and you could remove it entirely, freeing up space on each floor, or just to the ground floor. If you wanted to remove it externally this would require planning permission and may be tricky to get permission for depending how visible it is from the street and the particular protected characteristics of your conservation area. The idea of creating a courtyard could work nicely, but I wouldn't recommend building a standard conservatory - the amount of time you can use them comfortably is very limited. To build a high quality one that gives you comfortably useable space year round is costly - more so than a standard build that isn't a conservatory because glazing can be costly. Although it does depend what you want to use it for - as a mud room / utility it might work as you only tend to pass through rather than want to spend time in there enjoying the space. A thing to note about conservatories is that they can't be heated in the same way as a habitable space and comply with building regulations. The key to any redesign is getting a clear vision in place for how you will live there. If you want a home you can live in with ease and pleasure then it's essential to get that vision clear from the off. Okay, hold your horses.  This idea of removing the tub and reusing the floor tile to fill in where the tub had been has a major flaw.  No waterproofing.  Your plan only takes into account the pretty surfaces and not the bones that actually make a shower work.  When you build a shower, the layers underneath the tile and grout must be waterproof.  Grout is not waterproof.  A shower is built to account for that and you can actually take a shower in a properly made shower BEFORE the tile and grout go in and you will be fine.  If you leave up walls from the 1950s or earlier, you are dealing with tile set into a thick mud base reinforced with wire mesh.  Somehow, this system usually did not leak through and get the framing of the walls wet.  But once the tub is gone, you are back to bare studs down there.    There is no way for you to add tile there and tie it in to the old walls.  Your new section where the tub had been will either just leak, will leak at the seam between the old wall and the new area of wall (if you manage to waterproof the new section), or will leak both where this seam is and where the new wall meets the shower floor.  The only way to make a waterproof shower is to have a seamless layer of waterproofing using one of several methods from the drain in the shower floor to the top of the tile walls AFTER a professional slopes the shower floor properly.  You simply cannot do it the way that you said you want to do it, re-using the floor tiles to make the lower walls. Research waterproofing so you understand a few ways of doing it and you will see what i mean.  This is not a quick semi-remodel situation.  As pros have tried to tell you, you must gut the tub/shower to make a shower here.

Thank you for sharing your experience with condensation forming on your low-pitch roof, and for reaching out for advice on how to prevent this from happening during your roof replacement. One possible solution could be to add venting cavity battens on top of the purlins, which would allow for ventilation and help to reduce condensation. This would create a small air gap between the roof underlay and the insulation, which would allow for any moisture to escape. Additionally, using a suitable roof underlay, such as the Thermocraft Covertech 201 that you mentioned, could also help to prevent moisture from penetrating into the insulation. Overall, it's important to consult with a professional roofer or contractor who can recommend the best course of action based on your specific situation and the type of roofing materials being used. They can help you to choose the appropriate ventilation and insulation systems that will work best to prevent condensation and protect your home from moisture-related issues. Good luck with your roof replacement, and I hope you find a solution that works for you!

text: The trick to growing year round for me is to increase row spacing. I grow winter onions, carrots, and beets in rows 2 feet apart. They won't get harvested until late spring. But my summer veggies have to get planted out in  March. They all go in between. So while the winter veggies are getting big, the summer veggies (mostly vining) are small, and they don't compete. When the summer veggies get big,  and expand to fill the available space, the winter veggies have been harvested. Call that garden planning.

To my knowledge, radiant cooling (running chilled water through in-floor pipes) is neither effective nor very common in the US. A major issue, besides the fact that heat rises and the upper levels of room air will remain hot, is that in much of the US, humidity removal is as much a comfort-producing feature of traditional AC as is air cooling. I would expect that a chilled floor in a humid room would get wet - that removes some water vapor from the air but causes other obvious problems, potentially major ones. If you want to fill the pockets of your local tradesmen by going with the most expensive alternative and spend two or three times more, you could consider the ground source approach.

I think you would be better off and better served by looking more into the mini-split options. Just for clarification, I would not usually recommend in-floor radiant cooling for residential applications although they can work. In-floor radiant would be more appropriate in a commercial/institutional setting where humidity and Dew Point is better monitored and controlled. Floors would be zoned out for cooling in residential with chilled water fed fan coil units for both heating and cooling. They are fed by insulated piping that is a must to prevent sweating and fan coil units that collect and deal with condensate in air-conditioning mode much like mini-splits or any other fan coil units. I am so far from an expert on this that my best advice is probably to ignore my advice, but I have had to deal with calcimine a couple of times so here are my thoughts. New drywall is probably the easiest/cheapest if you don’t have plaster moldings.  However, if your crown is plaster and can’t be removed then removing the calcimine is probably your best bet.  I don’t understand why you need to use calcimine paint in option 2 if you are removing the calcimine.  When ours was removed they used a binder and then regular modern paint.  There was no need for a calcimine paint after the calcimine was removed and it was pretty easy to remove as it is so much softer than the cured plaster.   It was certainly labor intensive, but not difficult. My, again limited, understanding is that partial removal is not a good idea.  A hard coating over a soft coating will usually fail and in this case the areas that have cracked and failed have likely relieved the surface tension for areas that haven’t failed and so fixing those areas will likely just increase the surface tension on other areas and increase the likelihood of new failures in those areas in the future.
