One thing you will not get out of large format porcelain or laminate sheet or whatever this is representing is that the pattern is matched across all three tiles. Virtual imaging is problematic because it represents a reality that either can't be realized or is misleading. I see virtually staged rooms in real estate where the furniture has been scaled down slightly to make the rooms look larger. And I have been in some of these actual listings, empty, so I know they are doing that. I know someone who worked on a project that had many virtual images and the clients ended up being disappointed in the real thing because it did not look Exactly like the fake images. Why? The real thing had electrical outlets, it had light switches, it had required exit and emergency lighting, it had fire suppression. Everything wasn't smooth and pristine and flawless like the virtual imaging. The virtual imaging showed perspectives and proportions in ways that were not identical to how one experiences things in real life. And the virtual images were so "real" that the virtual reality is literally what the client expected from the outcome. (Which is Not really reality).

I would block the holes up- it can be done from outside without removing the kitchen (although when you later replace the kitchen you will likely tidy up the inside part of the hole).    It is important to have ventilation in a house to avoid condensation- this is especially true if there are lots of you living in the house (which means more showers, more cooking, more towels on radiators etc).  Instead of these air bricks people tend to have mechanical extractors in kitchens and bathrooms- you could go even further and have an automated system of ventilation- try an online search for MVHR.   Its a moisture controlled system that keeps warm air in the house but extracts damp or stale air- these systems cost from £700 to several thousands depending on how big your house is and the way it can be installed.

In order to accomplish your wish list, first, the entire plaster finish must be removed. The best way is by a water jet blaster. It will completely remove the plaster and expose the original concrete shell or substrate. This will allow for proper prep and adhesion of a tile finish. It's an expensive process. Chipping the material off never gets every last bit. It's not advisable to apply a bond coat to existing plaster and then apply tile. Too many layers in my opinion. A bond coat is necessary on a re-plaster though. Second, in order to add a sunshelf or any step in an existing pool, the new structure must be reinforced with rebar. Adding the steel rebar means one must also tie into existing rebar, make a connection to bond the steel as per  National Electric Code (NEC) Not reinforcing will most definitely result in failures in the form of cracks. Third, tiling an entire pool is more expensive than plastering. Tiling an entire pool takes special skill and it requires a special prep. Yes, it will last much longer than a plaster job. And yes, they are gorgeous when they're done. A sound plaster job will last 12-15 years provided the pool (chems) are properly maintained. Do you see yourself in that house beyond 15 years? I've asked clients in your position if they are comfortable with the additional expenses, then they should go for it. I make people understand what's involved in a project of such so there are no surprises. Hope this helps in your decision.

I'm assuming you're asking should you have two glass pieces, one to stay put and one to open? If so, it really depends on the overall style of your bathroom, and there are pros and cons to both. Traditional two glass pieces with one being the door is better for keeping in moisture and heat, but it is more expensive and it also depends on the size of the shower opening. A single, stationary piece of glass does block water, and it's less expensive. It is also more modern in terms of curbless showers, and can make the shower feel more open on all sides. But it is much colder, and there is a draft usually. Also water will spray everywhere so you'll need to make sure it doesn't damage any walls that arent covered in tile. Any opening less that 36" would only need a single swinging door. Hopefully I got the gist of your question correct!

In which case, and this gets to the main question, even the smallest common mini splits at 1 ton / 12,000 BTU could be way over-capacity for any one single room, and therefore end up running in sub-optimal cycling patterns. Inverters or units that have the ability to ramp up and down with 1% increase in loads (heat or cool). The problem is there are many incarnations of Inverters that don't allow a 1% step in capacity. So this is why you really need a trusted pro to do the work for you. The other side of a true 1% inverter step up an down is you pay for over sizing (a bit) because and how the machine runs --- typically starts out slow and ramps up and down as needed you never over supply the space. The over supply the unit has is simply never used, because the algorithm the machine employs doesn't allow it to over supply the space in question. Inverters add more complexity & cost: yes. Everything is moving that way so it's not avoidable for much longer. The con going forward will be how the inverter is designed to operate. 1% step up and down = better.     ---- 2, 3, 5 speeds not so good for certain applications (climate is more prone to determine this in my opinion -- mild climates have much less trouble).

Once that is known, then the heating and cooling loads for the room need to be calculated for your house and location. Once the  heating load is known, then you can select the proper size equipment. In the case of a mini split, you have to determine from the manufacturers specification sheet what is the heat output at the outdoor design temperature you used in the load calculation. Oh no.  Your story breaks my heart because, for me and obviously you also, trees hold a special place in my heart.  Trees have such grand, deep souls.    Here is Maya Angelou's poem When Great Trees Fall, although it is not just about trees: I copied part of it, then added the link to the whole poem.   After the link, I added the end of the poem.  I love this poem almost as much as I love trees and those great souls I have had the honor to know. When Great Trees Fall Maya Angelou When great trees fall, rocks on distant hills shudder, lions hunker down in tall grasses, and even elephants lumber after safety. When great trees fall in forests, small things recoil into silence, their senses eroded beyond fear. When great souls die, the air around us becomes light, rare, sterile. We breathe, briefly. Our eyes, briefly, see with a hurtful clarity. When Great Trees Fall And when great souls die, after a period peace blooms, slowly and always irregularly. Spaces fill with a kind of soothing electric vibration. Our senses, restored, never to be the same, whisper to us. They existed. They existed. We can be. Be and be better. For they existed. I am so sorry for your lost tree.  I hope you will plant another.

A sink faucet, simply unscrew the aerator on the spout to check for debris. Check the user manual or specifications documents for your tankless water heater, or look it up online by the model number to find the required GPM flow-rate to activate the unit and if there's a reference for what is the required sustained flow to keep it activated. Perhaps the safety-limiter on B1S is malfunctioning or needs to be adjusted to a higher trigger temp. Set B1S running hot, until it goes cold, leave it running and quickly go check the tankless to see if it has shut off. Have you tried pressing the bypass button *before* the flow runs cold?  Pressing it *after* the shower has gone cold probably doesn't change the hot flow-rate.  Your tankless may need the flow to stop for several seconds and restart to trigger it to re-ignite (assuming it's a gas unit). What is the setpoint of your water heater?  As a test, try setting it to approx 105°F to check what is the effect on B1S and B1F.  It's possible that your setpoint is high enough that showerers are turning the hot water flow down so low that it's dropping below what's needed to keep the tankless activated.  Setting the tankless lower such that more hot flow is mixed-in for a comfortable shower temp may eliminate the problem. I set my tankless *at* the desired shower temp ... between 101°F and 103°F, sometimes low as 92°F to 95°F after a session of summer yard work ... and run the faucet at full-hot flow with no cold mixed in.  Haven't had a problem with a shower going cold in 17+ years.

This comes to two factors: appearance versus performance. If you want to cool a room or keep out the cold, thick curtains/shades on all windows in a room are needed. If you are just needing to block the sun due to glare, then you only need the ones that the sun comes through directly. BUT if appearance is important, then you'd do all 6. I have a Bryant high efficiency furnace that has had ongoing issues since I installed it in 2000. It is actually made by Carrier. The door at the bottom has a lockout switch, so I guess it could be as simple as the switch itself not staying in the made position. Or, it could be that your controls are locking out and opening the door causes the controls to be reset. I would suggest checking the window that allows you to see through this door when it has failed to start. If there are any codes set, you will be able to see them without removing the door. The repeated code for I have had for various reasons has been the 42 (4 amber blinks, and then 2 green ones). It means that the inducer fan has not come up to speed in the allowed amount of time. My causes have been rubbing fan impellor, poor bearings, and in one case a plugged condensate drain trap that flooded the inducer housing. In any case check for codes and you will find out if there is anything more serious wrong. You should be able to find a list of codes on line, although there may be a list on the furnace door. To complicate things a little more, I recall that in some cases two codes can be set, and they will only display sequentially once, and after that only the last code is shown. So you have to sit there and watch it and hope it fails while you are still watching it... Not a great system.

I have used the trick of the piece of apple or bread in brown sugar but have never tried it on white sugar.  The two different sugars seem to differ in that the brown sugar has a moisture content that, when it is left exposed, will  evaporate and the brown sugar will harden.  However, white sugar has no moisture in it and will harden up with moisture. Sure that this is simple chemistry of some explanation.  Maybe someone here can shed some light.  Is moisture really what you want to put into your white sugar?  It must be in the chemistry of crystals that the difference is.  Brown sugar has a certain degree of molasses left in it or added back in after the refining, thus the moisture.  White sugar is hard dry crystals and it has been my experience that white sugar will actually harden with moisture. I never tried softening up white sugar with this technique and really never thought about trying it, but we learned the brown sugar trick early in life. With hardened sugar I will always use something to break it up. I am not so proud that I cant be proved wrong, but putting moisture into white sugar seems so antithetical to my longtime experience with it. Drop a spoon of water into the sugar canister and you will find a little hardened lump will form as it dries.  The crystals have dissolved and are hardened into a little shiny sugar rock. I always give it whack with something hard to break it up.  But, if it has hardened into a large solid mass that may provide limited results to use it in baking.  You can still dissolve it in liquid and use it like that, in some applications.  It WILL dissolve in moisture and water. I have a few hard lumps in my white sugar bucket right now.  Maybe I will experiment. However, you can make your own shaped sugar cubes by moistening your white sugar  with a few drops of water and putting it into small molds and let it dry. It will harden.

".... it is confusing as there are successful indoor plant pot companies whose  pots do not have drainage but use lava rocks who insist that they are enough." Don't feel bad. There are thousands of growers every day who fall prey to the advertising hype of advertising that walks the razor's edge between truth and lies. Recently, I did some research on a "special Fertilizer for Fiddle Leaf Figs" which among other things touts their 3:1:2 nutrient ratio. A nutrient ratio in not the same as a fertilizers NPK %s. Come to find out the amount of actual NPK %s were only 0.28 : 0.09 : 0.06 ..... less than 1/2 of 1% fertilizer and about 99.6% water. Growers are paying more than 192x what a quality 3:1:2 ratio fertilizer (Foliage-Pro 9-3-6) costs, for water. Plants WANT to be watered often and thoroughly. Watering forces harmful gasses (sulfur dioxide, CO2, methane) from the soil and pulls in fresh air behind it. Also, ANY part of the soil that is saturated, even the bottom layer with lava rock or other "drainage" material always represents a limitation to terrestrial plants by interfering with normal root function (no oxygen in that saturated zone) or root diseases (fungal infections commonly gathered under the umbrella of 'damping off diseases') that thrive where anaerobic condition persist. I'm not trying to brow beat anyone, but I can say with a great deal of certainty that trying to grow where the water:air ratio in the grow medium highly favors water will be and remain a limiting factor as you travel the road to a green thumb. Energy drives plant systems and functions - oxidation of the plant's food (sugars/ starch) is what releases the energy - an ample supply of oxygen is required to complete the process of oxidation. No oxygen = no energy released = loss of potential or loss of viability in some cases. I'll say, "Please believe me", not because I need you to believe me, but because I hate to see you waste time on a methodology where success is consistently marginal and to achieve it requires many times the effort of what a conventional pot with drainage/ appropriate grow medium requires. Good luck HU+digits. Al

Styrofoam insulation is polystyrene.  It's a rigid foam insulation which can be of extruded or expanded polystyrene.  Most spray foam insulations are either low or high density urethane foam.  They're not the same. Once cured, spray foam insulation is rigid; it won't move.  Your wood ceiling will move seasonally in response to changes in temperature and relative humidity.  You'll need to de-couple the insulation from the wood ceiling.  You might consider rigid foam insulation between the rafters with spray foam insulation applied to seal the rigid foam to the rafters.  That would function both as an air seal and vapor retarder and still permit the wood ceiling to expand and contract.  You could install additional insulation above the rigid insulation as needed to achieve the desired R-value.

Since it sounds like you are only willing to buy from one of the Big Three manufacturers, that limits your choices.  I will point out that electric vehicles don't really require "servicing" in the conventional sense unless there is something wrong with them.  I know someone who has put over 100K miles on his Tesla in the last 5 years and has yet to have anything major happen that required "servicing." His servicing has been limited to new tires and new air filters. Here is what the Tesla manual recommends for servicing: Your vehicle should generally be serviced on an as-needed basis. However, Tesla recommends the following maintenance items and intervals, as applicable to your vehicle, to ensure continued reliability and efficiency of your Model 3. For more do-it-yourself maintenance procedures and information, see https://www.tesla.com/support/do-it-yourself-guides. For more information on vehicle alerts, see Troubleshooting Alerts. Recalls typically are done using software updates via wifi.  Tesla also has mobile servicing, so you may want to check that out before writing them off. But you or your local mechanic should be able to handle anything routine in the list above. As for level 2 charging, there is no reason to pay that kind of money as there is no need for a fancy wall connector for a number of vehicles.  If you have a dryer circuit or other 240V outlet (like for a shop) close to where you park, you can plug in to that.  If you need to have a dedicated circuit, you buy a 240V receptacle and breaker and the wire to run between the two. In my case I had a circuit I no longer needed that was wired to a Jacuzzi I removed in a remodel.  I ran the wire to a convenient location in my garage and hooked it up to an industrial grade 240V receptacle.  Total cost for my level 2 charging: $20 for parts plus my time. Of course, if you need an electrician to do the work, the same install might be $1000 where I live. I will also point out that a few manufacturers include a level two charging device with the car at no extra cost.

You’re putting the cart before the horse. An OC comes at the end of your building project and ensure that you’ve complied with your building permit. And to get a building permit you need a planning permit. The local Council will issue the planning permit. I’d start with the Council website. And most Councils are happy to advise you in the feasibility of your project over the phone.   And you will need a planning permit for a shed >10sq metres. It is the planning permit that determines what type of dwelling you can build on your land. On a base level you will need to connect to sewage and stormwater disposal if it’s available or have Council approved methods of disposal if not. You will need a kitchen and some sort of laundry with a trough. And toilet and washing facilities. There will be minimum and maximum sizes of dwelling for your land. In some areas the power distributor requires you to pay a service fee even if you don’t connect to the poles. And connection to the poles can be many thousands of dollars depending how far away they are and if underground connections are required. There are forums on the web for shed dwellers, small houses and off-grid properties - worth googling and reading.

When looking for a good house plan, use this list as a guideline on what works best. The best houses orient the public rooms towards the south for the best passive solar heating and cooling The best houses are L, U, T, H, or I shaped. The best houses are only one to two rooms deep. And covered lanai, porches, garages, etc count as rooms in this case. The best houses make sure kitchens have natural light, meaning windows so one doesn't have to have lighting 24/7 to use the kitchen. (And no, dining areas with windows 10' or more from the kitchen will not allow for natural light.) The best houses make sure all public rooms and bedrooms have windows on at least two walls. The best houses do not if possible put mechanical rooms, pantries or closets on outside walls The best houses do not have diagonal interior walls making for odd spaces. The best houses keep public and private spaces separate. (Meaning you're not walking into the bedroom directly from a public room) The best houses do not have you walk through the work zone of the kitchen to bring laundry to the laundry room. The best houses do not have the mudroom go through any of the work zones of the kitchen. The best houses do not use the kitchen as a hallway to any other rooms. The best houses do not put toilets or toilet rooms up against bedroom walls or public areas. The best houses do not have walk in closets too small to stand inside. (One needs 2' for hanging space and 32"-36" for walking space. Ideally the 36") The best houses have separation, such as closets, between bedrooms and between bedrooms and public rooms. The best houses do not have roofs that are overly large, and dominate the exterior of the house. The best houses do not have stick on exterior materials only on the front façade. The best houses have an organizing “spine” so it’s easy to determine how to get from room to room in the house and what makes sense. Meaning they don’t have meandering circulation paths.

When using organic amendments like fish/ seaweed, or ground hoof/ horn/ feather/ bone/ blood, rice hull/ alfalfa meal, etc, the nutrients will be locked up tight in the hydrocarbon chains that make up these materials, which is a form unavailable for direct uptake by the plant. When these chains pass through the gut or otherwise mineralized in the grow medium, the nutrients gradually become available in a form the plant can take up directly. At that point, at the point of uptake, the salts that originated in any of these organic materials will be exactly the same as the salts in a container of Miracle-Gro or any other brand of soluble synthetic fertilizer. When you read the NPK %s on the label of an organic material, you're being informed of the weight (by %) of nitrogen, phosphorous, and potassium, none of which is immediately available, and in almost all hobby growing endeavors, WHEN it will be available is subject to the whims of nature. So the total amount of nutrition might be the same for any given NPK % when comparing organic to synthetic, but the rate of delivery and control is vastly different. Soluble synthetics are immediately available and give the grower complete control of the supplementation process (not withstanding the small amount of misc nutrition which might become available as soil hydrocarbon chains are cleaved). If anyone aside from you is reading this, I might mention that using organic forms of nutrition doesn't grant immunity to fertilizer burn or ammonium toxicity. When temps are cool, people often fertilize several times with various organic sources. Low soil biota activity limits breakdown of the fertilizer, so when warm temps come, several applications can become available all at once, making plasmolysis (fertilizer burn) and ammonium toxicity (especially if the soil/ medium is wet) a real issue that often goes undiagnosed, or more often misdiagnosed. This is what I thought you might find interesting: In my gardens and beds, I adhere pretty strictly to the idea that on an ongoing basis you should use organic products/soil amendments that build the soil structure to minimize the need for soluble (read synthetic) fertilizers and nutrient supplements. That said, there are times you NEED individual nutrients to complete the assortment of essential nutrients plants take from the soil. If you're limited by a rigid 'no chemical' ideology, you either deal with the abnormal and sub-par growth or wait, while you hope adding more organic matter eventually solves all the issues. If you are NOT limited by rigid ideology, the issue is easily solved with a soil test and the addition of the appropriate nutrient(s) via a chemical compound like potash, various nitrates, phosphates, etc. There are extremists at both ends of the organic vs. chemical approach to gardening. Some never think about the soil, believing it ok to keep adding chemicals to ‘hopefully’ produce growth. Others would never THINK of using a chemical and will chastise anyone who does. When it comes to my gardens and beds, I'm in the middle, but as noted I do lean quite heavily toward the organic side, though I stop short of telling anyone what they must do to be a good gardener. ;o) Where container culture is the topic, soluble synthetic fertilizers get the nod from me - hands down. They are easier to use; we know exactly what nutrients your plants are getting and when they are getting them; delivery of nutrients does not depend on the activity of soil organisms whose populations vary in boom/bust cycles in containers; you're using a soluble product, not an organic soil amendment that has the potential to clog valuable macro-pores; you needn’t worry about soil structure, because if you’re smart you’ll have built it into the medium before you planted in it ….. but let’s save the container soil topic for another day. I mentioned there are those at one end of the spectrum who would never lift a finger to improve their soil. Adding organic matter to their soils would be as foreign to them as adding exercise to their life’s itinerary. On the other end, are those who stand ululating and hand-flapping (credit to Dan for that one) at the very thought of anyone using Miracle-Gro. From the plant’s perspective, both extreme positions are ridiculous, and from my perspective, both extremes are unnecessarily self-limiting. The plant just wants to grow to it’s genetic potential. To do that, it needs a full compliment of the nutrients plants take from the soil, and it doesn’t care if they come from compost or Miracle-Gro. Perhaps a more logical approach to plant nutrition might be to look at soluble synthetic fertilizers in the same way we look at IPM practices. Use the most naturally harmonious method/product we can to bring plant growth or yields into the acceptable range. I realize that in most cases, we can do this by adding more OM, but not always. Often too, time is a consideration. We may have someone who wants to plant immediately, in soil that is deficient in one or more nutrients. We probably shouldn't expect someone to forgo their own freedom of choice and wait two years or more while the soil is fortified/improved only via the addition of organic matter. There is a technical difference between a fertilizer and a soil amendment, but even that point eventually becomes moot from a strictly nutritional perspective. Plants take up elements that are dissolved in the soil solution and in ionic form. What they take up are salts. The large molecules that make up hydrocarbon chains in organic fertilizers/soil amendments cannot be taken up by the plant unless the hydrocarbon chains are broken down into elemental/soluble form by soil organisms. At that point, the elements from soluble fertilizers are the same as the elements from organic sources, which is why the plant could care less. At the point in time where nutrients are assimilated, they are ALL soluble and in elemental form, regardless if they came from a dead fish, compost or a hose-end sprayer. If we could only achieve happy healthy plants in a soil teaming with life, using only organic soil amendments and fertilizers, how do we explain hydroponics? ... no medium, or an entirely inorganic one, and only soluble sources of nutrients. At the very least it suggests there is a middle ground in which everyone can seek their comfort level. I’ve been growing perfectly healthy plants in containers in a medium whose only organic fraction is 1/3 or less pine or fir bark; the rest of the ingredients are large mineral particles like Turface and crushed granite. I’ve used ONLY soluble fertilizers in these soils, with the hundreds of pictures I’ve posted here at GW serving as concrete proof that happy, healthy plants can indeed be grown using only synthetic soluble fertilizers if the soil structure is favorable …… which leads me to the reason for writing this: Colloquially, the term 'organic' formerly applied to things once living, but even some plastics contain carbon and are considered organic compounds as well. It really is misleading when we throw the word around w/o much consideration, but I admit to being guilty of it from time to time as well. Technically, urea, ureaformaldehyde, isobutylidene diurea, and crotonylidene diurea (forgive me if the spelling is slightly off) are all organic molecules, and actually do an extremely good job of feeding microbes, which reinforces the idea that synthetic fertilizers are getting framed for the microbial murder rap that should be hung on the effects of reduced OM in the soils. The microbial murder rap should be hung on the effects of reduced OM in the soils; purposely redundant so it couldn’t be missed. It's a vicious circle; mineral soils can support optimal plant growth (nutritionally speaking) only if enough young decaying matter is returned to the soil regularly and frequently. Prairies and forests are virtually self sustaining because all vegetative matter is recycled back into the soil. If we regularly mow and bale the grassland, or log off the forest, nutritional deficiencies are assured as a result of our removal of the OM that would have provided future nutrition - thus the tendency/need for us to adhere to the practice of replacing the lost nutrients with chemicals. In our gardens/beds/lawns ..., we can add compost or other OM to replace the vegetative matter we remove and use or discard. For more than 20 years, I've used compost regularly in the gardens/beds, and apply fine pine bark mulch 2-3" thick, usually every other year. I have extremely healthy soil and rarely find it necessary to use anything synthetic. You can find opinions all over the net that chemical fertilizers are laying waste to the landscape, and wiping out microbial populations faster than chocolate disappears from the candy dish in the family room. Are these opinions based on political views and a radical ideology, or warranted and based in fact? In research by Texas A&M University, intensely managed (read ‘managed using chemical fertilizers‘) sports fields with mostly a sand substrate showed no shortage of soil life. That is there were 10s of millions of bacteria, and 10s to 100s of thousands of fungi per cubic centimeter present in the heavily managed soils. Part of the study included measuring soil life in 11 inches (deep) of pure sand, with no organic amendments whatsoever, over which washed sod was placed. As the sod 'grew in', soil life populations increased almost immediately, 10-100 times . Soil life populations just sort of hang loose, waiting for something they can digest. If they don't get it, they die and feed off each other. When organic matter is introduced into the soil, they break it down, and their numbers increase. When they've consumed the organic matter, they die and consume each other, but the base population remains, ready to spring into action the moment more organic matter becomes available. What do fertilizers do? They make plants grow. Sure, extremely high concentrations of chemical fertilizer poured on the soil in volume might kill some microbes in the immediate area, but the o/a affect of chemical fertilizers is actually an increase in microbial populations through increased plant growth. You need only look to the fact that the rhizosphere (root zone) of plants is such a popular gathering place for soil biota to see increased plant mass promotes a marked increase in soil life. It's actually the continual 'taking' of OM from gardens, agricultural fields, lawns ... w/o replacing it that reduces or inhibits the communal activity of microbial populations. Even then, they're virtually never in short supply and are ever ready to bounce back ... if you just give them something to eat. None of this addresses the hot button political, ideological issues too many wish to export from their own value set, other than the fact it points out the folly in occupying the margin’s extremes. Again, I'm pretty pragmatic and results oriented, so I tend to approach this subject from a plant/soil perspective and leave the politics to the ideologues. My personal view is that in the o/a picture, a chemical fertilizer or nutrient supplement judiciously and responsibly applied to our gardens when it's found to be needed isn't the earth's end; and I prefer to use my own sense of right/wrong to set my course, rather than be told what I need to do to be a good, responsible student of husbandry. That said, avoidance of unnecessary chemicals in the gardens/beds to the greatest degree I feel is reasonable, is still my normal MO. YMMV, but options are good, and I prefer to keep them open. Al

The biggest cost in paint is the labor, not the paint.   Pay a bit more for the highest quality paint you can afford.   I have used BM Regal Select, SW Emerald and SW Duration. I personally like an eggshell finish on walls.  Emerald line eggshell equivalent is called satin. I use flat on ceilings and semi-gloss on trim and doors. Learn to read the TDS sheet for any and all products (primer, paint, clear coats, etc.).  It has great information, especially on the sheen, as that varies alot.  "Satin" can range from almost matte to almost semi-gloss in different brands and/or grades of paint. The TDS sheet lists the gloss in terms of degrees in addition to "flat, matte, satin, etc.". Yup.  Same as my father made, eggs and all.  But schmaltz?  Sure, you can buy it in bricks like butter, but easier, cheaper and no sourcing if you just render it at home.  Plus, for making the chopped liver, better to have the onion, which the bricks don't have.  BTW, if you're going to buy it, duck fat is tastier. ;) Save in the freezer the raw trimmings of fat and those fatty skin bits at the ends, inc. the tail, when you cook a chicken.   (Or beg them from a butcher.) An enamelled pan is best because it's non-reactive, but it's not a big differnce.  1-qt. or the smallest you have.  Or you could probably do it in a bowl over a simmer or a bain marie. Have a clean jar/lid ready to receive the fat, with a spoon in it so you can pour the hot fat on the spoon rather than shattering the jar (a clear jar makes scooping the schmaltz out easier because you can see where it is). Put your lumps of fat and skin in the pan with a cut little onion, or part of a slightly bigger one, in wedges.  Not too much onion because it'll use up the fat in cooking. Never turn your back on it while it's on the heat. (Bold courtesy of my mother.) Start the pan on medium-high heat until the fat starts to melt then turn it down a bit so it won't spatter.  As the fat leaves the skin bits remove them (or let them fry up as cracklings (gribines) if you have lots of fat and want to eat them).  Also remove the onion if it starts to char.  Try to leave as much fat as possible in the pan. When the fat is completely liquid, remove from the heat and let it cool from sizzling to just liquid (i.e., just a bit).  Remove all the solids with a fork first or use a strainer as you pour it carefully on the spoon, into the jar.   Cover and chill. When the fat is cool, it'll float on top of a layer of the onion juice.  The schmaltz should be a pretty yellow, especially if you used a yellow onion.  The onion juice will be yellow to brown.  With a clear glass jar, you can see how deep to put your spoon.  The onion juice itself isn't good to put in the cooking with the schmaltz.  Schmaltz, being just fat, freezes just fine, but wrap it air tight so it doesn't oxidize or take on odors. Thus, one becomes one's own source of schmaltz.  :)

That looks like it tastes good!  That's a trouble I have with ultra-high hydration.  Too much water overwhelming the ability of the gluten to hold.  One secret I've learned is that a lot of the promulgators of ridiculously high hydration recipes are fibbing.  I'm not saying they all are, but ones I've been able to find extra info on are kneading in way more bench flour than they admit.  Okay, maybe than they realize, and they're not trying to mislead, but same diff in the end.  I was taught to knead in all the flour and develop the gluten directly, then use minimal bench flour, which had been reserved from the total in the recipe, just barely enough to keep the dough from sticking, and accounted for. A lot of these recipes for ultra-high hydration use a deep bed of flour, not listed in the percentages, to amend the dough.  By barely working it in, rather than adding it in the beginning, it limits the strength of the gluten development, which gives the big holes, but when they say to add just enough bench flour to make the loaves manageable, they mean a lot of flour!  I've had high hydration loaves that looked nice and round and loafy that sank, spread or liquified in the oven, and few that looked like the recipe pictures.  Ultimately, that's proof of insufficient gluten development and too much water/not enough flour.  Since I abandoned the ridiculous water percentages, and just baked bread however I felt like it, I've achieved much better results for this type of bread.  Note: chiabatta is flat!  A much more honest recipe.

Why do Bourbon roses do well in Austin? They were discovered on the Île  Bourbon - now called Réunion -  off the coast of Madagascar in the  Indian Ocean growing wild and free in the tropical heat. No one knows  for sure, since there are no records of how they were bred, it might  have been a natural cross-breeding, perhaps the result of a cross  between the old European rose, Autumn Damask, and the 'Old Blush' China  rose, both of which were frequently used as hedging materials on the  island. Hedges on the island were usually planted in two rows of these  roses. The fact that the Bourbon rose occurred naturally and flourished  on its own without human intervention meant it had been tried and proven  through natural selection by Mother Nature herself, which gave it  toughness and vigor.   Bourbons get their repeat bloom from their china  heritage and their big flowers and scent from the Damask.  Bourbon roses  are generally tough plants and can take the heat and sun, which made  them successful hedge plantings.  Bourbons can grow big, thick and tough  canes, many have thorns, which can be woven into natural fences.  The  Portuguese arrived on Île Bourbon in the early 16th century. They could  have brought Damask roses there from Europe and other roses from China  and Japan.   They flower repeatedly on vigorous, frequently  semi-climbing shrubs with glossy foliage and purple-tinted canes. The  French arrived in the 1660's. "Bourbon" comes from the name of the royal  house of France. Breon, a botanical traveler for the French Government,  arrived on the island in 1817 and was curator of the Botanical and  Naturalization garden there.  A man named Perichon in San Benoist, in  planting a hedge found in his young plants one that was very different  from the others in its shoots and foliage, which was purple when new and  evergreen with huge rough leaves.  Breon grew many examples of this  rose and sent both seeds and plants to Henri Antoine Jacques, gardener  at the Chateaux de Neuilly, estate of the Duc d' Orleans, - who later  became King of France - near Paris, France, who distributed the rose to  all of the top rose cultivars in France.  At that point the rose was  commonly called Bourbon Jacques.  In the spring of 1821 it became a model for the famous rose painter, Redoute as Rosier de Bourbon. Seeds from this rose were very fertile and vigorous, it took a couple  of years of breeding to perfect the flowers and the plant was introduced  commercially as cuttings in 1821.  Bourbon roses were not a success in  England at the time, English gardeners thought the rose was not  well-mannered, course, with big flowers and a scent was too strong and  bold.   My favorite Bourbons are Madame Isaac Pereire from 1881 and Madame Ernst Calvat,  a natural sport - or mutation - of Madame Isaac discovered in 1888.   Madame Isaac was bred by by Armand Garçon and introduced in France by  Margottin Père & Fils of Paris who were horticulturists and plant  retailers.  Madame Isaac is a big plant that can grow canes up to 12  feet in length - it is often grown as a climbing rose and is an  effective rose for an arch or pergola. The leaves are large and the  rose-madder colored deep purple flowers are among the biggest to be  found in roses.  They are 5-6 inches, very full with more than 40  petals, cupped with a quartered bloom form - very cabbagey!  The scent  is very strong - perhaps the strongest deep rose perfume to be found -  deep, heavy Damask with raspberry which adds sweetness is the way to  describe it.  The scent can last all day.  The branches are covered with  dozens of flowers (hundreds on a mature plant) and in my garden the  scent carries across the street.  Madame Isaac blooms in waves, a huge  long one in spring of 45 days followed by lesser waves of flowers in  late summer and Fall.  I have even had flowers on Madame Isaac in  December and January if there is no frost.  It's a good cut rose in  informal, old rose arrangements.

I’ve always had Waste King batch feed disposals, 3/4 hp.  I’ve never had to replace a stopper, or the disposal.  I only had to buy new when I moved homes and always replaced whatever disposal the previous owner had. With an Insinkerator, the batch feed stopper works by a magnetic connection, which I always found annoying and glitchy.  A Waste King stopper for a batch feed disposal works via a notch set into the throat of the stopper.  The notch connects with its counterpart slot inside the disposal, and that starts and stops the disposal.  When the stopper is turned 1/4 turn, the notch does not connect, and the stopper allows water to drain but not food particles.  Another quarter turn, and the stopper does not allow water to drain, so that you can fill the sink. I’ve always gotten the Waste King model 9900TC which is 3/4 hp in the 3-bolt mount version.  They also make an EZ mount version (5000TC), but I prefer the 3-bolt mount because it will have less vibration.  Waste King also makes a 1 hp batch feed (9980TC), but it is a beast, and I feel takes up too much undersink cabinet space.

This is going to sound crazy, but I was desperate, nothing was working, so when someone suggested it to me, I tried it.  Cloves.  Stink bugs hate cloves.  I had more stink bugs than you've described, my home is older and not tight at all.  So I bought a couple bags of bulk cloves on Amazon, and I also bought a bottle of clove oil.  I filled small bowls with cloves, put one by the front door and back door, a few by windows, and on the kitchen counter.  For the clove oil, I spread it where I was not concerned about oil stains, such as on the shelf liner in kitchen cabinets.  You can also buy an essential oil diffuser, and put the clove oil in that, but I didn't do that. Note that the cloves won't kill existing bugs - I vacuumed up any that I saw for a couple days (wasted several vacuum bags that way, but it was the only way I could do it).  But cloves and clove oil will make the bugs desperately want to exit, and not want to enter.  After 2-3 days of cloves, there wasn't one bug, and have not been any since, and it's been about a year.  Your whole house will smell of cloves for a little while, hence the bugs won't want to enter.  And it's not bad, it's like Christmas.  Also note that you must keep the cloves from any pets; cloves are poisonous to pets. After a couple of weeks, I removed the bowls and threw away the cloves which had lost their scent by then anyway.  I have not seen any more stink bugs and it's been about a year, but if I do, the cloves are coming out again.

Pecking Order of Plant Parts Plant parts and processes which require an allotment of the plant's food/ energy are called energy sinks, and the strength of these energy sinks is organized into a distinct and fairly predictable pecking order: During periods of growth, energy is first allocated to respiratory function, i.e. to maintenance of living tissues, then, to production of fine roots, followed by flower and seed/fruit production, then primary growth (extension of both roots and shoots as well as an increase in foliage mass), then secondary growth (thickening), and finally, the synthesis of defensive chemicals. You're correct in the idea that removing reproductive parts like blooms and developing fruit/ seeds frees up energy which can then be allocated to sinks of lesser strength - primary growth (extension of both roots and shoots as well as an increase in foliage mass), then secondary growth (thickening), and synthesis of defensive chemicals. The pecking order is generally true, but not carved into stone. E.g., in some plants, as the summer solstice passes and day length diminishes (actually, it's the increase in the dark period), demand for energy for secondary growth increases at the expense of primary growth. This allows temperate plants to store energy for a winter of short days and low light intensity, dormancy if applicable, and the spring flush of new growth. Al

If it starts to get stiff and hard to work, trash it and mix a new batch.

Once I know the accent colors that are going to be used I can pick neutrals that work well with the accent colors. If you're determined to stain, you can get 3/4" birch or oak plywood. You won't need a full sheet for your shelves, but maybe you can find a half sheet. The best wood for a pantry is raw cedar as it helps repel insects and rodents. But it isn't necessary. Other harder woods work well, some take paint or stain better than others. Or can be left natural if that's what you like. Maple, oak, poplar, and walnut are all nice and can work well. Unless you are cutting from a sheet, it's unlikely you are going to find wood in a width to match the depth of your shelves. Your easiest fit option will be using eight inch wide boards and use two of them. You could get by with 3/4 inch thick boards, but 1 inch would be better. Wood cleats really do support pantry shelves well. And are the neatest support option. If you want or need light in there, you could finangle in a front edge light behind a front edge supprt, like how an under cabinet light can be strung in.

We did our own shelves and just measured the space, went to the lumber yard and explained what we needed, and had them suggest (and then cut to size) wood that would work. In our particular case we actually ended up using Douglas fir stair treads with the rounded edge shaved off--was the perfect depth and thickness for our project. (We specifically wanted fir or a similar-looking wood since the shelves are visible and match other fir in the room; it's a softer wood, though, so I wouldn't otherwise recommend it for shelving.) The recent city staff HATED the name "Historic" because the garden was not there historically, and the pioneer plot cemetery,. with plots laid out in grids and bordered with raised surrounds, would not have been a garden, and would never have had archways extending from one private plot to another (the historic photo that Jeri posted sure seemed to have a rose arch in it, and the former City Historian encouraged Fred Boutin, the garden founder, to plant as lushly as that photo showed, and had arbors built specifically for that purpose).   People had the idea that the roses were 100 years old or more - there are some we think we that old elsewhere, such as Jeri's beloved Elisabeth's Red China - but they were just big. We argued that the roses were historic because they were collected from other historic sites, just like a museum collects antiquities, but they didn't agree.  In retrospect, we should have caved in on the name but I wanted to keep it because the garden was so widely known under that name and I thought it was silly to change it. It was indeed a power struggle, which got ugly and personal, and a whole lot of it was about having the focus of the cemetery be the historical graves, not the roses.  Some of the nonprofit cemetery board, which the rose garden was part of, agreed that it should be a cemetery, not a garden. Since the rose garden was only 2.5 acres of a 30 acre site, it seemed to me that they could have allowed it, especially because the registration of the cemetery as a National Historic District specifically called out the rose garden as a significant feature.  The city did not feel bound by this listing, which they felt was a "mistake" - if we had the funds and energy to sue over this, we'd have won because they were indeed bound, but we didn't.  Compromise would have been nice but the current city historian had no interest in doing so, and staff backed her. Tom felt that the roses were overgrown.  He has been at odds with heritage rose people in California for years over their propensity to let roses grow big.  He says that every rose should be cut to the "height of a woman" and that every cane should come from 6" of the base of the rose, or lower.  He told the city staff that he was the only real rose expert in the world (he says that in his book on Training and Pruning Roses, too) and that I and the other volunteers didn't know what we were doing. Since staff thinks that pruning can only be good for roses, they agreed. I worked with Tom for a couple of years when I was still curator and welcomed his assistance with judicious regenerative pruning.  Then, things got out of control as I and other volunteers were pushed aside by the city. The city does not plan to do away with the cemetery.  They went to considerable expense to get it federally registered and to develop plans and improved staffing for the cemetery.  It was the "inappropriate" plantings and the obstreperous volunteers that they wanted to eliminate. Anybody who wants to see the 2021 catalog can find it at https://www.cemeteryrose.org/. Thanks everybody for your love and support of the cemetery.  We have propagated nearly all of the roses there.  Many of the roses remain, although continually chopped back and with weedeater damage at their bases which can be fatal.  The roses aren't lost, but the wonderful volunteer effort and romantic lush garden are. If you haven't seen the documentary "Cemetery Rose," it is on Youtube. Anita

Zizia should be watered regular when it's first planted, but once they establish they won't need watering, if grown in normal mesic conditions. They will grow bigger in full sun, but they will do fine in part shade if they get around 4 hours or more of light. Once their roots are established they become strong and almost impossible to kill. They self sow very easily. They bloom early in May and the blooms go for a good while. My plants get to shrub size, so I usually cut them back almost entirely to the ground, and they handle it well. They might have a few later blooms, but sometimes not. I had to dig out a vollunteer that was so big it was choking my New Jersey Tea shrub. The severe clipping/deadheading also prevents more vollunteers from happening. I'm saving the seeds from one of the plants to scatter in a part shade garden. I also grow the Heart-leaved Golden Alexanders, Zizia aptera. The heart-leaf isn't supposed to be as prolific at self seeding as Z. aurea is. This will be my 3rd year growing the Z. aptera. I grow another Apiaceae plant, Sium sauve, and it really does want wet feet all the time. The Jewelweed orange Impatiens also need heavy supplemental watering, and it gets tiresome trying to keep them alive. That applies to any Impatiens really, except perhaps the caudiciform ones. Even though it might seem counterintuitive, under-watering and over-watering produce the same drought response and the same symptoms in plants. Under-watering caused the necrotic leaf tips and margins because the limited moisture supply prevents the plant from moving water to its most distal parts, leaf tips and margins. Over-watering limits root's ability to function normally/ efficiently, which also limits the plant's ability to keep its most distal parts hydrated. In either case, under or over-watering, necrotic leaf tips and margins are usually the first indications there is a problem with the root system, but sometimes wilting can be the first indication. The plant should be watered at the sink and allowed to drain there; or, the pot the plant is in should be set up on some type of blocks so the bottom of the actual pot is well above any water that collects in the cache pot. This prevents the salts that get flushed from the soil from having a pathway by which they can make way back into the plant's pot. A high level of salts in the soil/ soil solution makes it difficult for the plant to take up water, which causes the same symptoms as over/ under-watering. A few repotting tools below. On the right is a root pick made from a wood dowel. It can also serve as a "tell", to "tell" you when it's time to water.  A "tell" is far more accurate than moisture meters, which actually measure electrical conductivity, not moisture levels, which is why if you insert a clean probe into distilled water it will read "DRY" - no ions to conduct electricity. Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Al

I disagree that Netflix has always had a policy stating that the screens must be shared by a household. In fact, Netflix publicly stated that account/password sharing was acceptable and even promoted it. In 2017: In a March 10, 2017, Twitter thread that was promoting its original series Love, Netflix wrote, "Love is sharing a password." The single tweet in the thread garnered more than 15,000 likes and more than 4,600 retweets. Password sharing has become a common practice among Netflix users, so much so that the company estimates more than 30 million households in the U.S. and Canada—and more than 100 million worldwide—engage in it, CNBC reported. But after the company said in its quarterly letter to shareholders Tuesday that it lost subscribers for the first time in more than a decade, it warned that a crackdown on password sharing could be in the works. https://www.newsweek.com/netflix-encouraged-subscribers-share-passwords-years-before-crackdown-1699473 In 2016: In an under-the-radar announcement from last week’s CES – likely dwarfed by news of Netflix’s global expansion – Netflix CEO Reed Hastings said that consumers sharing Netflix account information was “a positive thing.” https://techcrunch.com/2016/01/11/netflix-ceo-says-account-sharing-is-ok/ The issue is that Netflix is no longer growing. At the end of the day, Netflix is a for-profit publicly traded company with hungry shareholders and they can do whatever they want and introduce whatever rules they would like, including limiting how many locations may access a single account. What users have been doing does not equate to "abuse" or "misuse". But it also does not mean people will continue to pay for a service that they previously justified by sharing across multiple households. Your question about budget overruns is really two separate, but related questions:  what overruns were due to factors outside the homeowner's control (e.g., framing material prices, concrete prices, roofing prices, etc.) and what overruns were due to factors within homeowner's control (e.g., homeowner selections of appliances, fixtures, and finishes.)   Homeowner selections probably account for less than 15% +/- of total construction cost so even a 20% overrun in the homeowner selections category translates to a 3% overall cost overrun.  The more significant costs are those baked in by the constraints of the home site, the home design, current prices for materials in your market, and the quality of the original construction cost estimate.  While homeowner selections can move the cost needle, the bigger lever is the price of everything else that goes into a home.

You have to basically cut out a hole in the wall that is as wide as two doors, then install the pocket door framework which can come in a kit form - one half then gets covered with plasterboard so that it is inside the wall, as the pocket where the door slides into when you open the door.  The bit around the actual door then needs finished to whatever specification you want - usually with framing etc that a 'normal' door has.   Depends on the construction of your current wall though - whether it's load-bearing and therefore you'll need some sort of beam to support the wall above.  Or if it would be simpler to box out the rest of the wall rather than cut out a massive hole - in this case the room would get a bit smaller.  If you are cutting a hole in a modern stud wall then it won't affect the size of the room.   Door handles need to be considered carefully as you need something flat that can fit into the 'pocket' and you also need a fitting on the visible edge of the door to pull it out of the pocket again to close it.

Cooking effluent plumes expand as they rise from the pan/pot that is generating them.  And for gas cooktops, there is a modestly larger diameter of combustion products added on.  To capture the effluent, the hood has to overlap the plumes at the height of the hood.  A cylinder is the wrong shape.  You need a rectangle larger than the cooktop, or, with side skirts or cabinets, side obstructions that keep the plumes from expanding outside the hood entry aperture. Note that hoods one can stand the noise level of do not suck up the plumes, but depend on the plumes' upward momentum to bring the plumes to the hood entry.  Thus one cannot depend on CFM to pull in whatever is passing the hood boundary heading for the ceiling and by diffusion to the walls, furniture, and draperies.

My witch hazels typically wait almost two seasons before they show flowering happiness or disgust with their growing conditions.  The growth often jumps ahead or is stunted depending on how the plant is treated, but the flowers seem to lag another year, so I suspect you'll see a better show next year if the plant has been happy. I moved one last year and growth in the spring was stunted, but the bush set many flower buds for this year regardless.  I'm expecting it to grow normally now, but barely flower at all next year.  A droughty summer can also show up as a sparse blooming year two years later.  This is my experience for the hybrids btw, I don't know if the native sorts do the same. Actually they're pretty slow in general when it comes to reproducing.  The seeds take about a year to ripen and then a year and a half to two years to sprout once the seed pods explode and release the seeds.

For clarification, I was specifically considering the security aspects of the tilt/turn in the tilt position. When opened in tilt mode, there is no way that someone enters through it short of breaking the glass and crawling through, which is not something any normal person wants to do. Definitely not a opportunistic In tilt position it becomes a really large hopper window opening in maybe 6" along the top or so, which isn't really intrusive at all, but it might affect window treatment locations, which is a consideration for some people. And while they are generally more expensive than other window styles, they are probably not more expensive than a double mulled awning/fixed/awning would be, and a heck of a lot more secure at any level. The full open in turn position works great for letting in a lot of air, for cleaning windows from inside, and for egress, but it is rarely necessary when all someone simply wants to open a window for fresh air. The tilt position is usually more than adequate for that. From the standpoints of functionality and security, tilt/turn's are considered by many to be the top-of-the-line product, but they aren't for everyone primarily because of their aesthetic and  price. I consider the 'scratch test' only as a last resort. If everything else is growing around me and it's getting late in the spring, I'll do the scratch test to see if the dormant/dead tree is completely dead. I agree that the pictures show some shriveling on the outer bark and buds. Best thing would be to talk to your supplier about it. Soil temperatures can vary according to areas, causing different trees to come out of dormancy at different times. Yes, generally living trees will have a very thin layer of green just below the outer bark.

I'm going to agree with BillMN on this  - the 'scratch test' is not a reliable indicator of tree vitality. Even a dead branch could show a thin layer of green cambium under the bark as it takes time for a tree even in death to lose all the moisture in its tissues and the cambium dry and turn brown. Instead, especially at this time of year, the focus should be on the buds. If the bud are plump and firm - not dry or squishy - then chances are very good the tree will come to life and leaf out properly when nature intends.

Rather then the 'scratch test' I usually use the pliability test or the bud rub test. Dead twigs usually snap rather than bending and dead buds flake off rather then being moist and green inside. But I rarely do any test since it is usually possibly to tell if a tree is alive or dead just by looking at it, once one has had a bit of experience. I took a good look at some London Plane branches this morning and some of the buds did look a bit ike yours although those which were going to flower were much bigger and fatter. As I said, it doesn't really matter that you can't tell at this stage since all you need to do is wait.

I'm assuming this is to insulate the pipes from freezing in the winter. If that's not correct, then let us know. You should know a few things: 1. Insulating pipes, by itself, won't keep them from freezing 2. You need some source of heat. Insulation just slows the heat from dissipating to the surrounding (cold) air. 3. The heat needs to be reliable - the best is passive, from the interior or from the water itself. So, the best type of insulation for pipes is generally foam sleeves. It's split so it goes on easily and has adhesive to hold the two parts together.  Look for a stated R factor - the higher the R factor the better the insulation. If you are installing it yourself (an easy job) use a hand miter box to cut the foam to get a nice tight joint if you can't use a factory edge. Also use miter box for 90 degree elbows. Get the foam that's the proper size for your pipe - you don't want it to not close around the pipe, or to have a bunch of free airspace. if it will get very cold, and there's no heat from the room - you may need heat tape. Heat tape can fail though - it can come unplugged, etc. Try to do it so that you aren't relying on heat tape.

I understand the proposed configuration.  The potential energy savings at the condenser is equal to the amount of energy which the ERV failed to transfer. So you can do a back-of-the-envelope estimate if you know the temperature conditions and the efficiency of the ERV.  Assuming an ERV efficiency of 80% that leaves a potential 20% that could possibly be recouped under ideal conditions.  However, doing so will require more energy to deliver the ERV exhaust to the condenser, and keeping the exhaust point close enough to the condenser to capture the benefit will interfere with the flow of regular outdoor air.   My back-of-the-envelope calc suggests a 2.5% potential on a 98F day; less at lower temps.  It's a classic case of diminishing returns.

"California and some other states require that air duct systems have leakage less that a specified amount. Those gaps would not meet that requirement and the builder should correct that." I respectfully disagree.  Ductwork is typically leak tested by sealing off supplies and returns and pressure testing.  The test measures leakage at duct seams and seals.  Void spaces between the exterior of ducts and ceiling, wall or floor penetrations won't affect the measured duct leakage.  They will, however, permit either conditioned air to flow into unconditioned spaces or unconditioned air to flow into conditioned spaces so they should be sealed with foam sealant to minimize the consequences of the air movement.

HI, Elmer, The point of leakage testing is to verify that the application of mastic and/or tape has adequately sealed the duct seams and joints to minimize leakage.  To that end, your return grill should have been removed and the test connection taped to the actual metal duct work.  Leakage around the perimeter of ducts at penetrations is not the same as duct leakage.  It would be detected via a blower door test of the building envelope using a smoke pencil to detect specific leaks.  Here in Virginiaboth blower door testing and duct leakage testing are required for all new construction.  The voids should be sealed as described above to prevent the above transfer of air to/from conditioned spaces.

Hi, Elmer, The point of duct leakage testing is to prove that the leakage rate is within an acceptable limit.  If the evaluator takes a shortcut, but the test nevertheless reveals an acceptable leakage rate, it passes; the "true" leakage rate becomes academic.  In my area, duct leakage testing is performed in new construction to verify the leakage rate is less than 4 cfm/100 sq. ft. of conditioned floor air which is the code requirement.  Blower door testing of the structure is performed to verify that the air leakage rate is less than 5 air changes/hour (ACH) at 50 Pa. The sealing between duct work and penetrations may be in the mechanical contractor's scope of work or the insulation contractor's scope of work, but the lack of it doesn't suggest poor construction and sealing of the duct work itself.

The majority of issues with gaps around HVAC supply boots installed in the first floor of a home over a conventional (vented) crawl space are associated with air from the crawl space being drawn into the home via stack effect and any negative pressure inside the home.  I don't want air from the crawl space entering the conditioned living spaces of my home.  Sealing around those gaps addresses the problem.  The issue with gaps around HVAC supply boots installed in a ceiling with conventional (vented) attic space above is similar.  In my (mixed-humid) climate zone that results in warm, moist air being drawn into the home, moisture condensing on the surface of the drywall around the HVAC supply and creating favorable conditions for mold and mildew growth.   Neither is attributed to duct leakage. I agree with Worthy about air leakage in conditioned spaces being dismissed as of little consequence because the leakage is into a conditioned space.  The problem is that any amount of leakage reduces the amount of conditioned air being directed into spaces by design.

Sequoia Nursery grafted and rooted mini standards under mist for decades. The trick is using mist so the bud is kept moist until it knits with the stock so it doesn't dry out. The scion requires moisture either from being knitted to the stock or from being bathed by external moisture until the two pieces grow together. An unrooted stock is not flowing sap as there are no roots to absorb the water to be pushed up to the scion. Unless the process is conducted under pretty much 100% humidity so there is no possibility of the two pieces drying out before they knit together, I don't know how else it could be done successfully. Sequoia used a 3# coffee can with holes punched around the base about an inch from the bottom. Bundles of unrooted long whips with minis grafted to their tops were inserted into the can and placed under mist on a outdoor mist table which received strong, filtered light through the surrounding trees. During their hot weather, the bottoms of the whips remained in about an inch of water while the rest of the cuttings were maintained bathed in a mist of water which went off periodically. The strong light helped all the green parts to continue producing chlorophyll, feeding them until they grew roots and knitted together, at which point they were individually potted and replaced under less mist to gradually harden off and moved out into the sales area.

If you are going to stain it dark then there is really no need to pay for White Oak.  Thanks to the uptick in Bourbon along with the increased demand, White Oak is expensive and increasingly difficult to find.  Walnut is a great wood that takes stain well, but has a distinctive look and is more expensive than White Oak. Red Oak is fairly inexpensive (1/3 the price of Walnut) and takes stain well but does have a fairly heavy grain pattern.  Ash is also a large pore wood and takes stain pretty well but doesn't have as heavy of a grain.  Right now, 8/4 Ash is $2 more per board foot for me than 8/4 Red Oak. Alder doesn't take stain very well and therefore requires a bit more expertise/effort to stain.  Elm takes stain easy but can be annoying to work with, it tends to chunk out when you really don't want it to.  Chestnut is OK, it stains well but has less lignin (the compound that holds wood fibers together) and so is prone to splitting.  When removing significant material from Chestnut boards (1/4 of its thickness or width) I recommend letting it set a couple of days just to ensure it doesn't crack.  Or better yet, just use something else. Good luck.

For example, a couple of decades ago I visited a rural setting where cattle were being raised.  They had a raised concrete cistern about 20 feet off the ground with a 1-inch PVC pipe stretching down another 30 feet lower (total of 50 feet of head pressure) over a distance of about 1,000 feet.  They turned on the faucet at the cistern and we drove to the livestock tank where the water was headed.  By the time we got there it was trickling out.  We went about our business evaluating the forage in the pasture and returned past the livestock tank on the way back.  By that time the water was roaring out of the pipe at what you would call, full blast. I don't want to get into the mathematics involved, but in essence, the farther the run, the bigger diameter pipe you want.  Just going from 1/2-inch to 3/4-inch more than doubles the cross sectional area of the pipe and significantly reduces the flow resistance. You also lose pressure when the pipe is flexible.  Drip irrigation pipe doesn't need to be rigid for low pressures, but if you are planning for higher flow someday, then rigid PVC will hold the pressure all the way out.  Flexible pipe expands and there is pressure loss in that expansion.

The pompom look, foliage concentrated near apical meristems (ends of branches where extension growth takes place), is typical of plants with severe root congestion. Whenever there are nutritional deficiencies of any of the mobile nutrients (phosphorous, potassium, magnesium, and especially nitrogen), the plant robs those nutrients from other (usually older) leaves to use as building blocks to support new growth at branch/stem tips, resulting in shedding of the older leaves, which also contributes to the pompom look. Regular rootwork is mandatory if you wish to give your plants the best shot at realizing as much of their genetic potential as possible. Al

So much of the comments here are for if you lived in an ideal world, or if you live in a HCOL area with plenty of design showrooms catering to $100k+ kitchens, or if Architectural Digest was a real place where everyone employs multiple designers returning their calls instantly.  Another thing that is true for every profession, whether it is kitchen design, doctors, lawyers, teachers, anything, is that there are good ones and bad ones, and just cause you have a KD certification does not mean you will be good. The budget issues though are real.  I would increase to $60k which will get you a nice middle-of-the-road kitchen for the work you described, and if you are careful about your choices of materials. Most "independent kitchen designers" do not work on the kind of kitchen the OP is talking about.  Furthermore, most kitchen designers are not independent, but work within a kitchen showroom or cabinet showroom.  Depending on where you are located, it can be difficult to drum up enough business independently as a kitchen designer, so most are aligned with a showroom.  While it could happen that a kitchen showroom could pad the budget by designing cabinets and extras you don't need, the good ones will not.  They want repeat business, they want word-of-mouth business, and they don't want negative reviews online.  And oh yeah, the good ones are ethical. If you feel your design is padded, you can always come on this forum and get opinions on whether it is. What you need to do is visit several kitchen showrooms and/or look at cabinet lines you like, and find their local showrooms, then sit down with people there, and get a feel for which ones you "gel" with, and also which ones are willing to help you given your budget.  So, you've got some homework and legwork to do.  It is only after that legwork and homework that you can choose which designer you want to go with, and yes, pay them a design fee. I went to a cabinet showroom (that would be "oh no!" according to this forum), and got a wonderful kitchen design from their representative.  But I came armed with rough measurements of my kitchen, what look I wanted (photos from magazines and online), what type of appliances I wanted (e.g., a range vs separate cooktop/wall ovens), and most of all, my budget.  If you expect to be spoon-fed every detail of your kitchen, that would be a mistake.  You need to come armed with some basis to go by, or they will politely tell you they can't help you, or even will ghost you. I would not go to a Home Depot or any big box store though.  Anyway, we went over the kitchen plans several times, they came to the house and measured, and were very on top of the cabinet shipping and delivery. Good morning. Yes, this is artificial turf. It is from Easigrass, I think the Kensington turf. I used it here because the clients were adamant they wanted it, and it was a tiny area only. It should not be used routinely and for large areas. Artificial turf is very un-ecological as it is plastic and offers no carbon capture or resources for wildlife. Not only that, but it requires the removal of soil to form a firm sub-base and so living soil is lost too. Be wary of turf that claims to be recyclable as well, as often only certain components are and as they are woven into the whole, actually recycling them is impossible. Currently nobody recycles artificial turf and it all goes to landfill. It is also less permeable to rain than real turf and I have seen problems with localised flooding due to it. I hope that helps.

There reasonably needs to be sufficient slack to pull the dishwasher from the cavity when service is required ... behind the dishwasher, in the adjacent cabinetry, or under the sink. The length of the drain hose has no relation to the "add salt" and "add rinse aid" advisories.  There are sensors on the reserviors for those products.  Have you added salt and rinse aid? You can disable the machine's onboard water softener if you don't want to utilize it, and thus not need to deal with the salt.  Check the user manual for how to do that. If you are watering primarily in the cup, and supplying a dribble here and there to roots. All fertilizer salts are accumulating in the grow medium, which makes it continually more difficult for the plant to take up and move water efficiently. Eventually, as the level of dissolved solids/ salts in the grow medium continues to increase, water absorption will become impossible, or even act to pull water out of cells, reversing the normal process of osmosis and pulling water OUT of plant cells via the same mechanism curing salts 'pulls' water from the cells of meat destined to become bacon, jerky, ham, ..... . The technical name for what is occurring is 'plasmolysis', but more commonly it's known as fertilizer burn. The fix: Flush the soil on a regular basis. The grow medium looks very dense, so you might need to use something that allows you to flush the soil regularly w/o the need for concern the medium will remain wet too long and cause root issues related to either function or health.
