Choosing an Appropriate Size Container How large a container ‘can’ or ‘should’ be, depends on the relationship between the mass of the plant material you are working with and your choice of grow media. We often concern ourselves with "over-potting" (using a container that is too large), but "over-potting" is a term that arises from a lack of a basic understanding about the relationship we will look at, which logically determines appropriate container size. It's often repeated that you should only move up one container size when "potting-up". The reasoning is, that when potting up to a container more than one size larger, the medium will remain wet too long and potentially cause root rot issues, or at a minimum, limited root function. In reality, it is the size/mass of the plant material you are working with, and the physical properties of the medium you choose that determines both the upper & lower limits of appropriate container size - not a formulaic upward progression of container sizes. In many cases, after root pruning a plant, it may even be appropriate to step down a container size or two, but as you will see, that also depends on the physical properties of the medium you choose. It's not uncommon for me, after a repot/root-pruning to pot in containers as small as 1/5 the size as that which the plant had been growing in prior to the work. Plants grown in ‘slow’ (slow-draining/water-retentive) media need to be grown in containers with smaller volumes so the plant can use water quickly, allowing air to return to the medium before root issues more serious than impaired root function/metabolism become a limiting factor. We know that the anaerobic (airless) conditions that accompany soggy media quickly kill fine roots and impair root function/metabolism. We also know smaller medium volumes and the root constriction that accompany them cause plants to both extend branches and gain o/a mass much more slowly - a bane if rapid growth is the goal - a boon if growth restriction and a compact plant are what you have your sights set on. Conversely, rampant growth can be had by growing in very large containers and in very fast (draining) media where frequent watering and fertilizing is required - so it's not that plants rebel at being potted into very large containers per se, but rather, they rebel at being potted into very large containers in a medium too slow and water-retentive. This is a key point. We know there is an inverse relationship between media particle size and the height of the perched water table (PWT) in containers. A PWT is water that fills spaces between soil particles and defies gravity by refusing to leave the pot. As particle size increases, the height of the PWT decreases, until at about a particle size of just under 1/8 inch, media will no longer hold perched water. If there is no perched water, the medium is ALWAYS well aerated, even when it is at container capacity (fully saturated). So, if you aim for a medium (like the gritty mix) composed primarily of particles larger than 1/16", there is no upper limit to container size, other than what you can practically manage. The lower size limit will be determined by the medium volume's ability to allow room for roots to ’run’ and to furnish water enough to sustain the plant between irrigations. Bearing heavily on this ability is the ratio of fine roots to coarse roots. It takes a minimum amount of fine rootage to support the canopy under high water demand. If the container is full of large roots, there may not be room for a sufficient volume of the fine roots that do all the water/nutrient delivery work, and the coarse roots, too. You can grow a very large plant in a very small container if the roots have been well managed and the lion's share of the rootage is fine. You can also grow very small plants, even seedlings, in seemingly inordinately large containers if the medium is fast (free-draining and well-aerated) enough that it holds no, or very little perched water. I have just offered clear illustration why the oft repeated advice to ‘resist potting up more than one pot size at a time’, only applies when using heavy, water-retentive media. Well-aerated media are not bound by the same restrictions. As the ht and volume of the perched water table are reduced, the potential for negative effects associated with over-potting are diminished in a direct relationship with the reduction - up to the point at which the soil holds no (or an insignificant amount) of perched water and over-potting pretty much becomes a non-issue. Hi! I come across these issues all the time! To some extent it depends on your water company - for example United Utilities are very different to South West Water in the way they approach it, what they'll accept and at what point in your project you need to deal with them... Each water company has their own way of doing it and they tend to have guidance and someone you can contact to get their specifics... in general terms... If you are at the start of the shared drain (as in the drains on your property only have your waste draining into them). Then it is not actually a shared drain - it is your private drain - so you can deal with it as you want and there should be no requirement to get permission from a water company. If you have shared drains then you need to find out what is allowed because you will need permission and any changes (if changes are allowed) will have to be done to specific standards. Some companies are very restrictive about moving manholes. So you may need to both spend more on the drain alterations and moving a manhole, if any are allowed, or alter your designs so they avoid the manhole. I have seen some homes with internal manholes. I don't recommend this, but I have seen it. I don't know if this would comply with your water board requirements. It would be very tricky to do in a way that would comply with many building regulations requirements - specifically insulation and air tightness. If you have the budget and you need the extra internal space then you'll get better quality and more useable space by building an extension. Conservatories are generally pointless - as you've pointed out they are comfortably useable for only a very short portion of the year. Just replacing the roof doesn't really change this much - you still won't have a very comfortable space internally. Hope this helps. Jane award winning chartered architect eco-home and conservation specialist www.i-architect.co.uk

I've had engineered wood in both my houses for the last 23 years all with a Satin or Mate finish. My experience hasn't been bad with scratches or wear. however there have been a few dings/dents in spots from heavy stuff or dropping something sharp, but that is part of wood floors. Mine have all been the glue down kind which requires the slab to have a lower moisture content. You also need to make sure the floor is nice and level with no high or low spots (low spots are easy to deal with by using self-leveling. If there is a high spot it may need some grinding. My old house it was red oak from Robbins with a 1/2" wear layer so it could be sanded and refinished 3 times and a total of 5 layers - the more layers the more dimensionally stable. No issues with scratching from 2 dogs of the small/medium size, but only lived there 7 years after installation. I had one area that got wet and sat for a whole day and the boards were damaged and swelled. Once it dried out the swelling went back, but the finish was rougher in that area. My current house we installed Pecan (Hickory) from Robbins when it was built - originally we wanted the same as my old house, but it was on back-order so we ended up having to select something else. This floor was only 3/8 wear layer and could be sanded once. We never had any issues with it except we had a leak that flooded a corner of the master and had to have the floor in the whole house replaced as it was no longer made and we couldn't find anything that worked with our existing floor. We either had to completely change it up in one room or replace in the whole house. Since we know we will be selling at some point we elected to replace the whole house (insurance covered this except for the deductible), This was a mess and if you expect your basement might flood again it might not be the best choice. It took them 2 days to remove the wood and then also go over and make sure the adhesive was removed so they could lay a new floor. We replaced it with a white oak engineered floor (don't remember the brand beyond that it is a well known lower side of mid priced one) which can be sanded up to 3 times, However we have a few areas where the grain has raised/finish is a bit more rough due to our cat being sick and projectile vomiting and it sat all day. No swelling beyond that, but I'm done with engineered pre-finished wood at this point. I think a site finished wood floor might be better since the joints would be sealed by the poly and probably prevent moisture intrusion. I've found some engineered woods you can site finish, but my husband is completely over wood although he likes the look so I'm currently researching LVT for our next house.

Zalco - there is one thing about prefinished engineered wood which bothered me, which may or may not bother you. (We all know I'm weird! Ha ha...) FWIW - I have had site finished wood floors, pre-finished engineered wood floors, and LVP in a wood look plank. From a factual, totally non-emotional standpoint they all have pros and cons - and honestly I like all 3 of them. Some of them just seem to make more sense in some applications than others, but at the end of the day it's all about what you like. I also don't necessarily subscribe to the "real wood" is always preferable. In a vacuum, sure, "real" wood looks nicer to my eye. One of engineered's selling points is its durability, and I agree that mine is pretty darned durable. However, what I don't like about the prefinished engineered floor is that each individual board looks like an individual board. And yes if you just read that and went "huh?", I understand. LOL. Until I had it I wouldn't have known what that meant either.... There is one smooth finish over a site finished floor. The sealer goes on last and gets down into all the nooks and crannies, and when you look at a site finished floor, to my (admittedly really weird!) eyes, it just looks.....nice. If you read that whole thing and think, thanks you weirdo but I couldn't possibly care less...hey, I've done my job. :-) For me, I am unlikely to ever again get a pre-finished engineered wood floor. There is nothing you've said so far to make me think the problem is anything but over-watering. The moisture level at the top of the soil isn't important. What IS important is what the moisture level is deep in the pot - at the bottom. Read below about how to use a "tell" to "tell" you when it's time to water. It is a very simple but useful and accurate tool, and easy to make. The wooden tool below, bottom row second from the right side, is used here as a root pick, but it is exactly the same as what a "tell" looks like, except a tell is usually longer, maybe 60cm.  Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Al

Pros and cons to carpet, and pros and cons to hardwood or other flooring. What is your current flooring, on the stairs, hallway, and bedrooms? How many more years do you anticipate staying in this house? Carpet is softer underfoot and a bit quieter which is nice to muffle footsteps on the upstairs level. A good installation will protect any hardwood underneath it, nice for future owners who might want to uncover it. Carpeted steps are easier for dogs to navigate! Continuity is good, for visual pleasantness. Without seeing your space I'd guess that continuing the carpet in the upstairs hallways is a good thing. On the con side, carpet wears out especially in high traffic areas; and stains/spills are more difficult to clean up; and visually many people would prefer all hardwood to any wall-to-wall carpet.

10" (or 12") is definitely too shallow!  As ABC mentioned, the minimum recommended by the National Kitchen & Bath Association (NKBA) is 15" for counter-height seating.  That's 15" of clear leg/knee space -- after accounting for cabinets & decorative doors or end panels on the back of the cabinets. Your island should be, at a minimum: 1.5" counter overhang in front of the cabinets + 24"D cabinets + 1" decorative door or end panel on the backs of the cabs + 15" seating overhang ============ 41.5" deep island If no decorative door or end panel on the backs of the cabs, then subtract 1" for 40.5" However, even 42" or so of depth on a 12' long island is probably going to look skimpy/out of proportion.  Can you fit 48"?  (Don't forget to provide sufficient aisle space on all sides - 48" for the front & sides and 48" to 54" behind the seats (depending on what's behind the seats and how heavy the traffic will be in that space).)

You mean a range hood.  Or the exhaust hood for the range.  The proper distance between the cooktop and the bottom of the hood is 30-36”.  Any lower and it will have a cramped feeling when using the cooktop.  You may not be able to stir taller pots or peer into taller pots if the distance is less than 30”.  And any higher than 36” means you will provide opportunity for the smoke and grease to escape before reaching the hood. The problem with @palimpsest’s advice is that if you see that a manufacturer specifies lower than a 30” distance, that means that the hood is so underpowered, the manufacturer is concerned that the hood won’t exhaust well if placed at the standard distance of 30-36”.  So that would be a good way to eliminate that hood from your choices.

If you are stirring a pot where the rim is 5 feet off the floor, you are going to be standing on a stepstool anyway. Whether a hood is underpowered or not has a lot to do with how you cook. Not everyone has a pro-style range or cooks like they work in a restaurant. It's possible that something between 24" and 30" could be more than adequate for some people both height wise CFM wise.

The elements are just big resistors, and their typical failure mode is to stop getting hot for a variety of reasons. Not much else can go wrong with them. By "too hot" do you mean that they are hotter than you've come to expect for a given setting, or that they are getting hotter than they've ever been? In either event the most likely culprit is the rheostat that changes the temperature as you turn the knob (if there are some kind of electronic controls then there are more possibilities). The likely cure is to replace the switches behind the knobs. In answer to your question, swapping the elements will probably make no difference. Swapping the controllers might. If the burners are getting much hotter than they've ever been I'd definitely call a repair person, you could have bumped up voltage from a defective transformer for example-- I'd expect to see other problems in the house were that the case, extra bright incandescent light bulbs, etc. A bum controller is the most likely cause.

Mad's suggestion of Baltimore Belle is on point. It's known for being ultra-hardy. LJS *supposedly* is hardy to zone 2b (Hah!), but anecdotal evidence suggests otherwise. I grow it, or something I was sold as it, but I'm in comparatively balmy Z7. Check the HMF listing under the "Gardens" tab to see where it's being grown. You can send a message to any Z4 gardeners listed to see if it actually survived in their garden. Himmelsauge is one I'd recommend if you like deep pink/carmine roses. The canes aren't monstrously long, about 10-11 feet here, but it's very vigorous, and I've never seen even a tip die from winter damage. Of course, my average low temp is 5-10F, but it's listed as hardy to Z4. It's in stock at Rogue Valley right now. I just don't know if there's a Canadian source. Débutante is a much taller/larger rose, growing about 20' here. It's a pure light pink. In a good year (if I remembered to fertilize it the year before, lol) the blooms completely hide the foliage for about three weeks (EDIT: It would probably bloom even longer for you with your cooler Spring. It turns hot here just about the time Debutante blooms). I got mine from Angel Gardens in FL, but that wouldn't be an option for you :( Geschwinds Orden is one of my favorite ramblers. Almost thornless.  It no doubt is the most beautifully tinted rambler of all, with a very dark pink center, fading to almost pure white on the outer ring of petals. I think I got mine from Palatine, but they no longer list it. If you're interested in this one, be sure you get the real thing, as it's mixed up in commerce with a couple of other Geschwind roses. To make things REALLY confusing, Geschwind's Gilda in commerce is actually ORDEN. I grow both, and they are the same rose. So if you order Gilda, you're more likely to get Orden than if you actually order Orden. Confused now? lol. While I'm talking about Geschwind roses, I should mention G's Nordlandrose 1. Yes, there's a #2, as well. I don't grow either, but GN1 is rated hardy to Z3. Hope this helps. EDIT: I just did a little research on Long John Silver, and it seems that a lot of what is sold as LJS is actually Iceland Queen, another mystery mis-named rose, and possibly even Colonial White (I refuse to call it 'Sombreuil', its official name. Long story) . IQ and CW are only hardy to Z6, which might account for the seeming lack of hardiness of *some* LJS. It's probably impossible to tell who, if anyone, sells the real LJS. Your best bet is still to find someone in a cold zone who has one that survives, and ask what nursery they bought it from.

It's a simple case of SCALING Scaling is a form of disintegration. A common cause of scaling could be freezing and thawing conditions. Flaking or peeling is normally a form of scaling. Scaling, which can also be referred to as spalling, is rated based on the depth of the defect. The rating usually goes is as follows: 1. Light spalling is when the loss of surface mortar does not expose any coarse aggregate. 2. Medium spalling occurs when the damage has a depth of up to 0.4" 3. Severe spalling is determined when the depth of the damage ranges from 0.2 to 0.4". There is also some loss of mortar surrounding aggregate particles with a depth range of 0.4 to 0.8". 4. Very severe spalling is the loss of coarse aggregate particles, as well as surface mortar and surrounding aggregate, generally to a depth greater than 0.8". I've only been involved in one accident (knock on wood), and that was years ago when a woman pulled right out of a parking lot without looking and T-boned my car.  There are things that simply cannot be predicted, and of course drivers have become increasingly erratic in recent years thanks to "technology".  I cringe when I see a driver with cell phone in hand while they're driving; it just doesn't get much less attentive than that! I remember driving at times like a fool when I was 18 or 19 years old, but I thought I was invincible.  Now that I'm "an old lady", I am perfectly content to drive in the slower lane most of the time, although I do know how to get on the accelerator to execute a quick move when needed.  I try to remain highly alert at all times, and to constantly be scanning the road to know what's around me.  Even so (or maybe exactly so), I enjoy driving less and less.  I used to love nothing more in my younger years than to get in the car and just cruise.  I even thought I would still enjoy that, so bought a cute little red convertible a few years ago.  It was a cute fastback with retractable roof and I did enjoy owning it, although I became increasingly afraid to drive it.  Because it was a tiny two-seater, I wouldn't drive it on the highway for my daily commute and therefore it didn't get driven much at all.  A cost / benefit analysis told me what I needed to know:  I don't want or need a "pleasure car", only a dependable vehicle to get me from point A to point B and back again on a daily basis.  I don't want or need a little two-seater in which I feel as unseen as someone on a motorcycle surely feels.  My goal these days is to make it there and back incident-free, and to enjoy the commute by refusing to engage in "road rage games" or in assumptions made about the intent of other drivers. Oh, I still get perturbed by a number of things that other drivers do, but I try not to take it personally (though that's sometimes easier said than done).

If it is brand new it might be because it is still "breaking in" the engine which is where everything is new and kind of needs to seat in. That can take a bit of time depending on the oil that is in it. If It is kind-of-new, then it might be because of not breaking in the new engine correctly. If the engine is run at a set RPM all the time, then it can wet-stack, and smoke or pump oil out of the exhaust. If its been an engine you have been running forever, then it could have a broken ring, or worn rings. Or it could be as simple as, being an air cooled engine, it has not got up to temperature yet, the cylinder and piston have not expanded quite enough to give a good seal against the oil rings. But as soon as it comes up to proper temperature, it seals and stops smoking.

Black smoke, blue smoke or white smoke (not talking about some possible water vapor at first in cold weather)? If it's 'blue/black', it is the result of a rich condition where the choke is too closed and too much fuel is in the cylinders. This 'washes down' engine oil in the cylinder and burns it. Blue smoke is just oil. White smoke is also oil but usually coming in at the valve seals. Your engine might just be wearing out early for any number of reasons. John Brady, Not beaglenc here. In my experience, yes, both of those powders can fade colors over time, unless it is a truly colorfast fabric. I weigh the risk vs benefit in using those powders. Ex: is this navy blue cotton men's dress shirt so dirty, greasy or smelly that shortening it's usable life is needed by using a higher wash temp and a quality powder detergent such as Tide? In our situations here, the answer is yes most of the time. In other households, the answer could be no; let's use a lower temp and a liquid detergent. Liquid does not contain oxygen bleach. Tide powders do.  We also have a higher than usual chlorine content in our water supply, so our results may be different than in areas where this is not the case. Keep in mind that the definition of warm and hot in regards to washing machines varies greatly, depending on the machine and it's temperature settings. In some machines, warm is defined as 85F. In others, warm is 120F, whereas, in yet other machines, hot is defined as 100-110F. This makes it challenging to determine what warm or hot means when reading about other's laundry practices and their eventual outcomes. Warmer wash temps and powder detergent can equal more fading in colors. In answer to your question about Tide Orginal vs Tide F&G powders, I find that Tide Original cleans very well, checking the boxes one wants taken care of. Tide F&G powder does a good job too--removes many stains in day to day regular laundry. You likely know lots of people use it for cloth diapers with success, and I can't think of a higher demand laundry situation than cloth diapers. Where we, in this household can run into trouble is when I lean heavily on Tide F&G powder and then others come in after me and are using liquid detergent often. We can get a build up of funk that the Tide F&G can't remove in this situation. I suspect this is because it contains less oxygen bleach and does not have an activator. The washer isn't getting 'cleaned out' during a wash cycle as well because of less oxygen bleach and no activator and liquid detergent does not have either of those things. In your opening paragraph, imo, that is a fine laundry practice. I don't use powder Cheer too much anymore because finding it around here has become too difficult. I've switched many of my former Cheer powder loads over to Tide F&G liquid with Clorox 2 powder additive if the load needs that boost. I'll add stpp once in a while too. But I did have good outcomes with Cheer powder. It just seems to be too hard to obtain and I've moved on. I use Tide w/Bleach powder on whites and lights only. I've read of others who use it consitantly on all of their laundry in warm water and don't complain of fading. I would have fading of colors with it, but they say they don't experience that. Perhaps a test run on less important items to see how it works out in your laundry room.

I would measure from the door frame to the curtains.  That will give you your diameter.  Then, I'd  measure exactly halfway along that measurement and put a piece of tape or other marking. Let's call that spot X.  Then, from X, you can measure a half-diameter in any direction.  That is the size of your rug.  You probably do want to take a bit of string of the half-diameter length and draw a circle to see where the rug will be under your chair. If the walls behind the chair are not the same size, you probably want to use the shorter.  For example, if one wall is 11 feet long and the other 10, you'd want to measure your diagonal from the edge of the 10 foot wall to 10 feet from the corner of the 11 foot wall. A circle enscribed in a square (ie the run inside the square made by the two walls behind the chair and 2 imaginary walls for the rest of the square) will have a diameter that is the diagonal measurement of the square (top right corner to bottom left corner). You can also do the whole thing with math with Pythagorus's theorem.  (A^2 + B^2 = C^2) Measure the shorter wall, square that (A^2), double it (this is B^2, but A=B), then take the square root for your diameter. Pay attention to any obstacles, like baseboards, radiators or other things.  You need to measure at the floor. If you want a bigger rug than the one that fits into your corner, you need to find a diagonal further into your room to measure, projecting from the walls. For example, a point midway into the door to an equal distance along the wall with the window. Since a circle enscribed in a square has the diameter of the diagonal of the square, as long as you have a square of floor space, you can figure out the diameter of the rug.

The rings are indicators of where nodes are located. As the plant grows the outer layers of living periderm (bark) split, desiccate, and die. As the dead layer of bark thickens, it obscures the nodal rings. It also prevents light and air movement from reaching the living portion of the bark, which tends to reduce back-budding. Often, when you expose large areas of green/succulent tissue surrounded by bark, you get sunken ares that isn't pleasing to the eye. Not easily seen in this image, there is a large sunken area on the inside of the trunk curve as it's direction changes left to right. The trunk mass above that wound is actually a branch I wired into place 2 years before I chopped the trunk for the sole reason of increasing the taper of the trunk, which gives the illusion of greater age. This image was taken after about 90% of the foliage and branches were removed to establish the trunk line and the first three branches. The more vertical branch at the top is the new trunk leader.  You can see the sunken area (tan color) at the center of the plant from this top view. The wound will eventually be covered by new bark and become inconspicuous insofar as the appearance of the bark, but it will take a long time for the sunken area to become inconspicuous, which is why the trunk chop was planned where it would be hidden when the 'tree' is viewed from its front view.  This is a tree that has branches too many and too heavy at the top of the tree. A major issue for jades and elephant bush.  The rings you mention have started to become less conspicuous on the trunk, but still evident on newer branches. I was wanting to say a little more about terracing.  Simply, it's leveling a space by shifting soil from the higher side to the lower side.  When I can get them I lay logs or trunks--long stout lengths of wood--along the lower edges, fixing them in place with pieces of rebar, to hold the moved ground in place.  I never have enough of this kind of material.  The soil I've been shifting lately has been nearly pure gray clay, a discouraging sight on ground that's had grass, weeds, subshrubs, shrubs growing on it for twenty years.  It still needs vast amounts of organic amendment:  more than the over hundred tons of old hay we've used in the garden since we came. I do the terracing a little at a time:  when I feel like it.  We don't move earth in any big way, after an early experience where we had a tractor level a road, and provoked a landslide.  Now I dig individual planting holes, and any earth-moving is on a small scale and gradually. I plant thickly and continuously, partly for aesthetics, partly for ecological reasons, and partly to keep the ground in place.  It wants to slide downhill.  The plants' roots hold the soil; they absorb excess water, which limits runoff and flooding and stores the water for later; they help create a layer of organic matter at the soil surface, which also helps water absorption.  Having lots of shrubs and trees in particular means I can terrace, because their roots will hold the steeper, but small, areas of ground that result from terracing.  Also, clay tends to stay where it's put.

When the planting gets to the point where root congestion allows you to lift the root/soil mass from the pot intact, the plant will benefit from a repot. A repot is more involved than simply potting up in that it includes bare-rooting, root pruning, and a change of soil; whereas potting up is essentially lifting the congested (rootbound) root/soil mass from one pot into a slightly larger pot and filling the space between the pot walls and the root/soil mass with potting medium. When you pot up, most of the limitations associated with root congestion follow the plant to the new pot, but all stress associated with root congestion is relieved during a proper repotting session. .... best not to water on a schedule. Water on an 'as needed' basis, using a wooden "tell" you can easily make in minutes from a wooden dowel rod. See below. Don't forget fertilizing, it's very important. If you're watering correctly, so you're flushing the soil as you water, fertilizing about every 3rd or 4th time you water in summer and every 4th or 5th time in winter is about right. You can keep track of how many times you water by dropping a marble/ button. bottle cap in the pot at every watering. When it's time to drop in the 3rd/ 4th/ 5th object, depending on how often you decide it's appropriate to fertilize, fertilize, pick up the objects, start the cycle over. Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Al

It breaks my heart the amount of money and effort people put into raised beds with without a) understanding what problem they are trying to solve and b) understanding in advance the money required. Not to mention Internet gardening advice is difficult because many answers need to be specific to your local area as well as personal physical situation. This would be my advice: 1) figure out how much money you have available for the project. 2) figure out why you want raised beds. it could be aesthetics, physical situation like bad back or arthritis, or as your case sounds like you perceive you have a soil problem. 3) you sound like you are just starting (yeah- exciting!) so take some photos of your problem and at a quart bag of soil to at least 2 local and well reputed garden center (not a place like Lowes, etc but a true local garden center) and see what they think specifically about your soil. They earn their living by selling stuff and their advice very likely will steer you that way but treat it as a learning situation and if you have the budget just do it but only on one bed this year. 4) figure out how you feel about organic vs not. it really matters in the next step. 5) by now you should have an idea what sort of beds you want if at all. Estimate what your exact ideas will cost- especially the soil and map into your budget. Many ways to save money and you may want to consider building your beds with stone from your yard. What I do might not be right for you but just to contrast the current hysteria about growing in raised beds I have about half an acre in garden, my soil is extremely challenging (literally cannot sink a shovel unless soil is wet but if too wet can’t lift the shovel because every bit of soil sticks to the shovel) yet I have ripped out the raised beds created by prior owner and garden is very happy being in the ground despite starting with crummy soil and only 150 day frost free climate. That’s enough from me but please consider taking a look at Charles Dowding’s (he’s in England by the way) Youtube channel. His soil building principles are easy and very much translate to any gardener, no raised beds and provide an idea on how I am able to happily garden (including watermelon) in my challenging Colorado conditions.

If the corrosion is as bad as you say, you'll need to get serious to rehabilitate the fixtures. The J tubes are likely steel tubing (inexpensive material & easy to form) so the corrosion is probably good old iron oxide. I would: - Disassemble the fixtures (cut wires as necessary) and get the J tubes out and separate. - Pour/dribble/soak CLR rust remover down through the tubes to eat away the rust. Mechanically assist the CLR to work its way through from both ends of the tube. This all may take soaking overnight, rinsing out depleted CLR and repeated applications of new CLR application. - When the old wire finally comes out, clean the tube ID as best you can, rinse and dry. - Repaint the J tubes and reassemble the fixture.

Plexiglass and other acrylic sheets are solvent welded with chemicals like methylene chloride. Corian and other solid surfaces are adhered, not welded, with adhesives like methylmethacrylate which can be unbonded with acetone and/or lacquer thinner. Don't ask me how I found this out, please.   This is a Corian acrylic bowl adhered to Corian engineered stone. There is no silicone between the sink flange and the bottom of the estone, just color matched methacrylate. There is no maintainence ever; you can't get a more sanitary situation. If it can be done with estone, it can be done with natural stone, however, getting a fabricator to do it may be problematic.   This is a Karran 540 bonded to a Corian countertop. Although it isn't recommended by Karran, I'm not seeing any reason it couldn't be mounted in estone or natural stone. No lip, no caulk, just a hard seam between the sink flange and the bottom of the top.   Here's a close-up of the joint between the sink flange and stone on a TopZero sink. I drop my flange to allow a little bit of rounded stone sink profile; I don't think a 90* sharp sink edge is a good idea. TopZero provides and recommends methacrylate for the joint, not silicone. It can also be tinted to match the stone, unlike silicone. This job was a retrofit with a faucet deck:   There is such a thing as a flush mount top mount sink. We used to do them in Corian years ago. I suppose you could do the same with stainless steel, but I don't know why you'd want to. A slight positive reveal with a silicone joint between the sink flange and the stone bottom held in place with a strap system, not clips or blocking, remain the most cost effective, sanitary, and best looking choice for natural stone and estone tops and is the closest you'll get to seamless:   From TopZero:   I still strap my TZs.

@Kendrah - It really depends on the product but most industrial coatings will fully cure within 7 days.  However, full cure and hardness are actually different things, for many coatings full cure is needed for chemical resistance rather than hardness.  So most catalyzed polyurethanes are going to be installable after 24 hours.  They will not be fully cured, but they are not going to chip. Hardness in general is a bit of a trap.  A coating needs to actually be a bit flexible so it really needs to be strongly bonded to itself and the substrate, a hard coating on a soft wood is going to be more susceptible to chipping.  If you are sensitive to chemicals I would want a week for off-gassing to happen, which is probably more important than durability during installation. As for strapping cabinets to the truck, that is why god made nice thick corrugated cardboard.

The finish on an acrylic or fiberglass tub is not as durable as a porcelain/enamel finish on cast iron, period. The aesthetics of an acrylic or fiberglass tub is typically not as detailed as on an old cast iron. A couple things. First, make sure you understand the difference between a steel tub and a cast iron tub - they are not the same. With stamped steel, you get what you pay for, and even expensive ones still don't equal the quality of a cast iron. With a new cast iron, your cost will meet or substantially exceed the cost of refinishing an old one. Refinishing can be near-to-factory when performed on site. However, to do that the tub should be fully exposed, meaning all walls and fixtures removed to completely expose it. But if you go to that length, then the better way is to deliver the tub to the refinisher's shop, and the finish will equal a factory finish. There they will have better opportunity for prep, which is the key to refinishing.

Hi there Phil, I spoke with our Building Regulations team about your query and they came back to me with the following advice which could be very helpful for you. The fire strategy for these proposed works needs to be considered holistically with respect to the entire property, not just the works at this level. At this early instance, we would advice you to contact us at RESI directly with a full overview of your property and we can advise on the full potential feasibilities of your proposal. It does surprise clients often, but seemingly simple internal alterations such as these proposed require considered specified works to achieve UK building regulations compliance. Generally, regardless of the fire strategy to the upstairs floors, if the garage is to remain in use for vehicular storage then it should be separated from the rest of the property with 30 minute fire resisting construction. This can be done with timber studwork with 12.5mm plasterboard to each side or 15mm fireboard on one side and calcium silicate/concrete boarding on the other - naturally the garage is a cold-bridging space and so any partition should be thermally insulated to current part L standards as well. A structural engineer should be appointed to confirm the part A compliance with respect to structural integrity and at RESI, we do not advise conducting works to load bearing members without the advice and engagement of an engineer. We have several engineers we work frequently with who can engage on your project at a technical level alongside ourselves to ensure that a set of compliant building regulations scope drawings can detail and demonstrate how the works should be done properly, for both your contractor and a building inspector. Incidentally, the party wall structure should be surveyed for inherent defects prior to specifying a new dpc or injected dpc solution, with all new insulation measures satisfying the requirements of Part L of the building regulations for upgraded elements. We hope this is helpful, but if you do have any other questions regarding fire safety do not hesitate to get in touch with our team. text: Very simply, hybrids that produce desirable plants may come from crossed plants that are individually not so desirable. Those undesirable genes are there in the hybrid, but they don't dominate there. If you breed plants from hybrid seeds, you're just allowing those undesirable genes to reassert themselves. Breeders keep breeding using different varieties. Some come out better, but some come out worse. So yes, if you breed plants from hybrid seeds, you may get something better. But you may also get something worse. You'll certainly get something that the original breeder didn't intend for you to have.

If your range is next to the left base cabinet below, and there is no cover panel, then 1/2" of it is under the cabinet above, and not the hood. The wall cabinets above have to have applied cover panels.  So do the base panels of the cabinets below, for the openings to be the same width, and be aligned. You can not apply cover panels to the wall cabinets and not apply them to the base cabinets below.

If you're wokking, you need CFM.  And you need something to "catch" all the stuff the wok kicks out.  That ceiling-mounted vent is not going to capture anything.  First because it will be far from the countertop (especially with a shorter countertop height).  Second because there's nothing to guide all the greasy, steamy stuff into the actual vent. Fumes don't just rise, they spread.  Imagine a cone, starting at 30 inches wide (at the level of your counter) and spreading out as the steam rises through the room up to the ceiling... 8-foot ceilings shouldn't be an impediment to a vent hood, especially if the counter is shorter.  They usually need to be 30-36" from the countertop. You can look up the height of the various hoods and see what will be right for your island. The right-angle turn to vent horizontally is much less of a concern.  Depending on how long the run is you can look at adding in a silencer, or just sticking the blower on the outside of the house.

Different outcomes can result not only from slight differences in the inputs (many of which are estimates anyway) but also from what conclusion is drawn from the result. If the cooling load comes out to 3.6 tons, do you round down to 3.5 (one tenth of a ton difference is inconsequential) or do you round up (the old fashioned seat of the pants attitude, no one ever calls to complain they're too cool during hot weather). Arguably, half a ton isn't a huge difference either. One ton, different story.

In case it sparks helpful ideas for you… We did a to-the-studs remodel, demoing it all ourselves. We had a major mess with blown in (not foam) insulation. The shop vac did not work at all. Way cheaper than a hospital stay. Look at adding a cyclone prefilter -- the Oneida Dust Deputy is one variant-- that will pull out 98% of the dust before it gets to your shop vac, then also splurge for the HEPA filter for the vac You don't want to be spreading that dust around, whatever it is. If the mess is more than shop vac sized then a dust collector may be the way to go. The other approach is to spray it down with water using a garden sprayer to knock down the dust and shovel it out into trash bags, again avoiding spreading the dust everywhere.

@Artist-FKA-Novice Zone 7B GA I don't know if you're new to roses, but a lot of folks who are do worry about RRD. There are dozens of posts on this forum about people's experience with it. And I am so sorry you are worried so deeply--I can see that in your post. I think it's going to be fine. Your can actually check if there is RRD in your area.  Check out this link for more info (and you can report it here as well). But even if it is, I really wouldn't trouble yourself about your pruners. In 30 years of gardening I have never sanitized mine (I probably should) but have not passed on any diseases yet. I was going to encourage you that even if a rose has RRD, you will still be able to have beautiful roses if you properly dispose of it and the roots (bag it all up and drop in the trash). Having lost roses to bicyclists running them over, squirrels eating them, rot, and so many other diseases, RRD is just not a huge concern (to me). If it happens, it is usually unmistakable. But roses can be destroyed by so many other things that most of us don't worry about, and RRD is just one thing. So if you don't have a positive diagnosis from a lab, I wouldn't let yourself fret over this too much. I can give you an example from last year in my own garden. My Rock & Roll rose developed some pretty gnarly growth that I found bewildering. Flattened stems, extra thorniness, very red, etc.  It looked so much like RRD and I started to worry. Why wait? For one thing, if the current floor is vinyl or laminate or other thin material and you put down tile (or any flooring thicker than the current flooring), you run the risk of trapping the DW in the "DW alcove".  The height of the DW may or may not be adjustable enough to remove it with the tile. If the refrigerator just fits inside the current alcove, adding a thicker flooring could mean the refrigerator may not fit.  Or, again, if you don't run the flooring under the refrigerator, the refrigerator could be trapped (similar to the DW).  (If the flooring does not go all the way back to the wall, you will need plywood or other material the thickness of the flooring for the rest of the space so the appliance is level.) For appliances that you can see under such as refrigerators and ranges, you should always run the flooring at least far enough back so the old flooring (or subfloor) isn't visible from any point of view. If you are planning on putting the flooring over the top of your existing flooring, the above possible issues have an even greater chance for occurring.

I do water new autumn plantings if there is a lag in precipitation during the winter (such as happened during the two winters prior to this one here).  Plants recently put into the ground from a pot generally haven't sent roots very far into the surrounding soil, so remain dependent on whatever moisture is in its potting medium.  Potting media are designed to be well-drained and, in my experience, tend to dry out sooner than the ambient soil.  For me, the threshhold during winter is somewhere around three weeks without rain or since the last irrigation.  I keep careful watch on new plantings and poke a finger down into the potting medium to see how dry it is.  Last winter, for example, I remember watering new plantings at least several times and they needed it.

Organic lawn care is a big deal here in the US and many gardeners use natural or organic based fertilizers. You can purchase them already formulated and bagged (much like the Nutriboost product) but those tend to be overly pricey for what you get. If you can get them, seed meals can accomplish the same thing - soybean meal, cottonseed meal, alfalfa meal, corn meal, etc. These are also commonly used for animal feeds. Biosolids (like Milorganite) are also popular. These products can be used virtually year round because as with almost all organics, they are feeding the soil web which is always active and an enriched, biologically active soil will generate a healthy lawn. If soil temps drop too low, the soil biology will be dormant or inactive but the fertilizer product will remain more or less intact until they become active again as temps warm. Reviewing some of the posts in the Organic Lawn Care forum should provide additional detail.

When this was a more popular bathroom option, vanities were often only 32 inches high, and the lowered section even lower.  Now, most vanities are being made as high as kitchen counters - 36 inches.  What do you plan for the height of yours?  Then, as Rho Dodendron asks, how tall are you?  Do you want to sit on a short vanity stool, or a counter stool?  Do you want to let things occasionally fall off the edges onto the make-up section?  Can you put the make-up section on one end, preferably near a window?  Or have it entirely separate? Designers will come on here and tell you that nobody wants these sit-down vanities anymore.  I do.  I use my 36 inch tall end of my vanity for this purpose, to sit and do my hair.  If you want this feature, get it.  The configuration of having the lowered section in the middle is a 1980s-1990s look, so being more practical and having one continuous countertop between your two sinks is more ”today.”  You may also want to price out the difference between the countertop fabrication with the different layouts.  Do two extra cuts (to lower it in the center for the make-up vanity) cost much more than a continuous 8 or 10 foot long counter, or is the longer counter more expensive because it is harder to move than 2 four foot long ones and a two foot long one?  You may want to ask.

To determine the number and placement of lights in a room, we need to calculate the appropriate lighting level (illuminance) required for the tasks performed in the room. The illuminance is typically measured in foot-candles (fc) or lux. The Illuminating Engineering Society of North America (IESNA) provides guidelines for recommended illuminance levels for different types of rooms and tasks. For a kitchen, a recommended illuminance level is 50-100 fc, and for a basement rec-room, it is 10-20 fc. Using the illuminance data you provided, we can calculate the number and spacing of lights required to achieve the recommended illuminance levels in each room. First Floor Great Room/Eat-In/Kitchen: Assuming the total area of the kitchen and great room is around 500 square feet, we would need approximately 30,000-60,000 total lumens (60-120 lumens per square foot) to achieve the recommended illuminance level of 50-100 fc. Since each LED flush-mount provides about 930 lumens, we would need around 32-65 lights in total. Based on the horizontal/vertical diffuse angle of the LED flush-mounts (108.2 deg) and the spacing/ mounting height ratio (S/MH) of 1.22, the recommended spacing between lights is approximately 7.5 feet. However, since the ceiling height is 9 feet, we can space the lights slightly farther apart, up to around 9-10 feet. For the kitchen, your suggested placement of one light to the left/right of the sink and stove and one in the pantry is a good start. For the rest of the great room area, you could consider placing lights every 9-10 feet, in a grid pattern. You could also consider adding additional lights over the kitchen island or dining area, if applicable. Basement Rec-Room: Assuming the total area of the basement rec-room is around 300 square feet, we would need approximately 3,000-6,000 total lumens (10-20 lumens per square foot) to achieve the recommended illuminance level of 10-20 fc. Since each LED flush-mount provides about 930 lumens, we would need around 4-7 lights in total. Based on the same diffuse angle and spacing/mounting height ratio, the recommended spacing between lights is approximately 5.5 feet. However, since the ceiling height is around 8-9 feet, we can space the lights slightly farther apart, up to around 6-7 feet. For the basement rec-room, you could consider placing lights in a grid pattern, spaced around 6-7 feet apart. You may also want to place one or two lights near the stairs or bathroom, for safety and visibility. Overall, the number and placement of lights in a room depends on the size of the room, the desired illuminance level, and the characteristics of the lights themselves. It's always a good idea to consult with a lighting professional or builder to ensure that the lighting design meets your needs and preferences.

Since you asked here is the specific IRC code excerpt applying in the U.S.:   It is not as specific like Ontario's, but interpretation of "self-closing" is inherent. If the builder has passed inspection and you are moved in, it may be hard to move mountains for this. Maybe keep it with the list of other warranty items to do. Also FWIW the garage separation wall in a single family dwelling is not a fire wall, and seldom is the code amended to isolate having a listed fire-rated door.

There is no national residential consensus code in the US that requires a fire rating for the separation wall between a house and a garage nor is an opening in such a wall required to be fire-rated or a "fire door". Such assemblies are required by building codes between different Occupancies and that is not the case for single-family dwellings. Instead, US residential building codes provide written prescriptive requirements for that separation wall and openings in it.  Many jurisdictions modify the closer requirements but none to my knowledge requires the wall or door to be fire-rated. Here are the latest unmodified IRC requirements:   Here is a typical US residential building code requirement for a door between a house and a garage:   Often the option for a 20-minute fire-rated door is misunderstood.  Fire ratings are only granted for "assemblies", not parts of an assembly. The intent of the IRC is to allow for the door "panel" of a fire-rated assembly to be used in an unrated frame with unrated hardware so the assembly is not fire-rated.  Also there would be little purpose in requiring a fire-rated door in an unrated wall assembly. I don't know of any of this applies to the OP.

I do 16 hours on, 8 hours off once the seedlings germinate.  This is where a multi-shelf set-up comes in handy -- the germinating shelf has 24 hr light (generates heat), the other shelves are 16/8.  Plants need some amount of darkness for regenerative purposes -- it's not the time of day that matters under the lights, it's the darkness.  If you're growing on a windowsill or near a source of daylight, that dictates your darkness schedule.

In general, some seed that likes light for sprouting up like carrot and lettuce and tends to be surface sown or very lightly covered can appreaciate the light being on from sowing forward. Most seed that likes being more buried does not really need light till it starts popping out of the soil. But then you want to make sure it is getting light from that point on. Plants have circadian clocks- different species run on differing times of light and dark. When they are small seedlings it is usually beneficial for there to be longer times of light or no darkness. As they get older and start their own circadian rhythms some gardeners like to start giving hours of night or lights off to accomidate that. As they harden off it can be beneficial to adjust the night hours for plants akin to real night hours like we adjust their light from indoor to outdoor lighting during the day. In general, most plants are used to it being cooler at night than during the day. Seeds can benefit from additional warmth from a mat to sprout, but after that it is better to get the sproutlings off the heat. A couple few degree difference usually isn't a big deal for seedlings, it's the usual flux in a house. But a large temp drop or a lengthy one overnight can cause harm to many seedlings. Especially during the younger days of growth. I do my seedlings in a large south facing kitchen window that gets full sun, and I also run lights there. It stays temp stable on the warm side due to a basebord heater there. I use a couple of little four tier mini greenhouse cages for my shelving. I have a 24 hour on light for sproutlings. Another couple lights that get night time off closer to the actual night hours for older seedlings. I turn them off before going to bed, and on when I make coffee in the morning. Engineered hardwood flooring is indistinguishable from solid wood flooring from a "look and feel" perspective.  For planks as wide as 8-9" I'd be surprised if you could find solid oak planks. The only difference to consider would be the ability to refinish solid floors several times where most engineered products would allow for a single refinishing. Engineered flooring is generally a plywood base topped with the finished wood and arrives pre-stained and finished, ready to lay in your home.  There are usually options for how it can be laid, nail down, glue down, floating etc. Solid hardwood would offer the same options. Some engineered flooring is not recommended in below grade applications. Solid hardwood can be found both unfinished and pre finished.  Unfinished would be laid in the home and then sanded and stained to your desired colour and a finish coat on top. In my opinion, engineered hardwood is the superior product for most applications. If you are unsure, go to a good flooring store (not a big box) and see the various options available and talk to a flooring professional at the store for the best recommendations for your situation, including the subfloor it will be laid on, humidity levels in the home, desired look and feel (do you want a very smooth floor or maybe some distressing in the finish etc). Don't hesitate to choose Engineered.  It is not a "cheap out" option at all and may be end up being a better option than a solid alternative.

There will never be agreement on what soil/ grow medium is best, so let's go for 'good'. Any grow medium that allows you to water to beyond the point of complete soil saturation, w/o the medium holding too much water for a period so long it significantly interferes with root function, or worse, wrecks root health by setting the stage for any of a number of potential fungal infections, is a "good" medium. When your medium stays wet for too long, roots die. This causes the plant's chemical messengers to 'tell' the top of the plant to stop growing so the plant can focus almost its entire energy allocation on regrowth of the roots that were killed. Continued over-watering sets up a cycle of death and regeneration of roots that can rob the plant of huge %s of energy that otherwise would have been put toward growth and defense against insects/ diseases. BTW - getting to a place where you can water correctly w/o your plant paying an "over-watering tax" is a real game changer insofar as the ability to keep plants healthy and attractive, so it's worth making an effort to get there. The 2 approaches to 'getting there': 1) By making your own media and starting with a very large fraction of coarse materials and adding only enough fine material to bring water retention up to a point you can live with. 2) Use tricks to limit the volume of excess (perched) water your media can hold. Interesting user name, but it sort of weirds me out. You should water when the plant needs it. Watering on a schedule, unless you're using a grow medium specifically formulated to allow you to do that, almost always leads to episodes of over or under-watering. Burned leaf tips and/or leaf margins are most often a symptom of a problem in the rootzone. You can determine appropriate watering intervals by using a "tell". More on that below. Your plant looks very chlorotic. When did you last fertilize? what did you use? Does the pot have a drain hole? Does it have a collection saucer? Do you allow the plant to reabsorb the water that makes it into the collection saucer? Do you know your home's range of relative humidity? Your plant is sensitive to fluoride and fluoride is accumulative in plant tissues. Low humidity increases transpiration (water loss through the leaves), which speeds up the nutrient stream (water and what's dissolved in that water), which means more fluoride accumulates in leaves under low humidity conditions. Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips in order to avoid over-watering - leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions - which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips, rather than resolving a dilemma, simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Al

In addition to that great stuff, a clay pot feels cold when it is moist, and it is a darker color.  When it dries, it does not feel so cold and turns a lighter color.  The porosity of the clay allows water to evaporate from the soil much more quickly than non-porous ceramic or plastic pot. In the porous clay pot and not allowing the pot to sit in a tray of water, the risk of overwatering a parlor palm is so low, it shouldn't be on your mind unless you start watering your plant incessantly, daily.  I don't worry about the level of moisture in most of my pots before I add more water because the bigger harm to those plants is a dry moment.  Many plants can't handle a dry moment & will suffer foliage damage.  So I just make sure to water often enough so those plants are never literally dry. Also, really dry soil can become hydrophobic, unable to absorb moisture before it just runs by and out the drain hole.  If a pot has gotten very dry, water it again after a few minutes, thoroughly but gently all over the soil surface, not just in 1 spot.  Excess should drip out.  When it finishes dripping, put it back in the usual spot.  This is too time consuming if you have more than 100 pots in the house like I do.

The Queen Palm, like most palms has very little root structure so your tree should be OK. The only issue is that a Queen Palm unlike many others is not a self-pruning palm.  Many other palm trees drop their fronds once new fronds have grown in.  Not so with the Queen.  You have to literally cut off any dead fronds or seed sprays.  That's why they are typically the least expensive palm to purchase.  They will grow about 2 1/2 stories tall, last about 25 years and then die off.  We no longer allow them in our community as they are a yearly expense to have trimmed.

You need to get your watering intervals under control. I'm nearly certain your issue is over-watering. Try using a wooden 'tell' stuck deep into the soil, all the way to the pot bottom, to read moisture levels deep in the pot where it actually matters. More on that below. I'm assuming your pot has a drain hole. Yes? After you water thoroughly, so the entire soil column is fully wetted and at least 20% of the water applied exits the pot, tip your pot at a 45* angle to force more water from the soil. Compare B to A below to see what difference it makes. What do you do insofar as fertilizing? Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips in order to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions - which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma and creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Al

“Soapstone is soft. it will scratch and it can stain w/oils and such.“ I can’t believe this rubbish is still being quoted by ”Pros” in the year 2023.  It just shows how little experience some ”Pros” have, with soapstone. @Beth H. : Not all soapstones are soft.  There are some very hard varieties, such as Stormy Black, Anastacia, and Blevedere, which I have. While not as hard as granite, it takes some doing to scratch Belvedere...which I described in my post above, and includes a closeup of my counter.  Essentially, the only thing that’s ever scratched or made very small chips (at the sink edge) in my soapstone counters, is a cast iron pan.  A black Sharpy pen took care of the small sink edge chips (nobody can see them).  And, the scratch made by DH dragging a cast iron pan, disappeared after a light sanding…and a bit of mineral oil. The most egregious part of your statement, was saying that soapstone can stain.  For goodness sake.  Read up.  Soapstone is impervious to anything and everything.  It is denser and heavier than any stones used in home or commercial settings.  Nothing can penetrate the surface.  It never need to be sealed.  Any dripped cooking oils, tomato sauce, lemon juice, vinegar…anything, will sit on the surface of the stone.  That’s what forms patina on soapstone…oils oxidize on top of the stone. Which is why a hard variety of soapstone is perfect for a family with kids of any age.  Kids can be as sloppy and drippy as kids tend to be, and not stain the counters. Patina buildup, usually where most of the kitchen action is, like at the stove, can easily by removed.  Just some Comet or Bon Ami, water and the scrubby side of a blue Scotch sponge, is all we use.  My husband will do this once or twice a year, when he feels like bring the stone back to its original, lighter color. Perhaps best of all, unlike the threads we’ve seen on this site about those manmade, resin filled quartz counters getting scorched from heat…even from a hot pot lid that a poster’s son left on her quartz counter…that cannot happen with soapstone. Heat cannot damage soapstone.  Which is why throughout Scandinavia, and New England, free standing heating stoves are made of soapstone.  And why in this country, soapstone is usually the material of choice, for fireplace surrounds. Also, because soapstone absorbs heat slowly, and doesn’t get as cold as other stones, it will not suffer from thermal shock (cracking), which can happen with granite, quartzite, marble, and quartz. Soapstone, a hard variety, is the perfect material for a house with children.

Hibiscus are one of the few plants that actually need a special fertilizer; this, because they use more potassium than nitrogen, whereas most plants use around 6x as much N as potassium. Hibiscus use only a very limited amount of phosphorous, so "bloom-booster-type fertilizers' should always be avoided. Hibiscus also have very aggressive root systems, and need a full repot annually (in mid-spring) to be at their best. When they become seriously rootbound, they often shed inner foliage (close to the trunk) such that in the end all or almost all foliage is concentrated near branch tips. The foliage close to the trunk often goes through a period of resorption, during which mobile (in the plant) nutrients and other biocompounds are reclaimed by the plant to support new extension growth. This results in breakdown of the green pigment chlorophyll, which normally masks other pigments, and provides opportunity for insect pests and disease pathogens to infect the plant. The reason is, part of the shedding process includes individual leaves being walled off from plant processes/ functions by a layer that forms at the base of the leaf.
