Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips in order to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions - which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma and creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. did i miss the post about the falling tree story??? Man, you just don't know. You remember that I hired a company to come and cut a bunch of trees from around my house, right? The plan was for him to climb it and take it down in several pieces. He stressed the urgency of the job because of how it was leaning, he acted like it could fall any day! Well, time goes by. May comes, and the tree's still there. So I text him and push it, he comes out and decides that it's too windy and dangerous. June comes by. Now it's too hot. You see the pattern. Well, September comes, and now there's a hurricane in the forecast! So I push a little harder, and tell him that I'll rent a 50' lift for the day so that he can take it down easier. That's going to be delivered on a specific day, just before the hurricane hits, so he HAS to do it that day. Lift is delivered at 8am. He comes and looks at it for a few minutes, then leaves to get some food. 4:30 comes along, he finally shows back up and starts working on it. But he's decided that, instead of taking it down in sections, he's going to use his big truck, jack, and wedges to pull it where he wants it. By 7pm he's still working on it. Read Me First!" thread: Please post a fully-measured layout of the space under consideration and a sketch of the entire floor. Both can be either hand-drawn, computer generated, or drawn up with computer/app tools. By "fully-measured", we mean a layout with the widths of each wall/window/door/doorway and the distances between each wall/window/door/doorway labeled. See a sample below. If something cannot be moved or changed, label it precisely on your layout (see post in sample) and tell us why it cannot be moved/changed -- we may have some ideas for you. The sketch of the entire floor lets us see how the Kitchen relates to the rest of the home. It doesn't have to be to-scale, but it should accurately show how the rooms relate to each other and should include all interior & exterior doors. In addition, it will help us see how traffic flows in, around, and through the Kitchen. Label the front entry and family entry. The family entry is usually a garage or side entry, but it might not be. It's helpful to know which door you use to bring in groceries. Regardless of how you draw it up (by hand, computer, etc.), please be sure all measurements are labeled. (Note: Computer generated layouts often lack key measurements and, sometimes, measure to/from things like the middle of a wall or the middle of a window. Neither are useful. Measure each item and the distances between each item.)

The cost is not unreasonable, and actually sounds low for installation of that material. .  The price of the panels is minor compared to the installation materials and labor. The cost of STANDARD  tile is also minor compared to labor and materials for a properly built shower.   It IS more expensive to install GPTP (Gauged Porcelain Tile Panels) as qualified contractors must be properly trained and have the equipment. The industry (both professional trade organizations and manufacturers) have training programs (usually 2-5 day programs) for contractors to get proper training and certification in GPTP installation.  Hopefully your contractor is aware of the installation requirements. They are not installaed by one person, but by a team of installers.  To give you (and others who responded here) a bit of perspective about the training required: "Due to the extremely large modules that Gauged Porcelain Tile/Gauged Porcelain Tile Panels are available in, installation of this product is significantly different from the installation of standard large format porcelain tile, requiring special installation tools and techniques.  The unique installation procedures and workmanship considerations, are as outlined in ANSI A108.19 American National Standard Specifications for "Interior Installation of Gauged Porcelain Tile and Gauged Porcelain Tile Panels/Slabs by the Thin-Bed Method bonded with Modified Dry-Set Cement Mortar or Improved Modified Dry-Set Cement Mortar”.Some key issues addressed by ANSI A108.19 include: Contractor Qualifications Jobsite and Material Handling Requirements Substrate Flatness and General Requirements Floor and Wall Installation procedures for ANSI A137.3 Table 4 gauged products Wall Installation Procedures for ANSI A137.3 Table 5 gauged products Mortar, and Mortar Application Unique coverage criteria and evaluation procedures Lippage criteria and use of lippage control systems Special floor setting provisions that involve embedding by walking Movement Joints " You can assume that a properly credentialed installation team is not concerned about the cost of one slab breaking and I would not suggest that you try to negotiate pricing by offering to "eat it if they break it".  In addition, the contractor (if qualified) will be responsible for transport of the slabs as they require specific equipment and handling procedures. You do NOT want to attempt this yourself as it can be quite dangerous.  Doubtful a supplier would even allow it. I hope this provides a little perspective on GTPT installation for consideration in shower pricing.  Good luck with your project.

Hi Alex! Aside from whether or not the trees will live, and I think they will. It's generally not a good idea to stake trees so rigidly like shown in your pictures. The stake(s) should be about a foot from the trunk and the ties should be made of a strong but stretchable material (I use nylon stocking material), so the tree can sway and move to an extent when the wind blows. This is done because it allows the trunk and roots to adapt to conditions it will face later when not supported, growing stronger over time. If the tree won't stand straight by itself, another stake can be put opposite side of the tree, same distance away. That way the ties will hold the trunk in a more central position when the wind isn't blowing. Just thought I'd mention that. :-) bill

Water does drain considerably faster from a raised beds (RB) built on hard clay than the hard clay drains for 2 reasons, one of which has already been mentioned. 1) The added ht of the raised bed increases gravitational flow potential of the water column. That is to say the weight of the water column in the RB soil pushes down on water nearer the clay layer and forces it to move laterally through any openings in the sides, or under the sides if the rest directly on top of the clay layer. Stand a dry sponge on edge, then slowly start pouring water on top of the sponge. The sponge will absorb water to a given point (called field capacity), then water will start to flow laterally across the top of the surface the sponge is resting on. 2) Water's tendency to stick to itself (cohesion) and it's tendency to stick to other objects (like soil particles) added together + the force of capillary action, which in any soil which isn't saturated, pulls free water in all directions. The predominant direction is downward though, because the force of gravity will be working in concert with capillarity. The first part of clay soils to dry is the soil exposed to the air. When the surface of the clay soil surrounding the RB dries, it dramatically increases the capillary pull of the dry soil due to the very large (collective) surface area of clay soil's particulates and the added force of adhesion the surface area causes. So you have the weight of the water column pushing downward and forcing water to move laterally, plus, you have water being pulled laterally by the soil's capillarity, significantly increasing evaporative water loss from the bed. As the soil surface dries, it continues to pull water from the RB. When a RB is built on clay through which water is reluctant to percolate, it is best to avoid amending the clay soil on which the bed rests. This slows but doesn't stop 'the bathtub effect' from occurring over time. Raised beds, with their increased aeration and usually higher levels of OM, are hospitable harbors of refuge for populations of soil biota more concentrated than clay supports. Over time and through the activity of soil live, clay soils beneath RBs gradually become more porous and tend to hold more water in the root zone, so the beds would benefit from being moved from time to time. Adding in plants, changing the material of the hard landscape - patio / the drive and path... these have as much effect as changing the house itself (and can be cheaper (or not!), or faster, or less disruptive!). Finally if you're changing the look of your house you can also consider ways that you can improve its energy efficiency. Adding more insulation externally with render or some other cladding / finish can reduce your heating costs and make it look better and feel more comfortable to live in. (for most applications, I use some flavor of sand or loamy sand) I design a lot of soil profiles for general landscapes, bioswales/biofiltration, light weight rooftop applications, sports field root zones, etc. and one thing that I've learned over the years for deeper plantings is that, rather than placing organic amendment the entire depth, it can really help to do a "split layer" using the mineral soil / organic blend in the top 10 to 12 inches and just the mineral fraction without any organic below that. When it rains/snows the moisture migrates to the bottom and the rain hitting the concrete around the base also splashes back onto that part of the post. The bottom of the post stays wet and deteriorates. That doesn't look like a pressure treated post, which I would recommend in an exposed location like that. Also, is that post even attached to the slab with a steel post bracket, or is it just sitting in direct contact with the concrete? If so, that's another no-no which also hastens rotting.  If I were having that replaced I'd get a pressure treated post, I'd have the uncut end of the post at the bottom (so you wouldn't have an unprotected cross section), and I'd have a bracket installed that would support the post bottom at least an inch or two above the top of the slab. The cut end grain of wood sitting on concrete is a big no-no.  You are very lucky that the posts have lasted 35 years.  End grain soaks up water by capillary action--which is how the live tree moved moisture from the roots and spread it through the canopy.  End grain is like a cluster of open end straws, wicking moisture.

BM Advance is a waterborne alkyd paint, and epoxy paint is epoxy mixed into an arylic paint. Yes, you need to remove the finish coat (which is probably polyurethane) before you can stain them another color. This will probably remove some of the color of the stain depending how the cabinet was stained and what it was stained with and how you remove it. You have a couple options to remove the finish. 1) You can use a chemical stripper like Citristrip. 2) You can sand the doors by hand (Don't use a power sander of any kind! You're not trying to take of six layers of paint or remove any of the wood.) 3) You may be able to take the doors and drawer fronts to be dipped. A company will soak them in a vat of chemical stripper. It's expensive, but can be worth it for pieces with lots of edges, nooks and crannies that will hold up to it. Then you use a chemical stripper on the frame. For that vanity, #1 is absolutely your best choice. #2 is also reasonable. #3 isn't worth it for something with such straight lines. If you're trying to get the color out, too, that's a whole additional process. If not, and you just want them darker, you can stain them. Doing something like this yourself isn't "hard," but it does take skill and practice. Getting them an exact color is very challenging and you have no test pieces. It also involves a lot of labor and time. You can hire a furniture re-finisher to do it for you. But they are not going to guarantee you an exact color. If you're very particular about the color you want, it still might turn out greyer or redder or something you don't want.

To make kimchi, you need a crock with weights to hold the top down during fermentation.  If you google kimchi crocks or fermentation crocks, all kinds of options come up.  A good Asian grocery store would also be a place to look.  There are many different recipes for kimchi and most of the ingredients are easy to find, but we had to order the Korean chili flakes we wanted to use online.  Also online are many articles about the art of kimchi making; do some reading and research to gain a basic knowledge of how to start out and go from there.  As you gain experience, you will feel more confident about experimenting with ingredients and seasonings. Here is an article that explains kimchi making: https://mykoreankitchen.com/kimchi-recipe/ As far as wok cooking goes, it really makes a difference if you have a gas stove that puts out high heat.  If your stove and wok don't get hot enough, you will end up steaming your stir fry rather than giving it a good searing stir fry.  We had many frustrating experiences on an electric stove and switching over to gas made a huge difference in our results.  That's not to say don't stir fry if you have electric; just be aware that you might not get the exact results you are expecting.  We had the best luck stir frying small amounts at a time on the electric stove.

I've made several batches of kimchi, and have always used quart or 1/2 gallon mason jars.  For a weight I use glass fermenting weights from "that A river place".  While it's fermenting I use silicone "pickle lids" from the same source, as the mixture will need to vent as it ferments.   They look just like baby bottle nipples, and the pink lids have been the source of some curious looks and  good laughs!  I ferment it on our counter top for 3-7 days, depending on the temp and how "sour" we want it.  Be sure to put an old towl under the jars--they can leak out of the nipples and make a mess. When I'm satisfied with the flavor, I replace the silicone lids with a plastic lid and store the jars in our garage beer fridge.  DON'T put the lids on too tight-it will continue to ferment, although slowly.  It the lid is too tight--it will leak and make a big, stinky mess--ask me how I know! I don't use a recipe, so sorry I don't have one to share. I learned by watching youtube videos and looking at different online recipes.   I do use some grated apple in mine, as we like the sweetness it adds. Good luck with your home fermented kimchi--it is soooo much better than store-bought!

Don't use landscape fabric. It does not really break down and ends up being an issue for most gardeners. If you want to use a quick supression layer under your mulch, use cardboard or newspapers that break down. What kind of mulch you use on top depends on your preference. For the most part, woody plants (in containers) are more cohesive when it comes to what they want, than they are when it comes to what they will tolerate, though there are those with their own quirks. Almost all trees will grow well in a medium that allows you to water pretty much at will. If you can (but don't necessarily do) water on a schedule (as opposed to watering on an as-needed basis) you have a grow medium that's a keeper. Most fruiting trees like full sun, a 2:1:2 ratio fertilizer, and an acidic grow medium (around 5.5-6.0). About the fertilizer ..... good 2:1:2 ratio fertilizers (10-5-10 would be an example) aren't easy to find in packaging less than 50 lbs. If you're already using Foliage-Pro 9-3-6, just keep using it, but supplement the solution with half as much ProTeKt 0-0-3  as the 9-3-6. I.e., if you're using a teaspoon of 9-3-6 per gallon, use half that amount of ProTeKt 0-0-3. Be sure to read fertilizer packaging instructions so as to avoid the precipitation of ingredients that can occur when not mixing correctly. The inclusion of the ProTeKt is an excellent strategy for plants like hibiscus, which just generally needs more K than N, and fruit trees that want/need that extra measure of K when they arrive at sexual maturity/ begin fruiting. When it's time to repot, I would repot the plant before it starts pushing new growth in spring. That way, the plant will wake up more gradually, with blooms and new leaves emerging as the root system is able to support the new growth. When repotting too late, it can have a bigger impact in blooms and fruiting. Al

Like others have posted, you have to basically cut your molding upside down.  On your mitre saw, you have to position the portion of the crown molding that will be against the ceiling on the base of your mitre saw, and the portion of the crown molding that will be against the wall on the fence of your mitre saw.  Keep in mind that if you need to mitre the left of the molding, the mitre will be on your right on your saw.  Then you flip the molding over and it should line up, providing your corner is exactly 90 degrees.  Also, make sure you hold the piece of molding at exactly the same angle on your saw as it will lay on your wall.  For this, cut a small piece of molding about 1 foot long, and lay it against the corner of the ceiling and wall the way it should go, and make a mark on the ceiling and another one on the wall where the crown molding ends.  Remove the molding, and measure the distance, on the ceiling, between the corner and your mark.  Transpose that mark on the base of your mitre saw. For beginners, it can help to put a piece of painters tape on your fence and write "wall" and another piece on the table and write "ceiling".

You said you saw kitchens by two different contractors.  Typically, the contractor doesn't build the cabinets him or herself, they sub it out to a cabinet shop.  You should be more concerned about who the cabinet shop is.  Did you mean you saw kitchens with cabinets from two different custom cabinet shops? There's a wide range of quality in the custom cabinetry world.  The best, most expensive kitchens all use custom cabinetry.  Pretty much any kitchen image you've seen in a magazine has custom cabinets.   But there are a lot of people holding themselves out as custom cabinet makers who do a crappy job.  Factory-finished cabinets tend to have more consistent quality, although read through this forum and you'll see plenty of complaints about those too (including Plain & Fancy!).  There is no sure thing. The question of whether to go custom is really driven by you and your house - are you okay choosing between a limited selection of colors?  Is your space compatible with standard-size cabinets (nearly all factory-finished cabinets are not "true" custom, they are semi custom meaning that cabinet sizes may be limited or proceed in 1" increments) or is it an old house with weird corners and no straight walls? If you go custom, you'll have to do your research.  But that's also true of factory-finished.  And in my experience, factory-finished tend to cost about the same or more.

homey_bird, Vented dryers pull/exhaust upwards of 200 cu ft of air per minute during operation so don't plan to close the doors on the niche while it runs unless they're designed to provide that rate of airflow without obstruction. Frontload washers should also have the door left slightly ajar and the dispenser drawer slightly open when not in use to allow moisture to disperse for avoiding mold and odors in the drum so plan for sufficient space in front of the machine to allow for it. Space behind the machines, as stated above, may vary per the selected models.  The exhaust ducting for vented dryers is 4" diameter.  How do you plan to route the exhaust?  It can be tricky to arrange the ducting behind the dryer without kinking or crushing it when the machines are stacked in an enclosed niche with no side access to get behind them. There are exhaust housings that mount into the wall but working room to connect to the dryer is still required. There must also be space behind the washer for the hot/cold water supply hoses connecting to it.

"The recommended distance for a hood is 20 to 24 inches above the cooktop." That is incorrect.  The recommended distance is 30 to 36 inches above the cooktop. I do not see the point of spending money on a hood that is underpowered and needs to be installed so low in order to function. I would look for the 36" hood that is 600 cfms, and install it with a distance of 30-36" above the cooktop.  You said you have existing cabinetry.  What is the distance from the cooktop to the bottom of the existing cabinetry?  You may need to seek an undercabinet hood that is not taller than 7", depending on the cabinetry you have in place.

It's unclear whether the planting consists of several individual propagules, or the multiple trunks are all branches that connect to a lower order branch beneath the soil line. It could be either. If they are individual propagules, you can separate them when you next repot (spring), select one of the propagules, then remove any branches competing for position as the main leader so there is only 1 conspicuous trunk. If the lower branches were removed from this propagule such that all that remained is the cluster of branches at the top of the cutting, you could potentially end up with more than 8 trunks.  If you pruned off all branches except for 1 with the growing tip of the branch still attached, you would end up with a single-trunked specimen, and it wouldn't matter if the pruning was done before the propagule was stuck (in the grow medium) or at some later date.  If you live in the Northern Hemisphere and when you pruned, a large number of leaves were lost due to the pruning, it could be considered an error (from the plant's perspective). Leaves are each a food factory, working to produce the plant's true food (sugars/ starch). When the plant is pruned so leaves are lost, it increases the potential for the tree to be in a place where it is using more energy than it is creating (through photosynthesis). This is a dangerous position for a plant to be in as it is unsustainable; and, it puts the tree in a position where it must have enough stored energy reserves to push at least some new foliage to a point where it at least 75% mature, the break-even point where leaves change from being net users of energy to net producers. If you simply cut the 'extra' trunks off at the soil line, they will each back-bud from currently suppressed buds at or immediately below the soil line, which would add to the number of trunks/ stems on the plant. Al

I have remodeled four full bathrooms and two powder rooms.  We only moved the toilet once, and that was just nine inches from one joist compartment to the next.  So one thing I will say is that if you don't have an open ceiling under the bath so you can't see the way the joists are laid out, you won't know if you can move the waste pipe until the bathroom is demolished and you can open up the floor.  Even a professional plumber can't put a waste pipe where there is a joist.  Or to put it another way - they shouldn't.  I do think moving the toilet would make the layout better, but maybe there is a reason it is where it is now. As for the tub size, you know what you have now.  How does it compare to the one you're looking at?  Are they the same size?  I put a slightly larger tub into a small bath in our previous house and wished I hadn't.  Every inch matters when you're short on space.  Also think about the depth.  Deeper tubs are great for a nice soak, but if you have children they might be too deep (for reaching in to help a child wash) and if you're mostly using it for showers you have to step over the additional height all the time.  Only you know what is most suitable for you. As for the DIY, the last bathroom DH did partially on his own because he's retired now and has above average DIY skills.  He still had a plumber move the pipes that had to be moved and a tile setter come in.  He did the drywall work, electrical and installed the fixtures (plumbing hook ups, vanity and medicine cabinets installation).  The most important thing in DIY is being realistic about your own abilities and time available.  If your husband has a day job you could be waiting a long time for this bathroom to be finished.  If he has never done tile work before ask yourself if you want him to learn on this bathroom.  You might be able to save yourself some disagreements if you have a professional do the tiling.

If you are looking to blend with what most homes in Montana do, that would probably be the safer option! However, with such a historical building, it may make more sense to go with a more historic look (I.E Knock Down, Santa Fe, Orange Peel). If you are concerned about the skill level of the crew, orange peel can be done by less experienced teams and usually will turn out fine. We don't think a Smooth Finish would work in this style of home unless you are going for more of a clean and modern look. Say - Modern Farmhouse or Rustic Modern. Side Note - If you are planning to do a Wallpaper on any of the walls in the home, make sure the crews leave those walls as a Smooth Finish! Wallpaper has a harder time adhering to a heavily textured wall! We hope this was helpful! This project looks so fun! Happy Remodeling!

I love Santa Fe texture.  Fell in love with it when we visited Santa Fe many years ago.  The texture does not have to be 'heavy'; it can be as heavy or light as suits you. I do my own and think that it important that only one person does all of the texture in a room/ house.  Because there will be noticeable differences between how one person applies it and how another one does. It is quite easy to DIY.  I use an old cement trowel with rounded corners.  After the texture dries, you can/ should scrape down the highs with a broad drywall knife.   At this point, you can do a wash down with wet rags or a sponge to make the texture more subtle to the point of ending up with an Old World texture look.  If you want a heavy texture, then use premixed mud straight out of the bucket; thin the mud a bit for a lighter effect. This texture is also the one that is the most easy to repair or fill in if doors, windows, ect. get removed later on down the road or a visiting inlaw indulges in a bit too much Christmas cheer. `Knock down & orange peel are sprayed on and are very, very difficult to repair & blend in.  In the house before this one, I applied a Santa Fe texture over the sprayed on orange peel texture.  We had replaced a large picture window with patio doors and removed/ filled in the other existing door.

The main problem with texture is repairs -- if you, say, need to change the placement of a fixture or have new wiring run, it can be hard to patch the wall in a way that keeps the texture continuous. As leaves form along a branch or stem, they're a 1-time thing. IOW, no leaf will ever grow from the spot where the original leaf was attached. The best you can hope for would be a new branch/ vine growing from dormant/ suppressed buds arranged in a row above the attachment point of any leaf. The only way to make certain new branches will form where you want them is to prune back to just above the node where you desire a new branch/ vine to grow. Example:  This rooted Ficus cutting was pruned above the lower 2 leaves. This forced activation of buds located immediately above the mature leaves' attachment point. While these activated buds might appear to be leaves, they are actually new branches which will, also produce 1-time leaves along its length as long as the branches are extending and the tip of the branch remains in place. When the tip of the branch/ vine is removed, extension of that branch/ vine can no longer extend. The compacted soil and the holes/ tears made me conclude too soon that a Ca deficiency was in play. Had I known about the caterpillars, I would have not mentioned the Ca deficiency, though the grow medium adds considerable support to that line of thinking. What IS that medium? AL

To answer your question, leaves likely will not every grow in the same place low on those stems.  But you can wait until it gets longer again at the top with some new leaves, then cut those branches, root them and plant them back into the pot to kind of "start over".  Hope that makes sense.

Another option is just cut the plant back hard (low on the main stem), which will force new branches to grow on the stem remaining. New leaves can never grow to replace existing leaves on any existing stem or branch - only new branches can form just above where leaves are/were attached. Best time to cut back hard is a week or 2 before the summer solstice. The new leaves that grow along the new branches (in any case) will be/ should be in pristine condition and adapted to make most efficient use of light conditions wherever the plant is placed. That isn't to say all light levels will yield equal results, only that as new leaves come on line they will be perfectly adapted to make use of whatever level of light is available. Al

"one lens for distance and one for near" -- yeah, no.  My eye doctor suggested that, and I tried it.  It was pretty much ok until it very much wasn't.  Mine were done with the left lens for near vision, and the right lens for distance vision.  One day I was driving on a two-lane road in an agricultural area.  There was a slow-moving farm vehicle in front of me, and I wanted/needed to pass it.  I leaned my head to the left to see the oncoming traffic, and the closest oncoming vehicle was quite a distance away.  So, I proceeded to pass the farm vehicle... The issue was that once I was out into the oncoming lane and had the benefit of full, balanced vision of both eyes, I could see that the oncoming traffic was *much* closer than I thought it was.  I had to really accelerate to pass the farm vehicle and get back into that lane before I was creamed.  Scared the you-know-what out of me.  I called my eye doctor the next morning and got an appointment to get true bifocal contacts, which I've worn ever since.  And, yes, they are gas permeables.

Dry inside air in cold winters is invariably due to outside air infiltration.  First order of business is to get an energy audit, in particular, air infiltration.  I know you done some work to reduce this but its still causing you problems.  Pay the money and get it done properly.

Whether air exchange is intentional (e.g., via a HRV) or unintentional (e.g., via infiltration) indoor relative humidity is going to be low in the coldest part of winter (20% is pretty darn low) without supplemental humidification.  Given the OP's correlation of health issues and low relative humidity, I'd recommend humidification, and I otherwise wouldn't.   Condensation in wall cavities is a risk, but more so in homes with low infiltration and poor insulation.

Brad, I have posted this many moons ago here on GW. Much of the horticultural world involves problem solving. This old timer has always enjoyed that part of the business. Daisy refers to "thermal shock", where the rapid introduction of heat to the surface through a hot tap (or hot pans) causes rapid expansion of different parts of the material at different rates - eg the aggregates in the resin of composites, or the "glaze" over a ceramic sink. This can cause crackling, cracking and other defects to occur. Almost all such sinks will highlight that hot taps should not be used with them. You can get some products with stainless steel bases and composite sides. As to which is best - every product has their pros and cons. If you want to go white, I'd recommend ceramic as they're easier to clean, for darker colours, composites are nice and hard wearing but have a more textured, matte finish. Stainless is still a good bet, though be careful of poorly coated metal sinks in different colours (copper, brass, gunmetal), as the coating can wear with time

First, the OEM module output voltage is 1.5V, so you would want one alkaline battery, or a bank of them in parallel, not 3 in series achieving 4.5V as in the unit shown in your third image. Some experimentation with a battery and some resistors might help determine whether a series resistor is needed.  Start with a high resistance and work down to similar brightness as the OEM module produces.  High in this case is probably tens of ohms.  You may have to sacrifice a light string to home in on the ideal value.  Keep in mind the power requirement for the resistor.  P = I^2R.

Kaseki is on the right track. IMO, the 4.5V power supply looks to be just that, strictly a power supply with no current limiting. That means the current limiter is likely already in the wiring after the power supply, which is typical in my LED string light experience. If so, you could use the 4.5V battery supply and add 2 silicon diodes in series with it. The silicon diodes add in a ~0.65 voltage drop each into the circuit. The final voltage would be 4.5 - (2 x 0.65)  =3.2V nominal, which should be AOK. Any silicon diode will probably do, the 1N400x series diodes are common and available at Amazon..

Not that specific cultivar but there are several purple or chocolate leaved asperas on the market, Plum Passion being the most widely marketed variety. There is also some discussion that Burgundy Bliss is just a reintroduction of Plum Passion under another name to avoid patent rights. These have been around for a while (at least 5 years) but as they are not hardy for most of the country - forget any allusions to zone 5 hardiness, this is a firm zone 7 plant! - chances are many have not seen it or encountered it in stores. Asperas are relatively common here. Big bold plants with striking foliage, purple or not, and often fuzzy. They produce large lace cap flowers on old wood; in PNW soils blue fertile florets surrounded by pale, almost white sterile florets.

I have only seen it in pictures for the last few years. BP popped into the scene some time after Plum Passion was released, then replaced with Plum Passion Improved by Monrovia. Most asperas are big (>= 6 feet) and not very winter hardy. They would not survive my zone 8 winters without getting zapped to the ground often. I would not try them unless you can keep them very well protected somehow, like a heated greenhouse or some such stuff and keep them there all the time or in pots. They tend to be advertised as 6' tall but some can get to 10 feet. Golden Needle is probably the more compact one that I can remember (sometimes advertised 4-6' high)..

I would not try them unless you can keep them very well protected somehow, like a heated greenhouse or some such stuff and keep them there all the time or in pots. Nope. My hardiness zone would not 'permit' it. (If I drove 3.5 hours south I could get to a zone 7 CDN)(As well it is too large for our garden.) I was just curious about the plant.

You likely have a zero clearance fireplace, so wood/combustible framing around the unit within the manufacturer's limits are acceptable; find/download the manufacturer's installation instructions and follow them to the letter. Hi, I’m sorry I don’t know anything really about heat loss but I’m sure the companies who produce the large windows and doors use thermally efficient glazing. However, depending on where you live and the direction of the house, I think that you may also need to consider what you are going to do about heat gain. After this summer’s heatwave and the prediction of hotter weather to come, such large walls of glass can create massive heat gain inside, unless properly planned for. I imagine there may be similar options with glazing to reduce heat gain but also consider shading directly outside of the doors, eg a canopy, pergola, etc.

Like the earlier comment I don't know too much about this in any professional capacity but my first thought was also solar gain. Depending on the orientation you could end up with something incredibly warm possibly unbearably hot as well as cold in winter months. Are you having roof lights/veluxes as well? That's another consideration. Things I would think about would be triple glazing and creating some kind of external shading on the windows (brise soleil/pergola type affair).  I would really plan for window treatments blinds and curtains - will be expensive with so much glazing - but plan from the beginning to get a neat look.  Blackout type builds for insulation quality preventing both heat loss and gain and then also maybe something gauzy to diffuse daylight plus heavier curtains for evening time. It's no fun sitting in a cold room! For example you could look at recessing blinds into ceiling etc or some kind of track that allows for multiple blinds, panels, curtains etc.  I would also consider whether you could use a smaller amount of glazing but to frame a particular view/s. This would give you a bit of wall back for radiator/art/bookshelves.  The plan looks like a fantastic amount of space, good luck with everything!

Andersen uses Cardinal's L0E²-272 as standard LoE coating. This is arguably the best coating for your environment for both winter and summer applications. You could use 366 on the west facing windows to block more direct solar gain than 272 in summer, but frankly since you aren't talking about much overall glass area, I think the hassle of using two different coatings on different sides of your home outweighs the benefits of the improved (blocking solar) SHGC from the 366 coating. Heatlock is a surface 4 coating and does drop the condensation rating a fair bit. Andersen doesn't release CR ratings, but Cardinal says it goes from ~53% to ~36% when applying the HeatLock coating. Whenever you plant something new in deer country--even highly resistant plants-- spray it with a good repellent and keep it sprayed for awhile. This helps prevent two things--1.  deer developing a taste for something they usually won't eat, 2. deer trying out your new plant, pulling the unrooted plant out of the ground and dropping it in disgust on the ground where it's usually dead before you find it.

Your plant is wilting because there isn't enough oxygen in the grow medium to allow roots to function normally/ efficiently. You can remove the plant from the pot and set it on some combination of newspapers, rags, paper bags, towels, ..... which will pull the excess water out of the grow medium. After a few hours, return the plant to the pot and then to its cache pot. When you water, you should water at the sink until the entire soil column is wet, then allow the pot the plant is in to drain thoroughly. Tipping the pot at a 45* angle will force an additional measure of any excess water the soil holds out of the drain hole. Compare B to A below to see how this works.  The main pot (one the plant is in) should never be allowed to sit in the effluent that exits the drain hole after you water, that's why you should water at the sink and allow the pot to drain there; or, make sure the pot is up on some type of blocking so salts in the waste water that exits the drain hole have no pathway by which to make their way back into the soil.  Determining appropriate watering intervals is a key element of a good care regimen; and, if you're watering correctly, the plant should be fertilized about every 4th or 5th time you water in winter and every 3rd or 4th time in summer. Foliage-Pro 9-3-6 is an excellent fertilizer for houseplants, and provides a complete nutritional supplementation from a single source. A good way to determine appropriate watering intervals: Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Al

What are the colors in the rest of your home?  What is the style of the rest of your home?  Even if you want the basement a bit different it should still have some connection to the main floor of your home.    You don't want it to feel like belongs to the neighbors house.   Basements can be more fun, brighter, or more dramatic, but not so different that it doesn't relate at all. When I develop a color palette I always start with the colors that must stay.   Are you keeping the tile floor?   Are you keeping the oak trim and doors? If so you need to find colors that are going to work with the colors that must stay. (off topic note: If you are keeping the tile floors I would consider recoloring the grout.   Inexpensive DIY project that can transform a space. ) The second thing I need to know is what colors you love.  Not neutrals - actual colors.   Those colors that are in the art and décor that call your name when you are shopping.   Do you love cornflower blue and peach or wine reds and purples or golds and green? Once I understood the colors that you love and should bring into your home as accents and art and décor I can go about deciding on a neutral color family that works with what must stay and the colors you love. You neutral color families are: pink beige orange beige yellow beige green beige greige (between beige and gray with green undertones) green gray blue gray violet gray taupe (between beige and gray with pink/purple undertones) Once you have the neutral color family selected you can pick out carpet and furniture that are in that color family one darker one lighter or you may want to be brave and pick one of the colors you love for the carpet or the furniture. The color selection for carpet and furniture is limited.   Wall paint comes in any color you can imagine, so I would not be picking a wall color until I found the carpet and furniture that will work with the colors that must stay and the colors that you love. Once you have those picked out you can decide what shade of the neutral (lighter or darker) you want for your walls. This is much like putting together that perfect outfit, but your house will be wearing it every day for years and years.    If you find the perfect blouse (the own that has the colors that work perfectly with your skin tone and your hair and eye color.)   You have to get pants that work with the blouse, you need shoes that work with the pants.  Next you will want to dress it up a bit with jewelry or other accessories and then finally you will pick nail polish and lipstick that works with the whole outfit and looks great with your skin tone. It is the same concept and you seldom build an outfit based on your neighbors favorite shade of lipstick.

Oh please. Millions of structures around the world have been built by non-pros, were never inspected by anyone, and are still standing and serving their purpose a hundred and more years later. Some I've built are still doing just fine at least 50 years later. About 50% of the standing housing stock in our town predates codes and inspectons. Most of them are much better done than the more recent ones. The blanket presumption that codes and inspections are some sort of universal panacea is belied by just going to look at "modern" buildings, built to code and fully inspected, that have failed in storms or that are put together in a way that they will rot and become uninhabitable in a few decades. There are a vast number of things essential to a good building that are not in the code and that no inspector will ever look for. To be clear, I follow (usually well exceed) code requirements and always obtain all permits and inspections that are required. But code requirements are a bare minimum. In the OPs case, I'm guessing s/he is early in the learning process. Clearly you can't size footers without knowing your soil type and condition. The codes don't really help you with that and it is the rare inspector who will be that familiar with local soil conditions in every part of their local jurisdiction; no inspector I've ever worked with would tell you what you need to do-- they look for the specification from the foundation designer who, one hopes, has inspected the site in person and done any testing necessary. Agree completely that a plan off the interweb won't cut it unless it's ridiculously over-spec'd. DIY construction can and very frequently is well designed and well done; many of us DIY because we want a better product than we can get from a pro-- they simply can't afford to spend the amount of time on things that I might. It takes serious study and practice, willingness to rip things out and try again if you don't get it right the first time, and willingness to admit when you really do need a pro (I'm never going to be good enough at plastering walls).

The only way to know if it’s truly soapstone, is to test a sample.  Soapstone is impervious to everything.  It can’t etch or stain.  So, anything left on it, like wine, ketchup, mustard, vinegar, lemon juice, etc., will not leave a mark of any kind. Even if that slab passes the porisity test, you should still test the sample for hardness.  You don’t want a variety that scratches easily.  Many are so soft, a fingernail will leave scratches.  I have a very hard variety, Belvedere, that after 7 years, has no visible scratches.  The only thing that ever scratched it, was a cast iron pan my husband dragged across it, next to the rangetop.  That scratch disappeared after a light sanding, and a drop of mineral oil.

We just had one of the top ten warmest Februaries on record for TN, with multiple days above 70,  weeks of temps 10 to 20 degrees above average, and two days near 80 already in March.   And now we get two nights of mid-to low 20s. At those temperatures there's very little you can do to protect plants that are as far along as the ones in my more than 2 acre garden. My plants think it's April. Things that normally bloom in sequence/consecutively, have bloomed simultaneously this year. It's been glorious, but it's about to be cut short. I have two different varieties of evergreen azaleas already in bloom, the earliest EVER in my garden. Most of my deciduous azaleas (even the species crosses, which should know better!) have buds showing color. No way to cover those thirty or so, 6-8 foot tall shrubs. I have somewhere in the neighborhood of forty hydrangeas. Some are remontant, others once bloomers. They're scattered all over the garden. I couldn't even track them all down in one day, much less remember which is which. Unlike Ann, my fruit trees ARE blooming, at least the peaches, pears and nectarines. They're goners. The apple buds might survive, since they aren't so far along. A good 20-30% of my 250+ roses are climbers/ramblers. They can't be protected in any manner, even from a lesser frost. My pot ghetto I'll cart into the garage. They may be my only hope of a "first flush", lol. The several Japanese maples are in full leaf. Bye-bye. The sixty or so peonies are already 18" to 24" tall...no blooms this year, most likely.  I have hostas that I'll try to cover, but some are already in near full leaf, stupid things. But hostas don't have a lot of secondary leaf buds, so if I don't try to save them, they'll be truly pitiful for a whole season. My non-climbing roses are a whole drama in themselves. New growth all over, a few beginning to throw new canes. Like Ann, I may lose this year's bloom on some of my once bloomers. The R. hugonis buds might survive, and possibly my spin hybrids will still bloom. They're tough, and from much colder climes than here. But I even have a few buds on my teas, a month early. Yikes. I'll cover the least hardy roses that are small enough. But many of the ones that need protection the most, like my teas and chinas, are also the largest and impossible to cover. I'll have to pick and choose. I just can't cover over 175 roses. With a garden as large as mine, you have to take the good years with the bad. Late frosts and wild temperature swings are nothing new here. But this is a hard FREEZE, after an abnormally early and warm Spring. Plus, I've aged about 20 years in the past two. So, I'll do what I can, and try to be sanguine about what I can't save. In the past, right up to this year, I'd be knocking myself out tomorrow and Tuesday covering everything I could cover, with anything I could get my hands on. Years prior my front lawn has looked like a bed linen factory exploded. But I just can't do it any longer. Most of my plants will probably *survive*, but it ain't gonna be pretty (literally). EDIT: Ann, when this crappy weather is over, let me know if you still want a start of Prairie Peace.

someone suggested no social media or smart phones.  In this day and age:  impossible.  Libraries have computers.  Schools have computers.  Friends have computer.  If you want your kid sneaking around and doing things behind your back;  that's an open invitation. When my kids were younger I worked day and night, and was open for any shift day including weekends.  They never had a babysitter while I worked.  My oldest watched them on the days I wasn't there when they got home from school, but only for a couple hours until either my husband or myself came home.  Once my kids were teens, I changed jobs and made sure I was home weekends and evenings.  Someone once said, "why do you make sure you're home then?  They're teens!  They can take care of themselves!"  Uhm......... NO.  NO they can't.  A two year old doesn't need the same care a 13 year old does.  Teens are too impressionable and that's when they need their parents home the most!  We had our first computer and I made sure that I could always see what they were doing online.  I wasn't reading over their shoulder, but they knew that if I walked by and glanced at the monitor and they covered the screen, or changed browswers quickly, they weren't allowed on it anymore.  I had the mother board under lock and key when we weren't home.  And my youngest tried EVERYTHING to jimmy the lock.  ;)  As parents, it's our responsibility to shape our children and if they've been misinformed about anything, it's our job to educate them. I made sure my kids could talk to us about anything and I do mean ANYTHING.  They didn't take sex-ed in school:  I taught them.  While my kids aren't perfect and my youngest gave me more grey hairs than I like to admit, I think we did a pretty good job with our kids.

Hello Dale, "That said, how far above the seed starting tray and the ensuing seedlings should my light be?" The primary guideline here is you don't want to overheat or burn your seedlings with exposure to heat from the hot T5HO bulbs. HO stands for High Output and that means the bulbs are hot. I would say your T5HO bulbs should be at least a foot above the seedlings. But you can use your hand as a temperature sensor and tell if your T5HO bulbs are too close. There is a lot to know about gardening under lights. I started about 18 years ago when the "in" fluorescent bulbs were T8s, and you got enough light from them by overdriving them. I still use overdriven T8s because I have a significant investment in them. I suggest you get one or more books on the subject of Gardening Under Lights (that is a clickable link) My favorite book on the subject is the one by Leslie Halleck. But it doesn't hurt to have several books on the subject. One of my hobbies is breeding zinnias and my old overdriven T8 fluorescent lights let me pursue my hobby during the Winter. Grading and retaining walls are complicated topics, so please forgive my essay here. (TL;DR: you're probably fine, but don't take my word for it.) Without seeing the walls and the slopes first-hand, it's very difficult to tell what the existing situation is and what, if anything, should be done. Take any advice you get here—including mine—with a large helping of salt; and always verify it with a licensed professional (landscape contractor, general contractor, engineer, landscape architect) on-site. To my eye, there's probably not much risk of a significant landslide around the walls in your photo. There just isn't a lot of mass behind them; I would be more concerned about the hillside between the hedge at the top and the fence at the bottom. The slope of the upper terrace (behind the top wall) looks fairly gentle, and the distance between the top and bottom walls looks relatively short although the slope is steeper. The walls appear to be constructed of interlocking concrete blocks, which are designed to lean back into the hillside for structural stability when stacked into courses like this. Yes, the walls should have been backfilled with crushed aggregate ("drain rock") wrapped in filter fabric; if you are sure this wasn't done, you could excavate horizontally a foot or so back from the wall, and vertically down to the footing. Installation methods vary but generally you'll want 6-12" of topsoil and mulch at the top of the wall, then aggregate down to the level of the ground at the foot of the wall. A drain pipe at the lowest point won't hurt, assuming you have someplace even lower for it to drain away to (where the outfall won't cause erosion, which would destablize the slope); but some manufacturers say this is optional for walls less than 4' tall. A soils engineer could give you insights into how to handle the drainage given the characteristics of your particular soil. If you were going to add drainage to only one wall, I would suggest the lower wall, because I agree the grading between the top and bottom walls looks a bit aggressive. That slope appears to be around 1:1 (one foot of horizontal for every foot of vertical, or a 45° angle); generally steeper than 2:1 (two horizontal for every one vertical, or a 27° angle) is discouraged. That said, although the plantings look fairly new, I'm guessing the walls have been there for many years, and if the fill between them hasn't moved yet, it may be stable enough that no intervention is needed. Your hillside will always start at point A and end at point B, no matter how you regrade it. If you remove the top wall, the bottom wall would probably need to become taller, for which your town might require engineering plans and a construction permit. Removing soil between the top and bottom of the hillside is much more complicated than it sounds, because at some point your resculpted hill would have to connect back to the land around it, so then you might need retaining walls on the sides and/or the top. This is expensive, complicated, expensive, unattractive, and also costs a lot of money, so I wouldn't recommend it. Assuming the walls were properly constructed and the backfill is stable, the best thing you can do is maximize the plantings behind the walls and minimize the amount of water you apply. I don't know where in California you live, or what your sun exposure there is, but you could ask a local nursery to recommend noninvasive groundcovers (no Japanese honeysuckle, please!) that will not only shield the soil but also root as it spreads to prevent erosion. The creeping rosemary that's planted there now won't do this. Consider Salvia leucophylla, Mahonia repens, Symphoricarpos albus, Arctostaphylos uva-ursi, and other California native plants that put down deep roots. A web search for "California native groundcover for erosion control" will generate more ideas, like this page from the Theodore Payne Foundation. Nothing here should be taken as advice, only information. Recognize that sometimes the fastest way to destablize a slope is to start trying to stabilize it. Please proceed with all due caution. Good luck!

" 2) The inside and outside of eggs do too.  " That's the wrong point - yes, there's more external contamination from poor husbandry, but not the inside of the freshly laid egg.  The cuticle (or "bloom") is the layer of the shell that closes the pores of the shell to keep out external infection.  Using a dry wipe to lightly remove dirt or feces should not affect the cuticle (if you have backyard chickens), but the US law requires cleaning and sanitizing of any egg to be sold......that destroys the protective cuticle, and therefore refrigeration is required. In the EU, for example, Grade A eggs (all retail eggs) must not be cleaned, preserved, or refrigerated (below 5C) before purchase. Grade B eggs are used in food production, not retail sales.  https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/summary/rules-on-marketing-standards-for-eggs.html

Kevin, "Arid" is not nearly as simple as you imply. Science (regenerative agriculture) has shown that planting cover crops, especially legumes or other nitrogen fixing species, increases the organic content of the soil. That allows the rain that does fall to filter into the ground more efficiently, and that water is then held in the soil by the organic matter. So, even with no more rain than is typical for the area, there is more moisture available for subsequent crops or trees to grow. Over time, as more organic matter is added and as perennial plants are established, the water-holding capacity of the soil increases even more, so the "arid" land becomes productive. No volcanic eruption required. Martha

The Miele T1 does not have a variable speed compressor.  The compressor is on or off.  As the laundry gets dryer there is less moisture to absorb the heat from the refrigeration cycle.  To keep the main re-heat coil at the proper temperature some of the refrigerant is diverted to the small radiator on the right side of the dryer. As stated above there is a variable speed van that blows over this radiator to remove the excess heat from the refrigerant.  This excess heat makes its way out of the dryer and into the room.  It is a small amount of heat.  Less than a freezer or refrigerator which moves all of the heat from the inside to the room. This is actually a very good thing as it keeps the air temperature inside the dryer consistent as the laundery approaches dry.  If the dryer did not have this then the laundry would get hotter as it gets dry.  Which is exactly what happens in a normal vented and most condenser dryers. The other option would be to use a variable speed scroll compressor.  These are significantly more expensive.  Reliable ones, like a copeland scroll compressor used in HVAC equipment, are not readily available in small sizes like what is used in a residential dryer.  Miele’s solution is more than any other manufacturer does.

Hi, Paul, Reducing the setpoint temperature reduces the amount of heat loss from a home (and the amount of heat required to be transferred by the heat pump) in winter.  However, the energy savings is muted by your investment in a well-insulated home with low air infiltration.  That's a nice problem to have.   One potential issue, which others have referred to, is when the setpoint temperature is increased in the morning.  If the setpoint and indoor temperatures differ by 2 F or more, your back-up heat will likely come on.  For a heat pump, that's usually electric resistance (strip) heaters which are more expensive to operate.  To avoid triggering the back up heat, you'd need your Ecobee thermostat to gradually increase the setpoint while you sleep to avoid the back-up heat from coming on.  It may or may not be able to do that. On a separate, but related note, your low air infiltration rate requires that you install a fresh air ventilation system to maintain indoor air quality.  You should have an HRV or ERV installed which supplies fresh air to your home.  If you don't I suggest you make that a priority.

I lived for several years in Australia's capital city, Canberra.  Canberra is an entirely planned city, selected in 1908 as the site of the national capital as a compromise between the competing cities of Sydney and Melbourne. It was built (on what was once cow pasture) according to the winning plan in an international design competition held in 1912..  The winning architect, an American named Walter Burley Griffin, envisaged a series of small villages aligned to the topography of the location,  linked to each other, but respecting the hills and green spaces of the area in which the city was located.  At some point, an artificial lake was added to the plan - Lake Burley Griffin, of course. The city has a core, but then a series of suburbs built around the core, each with its own shopping center at its heart, and green space separating one suburb from the next.  If you live in Canberra, you get used to driving on major roads between the suburbs and the city, and between each of the suburbs, but then circular roads within the suburb, radiating out from the core shopping center.  Once you're in your own suburb, you can pretty much walk or take a very short drive to local supermarkets and other facilities, while being within a 15 or 20 minute drive of the city center. These days, Canberra is a city of almost 400,000, but as it has expanded, the city planners have stuck to Burley Griffin's original vision, individual suburbs with a core shopping center and housing radiation off that core.  And plenty of green space between each suburb.  It's a pretty interesting example of a genuine 15 minute city.

Consuming daffodils is toxic. But they have safely been used in perfume making for a long time. The OP is going to be doing a cold fat extraction method to get the scent for perfume. A fast and dirty version is steeping lavender blossoms in a body oil till it's scented. What the OP is planning is a more complex method that results in a high quality scented fat when done right. Organic chemicals are used in organic farming. Pesticides, herbicides, fertilizers. I understand that some folks are not OK with synthetic chemicals and want organic ones. But don't fool yourself into thinking they are chemical free. Especially from a commercial farmer, all of them have to use some form of chemicals. There are over a dozen goodly narcissus noted for fragrance suitable in perfume making. I suggest the OP figures out which ones they want to start with and go from there. Look for sellers that have those varieties and are organic. Or can answer the questions of what they use on their farms. Keep an eye out for a local friend that might need help dividing an organic patch or two. If there are local plant sales, ask the vendors how they grow. In most jurisdictions, the appropriate hood for a 48" range needs to be around 1200 CFM, give or take. The national building code, which is adopted by most states/counties/cities, requires a makeup air system for anything over 400 CFM. I have a 36" rangetop that requires a 600 CFM hood. My makeup air system is passive and is an 8" duct that dumps air into our mechanical room. 1200 CFM requires active makeup air system with blowers, and maybe a heater depending on where you live. If you price it out at fantech (one of the suppliers of such systems) you will see how it ends up there, and that's just for parts. If you are doing a renovation you also have to find room for the duct for your hood which may be 10". If you're on an exterior wall this is manageable, but if not it may be challenging. I originally wanted a 48" range as well, until I went through the process of figuring out the total cost. Of course you could always buy an insufficient hood I suppose. In your case I would buy a 36" induction cooktop and a double wall oven placed to the right of the cooktop.

ORB is a living finish. The green you see is actually the protector of the metals. ( copper and tin ) You can get it off with a lot of work. It's going to return: ) "If your oil-rubbed bronze faucet is turning green, it is due to a chemical reaction,  as described by Make It From Metal. The copper in the faucet has  reacted with carbon dioxide, water and oxygen in the air. Bronze is  actually made from 88 percent copper and 12 percent tin, so this  reaction is not that surprising. "Even if it's been recently installed, a bronze faucet can pick up the green patina associated with age fairly quickly. Bronze is a metal alloy. This means that rather than being a naturally occurring metal, it's comprised of predominantly copper, with a small percentage of tin. These two metals, as it is known from looking at the Statue of Liberty and many old roofs, turns a shade of minty green after exposure to the elements. It's patina. Hastened by water, and then oxidation with exposure to the air Mix 2 tablespoons of baking soda and enough lemon juice to form a paste, roughly the same consistency as toothpaste. Spread the paste evenly over the oil rubbed brass faucet turning green. Rub the mixture into the brass with a soft cloth, taking care to go over the very stained or very green parts with even more effort. After really working the paste into the faucet, wipe it off with a soft cloth. Rinse the faucet thoroughly with warm water and dry it completely. If a patina is still visible, repeat the process until it is clean and shiny."

This article is interesting. Profile A significant difference between 2PAC and laminate is when it comes to profiling. A 2PAC kitchen allows you to add character with different levels of profiling and routing, helping you achieve a ‘Hamptons’ style kitchen. Whereas laminate will always be a flat surface, sometimes with a slight texture if a woodgrain material has been selected. Thermo-laminated vinyl is the only product that can help you achieve a ‘Hamptons’ profiled kitchen using laminate. This product sits roughly in the middle of the price spectrum and does come with disadvantages so it is a lesser used product. A downside to thermo-laminate is that it does not withstand high-heat temperatures in certain parts of the kitchen and as such will bubble and melt.

. Price There is no doubt that 2PAC is a significantly pricier option than a laminate flat pack kitchen. 2PAC costs roughly 40% more than your standard laminate finish. This price is again markedly increased when it comes to selecting 2PAC cabinetry that is profiled in any way. The total price of cabinetry will increase parallel to the amount of routing required for a Hamptons style finish. As a result, a profiled 2PAC kitchen may cost double the budget as a laminate equivalent of the same size of kitchen. While laminate is certainly the most cost effective choice of kitchen material and you are not deprived of colours and finishes, 2PAC cabinetry allows you to have more design control over the colour and profiling of your kitchen. If you are looking for a Hamptons style kitchen, 2PAC will almost always be your only option. However, if you are looking for a flat surfaced kitchen and comparing between the two options – Laminate is a great way to reduce the overall cost of your Kitchen.

Can you post photos? Without seeing the situation and being able to visually assess the damage, all we can offer is speculation :-) Just by description, it sounds like your tree may have heart rot. Suggestions to cement or mortar this hole to keep any  water out are no longer advised (more harm than help) but a dedicated landscaping spray foam applied after a thorough cleaning out and drying can delay the decline. We moved to OKC in 2015 & I got my first real experience with clay soil. First off, clay isn't the horrible monster everyone acts like it is. Clay is normally super high in nutrients, you just have to get it to a usable form. Right now, I'd give anything for a truck load of clay soil, I prefer it over this sandbox of a yard I have now. Most soil particles are like wadded up pieces of paper. Piled together, they still have little pockets of air between them. Clay is more like a ream of paper. The particles are flat sheets, so they stick together & don't allow air between them. So water seeps in but doesn't evaporate like it does in regular soil, and air can't get to the roots. It took me about 3 years to get it to moderately usable, but I'm cheap, broke & lazy so you might be able to get it done faster with a little more effort. That means organic matter, & as much of it as possible. Dump all your kitchen scraps into the bed, cover with soil, for composting in place. Contact coffee shops & ask for their spent coffee grounds. The grounds themselves aren't as helpful as some claim, but the grit helps break the clay particles up which is what you're really looking for. Keep a look out for bagged leaves on the side of the road, take them home & chop them up, then use as mulch. Once spring comes, turn them into the soil to help break up the particles. Same with grass clippings, but be aware some homeowners put herbicides & pesticides on their grass which will then be transferred into your soil. If you know anyone with horses, cows, chickens, rabbits, etc, ask for manure. Just be careful because hay is typically sprayed with herbicides that will then be in your soil. I've known several who lost entire gardens to it & it can take years to fix.

Organic matter is always good, but it really depends on what you want to do with the soil, if you want a lawn, I think sod is best if you can afford it.  If I were wanting a lawn as quick as possible, I would plant rye grass.  I live in zone 7 and now have new rye grass up to about 2.5 to 3 inches tall, it was planted about 15 or 20 days ago.  This is  not a great time to start seeds because they germinate and grow slow in cold weather. I sorta go by the rule  " plant a $5.00 plant in a $20.00 hole".  The best money spent is in the hole, not in the plant.

"  I sorta go by the rule " plant a $5.00 plant in a $20.00 hole". The best money spent is in the hole, not in the plant. " Not when you are dealing with a clay based soil!! In fact, amending individual planting holes in any type of soil has long been disproven to be a beneficial practice when planting virtually anything anywhere but that's fodder for another discussion. When dealing with a clay soil it is even more of an issue as the planting hole in clay acts essentially as a bucket or bathtub, holding in the moisture retentive enriched soil and preventing free drainage. The plant roots just sit in overly saturated, slowly draining soil and are subject to rot.....very few plants can survive or even tolerate root rots. The Bathtub Effect The Myth of Amending Planting Holes

I have 3 gardens and I like a soil test before I start amending them.  This is my second garden and as you can see it is in pretty good shape.  This test was taken almost 9 years ago, and I expect the garden is still in good shape because I can grow about anything I want to.  I pretty much judge the soil by the way the plants look and respond. My wildlife garden is much like this test, but I cant find the test sheet on it, it is a little low in areas where this test shows " above optimum", and the PH was lower, adding a little lime seemed to fix the PH, the plants look good but no other soil test was taken.  I think it is always better to work the soil a little before planting.  I planted 11 food plots for wildlife this fall, the last one was about an acre of rye grass, which I did not cover. Where do you live?  Zone 7 only tells you what not to plant for winter survival.  It says nothing about your climate or soils.  Please be specific.  Saying you live in California is similarly not helpful.  If you live in Reno, say Reno. Roots are the best thing for clay soil.  Summer grasses and winter grasses are helpful.  I would go on to suggest that you only use organic fertilizer until the soil softens up for you. Have you tried the jar test to see how much clay you have?  There are salt imbalances which mimic clay, and the solution for one is not the solution for the other. Jar Test: take a straight sided jar (olive jars are perfect), and fill it half full with soil.  Use a ruler to measure how much soil you have.  Let's say you have 6 inches.  Fill the jar with water and a small squirt of shampoo or dish soap.  Cap the jar and shake it until all the clods are broken up/dissolved in the water.  Set the jar down and get your ruler ready.  After 1 minute goes by, take a picture of the jar with the ruler next to it.  What happens is some of the soil settles within a minute.  That would be the sand and grit.  Then wait 1 hour and take another picture.  After an hour you should have a distinct layer of silt on top of the sand/grit.  On top of that you should have cloudy brown water which is too cloudy to see through.  After 1 day, take another picture with the ruler.  It takes a day or more for the clay to settle on top of the silt.  If you have a layer and the water on top is very clear, then the test is over.  If the water on top is still cloudy, then there is more clay suspended in the water. After watching this forum for 20 years, what most people find is they don't have clay soil.  What they need to do next is a soil test which goes into the salts (sodium, calcium, magnesium, and potassium).  Excessive magnesium can cause moisture retention in any type of soil causing it to act like clay.
