Tip the pot on its side. Poke a hole up through the drain hole. Fold a strand from a rayon mop head over the blade of a straight slot screwdriver and push one end of the mop strand up into the grow medium through the drain hole. After watering, make sure the mop strand is either hanging several inches below the pot bottom or is resting directly on top of whatever soil the pot is resting on. This trick increases gravitational flow potential because it increases the ht of the soil column. One way to phrase it is, it tricks water into acting as though the pot is deeper than it is. As water moves down the wick is either a) pushed off the end of the wick by the weight of water from above, or b) Water moving down the wick is absorbed into the soil below, pulling additional water into the earth by the greater capillary draw of the soil below the pot. .... should take about 5 minutes to set up.   Rayon mop strand to the right of the plastic bag.     Compare E to A. If you can manage a hole through the bottom at the sidewall, tipping the pot (see B) with the drain hole at the pot's lowest point increases effectiveness. A true siphon won't work unless you have a way of keeping it primed or are willing to prime it for each use ..... and yes, there are one-way squeeze valves you can use as a priming mechanism, but why bother when you can accomplish the same end, passively. As soon as the siphon tube draws enough air to fill the tube in the pot to the ht where water would start moving downward instead of upward, you no longer have a siphon ..... at least not one that will siphon a liquid. Bill, YES, the ocean is a BIG factor.  If the storms ride up the coast either near the coast, or west of the coast, this drags in mild air and the result will be RAIN.  If the lows move east and up the coast offshore, then, this drags in cold, interior air and there is snow at the coast. It's actually a well-documented phenomenon.  Historically, the biggest coastal snowstorms occur when the storms pass east of the the benchmark, 40 N./70 West.  The reason these storms explode is that you have a strong dynamic between the cold inland air, PLUS the warm, gulf stream which rides up the coast. Those can be like snow hurricanes, with blinding snow, wind, and snow thunder. Ocean storms/nor'easters are not the only contributors to local snow, but they are the most potent. @Izzyaz: I think there may be some confusion about "open" and "sealed" burners. NXR's have always come with sealed burners.  What I suspect you meant was that your older NXR has dual-stacked (two ring) Isphording burners that look like this:  IIRC, NXR is currently calling this design "sealed tower burners."  FWIW, there were threads here a decade or so ago that confirmed these were the same dual-ring Isphording burners used by Wolf and DCS for their ranges, and they all definitely are sealed burners . We've had several threads over the last decade about ways to solve the repeated clicking igniter problem with this dual-stacked burners for NXR and Wolf ranges. Trouble is, the various fixes work in some cases but not others. If you've tried those fixes and found they didn't solve the random clicking problem, you certainly have my sympathy. Even a decade ago, some posters were reporting that the fixes didn't work or worked only temporarily and that they were moving on to other brands of stove. But, going back to your main question: are the flat-capped burner models less prone to random clicking than the dual-stacked burners?  I'm afraid I can't offer any direct experience (my 12 y.o. NXR is fine as the fixes worked for me)  but can suggest you also try including the Thor Kitchen and Kucht brands in your searches. All three brands' stoves come from the same production lines at Hyxxion corporation factories in China and all three use the same components.  Thor and Kucht have been offering the flat-capped burner models longer than NXR has, so there may be more chance of finding reports of problems if there are any to be found.

>>>" When I started mixing them up when I pull them off to clean them, I  always have a few that work great.  Just curious if that’s something you  do? "<<< I tried it for diagnostic purposes which basically ruled out deformed burners in my case. The repeated clicking can be caused by one (or more) of several different things.  What seems to mostly work for me is reaming out the burner's gas line venturis/nozzles with fine wire welding tip cleaners (aka "drills") and running pipe cleaners through the flame ports on the brass burners.  Different things seem to work differently for different folks.  I'm recalling a thread a couple years or so ago where some folks have resorted to wiring in a switch that lets them control power to the sparking module once the burners are lit. Flick the switch to on when they want to light a burner then cut the power so the module doesn't spark once a burner is going.  Some folks moved on to other brands. Still others haven't run into the problem.

And, FWIW, on the subject of " all the new models regardless of brand have moved on to these [flat-cap] burners," NXR is now offering different lines through different marketing channels. For example, the NXR "Entree" models offered through Home Depot, the "LS" models offered through Lowe's, and "Culinary" models offered through AJ Madison  all seem to come with the flat capped burners. The "Professional" models sold through Costco, AJ Madison and restaurant supply houses like Dvorson's still come with the "tower" (dual stacked) sealed burners.

" I usually plant pointy-end down, but you're right, planting them flat  should be OK. But you're saying that pushing up through more soil better  removes the seed coats?" I think that anything which speeds germination results in more issues with clinging seed coats. I've observed this with cucurbits planted pointy-end down; those planted flat had little to no problem. This was most noticeable with bitter melon & other gourds. This problem was also noticeable with tomatoes germinated at high temperatures (about 85 F.) When I germinate them at 70-75 F., I see far fewer helmets. I've also seen this in okra, which germinates in 3-4 days when started in pots (with A LOT of helmets) and germinates in 6-7 days in-ground, with few helmets. I think that in both cases, the extra time in moist soil before emergence helps to both soften the seed coat, and allow the cotyledons more time to break free. Old seed tends to have more clinging seed coats too, regardless of how they are planted.

Best to repot immediately before the tree's spring push gets underway. If the soil/root mass crumbles when you depot the plant, there is no pressing need to do a full repot (includes bare-rooting and root pruning along with a change of soil). If the soil/root mass comes away from the pot intact, root congestion will be taking a toll on growth/development rate, vitality, the tree's ability to defend itself, and likely eye appeal if that's a consideration, so a full repot would be a notably beneficial. The tree is likely beyond the state of being truly dormant and has passed into quiescence, a state of quiet rest during which the tree is fully capable of growing but cold temperatures act to suppress bud activity. Once the tree has experienced warmth above about about 45* for several consecutive days and growth begins, the ability to withstand freezing temperatures will be significantly reduced, meaning the plant will need protection from frost. It's best not to wait that long to do any repotting. Al

For safe troubleshooting, if one hot leg trips, it is desirable that both legs be in a safe mode with both breakers tripped. A common application of such a circuit is an underwired cottage/cabin where a 12/3 line is run to a kitchen counter outlet, the common hot tab on the receptacle is broken off separating the outlets, and each receptacle is on its own breaker feed. One now has two 20A circuits available in the kitchen. If troubleshooting such a receptacle, one desires that both hot legs be unpowered when working inside the box. @rwiegand The reason I posed the question is I'm trying to understand the wiring in our (new to us) house and had noticed these 2 circuits using 14/3 and, as HU-867564120 suggests, the 2 hots are opposite phases.  I've never seen 3 wire used for this before, so that led me to the current question.  I would NOT want to wire like this.  I also would not want to use 14 gauge wire on a 20amp breaker.  And I would not want to have 14 gauge wire going to kitchen utility circuits.  This house is just full of code violations.  It will take me years to fix them all (since I have a wife and a day job).

An MWBC is a completely normal, legal. safe, and efficient way to run wiring. 14 ga with a 20 A breaker certainly isn't and will be well undersized for a kitchen. Given the amperage requirements of many kitchen appliances you're probably going to want to properly re-wire the kitchen. Depending on what else you have you can re-use those 14 ga 15A circuits for lighting, dishwasher, disposal, perhaps a range hood or 120V supply to a gas range. You're going to want at least two 20 circuies for countertop appliances, one for the fridge, and one for the microwave. The fridge is the only one of those I would definitely not put on a MWBC. Another advantage is that if you have need for a 240 V outlet (eg for your serious espresso machine) that's easy to add when using MWBCs. It also makes it easy if you want to split a duplex outlet or four-plex outlet box into two circuits for two high amperage appliances fed from the same outlet box.

I agree with acm regarding the maintenance.  But there's a little more to it with the actual sheen.  It helps to know the exact brand and which line of paint.  For example - Benjamin Moore Chantilly Lace in their Regal line or the Scuff X line?  (or ??) As far as the sheen for the ceiling - flat is most often used because of (1) it doesn't reflect the light as much, and (2) flat hides imperfections better.  Unless you pay extra, drywalled ceilings aren't perfect. We recently finished a 2500 sq ft remodel of our lower level (with kitchenette).  We used all BM paint - BM Muresco Ceiling (flat); BM Scuff X Matte for the walls; BM Scuff X Eggshell for the closets; and BM Scuff X Satin for the trim.  (We have 15 grandchildren.)  We're very happy with the paint quality. To know how the sheens compare, even in the same brand, you will have to read the TDS sheets.  For example -Scuff X Matte has slightly more sheen than BM Aura Matte. Another note, if you're painting over stained trim, sanding and priming are necessary for the best adhesion and wear.  Insul X Stix is a great primer. ETA:  Sometimes here on Houzz, but mostly on a few other painting blogs I follow, people often mention that Sherwin Williams paint has less sheen when compared to other paint - for example, SW semi-gloss is closer to Benjamin Moore's satin.  Best way is read the TDS and get the gloss level as a percentage.

Generally fertilizer doesn't do much during the winter.  The time for the boost was late last fall, after your lawn stopped growing, but before the first hard freeze. At this point, if you did nothing over the winter, you can fertilize early with an organic.  Had you done the boost last fall, then the lawn should not need more fertilizer until May or late May. You can save money by using the raw materials that go into commercially bagged organic fertilizers.  Corn meal, alfalfa meal or pellets, soybean meal, and/or cottonseed meal should be available in 50# bags at your local feed store for much less than buying commercially bagged materials.  The application rate is 15 to 20 pounds per 1,000 square feet. The animals in your yard may or, more likely, may not be attracted to these feed materials.  Certainly these materials are feed to animals in captivity, but the reason is there is usually not enough fresh forage available to animals in captivity.  What I have seen most often is birds attracted after applying corn meal.  Even when I lived in the country with several species of deer and antelope roaming freely, no animals seemed to be overly attracted to my lawn after fertilizing.  My neighbors feed deer corn to the deer, but those same deer were not attracted to the corn meal in my lawn. Do these materials actually work?  Here's a picture posted here back in 2011 by mrmumbles.  He dropped a handful of alfalfa pellets onto his zoysia lawn in mid May and took the picture in mid June.   Even though the pic is low quality, it is easy to see the improved color, density, and growth a month after fertilizing.

I can buy a cu yard of mushroom compost here for $40, 32 pound sterling, so a bag of organic fertilizer for 38 pounds seems exorbitantly expensive. For some scope 2 cu yards of mushroom compost will fill an 8 foot long pickup truck. I don't know how big your lawn is but I'd suggest you spread an inch, 25mm, of mushroom compost over the entire lawn. It would be best to do this early in the season or in fall when the lawn is growing very well. The fact that the lawn is growing well means the black manure will be hidden by the growing lawn in a couple of weeks. I did this in late March here for 3 feet out beyond a fenced bed around my fruit trees.

Compost is fine if you can get a deal on it.  I don't have a truck so I have to have it delivered for an additional $60.  Total cost of compost, 2 yards, would be $40 x 2 + $60 = $140.  Normally if I wanted compost really badly I would spread 1/4-inch everywhere.  Two yards covers about 2000 square feet or 200 square meters (roughly).  So the cost for 2 yards of compost is $140/2 (thousand) or $70 per thousand square feet.  If I use alfalfa pellets, those cost me $20 for 50 pounds (20 kilos) at the feed store and I can carry that home easily.  Application rate is 15 to 20 pounds per 1,000 square feet, which covers 2,500 feet.  Cost for organic fertilizer is $20/2.5(thousand) = $8 per thousand square feet. Furthermore, 1 inch of compost over a lawn will smother the grass leaving one full season behind on growing grass.  But if you did use an inch, then the cost would be more like $280 per thousand square feet.

" Furthermore, 1 inch of compost over a lawn will smother the grass leaving one full season behind on growing grass. " I show a picture of one of the areas I spread an inch of mushroom compost over to provide organic fertilizer for the apple tree. I went out 3 feet all the way around the tree. That was on March 28th.  It's now June 5th. I would say that rather than losing a season of grass growing that the black mushroom compost warmed up the soil and the grass grew before the rest of the lawn. It hasn't rained in a couple of weeks so the grass needs some water. We had a lot of calculations to prove that using mushroom compost is much more expensive; however the mushroom compost will improve a lawn AND the soil for at least 5 years. The soil amendment is not scrap that runs up the cost of the improvement. It's what's needed to improve a lawn between applications of fertilizer.

text: Would be helpful to know where you live, and whether deer are present.  When you're in a milder climate, you may want to gravitate to using lots of evergreen shrubs for year-round good looks. If no deer, Indian Hawthorn is tough and loves the heat.  Also Wheeler's Dwarf Pittosporum makes a good low growing mounded shrub that can take the heat. Also dwarf Loropetalum Crimson Fire™ or Purple Daydream™ (or any of the many dwarfs with reddish foliage and blooms), Carissa holly, Ilex cornuta 'Mashahi's Gold', Yucca filamentosa 'Color Guard', Dwarf Yaupon holly would be just a few other choices. I'd visit a local good nursery and give them your parameters.  When you say 'color', you may be thinking of flowers. But flowers are fleeting. Don't dismiss shrubs with contrasting foliage such as variegated, reddish, or golden foliage to add year-round appeal.

Photosynthesis is a process during which the plant uses CO2 from the air and water from the soil along with little electromagnetic bundles from the sun (photons) to produce the plant's true food - glucose, with oxygen as a byproduct.  Respiration can be said to be the opposite of photosynthesis, as it uses oxygen to burn/oxidize the sugar to produce the energy plants need to drive their systems and grow, with carbon dioxide and water as byproducts. Photosynthesis: 6CO2 + 6H2O –––> C6H12O6 + 6O2 Respiration:    C6H12O6 + 6O2 –––> 6CO2 + 6H2O Warm indoor temperatures and low humidity increase your plant's rate of respiration significantly, while short days and less intense light levels decrease the plant's ability to carry on photosynthesis, which we already know is the source of the plant's true food. Whenever a plant is using more energy during the respiration phase than it makes during photosynthesis, it is in serious trouble because the disparity between energy production and energy use must be rectified by calling on the plant's energy reserves, which are finite in the same sense that the reserve power in a battery is finite and eventually depleted when called on, which always results in death of the organism unless conditions change enough that the plant is able to make more food/energy than it uses. The chill of winter slows energy consumption dramatically, which means almost no energy is required to ensure the plant remains viable. In spring, the plant reawakens as temperatures move to the mid-40s, with almost all of the energy it had at the end of autumn. Ideally, the plant would be kept at temperatures between 32-42*F, and watered occasionally as required to keep the root/soil mass from drying completely. Al

Ingrid, what I'm thinking is that in the future we're all going to have less wiggle room to try plants that are marginal for our conditions.  I certainly understand your desire to have an oasis of flowering beauty and freshness, and hope that you may be able to create it, though it will be a struggle.  As climate change accelerates, swings from the average will become greater:  more rain when it rains, longer droughts when it's dry; lower lows, higher highs.  All this will increase risks to plants that are less well-adapted to the conditions they're growing in. I have marble fireplace surround ( polished Cararra) and I  have marble top night  stands ( polished Crema Marfil) I have  one tiny etch on one nightstand that is barely visible unless you tilt your head. Marbles have Different  porosity rates.  If it is a dense marble, and sealed, stains are not an issue.. if the marble is honed, etching is not an issue, as it technically is already etched, so any new etches blend right in and are nit noticeable. I think a lot of generalizations are made about marble, when in fact, they all behave a bit different.  knowing about the particular  type of marble that is in the house and proper treatment of it, it really is fine. if you love the house, I would not discount it because of marble. its actually an asset to have a high quality material in a home. I asked a similar question recently and have since done more research, so this is my view. In my experience, mid-grade semi-custom cabinets, uninstalled, cost a lot more than true custom made-from-scratch cabinets from established, larger shops -- installed.  So for my kitchen, semi-custom cabinetry from Candlelight or TeddWood would be about $48k without installation.  Those are midrange lines.  While both have plenty of options, there's an upcharge for custom colors and I'd have to have many of the details (like brackets, open shelving, etc.) done separately, so add another $5-10k.  And then what - $5-10k for install?  So it's really $60-70k? My initial bid for all custom for the same kitchen was $30k, but that bid fell through.  New bids from very well-known, high-end makers in my high-end (Fairfield County, CT) area were all about $50k, installed.  And that was everything from soup to nuts, including any color I want and all the details my architect designed.  To me it's a no-brainer. People here will correctly tell you that you need to do research on the cabinetmaker and ask a lot of questions about what "custom" means to them, how cabinets are finished, etc. to determine the quality.  I'd argue you should ask most of the same questions when ordering semi-custom too.  The only other explanation I've heard for paying more for semi-custom is that these are established companies that will honor warranties if something goes wrong.  While that is a difference from a guy in a garage, a real established cabinetmaker will do the same, except you're dealing with someone down the street instead of in Pennsylvania or whatever. I sense on Houzz a skepticism of local cabinetmakers by (1) kitchen designers/store owners, who generally sell stock and semi-custom cabinetry for a living so have a vested interest and (2) homeowners who got burned looking for a super low price without doing their due diligence and then were shocked, shocked! when the quality wasn't great.

The value that someone creates for you is separate from the profit they make from doing it.  I could give a thousand examples of people who are well paid because they create value and it doesn't really matter to you unless you could create that same value. So now to insurance.  Because insurance adds administrative and sales costs to spreading risk it will always look bad in the aggregate.  I have never had a home owner's claim, but I still have insurance.  Aside from my annual physical and a colonoscopy, I have only seen my doctor half a dozen times since I was 18... so I have wasted money on health insurance too.  However, my wife has managed to beat cancer twice in that time and for her medical insurance was a godsend... it is the only reason we have retirement savings now. Which is the point of insurance.  It is some payment today to guard against catastrophic loss that probably isn't going to happen. Title insurance is very rarely needed, but it is also incredibly cheap when you do a simultaneous issue.  If your simultaneous issue price is $2,500 then that means the property value is several million.  Which means that you are talking about a small amount of a single payment to have title insurance.  For a half-million dollar home title insurance will be $600 - $800 in my area.  That is adjusted some by state, but it isn't going to adjust that much. Now if you are being quoted a non-simultaneous issue price then you really need to talk to someone about getting simultaneous issue.  The two largest title insurers only charge $100 and $200 flat fee for simultaneous issue and then you are only paying the marginal amount plus the flat fee.  Which, again, is just not much money. The HUGE drawback to a conventional fireplace is that they draw their combustion from the house. You may be heating one area but other areas are being cooled/chilled from the outside air being sucked through leaks. Go with a direct vent sealed combustion gas insert.  A direct vent gas appliance is a closed combustion system, sealed off from the living environment of your home. Outside air flows though a sealed pipe, directly to the burner. Exhaust gas flows back outdoors through a separate sealed pipe. There are two types of Direct Vent systems; Coaxial and Colinear. These types of units can really heat a house! So good are they that I have had to modify my return air ductwork to pull the room heat out (to keep that room tolerable) and get it back to the furnace blower to circulate around the house. I have two such Jotul units, a gas fireplace (Accadia GZ550) and a free-standing gas stove (Sebago GF400). Caution: a quality product will cost substantial $$. RPM stands for revolutions pre minute. This indicates how fast the blower motor is spinning to push the air flow. The blower is a variable speed motor. Varying the speed of the motor will vary the air flow. CFM stands for cubic feet per minutes. This is the volume of air moving through the furnace at the output of the blower. You thermostat has a default 90 second blower off delay. When the thermostat stops calling for heat, the blower with continue to run for 90 seconds to push out the remaining warm air. When the thermostat is satisfied I assume the capacity will go to 0% and eventually the RPM and CFM will go to zero. There is probably a time lag when the thermostat actually reports the data to the display screen. You will probably hear the furnace become quiet before all values go to zero. The static pressure shows 0.83 when capacity is 40% and the air flow is 567 CFM . That is not a good reading. You have an undersized supply and/or return. You never responded how the noise of the new furnace on the day it was installed compared with the old furnace. If the noise is about the same then noise is not due to the furnace in my opinion.

Hi, Marci, If you purchased a furnace that is advertised as "whisper quiet." I understand a performance expectation was created.  To enable an objective comparison of your old and new furnaces, we'd need performance data--including sound level data--for both the old and new systems. Noise in an HVAC system can come from a variety of sources, e.g., equipment noise, duct noise, air noise, etc.  If the air flow rates are the same, you shouldn't blame your replacement contractor for air noise produced by a duct work system he inherited.  That said, there are a couple of things you can try before investing in a complete overhaul of your duct work.  While they won't substitute for a properly designed duct system, they may make your existing system tolerable.  I can't tell from the photo, but it looks like the air handler is installed on masonry units of some sort.  Vibration isolating supports--or a layer of vibration absorbing material between the unit and the supports might help.  The duct work should include a flexible connector to reduce the transmission of vibration.  I can't tell if your system includes one, but I consider that something every system should have.  Air noise at supply and return registers can often be reduced by replacing them--especially the decorative ones-- with registers that have more open area or different vanes.  You could experiment by replacing registers in a single room and seeing if it makes a difference.  You may find registers designed for commercial applications will be quieter, especially if they have no dampers.

@Patricia Colwell Consulting says that same refrain over and over on this forum - hundreds of times - about getting polished stone counters.  She is not correct regarding marble.  Her experience is with granite, and she refuses to accept that marble is different than granite and that marble is better in a honed finish. But damage to stone counters prior to delivery, or upon installation, is NOT acceptable.  It doesn't matter that it's marble.  Yes, marble will patina with use, but should have no damage prior to delivery or upon installation.  That this fabricator has done this twice shows he is a very poor fabricator with poor quality control.  If he cannot even deliver an undamaged stone, how can you be confident that he has fabricated the slab correctly with the correct measurements?

One other way to look at your need-a-larger-DR situation: you can do the "fix" we are doing with our much smaller house.   You can remove the wall or greatly enlarge the opening between the current LR and DR, and buy a large extension table.    On those rare occasions when you need to have 10, 12 people, you can extend the table into the LR space 2 to 4 feet, maybe moving a couple of chairs.  Easiest would be if you didn't clutter up the sides of the DR with sideboards, etc; that's a tradeoff - wider table vs sideboards.   For a DR seldom used at full capacity, this is workable, and could save tens of thousands in construction.    Enlarging a cased opening between the rooms would be by far the cheapest, only a few thousand. Here is what I would do - create 2, 3 or 4 plans that are complete.  You have all the info in this thread to do that.   You don't need perfect drawings to present.  Then, find some contractors, I'd do minimum of 3,  through recommendations, and get them to come over, and give you a ballpark (not a full bid) for each scenario.   After probably 2 meetings you are going to understand what costs what.   And then you will probably wind up either digging deeper in your pockets, or scaling back your plans.  Or thinking of it in a phased way...do X now, and in 5 years, do Y.   Depends on your financial situation.

text: How far apart are the couches at this time? It looks as if they are about 8 feet from each other? Hi Karen, Difficult to advise without knowing more, but it is often actually the smaller spaces which are proportionally more expensive, as they can be more difficult to work in and sometimes you can't use "plus one" lower cost labour, given the tightness of a space. And even if you aren't replacing furniture, you may still have to remove/refit in order to do all you are wanting. If you are tiling behind a radiator also, for example, you may still have to full remove it - which may require a full drain down of your system, and then the same once the tiling is done. For these reasons, sometimes it is more cost effective to do a "fuller" job in a room. That said, the cost would be higher than I'd expect here in South Wales, where independent fitters working directly for a client can happily command about £4000 for a bathroom. Berkshire prices will be more. Get a couple of quotes from recommended installers. It may also be that the contractor is deliberately "quoting to lose" - if there is plenty of other work around, they may be trying to prioritise larger, better earning jobs and therefore pricing a bit high to "make it worthwhile" if they do, in fact, win it. As for 10 days - that is about standard for any "complete" bathroom we do and certain tasks cannot be speeded up die to drying times etc. So you might find someone who shaves a couple of days off it, but if they say they can do it for a grand in 3-4 days, run a mile...

We installed Dekton Laurent in our renovation last year. It is stunning...I love the matte leather finish and the warm brown veining. Everyone who walks into my home, loves it. Dekton makes the largest slab on the market so we could do our island without any top seams...which was a huge plus. But buyers beware. Our kitchen, with a huge waterfall island, butler pantry & servery required 6 slabs so it was one of the higher ticket items in our project. We are 2 careful adults and have, in one year's time, had 6 chips in this material. The first & so far, worst one was caused by a $10 ceramic dog treat jar tapping the edge of the island...when I heard the "thunk" I thought for sure I broke the ceramic, only to look down and see the chip in the edge. I nearly threw up...we had only been back in the house for a month when it happened. We have 2 chips along the bottom edge of the bar, where I guess the stools hit it when being lifted back into place. There is even one in the flat surface of a backsplash, almost like slate will chip off flat bits of its surface. This one is located where the (wall) splash meets the countertop, so it is not a vulnerable edge. If that isn't the fabrication, I'm not sure how we could have caused it...? When we got to chip #4, we started calling the Consentino showroom. Because we also had issues with the cut around the flush mount Miele induction HOB being so poorly done, we were convinced that our fabricator was perhaps the cause, or as @Sabrina Alfin Interiors suggested, used the wrong/dull blades.. (we did not choose the fabricator, he was part of the kitchen team that our kitchen contractor "always uses"...and he was paid separately and directly...another story/lesson learned). While questioning his qualifications for working with the material, he of course, was never able to provide us with his Dekton Certification for having completed the special training required by Consentino. (although I was told that he would not have been able to purchase the slabs without it...yeah, right). My husband and I both work for large, well-known architecture firms and had to use the full weight of our professional stature to get a Consentino rep to our home to see what was happening. She came, said next to nothing to us, took some pictures. Months went by and we heard nothing. After many calls and emails, she finally responded by emailing a link to the product specs, fabrication instructions & their joke of a warranty...ALL things that I already had downloaded from their website. They were basically saying "we don't care". We have threatened that no Cosentino material will ever be specified by either of our firms again. Did not matter. They will not admit to any flaw in this product and would not confirm our suspicions that poor fabrication tools & techniques could/would cause [additional] vulnerabilities or weakness. So we are just left to think about the expense and inconvenience that we will inevitably face to replace all of our countertops...ugh...and just feel sick all over again. Until Consentino addresses the issues and/or makes restitution to those of us who have had problems with this material, we've sworn to let as many people as possible know that it is definitely flawed!

Paint the mantle. The mantle is a cool color and the wall is a warm color - that's why it doesn't look right. For example, here are warm colors: off-white, cream, beige, tan, brown, olive green, gold, golden yellow, peach, orange, orange red, maroon. Cool colors: bright white, taupe, silver, gray, black, navy, emerald green, pine green, forest green, royal blue, purple, violet, burgendy, ice pastels, cool "blue" red. Try to limit your room colors to two colors only. Otherwise, you may not have a cohesive and unified look. Have a plan before you do or get anything for a room. I've been working with color for over 15 years, and my philosophy is based on the book Color me beautiful by Carole Jackson. The book is out of print, but you can get it on Amazon. I am a cool winter. Winters can still have bown hair. This is not based on your hair or eyes (because they can be changed), but by the skin color. Each person has a pink or green skin undertone. It may not have needed to be sealed.  Some quartzites are very dense and should not be sealed (like Taj Mahal quartzite for example), but some are not dense and are more like marble and must be sealed.  If you seal very dense stones, the sealant will just sit on top and cause a haze.  The haze will be particularly noticeable if a plate or similar is dragged across the counter. You didn't say the name of your quartzite, and that photo you  posted makes it impossible to identify. Already tried but that was unsuccessful even though I waited several hours and even rebooted the PC. This is what ended working: Because my inbox is configured on IMAP (not POP2), I followed these steps: - Open Outlook and go to the File menu. In the File menu, select Options. In the Options menu, select Advanced. In the Advanced menu, select the Send/Receive tab. In the Send/Receive tab, click on the Send/Receive button. Then, click on the Edit button. - In the Edit send/receive groups window, find the email account and un-check the option "Get folder unread count for subscribed folders". - Under the Received mail items section, check the option "Use the custom behavior defined below". - In the window that appears, you will see a list of your IMAP folders so, select the Inbox folder and leave the others unchecked. - Click the OK button to save the changes. - Exit out of the Options menu and perform a send/receive to test if there is any improvement. The Send/Receive got paused for much less than a half a minute and afterwards does not delay processing the Send / Receive Requests. I left the Outlook settings that way.

I am not going to say anyone's advice is invalid and I don't mean any disrespect, but I am going to disagree with it. I don't think the OP picked a non-neutral countertop by accident. I don't think a blue countertop was picked by accident. I think it just turned out to be brighter than the person who picked it expected, now its in in a larger form. (And anyway blue is considered a neutral color in dress, so I am not sure why it can't be considered a relative neutral here). I don't think it's that easy for a lot of people to just pick all neutrals for the big things and have them all complement each other. If it was I wouldn't see so many houses in real estate with a bunch of neutral finishes that look terrible with each other.  At the very least if more people picked a blue countertop it would give them some specific direction to go in. This is supposed to be a forum where things do actually get Designed, somehow, when someone needs help. It's not really designing anything when the answer is "everything big has to be neutral, so you just made a big uncorrectable mistake".  It  is designing something when someone is working with something that might not be so simple and you come up with some solutions to make it work. It's also not designing when the default advice is "Throw it away and start over". Sure, sometimes that is probably the best advice, I see lots of things proceed along the lines of the sunk cost fallacy, where people will spend more time and more money trying to fix something than they would if they just gave up on it. I get that. But I see that advice thrown around alot, and it's usually meted out as a form of punishment for not following the "everything big has to be neutral" rule. Finally I think there is the problem of the shock of the new. I have worked with a couple of people whose first reaction to a lot of things is "I HATE IT" seriously. I had a client who hated every single paint color in her house when it first went up. It was her nature. The real problem was that she was stuck with a decision and she couldn't change her mind every five minutes once the paint color went on the wall. It was a done deal.

This is a common problem in the downhill slopes of Folsom & El Dorado Hills where you can see many examples. Depending on the level of skill your architect or home designer possesses, they will usually have a civil engineer involved & designing this portion as their stamp is needed. Sometimes a sit down with the civil is best. Down hill drives do not immediately start at 15-20% but begins and ends with 15' of gradual slope changes to avoid scraping. The formula starts with 5' of 5% uphill off curb, then 5' of 5% downhill, 5' of 10% downhill THEN 15%+ down hill until within 15' of the garage door reversing the sequences. This takes a larger lot to fit or sometimes the home is pushed back to accommodate the slope sideways across the front. Also recommend you start with an accurate topographical survey, not a developer's supplied aerial survey which have been notoriously inaccurate leading to unpleasant and costly surprises.

@Margaret Oh This fiddle leaf fig has one really long root that wrapped around the top of the grower pot. Can this be cut? Yes, it should be removed for 2 reasons. 1) It is a problem root that will keep circling the pot and eventually become one or more of the adjectives: girdling, encircling, crossing, growing straight up or down or back toward the center of the root mass, or j-hooked. 2) it has very few small roots attached, so it currently serves as plumbing with not much moving through it, and it isn't needed for anchorage; IOW, it's not a significant help to the plant and the extra room made by removing it provides additional space in which the fine roots that do all the plant's heavy lifting can grow. In any repotting session, it would be my first target. How do you know which roots are okay to prune? I provided a list of problem roots above. The first target would be thick roots with not many fine roots growing from them. When removing these roots, target those not attached to the base of the trunk. Even roots that are at the base of the trunk can be shortened. A plants most vigorous tissues are in the root to shoot transition zone. These roots and branches that occur above thge soil line are the most vigorous on the plant. It's not an accident that rejuvenation pruning (cutting the top of the plant back hard) comes from the same root word (no pun) as juvenile - because you're cutting back to juvenile (most vigorous) tissues. The same holds true for roots. You do need to be measured about the volume of roots you take off, but your tendency to err on the safe side should keep you safe. These images show how harsh I am when it comes to repotting. The first plant is a boxwood, the second a Ficus benjamina              You needn't be so heavy-handed with the pruners during a rep[ot. This just shows how I typically go about repotting. It makes a huge difference in growth rate and vitality over the long term - no comparison at all to potting up or ignoring rootwork altogether. Also, it's almost  impossible to get the soil off from the roots on the very top. They're  super compacted. Is it fine to leave them as is? My suggestion is this: The first time you repot a plant is the hardest. Once it has been repotted, subsequent repots are much easier and faster. Try to set aside some free time when you won't feel pressured to do anything else, put on some music, take your time and fix as many root issues as you can, with most of the focus being on thick roots with few fine roots attached. Keep the roots wet for the entire time you're working them. That's important. I tend to work toward a round pad of roots 2-3" deep. This might be what a tree's roots look like after the first repotting session:  As the tree grows, the root mass will be a bit taller/deeper, but will still be maintained in a sort of hockey puck shape. For me, because I focus on bonsai, the appearance of the plant's surface roots is critical.  Powerful root base ^^^. Since your plant will likely never be formally judged, what the roots look like below the soil is of little concern, which doesn't mean you can ignore rootwork and expect results equal to what you get when rootwork is performed regularly - you can't - will never happen because root congestion is stressful and very often steals the lion's share of our plants' potential w/o us even knowing what we're losing. Ann, Thank you for your inquiry. I'm the tile setter. I believe a experienced tile setter should typically be responsible for the tile layout based on the veining or pattern of the tile. However, some tile setters don't want to spend the extra time required to match the veining or simply aren't detailed oriented enough to recognize the need for carefully matching the veining. The tile setter should always consult with the customer on the desired look and vein matching planned to insure they will be happy with the end result. And in some cases the customer may want to do the layout for the tile setter. So it's really up to the tile setter and customer to collaborate prior to setting the tile on the approach that will be taken to insure the desired look is achieved. For low density veining such as pictured I do the layout on the fly selecting tile from multiple boxes that will flow well in the pattern as it is installed while making sure I'm not using redundant tile patterns too close to each other. With a high density veining pattern I may pre-layout the tile which may include pre-grouping  tiles with same veining patterns and then as a set I will select tile from each group that will flow well together across the walls in the vertical and horizontal directions. With that said I believe the veining should ALWAYS flow in one direction as much as possible or it will look random and disjointed as if someone simply took each tile out the box without any consideration to the pattern direction or matching. You also have to consider that the vein match needs to be considred for all sides of each tile to try and match the veining in the horizontal and vertical directions as much as possible.  I like to try and make the finished layout result look as much like a solid surface slab on the wall. I think it's fair to say that tile with veining and pattern matching requirements would warrant an increase in pricing over non-patterned tile due to the extra labor time required to insure the veining is matched whether is done ahead of time or on the fly. Below are a bathroom tile projects that used veined tile which I matched as best as I could. 24" x 48" multi-directional veining. Pre-Layout required. https://www.houzz.com/hznb/projects/bathroom-24-x-48-statuary-porcelain-tub-shower-wall-tile-with-window-pj-vj~6760320   12" x 24" dense / heavy veining. Semi-prelayout required. I stacked all like tile together and then selected tile row by row to match left / right / top / bottom. https://www.houzz.com/hznb/projects/master-bathroom-remodel-shower-tub-vanity-counter-12-x-24-tile-quartz-pj-vj~6646110   12" x 24" light / medium veining. A recent porject completed with layout done on the fly as I set the tile using multiple boxes to select tile to create multi-tile vein flow matching. https://www.houzz.com/hznb/projects/master-bathroom-hannes-ii-pj-vj~7128299

In regard to chipped tile that’s why I specify at least a 20% overage. If you had an extensive amount of chipped tile I would have returned them to the supplier or simply asked for replacements. Finally,  As I referenced in my initial comment that most tile setters don’t want to take the time to do it right but at the same time they should if they are compensated for the additional to time to achieve a quality result. Homeowners need to understand time is money and if you want it done right there is a cost associated with that.  I don’t typically bid tile by the SF, especially for wall tile. I bid it on the wall complexity, type / style of tile, the layout and specialty features such as shower niches, accent tile and trim, etc. When I bid tyke this way I know I’m being compensated to produce a quality result and not a fast result. I agree with G&S. The perimeter was likely done with the intent of having the center covered by a rug. Once you stagger the end joints back from 0' to 4' and lay in new wood (where much of it lacks a major portion of the tongues and grooves), you'll have done a lot of work to produce a questionable floor. The overall chlorotic (yellowish) appearance and the shedding older leaves are both consistent with low fertility. I would flush the soil thoroughly at the next watering and fertilize. Following that, I would make sure my watering intervals are correct and I'm watering correctly. When plants are small and of a very manageable size like yours, you can usually tell if they need water by the weight of the planting. If you're not comfortable with that, and as the plantings get larger/heavier, using a 'tell' works very well. You can make a 'tell' by cutting a 1/4 or 5/16"x 48" wood dowel rod (any hardware) into pieces and sharpening the ends in a pencil sharpener. Push the sharpened dowel rod into the soil all the way to the bottom of the pot. Water when it shows almost dry. When you water, make sure you apply enough water to fully wet the entire soil mass and at least 20% of the water applied exits the drain hole. This flushes accumulating salts from tapwater and fertilizer solutions from the soil. If you're watering correctly, fertilize about every 4th or 5th watering in winter and every 3rd or 4th watering in summer. A liquid or water soluble fertilizer is best as delivery of nutrients when using fertilizers with organic components is erratic because the organic materials need to pass through the gut or otherwise be broken down into a form the plant can absorb, and populations of these forms of soil life are usually erratic in containers. To keep track of how many times you've watered each plant and when it's time to fertilize, drop a marble, button, other object in the pot when you water. No need for lists or remembering who needs fertilizing with this hack. Tying fertilizer applications to the number of times you've watered makes much more sense than using the calendar, as long as you're watering correctly. The idea that you should withhold fertilizer in winter is a horticultural myth. Plants don't only use nutrients for growth, they also use them in hundreds of processes and cycles. In order to suggest someone not fertilize in winter, you need to know if their medium is too water-retentive and how they water. Only when the medium is water retentive AND the grower is watering in small sips to avoid over-watering is the advice useful, and even then, it's the lesser of 2 evils. The evils or dilemma is, do I water in small sips to avoid over-watering and allow my plant to suffer the ill effects of accumulating dissolved solids (salts) in the soil, or do I water copiously, so I'm flushing the soil as I water, but run the risk of the soil remaining soggy for a period so long it seriously limits root function or wrecks root health. The right answer is neither. Ideally you would be using a medium that allows you to water to beyond the point of complete soil saturation, so you're flushing the soil, without the need to worry it will remain soggy for 2 long. That side-steps the dilemma entirely and you can expect that your plant would show its appreciation. Al

"Probably won't survive the 5:1:1." Untrue. If it doesn't survive, it's demise would be much more likely related to roots drying out while the tree was being worked. The 5:1:1 mix offers much greater opportunity for the plant to realize a larger measure of it's genetic potential than more water-retentive media. I've repotted thousands of plants in both the 5:1:1 and gritty mix w/o issue, and I continue that practice not because I have anything to prove, it simply works soo much better and eliminates completely the stress of root congestion. No matter what grow medium @Margaret OH uses, it will be essential to work the soil into the voids in the root mass. I typically use the homemade white nylon tool bottom row 4th from right to so that, adding a cup or two of soil at a time, but the wooden tool bottom 2nd from right works equally well as a root pick (to remove or work soil into the root mass) or a 'tell' to determine when it's time to water.  Insert the tool into the roots, add soil, then rotate the tool so the top of the tool rotates in a large circle and the bottom in a small circle - barely at all. You'll be able to easily see the soil moving into the soil. It reminds me of a whirlpool or how water starts to swirl in a cyclonic fashion as it goes down the drain. Because the 5:1:1 mix has a lot of large particles is no reason to think it won't be easy to work a homogeneous mix of the medium into the roots. Tip: To 'break' any grow medium's tendency to repel water when it's dry, put about half the soil you'll be using to pot the plant into a bucket/bowl. Add plenty of water and stir the mix vigorously. It should be saturated. Then, add the other half of the dry soil and mix. Allow the mix to rest for a half hour or so while you get things ready for the repot I agree that a low fired/ terra cotta clay pot is probably the best choice for the plant. The water in the initial (soaking wet) half of the medium will diffuse into the dry half within 30 minutes or so, 'breaking' the dry half of the soil's tendency to repel water. The medium should be slightly damp when you repot, just damp enough that it can no longer repel water while you're working it into the roots. If you're working with the gritty mix. You can soak the roots in water, then pot the plant in dry soil and water immediately. It's easier to get the dry gritty mix worked into the root mass, but you need to work quickly to prevent the roots from drying out. It takes only a few minutes to dry the fine roots out enough that they perish, which represents a setback while these roots regenerate. Generally, any plant I repot is pushing new growth inside of 1-2 weeks. An insignificantly small price to pay for a couple of years of growth and improved vitality unimpeded by the inherent stress associated with root congestion. Al

Hi Carly, If you're converting a listed building loft then you have some wriggle room in terms of meeting building regulations. Works to listed buildings do require listed building consent and any change of use of space does require building control approval - however, the listed building status does mean that the conservation takes precedence over the energy performance aspect. Having said that, for the sake of your comfort it is best to improve the energy performance as much as you can. It is possible to get to very good levels of thermal comfort even in older and listed buildings. When altering older buildings the best approach is to use a build up that works in a similar way to the existing structure, from a building physics perspective. This means that generally you are best to use a breathable build up - as you are clearly already aware. The foil insulation that you mention does not "breathe". If your home is detached then you could redo the roof with a different build up that doesn't require the 50mm ventilation. One way you can do this is by replacing the felt with a sealed breathable membrane that is designed specifically for this purpose. Then you can full fill between rafters. This does mean stripping the roof so might be more than your budget allows. There are likely to be other solutions that could also work for you. Hi there Carly, Firstly, to upgrade the existing roof rafters to comply with the current thermal targets of Part L of the UK building regulations, you will need this crucial measure of the rafter depth so as to ascertain the insulation to be added whilst maintaining an advised 50mm gap for cross ventilation through the roof build up. From the sounds of your measurements, a combination of insulated plasterboarding and quilt insulations (which can satisfy thermal performance targets in relatively thinner layers) would need to be specified.Following a survey of the property by your architects, the feasibility of this can be ascertained where these crucial dimensions can be confirmed along with the level of the floor structure - which may or may not need to be structurally upgraded to a thicker intermediate floor (most existing ceiling ties, though often boarded up for access into loft spaces, are not usually strong enough to take the loads of a new habitable loft space).At RESI, we use 3d digital surveys to form an interactive model of your property that is highly accurate to around 2mm, whereby we can test material buildups to the existing elements, in order to specify a solution that works best for the age of your property whilst also offering optimal head height.As part of the proposed works, it would be prominent to retrofit eaves and roof apex ventilators where possible, to permit a better airflow if not already in place. For a design such as yours Carly, a very holistic approach is required to consider the construction methodology in context of the age and style of the property, as well as offering the best possible final spatial volume. If this is done in accurate methods such as the above that we utilize in all projects, using our 3D software to test and simulate the various options, then on site this can be delivered properly and improve on the overall climatic conditions to the space effectively. Edited to note: This post might seem somewhat off topic because it is a reply to a post which would have been seen below Roberts, but has been removed, I assume by the person who posted the 'opinion' that prompted the reply below. The crux of the post removed was that it is ridiculous to think it matters when one chooses to repot their houseplants. What I wrote below is a refutation of that idea, and lists some of the reasons why the suggestion doesn't hold water. *********************************************************************************** No one I know of has ever said the only month appropriate for repotting houseplants is June. You are as free to avoid repotting as long as you like, or choose to repot whenever you like, just as you are free to avoid changing the oil in your car for as long as you like or fill the gas tank only when you feel like it, regardless of how much fuel it contains. The fact is, house plants not grown under lights normally vary significantly in their level of vitality throughout the growth cycle. Stored energy begins to wane quite predictably in mid to late fall, and continues to diminish until after the vernal equinox. What IS ridiculous, is suggesting that repotting when the plant's energy reserves are at their lowest and the plant's current ability to synthesize food/energy remains limited by short days and low light intensity, is not inferior to waiting a bit for the opportunity to work in sync with the plant's natural rhythms and taking advantage of the plant's strengths while making allowances for their weaknesses. I have repotted (fully repotted) many thousands of plants and I can say with a great deal of certainty that most tropicals which are reasonably healthy and repotted or divided somewhere around the summer solstice will recover in a small fraction of the time (a week or two to see new growth) it would take the same plant to recover were it repotted in winter or early spring. I'll reiterate that no one needs permission to repot their plants whenever they please, but that does not mean that the degrees of comparison from poor to middling to good, better, and best time to repot do not apply. One might consider running a marathon after a week-long drinking binge, but it's probably going to turn out better if one makes an allowance for the lack of verve and wait for a better opportunity. I agree the best time to repot changes somewhat with the grower's geographical proximity to the equator, and being nearer than 20* N or S latitude to the equator significantly broadens the period of time that can be considered the best time to repot when viewed from the plant's perspective, but there are still good times and not as good times to repot. Keep in mind too, that repotting is much more involved than potting-up, a practice that isn't as stressful in the immediate, but gradually adds to the accumulative stress that comes with the center of the root/soil mass becoming increasingly congested. Even if we take at face value that someone's winter has been exceptionally warm and sunny and mild, and humidity has been just wonderful, conditions are just starting to gain momentum on the upswing. Unless the plant is in steep decline, we can expect it's level of vitality to continue to improve (where you live) from now until late summer, so the plant would still be the better for a bit of patience. A plant's ability to defend itself against insect herbivory and disease pathogens is a byproduct of it's metabolic processes. A repot now or in the middle of winter ensures a longer recovery and greater susceptibility to insects and diseases during that recovery than if the repot was undertaken when the plant is at peak vitality levels. If someone wants to repot now or in the middle of winter as a show of defiance, that's fine with me. I would just hope that others understand the benefits of working with a plant's natural rhythms instead of at cross purposes with them. Al

The world of soccer is divided into geographic regions - Europe, Africa, South America, Asia, North/Central America, etc. The World Cup tournament starts with 32 teams. The 32 slots are allocated among the geographic regions based upon the successes or failures of national teams in each region versus international competition in past years. Each region has its own tournament in the 2 years prior to a World Cup to determine which will be awarded its available World Cup slots. The standings of each regional tournament determine that. The World Cup tournament itself has two stages. In the first, called the Group Round, the 32 teams are put into one of 8 groups. The allocations are seeded so that highly ranked teams don't find themselves playing one another at the very beginning, not unlike how March Madness works. In the Group round, each team plays the three other group member once. Of these 8 groups of four teams, the top 2 finishers move on to the Round of 16, which begins the single elimination phase. Round of 16 followed by a round of 8, followed by a round of 4, and the two winners of that play the final. That was held today. It pays to remember that in a sense, international soccer tournaments are like basketball in the Olympics. Each player has a club team they play for, that's their livelihood and where they spend their lives. Every few months, national teams, based on players' nationalities and not based on their team employment, play one another. And every 4 years, is the World Cup of national (not club) teams. Grafted often is more vigorous.  I don't know about "usually".  I think the main advantage of grafting is a shortcut for the growers, to help them get plants saleable a year or two sooner than they would be if grown own-root.  They grow thousands and thousands of Dr. Huey roots without any care of what the trends in demand for different blooms will be.  Then they graft whatever scion they think will sell in the near future. Once the plant is in your yard and established, which kind of rose is better depends on your soil, growing conditions, and pest challenges.  Those big woody Dr. Huey roots could speed up your plant's growth if conditions are right.  If you have freeze and thaw, grafted may be more sensitive to cold damage - or at least, can't regrow the canes you want from the root area, because that's a different rose.  Some people report that grafted roses die sooner if the scion plant doesn't establish its own roots over time.  This is kind of hard to predict universally. You could always re-bury your grafted roses deeper in the hopes that the scion plant will root as well. Oh, and based on what Jason said in the video, and pictures on HelpMeFind, City of York is a big ol' rose, and doesn't need any help from Dr. Huey. Weber's Mount Olympus Meatball Kabobs Serves 4-6 Meatballs:2 medium garlic cloves1 small red or yellow onion, roughly chopped (about 1 cup)1/4 cup lightly packed fresh mint leaves3/4 pound ground lamb3/4 pound ground beef1 T. red wine vinegar1 1/2 tsp. kosher salt1 tsp. freshly ground black pepper1 tsp. dried oregano1/2 tsp. paprika Sauce:4 ounces English cucumber1 cup plain yogurt2 T. olive oil2 T. finely chopped fresh dill1/2 tsp. kosher salt1/4 tsp. freshly ground black pepper1/8 tsp. Tabasco sauce For Meatballs: In food processor (or by hand) finely chop garlic, onion and mint. Combine in large bowl with lamb, beef and remaining meatball ingredients. Blend lightly with your hands until well combined. Form into meatballs about 1 1/2 inches in diameter (you should have 20-25 meatballs). Thread long, wide skewers through meatballs, about 4 or 5 per skewer, leaving a little room between each meatball. Place kabobs on baking sheet, cover and chill for 2 hours and up to 8 hours. For Sauce: Grate cucumber. Drain in colander and squeeze out most of moisture. In medium bowl, whisk together cucumber and remaining sauce ingredients. Cover and chill until ready to serve (can be made 1-2 days in advance). Lightly brush or spray kabobs on all sides with olive oil. Grill over direct medium heat until fully cooked, 8-10 minutes, gently rotating meatballs 2 or 3 times during grilling. Serve warm with the sauce.

It would be more helpful to monitor efficiency by at least measuring ∆T of room temperature or return air temperature to temperature in the main plenum after the HP. I do this with our system with a remote wireless weather station sensor mounted at the first register closest to the HP that continually monitors temperature with Min/Max recording and relative humidity. I monitor this for heating and cooling. This way I’m alerted immediately of any change in efficiency just by ∆T alone - heating or cooling. You might want to install one of these: Blue-White Flow Gauge This essential device will indicate actual flow rate, provide visuals of fluid colour, unwanted entrained air bubbles and suspended particles that might be damaging and possible loss of fluid. Generally, devices using switching power supplies can work over a wide range of input voltages and 50-60 Hz.  Just looking at two USB type supplies that were handy, one from Alcatel and one from Verizon supports this.  So cell' 'phones should be OK.  An available iPad power module lists 50-60 Hz in very fine print. I don't quite need hearing aides yet, so I don't have any to investigate.  But if they charge from USB type modules, the modules likely say in small print what their power limitations are.  I notice looking up the C-1B2 that it is a USB powered charger that depends on different adapter plugs to operate from wall receptacles.  You would need a USB power module with a Japanese plug to power it. Devices with power transformers to isolate them from the power lines, such as (in the USA) some older TVs, HIFi equipment, and, (as I recall observing the guts), my Sharp OTC microwave oven, may not like 50-Hz power because the transformer input impedance wasn't designed for 50 Hz.  (My Sharp specifies 60 Hz.)  More iron and wire is needed for 50 Hz.  60-Hz transformers may overheat at 50 Hz.  (Impedance is proportional to frequency and inductance.) Various clocks and other devices depending on the power line frequency instead of their own crystal timers will need to be hooked to the appropriate frequency power source, and may not tolerate excessive voltage. I was surprised to see that my Mitsubishi split air conditioners, ubiquitous in Japan, are only listed for 60 Hz.  So Mitsu saved a smidgen of cost with their US export models.

Couple comments: - Not sure if the only circulation to this section of the house is through the 38" cased opening, but you may want a 3-way for the general ceiling and pendants over at the lower left corner wall or somewhere that circulation could be coming or going. - Shelf picture light: not sure if that will be mounted to the edge of the top shelf, or to a "cover" at 7' or 8' to match the adjacent cabinet heights, but sticking out might be intrusive to the functional recessed and might cause too great of shadows under each shelf depending on how many shelves. Also picturing a prominent brass canopy that will "compete" with the very close sconce and pendants. - Sconce: on a blank wall (assuming) would be just decoration (so not a downlight), so the height at around 70" or so might be a hazard in circulation. Also, be aware that the wall is wider there (pocket door is hidden), so if you are using the sconce to tie into the decor of the adjacent room it might want to scootch over. - Sink recessed: These additionals are strictly functional for task, and compete with pendants. So in that respect, it is good to separately switch them, as sometimes you want the pendants to be showcased/only utilized for seating or when you are not doing prep/cleanup, yet still have the general kitchen lighting on. Also, you don't always want the hotspots on the pendant shades, especially with brass. If your pendants are opaque shades and strictly higher-lumen downlights, the (2) recessed are probably not needed at all for task. - Hood recessed: depending on reflectivity of hood and style, can scootch closer to stove.

HVAC systems need to maintain comfortable and healthy conditions for a home's occupants.  That includes minimizing the potential for mold, and mildew.   Houston is in IECC climate zone 2A (warm-humid.)  Turning off the upper level HVAC or increasing the setpoint temperature in an effort to save energy will also reduce the ability to dehumidify the space. Since your objective is to reduce energy used for space conditioning, you might consider replacing the existing heat pump or air conditioner serving that area with a ducted mini-split system, particularly if the existing system is nearing the end of it's life expectancy.  That would enable better system turndown and better dehumidification while also reducing energy usage.

Interesting property, looks like great bird habitat! I don't know if you're total newbies with regard to managing a woodland area or not, but here's some considerations. Poison Ivy - make sure you identify it and removing it safely. Small-ish vines can be squirted with Round Up; larger vines you might need to cut off near the ground and use the Round Up as new leaves come out. Once you've gotten rid of it, you're not done. Birds will bring seeds in and new poison ivy plants will spring up, so once a month or so walk your property and look for baby poison ivies -- easy to get rid of when they're only a few leaves high. Other invasive vines - honeysuckle and english ivy are the most common. Persistence is the key -- cut near the base, pull out what comes easily, do it again in a few weeks. English ivy laughs at Round Up so don't even try that. When your tree people come, see if they'll cut some of the trunks into 5 or 6 foot sections and leave them for you. They'll make good edges of pathways, and can help prevent erosion if you place them across the slope. Maybe they can mulch the rest of the oak branches and scatter it in your woods. And if you can get a tree expert to walk your woods with you and identify species, that's great -- you'll enjoy it a lot more if you know what you own. As to clearing areas ... yes that's likely to cause erosion, so have a plan in place before you start. A stop-gap measure could be to plant Winter Rye on any bare soil -- that stuff sprouts very easily, but it won't over-winter so it's only a temporary fix. If that were my woodland, I'd clear out the invasives, plant more natives, add a bird bath near the house, make a few rambling paths through the woods. Leave most of it as "woodland" complete with undergrowth; don't try to make it into a park. You'll have more interesting wildlife, and you'll have a place to easily rake leaves into each fall instead of having to bag them for the trash.

For a 72-inch vanity, I would usually avoid choosing the widest possible recessed cabinets just because the wall can technically take them. The better look often comes from keeping the two cabinets clearly tied to the sink centers while still leaving enough wall breathing room and, if you use sconces, enough side space for the lighting to feel comfortable. When the cabinets get too wide, the vanity wall can start looking crowded before the room is even finished. In practice, balanced spacing usually matters more than squeezing out every inch of mirrored storage. From a production and QC perspective, I would also think past the front view: door swing clearance, hinge reach, interior shelf usability and how much installation tolerance the rough opening really leaves you. Recessed cabinets look simple when finished, but they are less forgiving in the field than people expect. I would size the cabinets as part of the full vanity-lighting composition, not as an isolated storage decision.

North American white and red oak have open grain. It's especially present when the boards are flat cut. When you stain the wood to get a medium color like your door, the grain turn black from the stain. Rift and quarter-sawn cut the boards at an angle that minimizes the open grain and the black grain pattern. To deal with that you can fill the grain with a light color paint or any color lighter than black. Cerise is a technique. Also pickling. Then you can add a topcoat of clear finish. The door you show looks like it got a light grain fill and a satin topcoat. It looks good in the full picture. As an aside, European and French Oak are different oak species with more dense less open grain. You can see that on IKEA Vedhamn doors. VEDHAMN oak fronts - IKEA    IKEA uses European Oak. They are about the only place where you can get European Oak cabinet doors and drawer fronts in the US. . . .and you'll save a lot of money. DOCA cabinets in Spain also makes cabinets. Contrary to popular belief, overhead watering does not encourage the development of powdery mildew. PM is actually water adverse - cannot develop on wet surfaces - and spraying down susceptible plants periodically is one form of recommended preventative treatment. Late day applications of overhead watering should be avoided as insufficient time for the foliage to dry before nightfall can encourage other fungal issues but in general, overhead watering does NOT increase disease issues. Overhead watering is the norm for almost all commercial agriculture.

What is your budget?  If you can afford it an underground system is the cleanest and neatest way to do irrigation.  It also puts all of the largest pipes quite deep which limits damage from normal gardening. I also watered by hand for...wow, 40 years!  I couldn't imagine doing it now, and I'm very grateful for our underground system. We have a lot of drip as part of the system and it keeps me quite busy for 8 months of the year maintaining the drip infrastructure.  Every time I add a plant I have to get water to that plant, which means adding an emitter or adjusting the spray pattern of a spray-head. It's not easy but way better than dragging hoses, and looking at hoses always laying around.  We don't have any drip or soaker hoses, just a combination of spray heads and emitters, and it works well in both ornamental gardens and raised beds with veggies. Combination Service Entrance Device (CSED) is what I would recommend to replace the mess I see in the pictures, but do you have a sub panel inside the house not pictured?  Lets talk about an additional sub panels inside the house later but what I see in your pictures on the outside of the house is not a subpanel.  Everything on the outside would need to be removed and replaced with a new 200 amp CSED, new 2" rigid conduit for the mast, new weatherhead, correct wire and size from meter socket out weatherhead, (electric company doesn't wire to the meter socket) proper straps and distances between conduit straps to determine the number.  Proper attachment of all parts of the meter loop/disconnect to the house is just as important as the material used and the inspector will not allow connection until it meets code.  The mast height above the soffit is also determined by code and needs followed.About meeting code, are you saying the last NEC code your city adopted was 2017?  I strongly recommend replacing the meter loop to the most recent electrical code anyway.Your upgrade would also require the correct and and proper grounding rod and proper electrical bonding of metal piping in the house.  Also check with state code on smoke detectors, many states require adding hard wired smoke detectors when certain remodeling or repairs are done to a house.Once you replace your meter socket and main panel (again it isn't a subpanel, if you have others in the house please take a picture and post) non of the other circuits need to be upgraded to include a ground, but the CSED will need to include everything for proper grounding.It sounds like you plan on doing the job and fine if you find all the information needed with the skills to do it, followed up by an inspection.  Grandfathered electrical only applies to what you are haven't touched.  It sounds like you touched a lot of the circuits in the house and how deep you touched the 2 wire no ground circuits would determine if it the circuit needed to be brought to code, and If you added or extended any part of a circuit the circuit needed to be brought to code, but another story.   When the previous owner rewired the kitchen was it inspected?  If not you may need to worry about that because grounding requirements would need to be followed, and I do see some green and bare wires in the outside breaker box I don't see where they are going.I hate seeing all these houses listed for sale stating remodeled and updated as flips. Being located in Canada, I've never heard of the oil brands you've used previously, although the 6 month time frame  description of your products performance sounds just about right for exterior semi trans oil. I've used the  Sherwin Williams version of this product extensively over the years. My last house had a  hottub deck that needed constant snow shovelling & would consume  10 gallons of semi trans oil every fall for maintenance. I would  only ever use semi trans oil for properly prepared clients exterior lumber decks, and nothing  else due to product limitations.   In the world of ski resort homes I've been using Sikkens Cetol 1 for over two decades on multiple wood species with great results  ( *Side note, never top with Cetol 2/3 or any other clear coat)   I have large timbers on my own home, that on average  I recoat with one coat of Cetol 1  every 3-5 years, depending on exposure. Sure the product costs are  higher than a semi trans oil, but then so are the benefits.... A couple points  to keep in mind;  smooth cedar siding  installed horizontally instead of vertically will unfortunately be more prone to marking/future water stains & trapping dirt  etc. mainly due to that flat exposed edge profile. Smooth wood  will always discolor/dry out/mark faster than the equivalent siding in a rough/er finish & require higher upkeep. Another factor to consider is the cedar sidings  substrate.  Over the years I've definitely noticed product life discrepancies/variations depending on the sidings  backing and perhaps more critically,  how it was installed. Air movement is your friend.... Either way, good luck whichever road you take with this !
