"Tripping the breaker" on a hot tub can be broadly from two different causes: 1. Excess current - breaker itself trips 2. The GFCI is tripping - in other words, a ground fault Knowing which is actually happening is the first step. Keep in mind that you are talking about people, immersed in water, and electricity. If you have an electrical problem, it's important that you not "guess" - and very important that you don't just flip the breaker on and see if it stays on. Both the GFCI and the overcurrent protection  are "last resort" safety mechanisms. It's like driving around in your car and counting on your emergency brake to stop your car when you know that your brakes are bad. I hate to be unkind, but I think that you may not be getting the best and brightest to look at your tub. It sounds like they are grasping at straws. If the motor on the blower is wet, how did it get wet? Is it really wet, or are they just guessing - like with the valve? My personal experience with hot tubs is that they are great for the first 5 years or so - then they start having an issue or two - and then it turns into a constant battle.  There is a pump, a heater and a blower. There are also some flow switches, thermistors and the control board. If you have a GFI shutting down, and the tub is older than 5 years, and you need this tub to be reliably functional, I would look  at replacing the heater, the blower and the pump. That might be a different company that does the weekly maintenance. I would balance that against the cost of a replacement unit. Keep in mind that if your tub is built into a deck, you may have a problem getting an exact fit.

What do they mean a shut valve is causing the breaker to trip? Which valve? Because valves are water, not electrical. Is it a clogged one causing a pressure issue, a hot water valve issue causing the tub to overheat and trip the breaker? Somehing manually shut off? A damaged one leaking and causing wetness in parts of your tub that it should not- like that blower? Another valve? You might want to get in a second opinion to help clarify what is going on with your tub. And maybe a clearer report on what is going on with your tub from your maintenance company. You cannot allow your renters to use the tub in the state it is in. It just is risking safety. We inherited a hot tub with the house when we moved in. Freestanding, a bit older model. I think we actually got it working once and soaking for a few minutes, lol. It was the bits that ran the tub, or a jet or valve here or there in the tub that was leaking and needed to be replaced, and so on. Once it started it seemed like a cascading effect. Wasn't nice enough to be worth it for us.

Some brief responses to your various questions: 1. Need a cover panel here but IKEA cover panels have a max height of 240cm – we need 260cm so there will be a join ideally in line with the wall cabinets – any alternative solution to this? If you were able to identify the matching board, it might be possible to buy a larger panel through a different route - many are up to 3m long if bought from a panel distributor or the manufacturer.  But that will be less likely with Ikea, assuming they are making their own. 2. 400mm height wall units – proposing to have these opening vertically – good/bad idea? Hmmm, I'm in two minds here. I don't like side opening for short but wide doors, but your top boxes will be a nightmare to use if they are top hinged because of height. You could consider pinning the top box doors to the ones below & side mounting, such that they all open together. 3. Corner is currently inaccessible with the drawers – trying to maximise drawer space over cupboard space – is this a good idea? No, a bad idea - a lot of waster space. Go for a corner with pull out Le Mans. Will be similar price to the drawers, but you get to use the corner totally. Could reconfigure with 600mm drawers but thought a 400mm cupboard to access space in the corner would be unusable. Basically, is having more drawer space a better idea? As above, use wireworks - they were designed for a reason! 4. Extractor – gone for an integrated as wanted to have no break in wall units – good or bad idea? Good idea - we do plenty of these! Consider also telescopic options and be SURE to check installation dimensions to be sure the extractor you pick will fit the wall unit - not all do! 5. Proposed a small shelf to the rear of the worktop which would be tiled as we are reducing the amount of worktop compared to the current, and wanted to maximise useable space for small items that would usually clutter up the worktop e.g condiments, kitchen roll, etc. Any thoughts on this? Anyone ever seen this, and if so, what depth/height would you suggest, and did it work/look good in reality? Yes, I've seen this done and it can be useful & effective. BUT we would normally step all the base units off the wall by that full amount, in which case you need to ensure the design of wall units takes this into account where you return around corners! 6. Kitchen is 4.8m wide, and due the cabinet widths of IKEA, will always have about 150mm to fill along the width. Do you think where we have shown the filler panel is the most suitable location, or would it be better behind the oven (bearing in mind the wall units need something to attach to if we were to have the filler panel here)? Personally I hate to see any wasted space in a kitchen. If you have at least 150mm width, I'd consider doing a full height wine rack or cookbook shelves instead. A competent fitter will fashion something for the price of an extra fitter panel or two and an hour or two's time. 7. Worktop depth – as far as we’re aware, Minerva (with the integrated sink) only comes as 650mm deep. However, IKEA cover panels are max 600mm deep (needed for fridge and oven units), meaning our fitter would have to shave 50mm off the worktop. Is it doable for a good fitter? I very rarely do this, but I must urge caution against using Minerva. It is one product we used for a number of jobs a few years back, but now we wouldn't touch it with a barge pole. We've seen multiple problems with batch colour matching, stains, heat, and crackling of sink bases with hot taps. The company was not good at supporting putting issues right, and we came to the conclusion that we were not comfortable offering it to our clients. There are better alternatives out there, and a good fabricator and keenly priced quartz will get close in price. While you can remove 50mm from the worktop, the product will get through blades rapidly, and it is harder to work with than laminates. We really would recommend proper fabricators for such products. 8. Currently proposing this as open as only 200mm – would a 200mm pull-out cabinet be practical given the position in the corner? No reason why not. A good German kitchen would probably offer you an 800x800 L shaped carousel unit as one way to handle this "tight" corner. Or if you can stretch to a 300w unit, I would. - What colour of units would anyone recommend for a north facing kitchen, with a dark grey stone floor, and would you recommend matt or gloss? Possibly a steel or Spitfire blue or light green. I'd consider woodgrains too. Gloss or matt is a very personal choice, though certain colours can look better in one or the other. We have been going back and forward between green/grey (BODARP) or white, but is one too dark, and the other too stark? If white is too stark, a Limestone or Taupe might suit you. - Microwave – integrated or not? Could replace the double oven with a single oven and combi microwave oven. Single plus combi is a popular option - have a good look at the Samsung options which are jam packed with additional cooking features like Air Sous Vide, Air Fry and steam. Alternatively if you only use a microwave infrequently for relatively modest amounts (a plate, say) & reheating, consider a wall unit mounted one. - Considering going for push open for all wall units – what are thoughts on this? Anything with a push mechanism will need periodic adjustment and some mechanisms are better than others. German handleless wall units are better designed with a "finger space" rail so need no tip-on mechanism - Base units/appliances – would we be better with handles or grooves? Personal choice! If going handleless, you really can't beat true German kitchens or the Omega "flat" rail system. - Lighting – would warm or cool lighting work best in a north facing kitchen? Neither - pick "natural" (in between) at about 4000 Kelvin. And finally, interesting to hear people’s thoughts in general please? The design is a little lacking in symmetry for me and is quite "fussy", but given the limited unit options from Ikea, I kind of see why it is as it is. Be aware that IKEA use their own slightly strange "grid" system, so all sizes are pretty unique to them and them alone. Their carcasses are very basic, and I see more than the average number of customers looking to change IKEA kitchens a lot sooner than most other brands. If budgets are tight, you can get a good looking kitchen for not a lot - but with some careful design from an independent studio whose suppliers have more extensive ranges, you will probably get a much better looking kitchen that lasts longer for not a huge amount more. We could probably design a tidier layout that used far fewer overall units, but which delivered more usable space - to give an example, using German units, you could do extra-high wall units as single units, so no top boxes or triple-stacked units required! Hope that all gives you a little food for thought. I would certainly do your homework and look at reviews for Minerva - only 1.9 stars on Trustpilot. Feel free to ask anything else and I'm sure we'll be happy to give our thoughts! Caldicot Kitchens

I've been researching this and asking in other places as well, and so far I think the best and cheapest solution is to use either mdf, which seems heavy to me, or a wood trim, and then cut holes into it for lightness, while maintaing rigidity. This is much cheaper than buying it per panel. one panel would cost me about 80$ However, I'm buying 10 panels of rockwool for 100$. Then it's just the wood frame I need to buy and some fabric. Cardboard on the back would reflect sound back forward. I'm actually going to be putting some cork stoppers on the back of these to keep them off the wall slightly. They will reduce some noise leaking out of my apartment into the neighbour's place, but nothing too significant. The real reason is to get rid of that room sound. If you've ever painted an empty room, you will notice how much room sound you get. Laymen call that echo, but technically echo is distinct sound repeated back, whereas this sort of room noise is called reverb. Filling a room with furniture and book cases and things like that will dampen it. These types of panels also dampen quite a wide range of frequencies. But thicker ones are need for deep bass, and different shapes are required for corners. Also, varying angles and distances of walls helps, because sound is waves, and if you repeat a movement in increases the wave, so if a sound is the right size of wave, it can bounce back between walls, and make itself louder. There are also other solutions, like diffusers, like this: https://flypaper.soundfly.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/diffuser-header-1024x683.png which are just designed to break up the sound, and keep it natural, but avoid buildups or cancellations of certain frequencies.  If you're designing a space, and you want to be mindful of how it sounds, breaking up flat walls, and adding soft furniture, and especially book cases. They work very well as diffusers, and they also absorb quite well. So, for people doing remote work from their office or something, if they want more of a professional audio sound, book cases work really well, and so will anything resembling what I described above. For people that want to reduce noise from neighbours, that's a whole extra level, and will require contractors and lots of construction lol. You basically need to build a room inside a room at that point.

Eileen, I copied the recipe…thanks!  The only “crackers” I’ve made lean more toward savory shortbread.  Ina Garten has a couple good ones you can easily google for Parmesan Thyme Crackers and Jalapeno Cheddar Crackers. I’ve also made this one I’ve posted here before.  I found it in Bon Appetit years ago and like to make it for Thanksgiving.  The savory shortbread is good both with or without the roulade. Blue Cheese Shortbread Leaves With Cream Cheese Roulade You can start making the shortbread leaves up to three days ahead...or make them well in advance and freeze. Shortbread Ingredients:3 1/2 oz. crumbled blue cheese (about 1/2 cup)3 T. unslated butter, room temp. (I prefer salted butter for these)1/2 cup flour1/4 cup cornstarch1/4 tsp. kosher salt1/8 tsp. ground black pepper1/3 cup walnuts, finely chopped Roulade Ingredients:1 8-oz. pkg. chilled cream cheese2/3 cup purchased spiced cranberry-apple chutney (or other favorite chutney)1/2 cup very thinly sliced green onions For Shortbread:Blend blue cheese and butter in processor until creamy. Add flour, cornstarch, salt, and pepper. Using on/off turns, process until mixture resembles coarse meal. Add walnuts and process just until moist clumps form. Gather dough into ball. Flatten into disk. Wrap dough in plastic and refrigerate until firm, about 1 hour. Preheat oven to 325°F. Line 2 baking sheets with parchment paper. Roll out dough between sheets of plastic wrap to 1/8- to 1/4-inch thickness. Remove top sheet. Using 2 1/2x1-inch leaf-shaped cookie cutter, cut out leaves. Transfer leaves to prepared baking sheets. Gather dough scraps and reroll; cut out additional leaves. Transfer to prepared baking sheets. Bake until golden brown, about 20 minutes. Transfer leaves to rack and cool. (Can be prepared 3 days ahead. Store in airtight container at room temperature.) For Roulade: (See *Note below)Using rolling pin, flatten cream cheese between sheets of plastic wrap; roll into 10x8-inch rectangle. Remove top sheet of plastic wrap. Spread 1/3 cup chutney atop cream cheese rectangle, leaving 1-inch plain border. Sprinkle chutney with 2 tablespoons green onions. Using plastic as aid and starting at 1 long side, roll up cream cheese, jelly-roll style, into log. Gently press remaining green onions onto roulade. Wrap roulade tightly with plastic. Refrigerate until set, at least 2 hours and up to 2 days. Place roulade on platter. Surround with shortbread leaves. Top roulade with remaining 1/3 cup chutney and serve. *Note: You can go the easy route with the roulade ingredients by just topping the cream cheese with the chutney and onion.

The reason why every seed is putting up multiple seedlings is because those are multigerm seeds. It means when the flowers were making their seed clusters multiple seeds grew together into one fused pod. It's common among many members of the beet family, including Swiss Chard. Heirlooms and older varieties tend to be multigerm more often. The trait of breeding for monogerm seeds is a bit newer and you can find them more in hybrid selections. Hi, Kelly. Does the pot have a drain hole? If not, that's almost certainly the underlying issue ....... along with a hand too heavy on the watering can. It looks like too much water and too little air in the grow medium. Read below about using a "tell" to "tell" you when it's time to water. It is very helpful and will help keep you on track insofar as proper watering intervals go. How do you determine when it's time to water? Among conventional container gardeners, "soil", the word, is a perfectly acceptable label for what a plant's roots call home, as are additional synonyms 'medium', 'grow medium', and 'substrate'. Among container gardeners, "soil" does not carry the connotation of being a mineral soil. When people call what their plants grow in "dirt", so what. We know what they mean. The best way to change their mind about what they call soil, is by repeating the more appropriate descriptors over and over as we welcome them to the fold and do what we can to help them increase the amount of reward they get for their efforts. Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Al

Fact: the pedigree of a rose plays a huge role in a variety's ability (or inability) to generate new  infrastructure from the base of the plant (aka "basal breaks"). There are many cultivars that do it with abandon, and there are many that make a few large canes and then build on that structure year after year. Varieties of the latter type cannot be prompted to make new basal canes no matter what you do to them, so there's great wisdom in letting each variety grow as it is genetically designed to do, and accept what you get. If you find a specific rose doesn't meet your expectations in terms of its growth habit/architecture, then get rid of it and replace it with a variety that performs the way you want. Many of the older Hybrid Teas rarely add new basal canes to their biomass - instead they build on top of existing growth. Of course, you can chop them to the ground to force them to renew their wood, but you won't get the best shrub from a rose handled this way, IMO.

When we set our plumbing either in the spa or the pool, we have to support the pipe by tying it to a piece of rebar. The pipes are stubbed out beyond the shotcrete. After the shot, the crew will carve out around the pipes to allow for access to the pipe to cut them back prior to plastering. I'll post a pic of a recent build during construction to see the stubbed pipes. Most times we have to chip a bit more to allow the wall fitting to sit back far enough to finish flush with the plaster. Sometimes the supporting piece of rebar interferes and we will cut it out. The pipe is cut back and the wall fitting is set. Everything is pre-measured to ensure the fitting when glued is fully seated and ends flush for plaster. Setting the wall fittings should be the PB's responsibility. Not the plaster contractor. Perhaps in your case the rebar was exposed, the pipes were cut back too far, not extended and the plaster contractor set the wall fittings flush as they were plastering. So now the wall fitting is not glued to the stub and the space in between has the rebar exposed resulting in rust. It will never stop. Chipping out the wall would be a great undertaking and any plaster patching would be noticeable. I don't have eyes on these wall fittings, but perhaps cleaning up the affected areas, allow to dry, reach into the fittings and rough the plastic surface with some emery cloth. A long, narrow wire brush attachment may work well. Wipe it clean and apply some GE Silicone where there is a gap. This may be tricky if it's in deep. A long flat applicator of some sort will help. Apply enough to fill the gap but not too much interfere with the jet function. Allow 24 hrs to set. This won't be a permanent fix, but it should stop the rusting issues.

Hi, HU, I believe the source of your confusion is the fact that the information resource you linked relates to commercial and industrial applications--not residential.  If you click on "Applications" or "Case Studies" you won't find any residential ones.  Commercial/industrial dehumidification systems are typically ones designed to deal with large point sources of moisture (e.g., an indoor swimming pool, a hotel lobby with a large multi-story waterfall, etc.)   The location of returns will be close to the moisture point source.   Moisture point sources in residential applications are typically addressed by ventilation systems (e.g., bath vent fans, range hoods, etc.)  Returns would not be appropriate (and would not comply with the code) in those locations.   Stick to information related to residential dehumidifier applications. For what it's worth, if you have a forced-air heating and/or cooling system I'd look to utilize that system to distribute air leaving the dehumidifier rather than create a redundant air distribution system.  I also recommend engaging an experienced design professional so your system is sized  appropriately for your needs and performs as intended.

Thanks this is very helpful! Based on the images we would prefer Option B. Will your In-Laws be living in this Guest Suite or will they only be staying on occasion? If the ultimate goal is to have them move into this space, the larger closet is the best option. A bed in front of a window doesn't bother us as long as you are purchasing the right type of frame for the location. For example, we would not do an extra tall headboard because you will block the natural light coming into this room, and those are the only windows in the space. It is also recommended to have 36" wide walkways, especially when designing for aging in place, you need to ensure there is plenty of space to move around in the room. The only concern we have is with the type of doors you are doing on the closet. It would need to be a pocket door. A traditional door won't work with the way the nightstands are placed because the nightstand is partially blocking full access to the closet. Even an accordion door we would hesitate to put in the closet because it will need to fold up to a wall somewhere and we don't see that working unless the accordion folds up against the wall with the entry door. Another point to keep in mind- typically nightstands are anywhere from 24-30" wide and 18-36" deep, so keep that in mind when selecting furniture for this space, especially if you go with a King Size bed and only have 27" on either side. We would also suggest draperies on the windows to give the room more of a softness and welcoming feel. Hope this feedback is helpful! Side Note: If you are putting a bed on a window wall and it is going to block the window, at least try to make sure the bed is centered on the window, trust us - it will drive you crazy if it is off center when it goes in and it will be very noticeable, because the window is the focal point of the room and the bed amplifies that.

That's a doozy of a light fixture. Before making any decisions on finishes I'd sort out the lighting. Recommended general lighting in a kitchen is sometimes calculated as 35 lumens per square foot (in addition to undercabinet lighting). Switching to a surface mount track light system that gets you to 35 lumens/sf is a good, immediate fix. You'll also want to add undercabinet lighting and swap what's over the sink for a pendant. Be mindful of the color temp of the bulbs and try to get them all the same throughout the space - I prefer 3000K.

@User - there are several reasons for buzzing in an induction cooktop.  One is the cookware, but not 98% of the time.  Other reasons are the electrical wiring to the cooktop, the cooktop itself (whether it's a faulty one or that particular model is just intrinsically a buzzing cooktop), and also the sensitivity of the user to buzzing.  There have been posts on this forum where one spouse hears buzzing of their cooktop and the other spouse does not on the same cooktop.  Since the OP was in a showroom, the buzzing could have been any of those reasons. @Emily R. - I would get an electrician to check that your kitchen's wiring to the cooktop will be adequate for an induction cooktop, even if it was adequate for an older electric smoothtop.  I would also look through reviews about which cookware brands buzz least on induction; some induction-capable pans still buzz, and it does not appear to be necessarily a function of price, since my Demeyere (a top-notch expensive cookware) buzzed on an induction cooktop (a Thermador).

" My upper kitchen cabinets are 15” deep.  Under cabinet exhaust fans are not this deep" Perhaps I am not understanding you.  Undercabinet exhaust hoods - even recirculating ones - are usually 18" deep or more front to back.  The better ones are 24" deep, and you can find many that are 22" deep.  Rather than fooling around with wrapping in sheet metal, etc., get a deeper hood.

The cooktop installation instructions will specify distances to combustibles.  These values do not exclude combustibles that have sheet metal attached to them, unless spaced out by appropriate methods (see IMC 308.4).  So any sheet metal used to block cooking plumes headed for the gap will have to be appropriately mounted if within the combustible distance limit.  This limit varies greatly with type of cooktop and burner BTUh. A small under-cabinet exhaust fan (blower) that doesn't exhaust must filter well to have any utility at all.  I'm not particularly sanguine about what filtering can be fitted to such a small unit as the OP describes. It should also be understood that small flow rate devices cannot adequately capture and contain hot oil or grease cooking plumes, which will spill out into the room.

What needs to be treated in the water? Without seeing your water analysis, you won't get meaningful answers here. If you choose to list the problem aspects of the water do note if it's municipal or well water and where you live. A whole house system is generally installed to treat systemic issues like pH, hardness, high iron, etc. These would usually have media filled tanks that automatically regenerate and are serviced annually (maybe more often) to replace minerals and examine components. Under sink systems are usually for just drinking water. RO wastes a LOT of water for each gallon produced and is not done 'whole house'. If your incoming water is pretty bad and you don't have significant pre-filtration, your RO membrane will be really taxed. I have the iSpring PH100 RO system which claims the lowest waste water without using a permeate pump. It was a DIY. Filters are reasonably priced and it has a remineralization filter for taste. Also have a whole house neutralizer to address low pH.

My 2 cents… at the very least you want softened.  I honestly wouldn’t even recommend softened unless you have an end grain or framed butcherblock as chipping will be a problem. I prefer an eased edge, which is a 1/16 to 1/8 roundover.  An eased edge is going to appear visually square, but be less annoying to bump and have fewer maintenance issues than a softened edge. After that you get into the small roundovers.  These usually start at 3/16 and go up from there.  These will still appear pretty square on a large, thick butcherblock but are noticeably softer.  I don’t really love 3/16 or larger roundovers.  I feel they start to move away from the feel of butcherblocks to wooden counters, as butcherblocks were traditionally thick and “square-ish”. Good luck

Basil is a tropical and sub tropical plant and commercial growing in Florida.  I've seen pictures of basil growing at Stephen's produce in palm bay county set out in the field under full sun and they looked good.  But the Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences, university of Florida states It prefers sun (with a bit of  afternoon shade to protect it from the heat) and moist, but well-drained soil,  OK, but actual growers in Florida (with about 500 acres in production) contradict what the university of Florida suggests and don't see them shading 500 acres. What I did notice in basil field pictures in Florida was raised beds which does supports the university about well-drained soil.  Another thing about basil is they don't tolerate drought well, so raised beds kept well moistened with irrigation dippers would offer you the best chance of success growing basil.  A sun screen of say 50% in the hot afternoon would be optional but I personally don't think it's the problem.  You can get a simple dipper kit from home depot for less than $10. A plant that is over watered will look similar to a plant that is under watered, and you don't want either one.

Hello LL- The rule of thumb when selecting a coffee table is to select a piece that's length is about 1/2 but no more than 2/3 of the length of the sofa, and it should be 4 inches higher or lower than the sofa. Designers refer to this aesthetically pleasing proportion as the "Golden Ratio".  Other clearances that we prioritize for seating furniture selection include the space needed to walk around the coffee table.  There needs to be at least 14" of space between the sofa edges and the coffee table on all sides and 18" is the standard distance.  Side tables should be the same height as the chair arms, as someone previously mentioned and in general you are probably trying to fit too much in this one space.  I would suggest swapping out this rectangular table for a round one to add more curves to the rectilinear forms you are already using. That creates a sense of balance and harmony.  I noticed the square storage ottomans in your photos, and they take up valuable floor space and add too many footprints to the room.  If you need additional storage and seating, they do have a variety of flexible coffee table options that can multitask.  Many have removable tops that conceal storage below and sometimes reverse to serving trays. Others have flexible seating that is stored underneath when not in use. I would try to minimize the foot prints in the room by investing in a more versatile and functional coffee table that can meet a variety of needs - foot rest, blanket and other storage, seating. UK, southern exposure is fine, but further south, they actually can burn in too intense, direct sun, coloration is better in filtered sun, in intense sun, leaves will turn more pale or even develop some reddish tones but I find the deep green more pleasing. text: I never have any trouble with plastic over veggies. What's the problem supposed to be with plastic? Of course, where it touches the plants, with no extra insulation, frost burn is a possibility. I don't care much if a few leaves that hold the plastic up get frost burned. But the burn is there highly localized, and multiple layers removes that problem entirely. The purpose of the plastic is to hold in the warm air coming off the soil, and that will benefit 95% of the plant. Plastic holds warm air better than anything else. It's true that draping plastic directly over harvestable stuff, like cabbages, might not be smart. You'd rather not have frost burns on your cabbage. My winter veggies are chard, daikon, turnips, onions, beets, and carrots, and based on experience, 15F is only mildly threatening to those. What I worry about is that it's actually going to hit 10F.

Barry, this site is largely frequented by people in the US where allotments are not really a thing and where climate, gardening techniques and styles are rather different. I would suggest getting a basic allotment/veg gardening book. This is a good guide too  Starting a nature-friendly allotment (soilassociation.org) The main thing you will need is infinite patience and stoicism. I have had my allotment for over thirty years and every year I watch new gardeners bouncing along in spring full of visions of wonderful home grown vegetables. They are usually swiftly disabused when they find the soil is not perfect friable loam like on TV gardening programmes and are hit by the sheer hard work and obstacles they meet. Step one, join the local allotments association. Step 2, build your compost heap enclosures (It looks as if you might already have some). Step 3, cut down the  buddleja by the railings or your whole plot will become a buddleja forest. Step 4, buy a roll of landscape fabric. Cover most of the growing areas. This is temporary and will stop weeds growing while you work methodically over the ground. Then start digging a bit at a time. Get all the perennial weeds out. Don't worry too much about annual weeds. They are much easier to deal with.  After one thorough digging you may never need to do it again if you decide on no dig techniques. But you have to get those perennials out first. Talk to other allotment holders. Keep all the boards and poles etc which you find as you progress. It all comes in handy. Above all, don't get discouraged. Having an allotment is a wonderful thing.

Wind chill does have an effect on things like citrus.  It will cause the bark to get down to outside temperature faster.  With this freeze, a constant 15 degrees will kill almost all citrus.  If it only gets down to 15 degrees for a couple of hours and then warms up, the bark does not have time to freeze.  If the wind chill is 5 degrees, it will cause the bark to freeze faster than if the air is calm.  Once the bark gets down to the outside temperature, you would be correct at that time wind chill will not matter.  It will not get colder than the outside temperature.

When we first arrived in Western Australia in 1969, the options for food were pretty limited.  Take away food was pretty much fish and chips, or a roast chicken, or maybe a home made hamburgerurged.  There were no chain restaurants.  There were some Chinese and Italian resturants, but they generally included some English style dishes for the die hards who wouldn’t eat ”foreign muck”. A couple of years later the first pizza place opened, run by a friend of my mother’s.  Gradually more Chinese, Italian and some Indian restaurants opened and the chain fast food places moved in.  I remember what a sensation it was when the first Hungry Jack’s (aka Burger King- an Aussie who heard they were coming hoped to cash in by registering the business name and selling it to Burger King, but Burger King decided not to play his game and chose a different trading name) opened not too far from where we were living at the time. Now in the city at least, you can find pretty well any ethnic cuisine you can think of.  Chinese food here is pretty well exactly the same as it is made in China, unlike I have been led to believe Chinese food in the US is, where much has apparently been adapted to US tastes.  Indian food is very, very common, and Thai food has surged ahead in the last 10-15 years as well.  Mexican restaurants are the cuisine du jour at the moment, but are giving way to Middle Eastern and Japanese restaurants.  I remember when there was only one Mexican restaurant in Perth :-). Our little town has a Chinese restaurant and a cafe run by a lady of Lebanese descent which sells a lot of Lebanese dishes as well as traditional Australian foods.  The local supermarket has a much wider range of ingredients than it did when we moved to town in 1986- I remember when DD was in pre-school her class produced a family cookbook with family recipes submitted by each child.  I was on the committee putting it together and one recipe was submitted by a mother who had obviously just torn a page out of a magazine.  We substituted my lemon butter recipe (clearly the mother didn’t care) because the magazine recipe had ”exotic” ingredients like rocket (arugula) which were totally unobtainable locally at the time. In the larger town where I work the bigger supermarkets carry a pretty wide range of ingredients, but sometimes they stop carrying the more exotic ones (which is very annoying) due to low demand.  I think it’s because a large proportion of the population there is not big on cooking or very open to being exposed to new cuisines due to being in the lower socio-economic (often bordering on dysfunctional) cohort.  The town is the district hub for social services so most of those requiring such services live there for easier access.

The comments on here have sometimes drifted to "climbers" in general, instead of just English "climber-shrubs", as requested by the OP. Here are my comments on both: 1)  English Climber-Shrubs - I only grow one of these, which I have grown for over 20 years. It is Graham Thomas. Mine is pruned in its lower part by deer, so it ends up looking sort of like a lolipop. However, as you can see in this pic, left to itself it is as wide on the top parts of it as it is tall overall.   2) Climbers in general: of course, it is difficult to generalize without knowing what TYPE of climbing rose you are talking about, but I have grown climbing once bloomers such as banksias and old ramblers, as well as repeat blooming climbing old tea roses,  climbing tea/noisettes, climbing hybrid teas, and climbing  polyanthas. Then there are the old tea roses (not labeled "climbers"), and even some hybrid musks, which in many cases in a warm climate CAN be made to climb, very much like some of the English "shrub" roses which turned out to be tall enough to be used as climbers in warm climates. In my experience, in my warm climate, all of these roses, if left to themselves, will get at least as wide as they are high, and sometimes wider. Of course, I tend to let roses do whatever they want to do, so I don't have much experience of roses which are pruned frequently to keep them narrower. Jackie

Stucco does not reduce value. But there is still an old cultural norm where some people think a fully brick house is the ultimate in building material and value. Many, actually most American homes, have the "public" money facade only be on the front, with the two sides that are often close to neighbors being muted, and the back being no money left and no perspective view to see it as the front is seen anyway. It's nice to design all 4 elevations at the same level, but that starts with budget and the floor plan, which is not reality for 98% of projects. As far as using full brick, if you were to do that you would be better off demo'ing the existing brick and stone and replacing it with the new brick veneer, not hanging another new wythe in front of the old existing. This would be the least complicated detailing, but much more expensive. Thin brick over the existing is a viable alternative, as long as it is installed correctly. You will also have some specific details to hammer out on the existing first floor like at window returns and sills. And regardless if stucco or thin brick, the bigger detail is the transition from the 2nd floor to the 1st, in getting those planes flush. Stucco (cementious or EIFS) is a much better choice than siding to go over existing brick on the other 3 elevations.

I think part of the added 's' is that the corporate name is also a surname so that it was just natural to add the 's'.      We don't add an s to Target,  or Shop Rite or Walmart unless we're using the possessive as in Target's parking lot or Walmart's return policy. OK I ended up googling it -  Mary Leech, a professor of Linguistics at the University of Cincinnati explains that it is 'an unintentional association' ..............“Often with language, people will make associations with a form or  category, and it sticks, then it gets passed down over time or adapted,”  Leech wrote. “[Kroger’s] could be a misuse of a plural, but my guess  would be that it is an unconscious [association] with possession that  dates back to small, family-owned businesses and it has become a  cultural habit to make that association.” https://www.cincinnati.com/story/life/2022/08/26/why-do-we-add-s-kroger-answer-after-joe-burrow-ad/65420289007/ This article goes into even greater depth. https://styleblueprint.com/everyday/why-do-people-add-s-to-the-end-of-words/

You don't need to bring the architect your drawings. His/her job and his/her years of experience, education and training will help you come up with something even better than anything you can think of. Unless of course, your background is in design. Otherwise, bring him/her a list of your needs, your wants, and your wouldn't it be nice to haves and let the architect do their job working WITH you. It still is a team effort but if you bring him/her a plan already, you're hampering what could be an even better idea. Below is a list of best houses. Something to think about as you work with your architect: The best houses orient the public rooms towards the south for the best passive solar heating and cooling The best houses are L, U, T, H, or I shaped. The best houses are only one to two rooms deep. And covered lanai, porches, garages, etc count as rooms in this case. The best houses make sure kitchens have natural light, meaning windows so one doesn't have to have lighting 24/7 to use the kitchen. (And no, dining areas with windows 10' or more from the kitchen will not allow for natural light.) The best houses make sure all public rooms and bedrooms have windows on at least two walls. The best houses do not if possible put mechanical rooms, pantries or closets on outside walls The best houses do not have diagonal interior walls making for odd spaces. The best houses keep public and private spaces separate. The best houses do not have you walk through the work zone of the kitchen to bring laundry to the laundry room. The best houses do not have the mudroom go through any of the work zones of the kitchen. The best houses do not use the kitchen as a hallway to any other rooms. The best houses do not put toilets or toilet rooms up against bedroom walls or public areas. The best houses do not have walk in closets too small to stand inside. The best houses have separation, such as closets, between bedrooms and between bedrooms and public rooms. The best houses do not have roofs that are overly large, and dominate the exterior of the house. The best houses do not have stick on exterior materials only on the front façade. The best houses have an organizing “spine” so it’s easy to determine how to get from room to room in the house and what makes sense. Meaning they don’t have meandering circulation paths. And added from Architectrunnerguy: -The best houses enrich their owners souls. -The best houses are timeless. -The best houses incorporate the intangibles of good design. -The best houses have strong organizational concepts. -The best houses have owners who understand what good design is….and isn’t. -The best houses are shaped in response to the Sun. -The best houses have all its parts in good proportion to each other and to the whole. -The best houses enhance the street. -The best houses balance function, aesthetics and construction. -The best houses recognize there are always design tradeoffs. -The best houses break some “rules”. -The best houses are a joy to live in.

There is no overkill, but ... Many typical liners, including Wolf's, may not be deep enough (front-to-back) to fully cover front burner plume expansion. I don't see 42-inch liners in my 2021 Wolf Design Guide.  Perhaps mine is out of date. If we assume a liner capture aperture of 40 x 19 inches, then the capture area is 5.3 square feet.  At a minimum, you want 90 CFM/sq. ft., or in this case about 500 CFM.  To get this in a typical pressure loss system (baffles, hood transition, duct, MUA) you will need a roughly 700 CFM rated blower.  To keep noise down you will certainly need a silencer in the duct between the blower and the hood. In any case, I strongly encourage you to consider how much of that smoke you want to escape the hood, and hence whether you should go for a deeper hood. If an undersized liner is used in a wood cabinet hood, the uncovered interior should be faced with stainless steel.  If there is some volume below the baffles to the bottom edge of the wood hood, then we can consider the hood size to be larger.  Not sure if it would be deeper pending more information.  If so, we can calculate based on the entire hood entry aperture as see that higher flow rate is called for. Note that the noise from a silenced Wolf hood/blower system (such as I have) will be dominated by baffle hiss, and this could be louder in your case if the large hood entry area is doing actual 90 CFM, and the inner liner area is doing some multiple of that. Check out an Asian restaurant for how far towards the cook the hood entry aperture extends.  Scale down from 7 ft to 6 ft hood height. Basic rule: the farther a hood system deviates from standard commercial design, the greater the penalty on either power efficiency or capture and containment efficiency.

I post this list all the time. Anything in bold might be an issue with this plan. Personally, I agree with the others who say find an architect to design a house that works for you and your family. The best houses orient the public rooms towards the south for the best passive solar heating and cooling The best houses are L, U, T, H, or I shaped. The best houses are only one to two rooms deep. And covered lanai, porches, garages, etc count as rooms in this case. The best houses make sure kitchens have natural light, meaning windows so one doesn't have to have lighting 24/7 to use the kitchen. (And no, dining areas with windows 10' or more from the kitchen will not allow for natural light.) The best houses make sure all public rooms and bedrooms have windows on at least two walls. The best houses do not if possible put mechanical rooms, pantries or closets on outside walls The best houses do not have diagonal interior walls making for odd spaces. The best houses keep public and private spaces separate. The best houses do not have you walk through the work zone of the kitchen to bring laundry to the laundry room. The best houses do not have the mudroom go through any of the work zones of the kitchen. The best houses do not use the kitchen as a hallway to any other rooms. The best houses do not put toilets or toilet rooms up against bedroom walls or public areas. The best houses do not have walk in closets too small to stand inside. The best houses do not have roofs that are overly large, and dominate the exterior of the house. The best houses do not have stick on exterior materials only on the front façade. The best houses have an organizing “spine” so it’s easy to determine how to get from room to room in the house and what makes sense. Meaning they don’t have meandering circulation paths.

As you already are aware, you can do the outlet strips under your upper cabinets, aka Plugmold.  However, the things that you keep regularly plugged in, such as coffee maker or toaster, will have the cords dangling in an unsightly way (see pic).  The solution is to have the Plugmold, and also have a couple receptacles in the backsplash just at the place or places where you will be plugging in coffeemaker/toaster regularly. When you install the receptacles in the backsplash, they should be installed low and horizontal, so that they are less obtrusive and are hidden by toaster, coffee maker, paper towel holder etc.  A good height for the horizontal receptacles is 4" on center.  You don't want them so low that a thick plug can't be plugged in cause it butts up to the counter, and you don't want it too high so that it is obtrusive.  Also buy the receptacle frames that are "screwless", and companies like Lutron and Leviton make them in dozens of colors to get close to the color of your backsplash.  There used to be a company that would make receptacles to order to match exactly the backsplash, but they've gone out of business.

@User noted that Limited option lines like Ikea only have 1 option. And you have to use it, because the sides are not finished otherwise. The panelized (cope and stick) doors that the OP is showing have to be ordered at least 3/4" (7/8" is probably preferred) wider to be used as cover panels.  You can't simply move them forward without leaving a gap in the back and any attempt to fill that gap (with wood of course) will result in a stile appearing 3/4" thicker. I do prefer cover panels pulled forward to align flush with doors, but I don't think it looks good unless everything is pulled forward flush with the doors.  This means any molding or crown on top needs to pull brought flush as does any type of bottom or light rail.  It can also cause filler pieces to look off a bit, as you are basically creating an inset framing effect for your cabinets and if you have several fillers they can appear noticeably recessed.

I had a cedar shake roof on my first house, which was built in 1952 and was still in good shape when I bought it 22 years later; by the time it got to 30 years it needed replacing. When I sold that home, I chose a different style home that had a steel, standing seam roof.  Almost 20 years later it looks about as good as new and I haven't had a bit of maintenance. Find yourself a steel or synthetic substitute for a cedar shake roof and you'll be much happier.

Hi, Shirley ~ Perennial plants, which includes trees and shrubs, will need regular rootwork or dividing if the plants are to remain robust and healthy. Root congestion begins to take a toll on growth rate, vitality levels (health), yields (where applicable), eye appeal, and the plant's ability to defend itself at the approximate point in time when the soil/root mass can be lifted from the pot intact. Eventually, root congestion can rob the plant of its entire potential for growth, and negatively impact the plant as already noted, leaving a grower with plants the appearance of which make clear their level of vitality. Potting up only partially relieves the stress of root congestion - it's like kicking the can down the road each year. Choosing the right soil would have a major impact on your ability to chose a certain size cache pot, or more than one size cache pot, and regular bare-rooting, root pruning (or dividing where applicable), and a change of potting medium, would allow you to freely exchange plants in nursery cans between the cache pots. You can often maintain plants in the same pot for a decade or more if appropriate rootwork is done regularly, usually every 1-3 years. A healthy root system is always a prerequisite if we are to expect a healthy plant. Al

Natural stone is a great feature that helps connect your home to the site and I like your selection. However too many times I have seen stone used incorrectly and it looks cheap and nasty. If you are going to the added expense of applying a stone finish then don't shortchange yourself and regret not doing it properly every time you walk past it or are there enjoying your fireplace. A couple of rules to go by with stone. 1. If you are going to make a feature of something the clad the entire feature not half of it, otherwise it will look like you ran out of money - how embarrassing! 2. Always think in 3D. Natural stone is a 3D material and should be applied to all exposed surface not just one. I have seen columns clad only on the street face and it looks so cheap. Trust me - don't go there. Paint it a feature colour and save up to do the job properly if need be, after all you deserve the best. 3. When applying the stone wrap it around the corner. DO NOT finish one face with a raw edge and start the next face - again it looks so fake. There are three basic ways that you can treat an external corner so it looks real. (i) Mitre the corners so with half or 1/3 rd 2/3rds tiles or stone. You the start the second face with the balance of the sheet that when mitred to the first sheet looks as one solid piece of stone. (ii) Finish the stone hard up against another element that will conceal the raw edge. (iii) Select a stone that comes with a specially cut corner tile. These are usually natural stone that have been had the back specially cut out to form an "L" for the corner. ECO OUTDOORS offer a selection of stone walling with the corner stone. It may not be cheap but it sure looks good and saves you sitting in front of your fire saying "I wish we had spent the extra and done it properly. Trust me it will eat away at you for years to come.

First, I would determine the project design - where does the paneling begin and end?  How high does it go?  If it goes to the ceiling is there a need to re-install crown?  One way to start is to collect as many pictures of these projects as possible and then note aspects that you like or dislike.  Do you like more paneling segments or less?  Thicker or thinner segments?  Do you want any mouldings in the inner panel? I think that any decent woodworking organization should be able to make a scale sketch possibly a simple rendering.  You can do the same thing using sketchup or home designer, this is a valuable skill for future projects. For trim work, I would get several quotes.  Ask questions about how they are going to assemble and finish and take good notes.  You'll surprised at how techniques vary and learn alot about how they work and price their jobs. One way to determine a fair price is to ask how many hours it is going to take. I've done several of these "wainscoting" projects.  Done well, they involve pre-asssembling the segments, the joints are assembled with glue and pocket screws so the joint is perfect.  Don't allow a carpenter to just nail or glue 1x lumber to the wall.  Once the segments are pre-assembled the outside pieces may need to be scribed to inside corners.  Please have a look at the four wainscoting videos on Gary Katz youtube site.

You are asking for design, build, and rendering. That cuts out 90% of folks. But, figure 10-14K, if you want it done correctly and well, by a finish carpenter or cabinet maker,  in paint grade MDF. They may not have those rendering skills. If you want an even higher end raised panel judges panel look, triple that. For real stained wood, double again. If you just want some cheap screen molding slapped up, then DIY it. Handymen find the math needed to do that challenging. They absolutely cannot render it.

I haven't grown that cultivar but I have grown a number of other oakleaf hydrangeas and recommend them frequently for clients. They are by far my favorite type of hydrangea! With enough sun exposure, ALL oakleafs develop great fall color and recent breeding programs have focused on maximizing that and developing more compact selections. Jetstream appears to be somewhere in between a full sized oakleaf cultivar and the more compact or dwarf forms. It is too big for my current garden but I'd consider growing Jetstream in a container to keep it a bit smaller. Should be a strong performer in zone 7.

I used to have one many years ago but swapped it for a smaller cultivar. The fall color of the foliage was awesome but then, that is common in all of the oakleaf hydrangeas that I have had. The best fall color show happens when it got some morning and afternoon fall sun during the cooler fall temperatures.  Its planting location received very little direct sun (corner spot with two fences on two sides, one big holly on the 3rd side and a big Crape Myrtle providing shade on top) but always bloomed well (common on oakleaf hydrangeas too) and had nice fall colors. Enjoy! Very drought tolerant here in Texas 8a but do not let it sit in wet soil for too long or you will be sorry as they can easily catch root rot. I have no idea how they measure "stronger" branches; I did not notice anything specially stronger though. The blooms are smaller compared to other oakleaf varieties and thus, they did not flop in my 'well protected from winds/storms' location.

Adding to what was said above, I'm recalling an old thread here (by the late mamapinky, IIRC) which delved into your question. What I recall is that washing soda is sodium carbonate (Na2CO3) with pH of 11 while baking soda is sodium bicarcbonate  (NaHCO3) which has a pH of 8.5. IOW, baking soda is only slighly alkaline. while laundry soda is much more strongly alkaline.  In practical laundry terms, the differences were said to make washing soda significantly more effective than baking soda at softening water (by binding out water hardening minerals such as calcium and magnesium) and at removing fatty/greasy soiling. The binding to minerals is the "precipitating water softener" bit.  Both do it but washing soda is a lot more effective at it than baking soda. Wish I could find that old thread but, since it wasn't turning up for me in searches right now, I tried some quick internet searches. Besides confirming what Dadoes reported, the trustworthy sources further explained that washing sodas are more effective than baking soda in laundry because washing sodas more readily interact with fats and grease deposits on laundry. The interaction converts them into soap-like substances which can be more readily washed and rinsed away. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_carbonate The searches also reminded me of a stupid-pet-trick: baking soda can be converted into washing soda when baked in a hot oven for an hour or so.

Agree with Paul Barden, yesterday Sunday 2/19/23 it got up to 50 F in my zone 5a. I pulled out a bunch of green sticks (with tiny leaves) and ALL OF THEM have ZERO roots, despite rooting them since Nov. 2022.  That's 4 months of rooting.  Hard wood rootings (done through winter) are very slow in forming roots. The very few rootings that have decent roots:  these have 4 to 7 set of full leaflets.  But these winter-roots are not as long as summer-roots.  I took these rootings out of the fabric pouches after I saw roots coming out at bottom.  CONCLUSION:  Unless there's at least 4 set of full-leaflets like below, there are not enough roots on the stem to pull out.  Winter roots are wimpier than summer roots.  Winter rooting can't handle dense medium like sharp sand.   I lost countless cuttings when I tested different combo with sharp sand, such as 100% sharp sand (topped with fertile clay),  1/2 sharp sand and 1/2 vermiculite, or 1/4 sharp sand with 3/4 Pro-mix potting soil and perlite.  Their stems stay green, but THEY FAILED TO FORM ROOTS. The only medium that wimpy winter roots can push through is VERY FLUFFY like at least 1/2 perlite. A friend who rooted INDOOR through her zone 6 winter, with Grow-lights told me the same.

Meaning that once you start demolishing tile, the hammering could disturb plumbing and wall tiles which can lead to leaks.   Replacing fixtures (tubs/toilets/sinks) is neither cheap nor cosmetic.  And doing it piecemeal will not get you what you want. What you need to do is figure out a budget and see what can be done relatively inexpensively and with the least amount of disruption. Personal story--I have a vacation home with a large master bath done in the 1990s.  All the tile and fixtures are white, chrome fittings, white vanities with laminate tops.  Poor lighting, small shower, huge mirror over vanity, tiny storage cabinet and large/never used jetted tub.  After getting a quote for over $50K to gut the space, we decided we would rather spend that money elsewhere, so we went for a cosmetic update.  We installed a new glass shower enclosure (enlarging the shower would have been very expensive), painted the vanities slate blue, replaced the vanity top with a quartz remnant, installed new sinks and faucets, lighting fixtures and mirrored medicine cabinets.  Then painted the walls to work with the blue cabinets and quartz tops.  All told it was about $5-$6K.  We contracted out everything except painting.  No changes to tiles, fixtures, windows or layout.  Do I wish we could put  the space that the tub takes up to better use?  Yes, but it wasn't worth the $$. So my point is to take stock of the space and your budget and plan out how to make your preferred changes. Here's a photo of the vanity wall which represents most of the changes:

Your friend might want to try keeping the plant indoors year-round, if there's some sun there in the summer too.  This could encourage blooming and would presumably also keep it from being pee'd on, Note that urine is an excellent source of nitrogen, so if the dog has been frequently "watering" the soil in the pot, your friend needs to be careful NOT to add any fertilizer that contains nitrogen (which is pretty much all of them).  A lot of plants don't flower well if they're getting loads of nitrogen, so the dog pee could be the reason why this plant doesn't bloom -- especially if she's adding any other fertilizer.  If she does move it indoors, though, or if her elderly dog reaches the end of his days, the plant might eventually appreciate a little fertilizer.

@Beth H. : One of the main questions that Austin Lee asked was: "...how to reduce the heat on the surface directly above our new gas fire place insert ". Redoing the wall with metal studs, etc as Wacky Tacky has suggested would be the proper method for plastering the wall (and I agree). However,  it will not reduce the surface temperature of the wall, although the plaster will be less likely to crack. Adding a hood (also called heat deflector) can in fact reduce the heat on the plaster surface significantly, so I'm not sure why you are saying it will not. The hood will deflect the heat out towards the room instead of going directly straight up the wall, giving it a moment to mix with room air, which occurs quickly. I'm not sure why you are saying it won't help. Hoods have been used as heat deflectors for fireplaces for many years. In fact, most ventless gas fireplace manufacturers include them with their units and they cannot be installed without them if there is a combustible wall surface above the fireplace. Ventless gas fireplaces push 100% of the heat into the room, so they are even more problematic than a direct vent fireplace such as the Valor G4 insert. @Austin Lee I recommend you do a simple test by creating a mock hood (heat deflector) using a couple 2x4s with a piece of sheet metal screwed on top as illustrated below. I would test it with both 4" and 6" wide pieces to see if there is much difference between them. Get yourself an infrared thermometer to check the wall temperature at various heights above the fireplace with and without the mock hood. Here's how the mock device might look shown taped to the wall. You need to make sure the sheet metal is flush to the wall so no heat gets between it and the wall. Maybe tape it there as well.   I guarantee you will find a significant difference in the wall temperature during this test. I would not be surprised if it was as much as 50%. An actual hood will perform better due to the construction at an angle with a leading edge. And to your point Beth, yes, the hood will get very hot to the touch just as the other components of the fireplace as described in the owner's manual. With that said, it is also possible to fabricate a hood that is insulated to reduce the heat at the top surface, although I have yet to see an insulated hood offered on the market, I'd be happy to design one.

I wonder if it's some kind of Synadenium/Euphorbia?  If you remove a leaf, does white sap come out?  Before you remove a leaf, put some newspaper, paper towel, or plastic on the floor underneath the spot where you will do it because if it is a Euphorbia, white latex sap will leak out for a few minutes and you don't want that on your floor.  Also, don't get it on your skin because it could cause a rash, similar to poison ivy.  Definitely don't get it in your eye. That's a cute shelf but I believe both plants would appreciate a spot in more light.  But if you discover white sap in your plant, don't put that one where people will bump into it.  Euphorbias are interesting to look at, but that sap is no joke. If there is no sap, I might wonder if it's some kind of Pilea.

See other thread on basement water problems. For now, just buy a cheap plastic downspout splashblock to catch the water, keep it from creating a sinkhole that exacerbates the water problems, and help direct it away from the house. Until you can clean debris/seal your leaking gutter when you buy a ladder or hire someone.

You need to get up there, or pay someone to, and find out why the gutter is overflowing or leaking there.  Possibilities:  the gutter is clogged with leaves (very common, very easy fix), there is a seam that has opened or a crack in the gutter (fix with sealant, also easy), the gutter is not hung so that water flows down a slight incline to the downspout (can be fixed, less easy) - or any combination of the three. In the meantime, go to your closest big box hardware store and buy either a downspout ground block, or even a large-ish bucket or a plastic bin, and also buy a length of cheap vinyl gutter.  Postion the block or bucket under the leak to catch the water. Run the cheap gutter from the block or cut an opening in the bucket/bin and insert the end of the gutter into it - point the gutter toward the street.

Turn off the hot water at the shut-off valve. Take everything out from inder the sink. Use a flashlight to find the valve. Clockwise to close it. Wipe everything dry. The hose, the valve and the hookup for the dishwasher. With the light on turn the water back on. Look for the leak. Let us know. Add pics to one of your posts.

Put nothing on the inside of the walls (e.g. paints of any sort). They will do nothing but bubble and peel and make any future work more difficult. You have to alleviate on the outside. Make sure your downspouts have leaders that discharge water as far away from the house as possible (10' +). Make sure grade is sloped away from perimeter at minimum 6" in 10'. Other maintenance things like keeping gutters clean and no buildup of mulch/stone against the house or creating bathtubs. And just to note, in an old house with brick foundation walls, there is no repairing walls against water intrusion, you'd have to dig outside and put waterproofing and drainage. Your seller disclosures should have said something about known water intrusion.

It could be that the connection has loosened or wasn't tightened well when it was changed. I had water leaking into my under sink cabinet, turned out to be from failed sealant under the faucet so any water that splashed up onto the counter around the faucet was draining down there.

If your rocky slope can grow that much green and tall weeds and is surrounded by forest, it is getting a good amount of water. To try and change that large a space over to a weed free groundcover would be setting yourself up for a lifetime of aggravation. It would make more sense to work with nature and what wants to grow there naturally. To that end start planting tall weeds that will spread and self-sow and bloom in the summer and fall. Then you will have a blooming rocky slope and something pretty to look at. Plants like Black Eye Susan, Joe Pye and Ironweed, fall blooming asters, Shasta Daisy, Helianthus, Beebalm and on and on. Marjoram and oregano have a nice summer bloom for shorter groundcover layer in the mix. During the growing season you can just let it be. Let it grow tall. The other weeds won't matter when all the weed flowers are blooming. Then just mow the slope down over the winter and start short and fresh in the spring.

it's not difficult to install.  some cement tiles come presealed, some don't.  ( I have two diff brands that i've installed.  one on my shower wall that I had to seal multiple times prior to install, and these from CleTile that were already, somewhat sealed:  install is easy.  You soak the tiles in water prior to laying them in thinset.  if you don't, the dry tile could soak up all the moisture from the thinset leading to drying out and improper adhesion. Grouting with dark grout is tricky.  (I applied 3 coats of sealer on this first.  when it's sealed water will bead on top) I wanted black grout but cement tiles will stain. You cannot spread out the grout over the face of the tile like you would with regular tile.  I had to carefully pipe in the grout in the joints while quickly wiping away residue.  in some spots the black did bleed into the tile and discolor.  if you enlarge this you can see some of it.  the same can happen w/any color grout, which is why it should be limited to spreading it only over the joints and not the entire face of the tile. you'll also see some fine chips and cracks around the edges of the tile. this is normal.  the coloring on these is marble dust and pigment placed over the cement base. These aren't supposed to look perfect.  If you want perfect, get the porcelain tiles that look like this. Since it's a powder room, it prob won't get that much activity.  someone wearing shoes w/sharp heels would prob cause the most damage. what else would you like to know? those lili tiles are beautiful.  which color are you doing? the griege one?  that green is stunning

Just for clarification… A general rule for VOC’s is what goes in must come out.  Bona Drifast has slightly more VOC’s than Duraseal, so it will off gas more per gallon.  The Duraseal product that I looked at had 4.27 lbs per gallon and Bona Drifast has 4.6 lbs per gallon. Traditionally, faster curing products off-gas over a shorter time, however, some producers have began using the trick of binding the hydrocarbons to slow down VOC release even in fast drying products. For example, Tradionally conversion varnish was a fast curing product used in many consumer goods such as cabinets.  Most off-gassing would be finished inside a week and only trace amounts would off-gas after three weeks, which is often faster than these products would be installed.  In response to air quality regulations, the Xylene was bound and now off-gasses much less but continues for about a year. Having said that, if I were picking between these two products with off-gassing being the main concern… I would pick the Bona and feel safe that is the better bet.

If you want to have your afghan turn out the size the pattern states, you need to crochet to guage.  (I’m surprised the gauge instructions didn’t include how many stitches across made whatever measurement.) When gauge is important, you need to do a small piece to test whether size of your stitches is the same as the person who wrote the pattern’s stitches.  So you crochet however many stitches across the guage suggests, then do four rows, then measure your resulting square side to side and top to bottom.  It should be the same as the measurements mentioned in the guage.  If it is not, you need to either adjust how tightly/loosely you crochet, use a larger or smaller hook as appropriate, or adjust the number of stitches and rows you crochet to get the size afghan you want.

Thanks for your location.  In 20+ years on this site I can't remember anyone from La Jolla writing in.  Laguna is about as close to a coastal similar location.  Usually people will tell us they are in San Diego, but when you ask, they are often east of Grosmont, which, as you know, is nothing like the San Diego climate, so different turf types are required.  Are you in the area which gets late night and morning low clouds and fog? Have you walked your neighborhood to find lawns that you really like? Are you going to have someone care for it or are you caring for it? If you are caring for it, how much work are you willing to do for mowing and watering?  Mowing ranges from every 3 days for a short, hybrid bermuda to every other week for St Augustine or a hybrid buffalo. Before you go with West Coast Turf's suggestion, ask them to give you some addresses where their turf is installed. Check around to see if UC Verde buffalo grass is available.  One of the keys to underfoot comfort is not having seed stalks sticking up.  Seeded buffalo and even other hybrids can get seed heads.  I believe the UC Verde does not get them, but check to be sure.  UC Verde might only be available online, so ask around.  This grass is possibly the most drought resistant variety.  Bermuda is similarly good, but it has other issues with maintenance. TIF 419 bermuda is a contractor grade turf, but don't let that sway you away.  It is also the gold standard of hybrid bermudas.  The reason contractors use it is that it is raised by the square mile up in Hemet/Winchester, and is super easy to get a lot of fast. When you buy sod you want to buy from someone who sells lots of pallets of it every day.  For example Lowe's and Home Depot sell sod, but they might only sell 5 pallets in 2 weeks.  My local sod outlet in San Antonio sells 14 pallets every day with new grass delivered nightly.

Ideally means not the only option. I do think that 10 feet is really the ideal change but everyone has different standards. First - it matters what your ceiling height is. We had 10 feet and then 18 inches between floors so 11.5 feet. If you have 8 foot ceilings - well then 9.5 feet. Second - how tall do you expect the front of your house to be? This is a regional issue and neighborhood issue. In my area, we typically expect 4-6 steps above grade to a front porch. So that is 3-4 feet. If you raise that to 6 feet - well there is another 2 feet. Does that cost money? Heck yeah. But it depends on your foundation type and if it wraps around. Brick costs serious money. Not to mention the steps on your porch. Third/last - you can always move dirt around. Mostly it gets expensive when you take it off site. With 1/2 acre/ you can often use it to flatten out a sloped back yard. So ideal is somewhere between 6 and 10 feet in slope. Each foot away from that could be $10k more or $20k more (or probably more) and it depends on a lot of factors. So it depends on your budget of course. So define ceiling height of basement, foundation type - brick/stone (4 sides?) and porch height. When you raise the house and the porch, you also increase the steps from garage to house. Which costs money and reduces effective garage size. A thought is a partial walkout - our neighbor had this. Maybe 1/3 of the house could "walk out" - on the low side. Is that then 6 feet from the highest corner? In this setting, there was a retaining wall and the walkout patio has stairs to the rest of the yard. Also, moving dirt is not that expensive but taking it away gets pricey. You can level the back yard and dig out a portion of it and place a retaining wall. I suppose my goal/advice is to not focus on some magical 6 foot number and get some local expert advice.

You can do a "walk up" basement (a door up to grade) anywhere where the basement is below grade. It is a matter of how much excavation beyond the door that you prefer (or can afford). A "walk out" basement insinuates that the grade continues beyond at or below the basement level and more of the foundation wall is exposed.  But I agree if no one does basements in your area, why is that - usually that means you have a very shallow, if any, frost depth, or soil conditions (e.g. rock or sand) that would preclude having basements.

Wall color is chosen last.  You haven't said what your countertops are.  That is an important part of the puzzle as well as the floors and cabinets.  Once everything else is done start sampling wall colors.  Very dark cabinets are a very specific design choice that won't appeal to everyone, so I hope you're planning on living in this house a long time and as Beverly said, have a lot of natural and artificial light.  Otherwise you will be creating a cave.  Remember that pictures online and in magazines are photoshopped and lit to look their best and those finishes won't necessarily look the same in your house.

Congrats on having a house from the 1920's with enough room on the first floor to even fit laundry and a full bath.  I think you are headed in the right direction.  You just need to not think of these spaces as flowing together with the dining room but very separate. I would paint and style the laundry and bathroom to look very different than the dining room so there is a serious mental separation. Tell us why you are thinking French door for both entry into laundry area and into bathroom.  Do you have them elsewhere in your home and you are trying to replicate?  Is it a light issue?  Do you just like the look?  Do you want a wide opening? If you are running to pee, closing double doors is extra work.  The lack of privacy isn't good.  And if you are older and less mobile it makes closing the door twice the work. I'd make both doorways - from dining into laundry room, and from laundry into bath solid single doors.  Have doors made that match the original doors in the rest of your home.  Get hardware that is sympathetic to your house's history. I've lived in a 170 year old house and needed to put in a first floor powder room so my visiting parents didn't have to run up and down the steep stairs throughout the day.  So I *get* the need to respect an old home, its beauty and limitations, and consider aging in place, which is an entirely new concept and wasn't around when your home was built.
