Here - because of our late to start and short growing season (not safe to plant out toms until end of May/beginning of June), tomato plants sold at nurseries here are almost always sold in gallon sized containers, often with flowers and fruit present. I would disagree about not fertilizing. Depriving it of nutrients - there are virtually none in container potting soil - will stress the plant and weaken it, making it more vulnerable to pests and diseases and at a disadvantage when you can finally plant out. I would use a dilute liquid fertilizer  once a week or with every other watering. You don't say where you are located but I would try to get the plant in the ground as soon as possible. Using something like a cloche or wall of waters will guard against cold overnight temps (to some degree) as well as heating up soil temps. When I was 22 living with my best friend Michael (AKA Ramona Montez), we had the idea to open a tea and pastry shop and call it "El Morocco Tea Room" and serve a variety of teas along with coffee cakes and pastries that I would make. I think this could have been a successful venture, but no one would lend us the money to get started.  It was perhaps a bit beyond what Austin would support in the early 1970s because the people in Austin with money were extremely conservative, and the people who were progressive were equally cheap.  Austin was NOT Los Angeles. That idea did not work out, and so Michael moved to New York, and I moved to San Francisco, where we both felt we would be more appreciated - and that was a good move for both of us.  At that time, everyone in Austin was telling Michael and me to "mellow out" but I felt that if I mellowed out anymore than I already had that I would rot.  Austin was not the place for either of us.  Location is very important when you are opening a restaurant. In San Francisco, I did get a job baking coffee cakes and pastries for Island Restaurant, owned by a commune of hippies who made their money selling marijuana (unbeknownst to me at the time) upstairs from the restaurant at 16th and Sanchez Streets, one and a half blocks from where I lived at the time.  This was a great location, since I had to work graveyard, but working graveyard also meant that I did not see any customers going upstairs for the real moneymaker. One of the problems with this restaurant was that the wait staff was always stoned, and so customers (who were probably also stoned while there) seldom got what they ordered, unless they picked it up from one of the counters themselves.  This was not my primary job, and I worked there only two nights a week, and not for very long, as I did not like the hours.  Island Restaurant reminded me a lot of Van Gogh's Ear Restaurant in Venice, where I lived 20 years later.  In fact, Venice in the 1990s very much reminded me of San Francisco in the 1970s. If, however, I opened a restaurant in my 70s, it would probably be a pizza place, and I would want to have a brick pizza oven.  At this point, my menu would be much more limited than it would have been in my younger years, but I would want to offer a variety of styles of pizza.  I would only make Neapolitan pizzas at a max diameter of 14", but I would expect people to order individual pizzas at 12" diameter, and I would offer larger pizzas of different styles. I would still want to offer desserts, and I would want to serve coffee cakes for breakfast.  My favorite is Walnut Sour Cream Coffee Cake, but I would rather serve that with tea than with coffee.  I would also want to serve scones, waffles, and popovers.

Your gap is too wide; there should be no gap. Disconnect the drain lines/disposal and remove the sink from the cabinet. You may have to unscrew the clips. If you can't get access to the screws, place a stiff scraper between the sink flange and the stone bottom and hammer the scraper into the screws; they will fail and the sink will drop. Scrape the old caulk from the sink flange and stone bottom. Install a Hercules Universal Sink Harness (BB Industries) to the cabinet sides. Run a pipe clamp through a 2x4 that spans the larger bowl and the drain hole and pull the sink to within 1" of the stone bottom. Silicone the flange, tighten the clamp, position the sink for the proper reveal, tighten the HUSH, remove the clamp, spritz the squeeze-out with Windex, spit on your finger, wipe up the squeeze-out, connect the drain lines and you're done. This may be a 3-hour job the first time you do it; it takes any man of my crew just over an hour. Without replacing your countertop, there is no other proper way to fix this. More topical silicone is useless. Your sink failed because of the clips and the fact that you have a divided sink with steel on the flat which flexed and caused the leak. A strapped divided sink cannot flex without defying the laws of physics. This repair is permanent and you will never have black/brown crud at your stone/sink flange joint again because it will never leak again. To other readers, if you have black/brown recurring crud at your sink flange/stone bottom, your sink is leaking. If the gap were smaller it wouldn't leak; if it were larger, you could clean it with that toothbrush you've been trying. It's just the right size to allow capillary action; sucking and trapping dirty sink water. Gross. I've never grafted plums, but have done it with apples, pears, cherries. I find the success rate is better with apples than pears. Last year I made about 20 grafts to a Bradford pear and none took. The year  before, as a test I grafted a Shenandoah pear to the same tree with a success ratio of 1/1. I think the problem is that the Bradford pear comes out of dormancy before the scion sellers on the west coast ship their scions. This year I ordered pear scions from Fedco in Maine and I received them in the first week of March, so they're already grafted. The west coast seller I ordered D'Anjou scions from hasn't shipped so I think those scions won't take; if I ever received them. Last year I was grafting in the 2nd and 3rd week of April. I found that after all the grafting to the pear tree the tree threw out lots of new growth. Lots of long new growth right off the trunk/ So plenty of places for a graft to a stem with the exact same size diameter as my scion. I did all the grafts with a drill into the bottom 18" of the trunk, because of vine girdling and deer damage to the trunk. Also hoping I'll get very little water sprouts in the future. We have the Elkay Crosstown stainless steel farmhouse sink.  Single bowl with the corner "offset" drain.  The corner offset drain is one of the best things - it allows more undersink cabinet storage because the plumbing is not down the center.  You also don't have two plumbing drains the way you have with a double bowl.  You will be surprised at the expanse inside the cabinet under the sink. This list is a summary of what they build, it is not presented as a choosable upgrade, that will be a separate list (but may cover some of the same items). "Upgrade" is a generic term relative to each item, so understand the nuances of it's meaning and evaluate on that - as examples: - Interior doors are solid core. Understand that their base install already is an "upgrade" over hollow core, but you didn't choose it, it's just the door spec for the market they have positioned themselves to offer as a standard. But since they didn't state the style, let's assume they are flush. A chooseable upgrade might be paying extra for 6 panel doors. - Kitchen counter is probably an allowance. You will probably have 2 levels of types of counters that you choose from their supplier. One of the choices can be considered an "upgrade" over the other, and sometimes you can even "upgrade" an "upgrade" by going over those costs if you fall in love with an expensive slab beyond the 2 levels offered, and pay out of pocket. - The driveway is asphalt. "Upgrade" here would mean concrete, a completely different material, timeline, and contractor. - Often back sliders have a simple wooden step down, and backyards are seeded. An offerable "upgrade" would be a small deck or sod. - Often "upgrades" are offered plan-wise, like extending the Dining Room or adding a fireplace. Typically a builder will not venture far from the materials and methods they always build houses, even if it were a custom house. So you can't just state you want something different than their summary list you have posted. You'd have to get their list of items they offer "upgrades" on and evaluate their stated costs for your budget, your desires, and the neighborhood specific to only those items offered.

For one thing, using a very dark grout w/white marble sometimes causes staining along the marble edges.  You may get shadowing and the grout may look 'off'. secondly, using a very dark grout w/the marble mosaic is NOT required for it to 'pop'.  Just use a nice gray grout for the subway and the mosaic.  Plus, you'll have to decide how to 'edge' out the mosaic design.  do you plan on using pencil liners or a Schluter jollly?  If you don't use either, it may look weird have 2 diff grout colors suddenly change. But staining w/the dark grout is a real issue let me show you my shower w/white tile and a marble mosaic.  For both I used Mapei Warm Gray unsanded grout.  even if the mosaic didn't have the black, do you think I would have needed a dark grout to make it 'pop' ?  Of course not.  the design is enough pop on it's own. I also have a cement tile accent wall in the shower. I used the Mapei Charcoal grout for those tiles.  I was very careful applying the grout and wiping it off, but I still got staining (and I sealed these 4 times prior to grouting)  Here's the closeup.  look at the joints and you'll see it.  (the coloring in cement tiles are made from marble dust)  Luckily this is more of a rustic, old-world look tile and it doesn't matter This is what will happen to your marble tiles, 100% guaranteed.  (also, make sure you use the Bianco (white) thinset for marble tiles when you set these.  don't use the gray thinset.  Stick with the gray grout.  Since that marble tile leans on the cooler side, I'd do the Warm Gray, Silver, maybe the Gray color, but do a grout test on sample pieces first to see if it bleeds  Then do a sample white tile w/a few of the grout colors and see what you think.  Maybe you'll like the white tiles w/the slightly darker gray color you do on the marble. another thing about dark grout colors.  use very little water during the clean up phase, and use exact measurement w/water during the mixing phase.  Too much water dilutes the coloring and will leave you with light spots when it dries

It could be mortar washed - very lightly over the brown color, but that is not the main reason it looks this way. This look is achieved by using an FBA spec brick (meaning more variations in size, shape, and color of the face) as opposed to FBX (rigid dimensions and uniformity), and the bricks are formed by molding as opposed to an extruded process. The mortar is just a flush joint, which fills the variations on the edges of the FBA face. Mortar washing would fill more of the variations within the face.

There are a few reasons that some in the design industry do not like the LED integral recessed cans: - the flat sealed lens is too "dead looking" when off - the baffle depth is too shallow - the throw of the light causes glare - you don't have the slight difference in lamp style, like from a PAR to BR, to fine-tune - single stamped metal trims are bulkier - if the LED goes out in the future, you have to replace the entire trim, which will probably not match the others. Nor will the sheen or transparency of the lens. - you can't experiment with different 'bulbs', you can only change the CCT - and for your specific selection the 5"/6" replacement means the trim is very wide and prominent. If you have a properly sized BR30 'bulb' that means you have 5" fixtures, not 6". As far as longevity of LED integral cans vs LED 'bulbs', it's a crapshoot for any of them. Longevity is predominantly a function of how much heat the driver electronics is exposed to. Some lamps are designed better than others for that. But if one goes out, it is overall much easier to just change a 'bulb' (or all of them) than 1/all the fixtures.

Hi Abinaya, In reality it is not a good idea to use Marble for a Kitchen Benchtop. A lot of the images you may see on sites like Instagram may actually be Natural Quartzite, or man made Reconstituted Stone, or  or even possibly Sintered Porcelain. The reason Marble is not really suitable for Kitchen benchtops is that it is a soft stone that can scratch from the heard wear inflicted on a kitchen benchtop, plus it is porous so it will stain from many of the ingredients used in a kitchen and it will also mark from acidic foods and many household cleansers. It is for these reasons why alternative material which still look like Marble are generally used and recommended for Kitchen Benchtops. Quartzite for example is still a natural Stone, which in some forms like  Bianco Superiore Quartzite ,  Taj Mahal Quartzite ,  White Pearl Quartzite, Sky White Quartzite and Calacatta Mont Blanc Quartzite, all form with distinctive veining; much the same as Marbles have. Quartzite is better suited for Kitchen tops though because it is as hard wearing as Granite, is Acid Resistant, and is Stain Resistant. Alternatively, man made Reconstituted Stone products (also called Engineered stone or Quartz Tops) are made from a mix of quartz particles and resin which comes in a huge range of Look-Alike Marble Styles, where this product type is also more hard wearing and stain resistant than real Marble. Likewise Man Made Sintered Porcelain Slab Manufacturers also make a variety of Marble Look-Alike styles. All these products have a place in the market and each can fill specific design requirements that another material type may not be able to do, so it is well worth doing your homework on their individual characteristics & specifications so to better guide your material choice to best suit your specific application and needs. Hope this helps, Malcolm.

"I don't understand the point of the offset drain? My Kraus sinks do not have offset drains but they have sink grids." @vinmarks - in answer to your question (and anyone else looking at this thread wondering about this), my comments above were referring to an offset corner drain.  The term "offset drain" means it is simply not centered in the sink; it is in the back or the corner. Your Kraus KHU100-32 does have an offset drain in the back. There are two advantages to an offset corner drain.  One advantage is that it allows you to set down in the sink dishes, large pan, tray without covering the drain.  Many people (including me) prefer not to use a sink grid that you mentioned.  The second advantage to a corner drain is that under the sink the drain and the disposal (if you have one) is off to one side.  This allows a more uninterrupted area for storage under the sink, vs. a drain pipe down the center.  So you would have more storage space under the sink, and you won't have to be always peering around one or the other side of the drain pipe to get your cleaning supplies, sponge, pail, garbage bags, etc. that you've stored under the sink.

Hi Daniel, Congratulations on becoming a home owner - always exciting to start to put your mark on a property! To briefly answer your question (without the benefit of a closer inspection): While having a drain on both sides of your door helps from a drainage point of view, you would still need to consider how to run you water feed to that side of the kitchen.  And even then, I would not advocate putting it immediately behind the back door, as opening the back door would clash with the dishwasher door. From a cost point of view, therefore, the lowest cost/impact location would be where your fridge currently is, then relocating that to the far side. Regarding sizes - it doesn’t look as though you will fit a full width (60cm) dishwasher there, but I would suggest just getting a “slimline” (45cm) which are remarkably spacious and normally adequate for a couple or small family. Water & drainage feeds will be easy enough to run from your sink area without major drama. I wouldn’t worry about removing your cupboard affecting the integrity of the worktop - a small timber batten or a couple of brackets will be more than adequate to support. As to who to get to do the works - they need to be competent in plumbing and general basic carpentry (not a major part of the job), and if they have the relevant ticket for electrics to add a socket, all the better. You can usual find a few such “multi-skilled” folk in any are - seek out recommendations if you don’t already know good tradesmen, and check a reference or two. When it comes to the work, get a fixed price quote and check what is included/excluded. Be clear on what work you need done and try to stick to that - chopping & changing or adding to a list is a sure way to see your bill rocket! If you have other works you intend to do on the property, consider bundling them together to get a better overall price. With any “starter” home, I’d always urge caution not to overspend - there is always a ceiling value for any property (particularly starter properties) and if you have one eye on moving up the property ladder, only do works that will see a good return. The fine sandpaper you used polished the stainless. If you did get the scratches out that is half the battle and now you just need to blend in the repaired spot. I have done a lot of SS scratch repair  with simple hand pads. Get some scotch brite pads of various grits. I would start out with a fresh green pad that is on the back of the sponge scrubbers and see what you get. If that does not blend it in go to the next course grit maybe the maroon pad and then the brownish gray pad. You should be able to get the other pads at most home stores. When you are doing this have the pads on a block of wood so you keep it flat and use light to medium pressure. A small squirt of WD-40 will also help the pad cut the graining back in the stainless steel and work some oil into the metal and help it blend in. This sounds like a lot of work but blending in the small area will be much less than doing the rest of the door front. It may not blend in perfectly and be like new but you should be able to get it pretty close.

Ventilation is the main issue. We previously lived in an apartment that had an ineffective ventilation system rather than an extraction fan, as the bathroom didn't back any external walls. Biggest issue was mould on the ceiling and moisture escaping to the adjoining rooms after a shower. If there is no other option I would invest in a really powerful humidistat extractor fan (150mm rather than the smaller 100mm openings)  that overruns after the light is switched off.

Nearly 18 months now with an internal bathroom. The Vent-Axia Svara extractor fan was well worth the money. Runs 24/7 at low speed and then increases whenever it senses the light being switched on (it doesn’t interact with the light circuit) or humidity level increases. Bluetooth connection to your phone means easy to get the settings right. Definitely worth the extra £60-80 versus a normal extractor. Not a spot of mould - yet. I bought a second one for downstairs WC. I am convinced this plus opening windows a crack has improved the ventilation for the whole house - no longer any condensation on the single glass Victorian sash windows. Internal walls in an internal bathroom mean the walls are warmer, so less condensation and thus less mould versus our previous bathroom - which was surrounded on the outside by 3 solid cold walls and 1 ceiling.

text: Hello, I received what I believe is a sterile hybrid grapefruit tree from a friend, it was too thorny for them to keep with kids in the house, she got it from a lady whose son started it from a store grapefruit seed when he was a kid. I believe that explains why it has never flowered or fruited yet, a seed from a store grapefruit probably an infertile f1 hybrid? Your grapefruit from seed is not a hybrid nor is it sterile.  Most grapefruits are able to grow true from seed and should be able to produce fruit just like the one from which it came.  The main problems associated with growing grapefruit from seed are: 1)  Grapefruits have a VERY long juvenile period before they are able to bloom -- anywhere from 10 to 25 years (or more), depending upon growing season length and other cultural factors, and 2)  They need to be VERY large and VERY tall before that can happen.  If you chop it back so it fits in your home you essentially delay the production of mature growth. In fact, with constant pruning, it may never bloom.  I grew a grapefruit x Poncirus hybrid from seed once and it got to about 14 feet high before it was killed by the cold.  It still had not bloomed, but was probably getting very close. So this is one reason why most citrus are grafted (or started from cuttings) from mature, fruit-bearing wood.  Citrus varieties vary in the time it takes them to reach bearing age. Oranges and grapefruit are notorious for the longest period.  Key limes, lemons, mandarins, kumquats and calamondins often can bloom much sooner.... 4 to 10 years.  I grafted some fertile trovita orange onto it from a tree that fruits well. It's only been a year since then, haven't seen flower yet but maybe this summer. Good for you!  Your Trovita graft should bloom and bear when it's ready, and as long as the Trovita portion doesn't have too much competition from the rest of the tree. But I am wondering if the rootstock being this most likely permanently infertile grapefruit, if the hormones etc might never be proper to trigger a bloom in the grafts, or would the grafts operate based on their own design regardless of the rootstock as long as they're receiving nutrition and a place to live on the sterile tree? Scions don't care about the age or variety of the rootstock (as long as they are compatible and 'take').  In fact most citrus are grafted onto seedlings only a couple years old. If fertile grafts can bloom and fruit on a sterile hybrid tree I'll put some more on, which was the plan. But if the rootstock being sterile is going to inhibit blossom and fruit of the grafts, is there some kind of hormone or chemistry I could treat it with to trick it to trigger the grafts to bloom & fruit? Please CC your responses to marlajns@yahoo.com in case I don't see them here, thanks very much Your rootstock should not hinder the scion from blooming or producing in any way.

Top the line Goodman would be Inverter these days and probably better than the Carrier Infinity for a number of reasons. The infinity is going to require a proprietary thermostat to run as designed.... those don't come cheap. As things change in HVAC the manufacturer is only on the hook to provide those parts to your system for 10-12 years. So if new tech comes out and it will -- a proprietary controlled system could theoretically become an expensive paper weight if that thermostat that drives it becomes obsolete and "sold out". Goodman Inverter realm is similar but different... the control electronics are on the control board of the furnace. So this allows you to choose any thermostat your heart desires. The furnace merely needs a signal from a 24v off the shelf thermostat. It then relays this info and communicates with the outdoor unit or the furnace if in heating mode. So the Goodman design eliminated the expensive proprietary control. The con if you will in that is that there is no piece meal with this kind... like if you have a newer furnace and wanting to upgrade to higher efficiency.  The Goodman Inverter realm before 2023 was up to 24.5 SEER and with the new 2023 requirements of SEER2 it obtains up to 22.5 SEER2. The infinity is typically hampered by 5 speed operation rather than true inverter variable with 1% steps up an down. When the infinity off cycles it makes strange hissing noises AFAIK it's the only system that does this. Don't place it any where near a window.... even more so if it is a heat pump. Parts for the Infinity as well as the equipment itself will likely come from Mexico. Goodman... while parent company is Daikin, they are designed and built (assembled) in USA at a state of art manufacturing facility just outside Houston, Tx. Parts for this system likely come from Mexico, China and possibly other countries... just so you realize assembled in the USA only goes so far. Gone are the days where assembled here means truly built here as in using USA sourced parts. If you have an already built structure? Piece meal among major manufacturer's of HVAC equipment is getting harder to come by... primarily due to communicating aspects of the machine. You can argue the good from the bad from this in a myriad number of ways like for my climate in Katy, Texas (hot climate that depends on AC) furnaces here easily last 30 years if not longer, AC's vary from just over 5 years (out of warranty with major failure) to 15 years with some rare findings of over 18 years. So if you have a HVAC system that is around 6 years old here to go high efficiency with major manufacturer you are going to spend money on a new complete system. The disrupter if you will is Bosch. True inverter with 1% up and down steps, no hissing noises going into off mode. German Engineered made in China. The distributor network is improving in terms of parts and equipment. What the future looks like? Probably nearing the end of piece meal -- you know replace a condenser or replace a furnace / air handler -- because those pieces will have to be the same brand as before. Dicey to say the least. Bosch and possibly another manufacturer soon are the only two that I know of that aren't playing the "proprietary control" game. Brand is less important now anyway due to the phase out of R410a that is coming due in 2025 Equipment ban. If R410a sky rockets in price and you get a refrigerant leak at some point that might make it cheaper to rip everything out again and replace it to whatever the new stuff is. House chickens?  LOL, those are very spoiled chickens indeed.  Mine stay in their coop even at -20F.  It's not heated but is well insulated and I have Michigan chickens who are used to the cold, mostly Rhode Island Reds.  They do have an electric dish to keep their water from freezing. I have a sheet pan for the coop that scraps go into.  If I'm trimming beef or pork, the raw fat chunks go into the pan with vegetable scraps, stale cornbread, leftover yogurt, this morning's oatmeal, leftover beans, etc.  I don't feed them junk, like cake or chips.   If it's trim from cooked meat, that goes in too.  Liquid fat is either cooled until it hardens or if it is liquid at room temperature it is mixed into something, like oatmeal or their scratch grains.  With only Elery and I, we accumulate enough scraps to feed the chickens a couple of times a week, and we have 30 chickens, so enough that everyone gets some, but not so much that it spoils or that the "girls" get too fat.  Remember, their DNA is closest to the T-Rex, so the little dinosaurs would probably eat ME if they were big enough! Annie

Asclepias incarnata is a very short lived perennial. It self seeds and creates new vollunteers to replace the parent plant. I've searched, but I can't find any info about how 'Cinderella' came to be. People that grow 'Cinderella' tell me there's no difference between Cinderella compared to the straight species. In the wild Asclepias incarnata grows in moist soil and full sun, and it has to compete with tall marsh grasses and other plants. In the wild incarnata is usually held erect  by surrounding plants, but in a garden setting it's likely to flop. You might have better luck if you grew your local ecotype of SM. I've been growing the subspecies Asclepias incarnata subsp. pulchra for a few years, and it's very nice. It never grows more than 3 ft. tall, and it stays healthy and doesn't flop. It has pubescent leaves giving it a more elegant look, and it doesn't get ravaged by Oleander aphids to the degree that the straight species does. I believe that's due to it having a higher level of the toxic cardioglycoids. I've grown 'Ice Ballet' 2 times, and both times the plants died after flowering. 'IB' seems to be weaker than the regular species, but the white flowers are beautiful. Common milkweed, A. syriaca, does indeed spread quickly by rhyzomes. I control mine by pulling out all the new shoots in places where I don't want them. The parent plant will eventually get the hint, and will cease sending energy to that location. It works for me. Otherwise I would have to excavate the entire bed and remove every last rhizome. I'm also removing the shoots of a couple milkweed cousins, with the same agressive habit, which are Hemp Dogbane, Apocynum cannibinum, and Honeyvine, Cynanchum laeve. So I have a network of milkweed roots underneath my other plants, but every time I pull shoots of them out, the root network is weakened. I would never use herbicide on milkweeds, and I would hope noone else does either. MY straight species of Swamp Milkweed is a magnet for the orange Oleander aphids, along with tropical milkweed A. curassavica. The milkweed weevils haven't reached my area in Illinois yet. "If you haven't already, you might want to check if there's flashing installed under the siding as sometimes it's there but not visible." See the silver metal between the bottom of the siding and the shingles? That is proper aluminum step flashing and is quite visible. It prevents water intrusion mechanically, which is how you want it done,  because mechanical flashing accommodates seasonal building movement, unlike caulk or roof mastic. The ends of the siding do not touch the shingles so those ends do not wick water and rot. Do nothing about the gap please.

Efflorescence is a white, chalky substance that may appear on the surface of natural stone, clay brick, concrete pavers or any other porous building material. Naturally-occurring salts found in soil, water, sand, gravel and cement are dissolved by rain and groundwater. This moisture is drawn to the surface of the stone where it evaporates, leaving the salts behind as a white haze. Although unattractive, the process is completely natural and in no way damages the stone.

good point about codes. here in Calif: Under California’s Building Code, you must obtain a permit before building a fence that will be over 6 feet tall unless the top 2 feet of the fence will be barbed wire. For a front yard fence, the maximum height is 42 inches. For a backyard fence, the maximum height is 72 inches. If you’re sharing a fence with a neighbor, your fence must be a minimum of 60 inches high and be free of gaps that a small child might pass through. Part of California fence law, California Civil Code 841, describes the rights and responsibilities of those who share a fence along a mutual boundary line. While each neighbor may only see one side of the fence, this particular portion of California law outlines basic etiquette that each neighbor must uphold. Under this fence law, anyone who plans to conduct maintenance or replacement of a shared fence must inform all impacted property owners at least 30 days in advance. This is because adjoining landowners are equally responsible for the costs of construction, maintenance, and any needed replacement of the fence. If you’re planning on building or replacing a shared fence, you must send a letter to the other impacted homeowners. This letter is known as a good neighbor fence letter and should include: Doesn't say anything about the the 'good side' facing the neighbor.  Some states do have this rule, others do not. I would just pick a fence design that is pleasant on both sides. And, most codes will also require the neighbor to pay a portion for upkeep and such.  If you don't want any money from the neighbor, I would have papers drawn up that outline everything with him signing it (with a witness).  down the road you don't want to be sued. Fatsia is more like a clumping perennial blended with a suckering shrub. New growth comes from the root crown not individual canes. Topping the canes won't make a single stem get fuller and kind of wrecks the intended form. Leave the main stem alone. It is blooming. Why would you want to chop that off? You want the fatsia to be the taller shrub in this grouping. Remove the lower leaves from the main trunk and let the ferns be the groundcover below. A lot of how to maintain this plant is going to depend on your climate and if it can get frozen in the winter.

Fatsias as outdoor specimens are common in my area. They are an  excellent choice for dry shade although tolerant of a range of other growing conditions. They are also very tolerant of hard pruning should the plant outgrow its space, so they can be taken back virtually to ground level and will regenerate rapidly. Winter dieback/damage is common here in exposed areas and with an Arctic blast and this is a common late spring activity to cut back the fatsia hard to remove all damaged portions. The plant is generally back in full flush by the end of the growing season.

The last two fences we've built have been good neighbor fences, where there is no good or bad side. The cost wasn't much more than a standard fence, so that's worth doing if you don't plan to follow the basic "good side faces the neighbor" etiquette. We have one that the neighboring building's HOA built and paid for where the bad side faces us, but we didn't really care because they paid for it. (In California the law expects that each neighbor pays 50% of the cost, so that's unusual.) I will say I was still pretty annoyed when they replaced that fence because we live in an urban area and went to let our dog out one day only to discover that we no longer had a fenced backyard (and wouldn't for the next three days). Sure, it was great that we didn't have to pay, but basic courtesy (and in our case, local law!) says you still need to give people a heads up. I would definitely consider building it on the property line rather than fully on your property, though. Even if the neighbor is aware that the slice of land on the opposite side of the fence is technically yours, they're likely to absorb it into their yard in practice because there's a fence there, and a future neighbor might not be aware since most places the practice is to put the fence on the property line. You are also responsible for maintaining both sides of the fence (and the section of yard on the other side) if it's in your yard, too, whereas if you put it on the line, they maintain their side. Is there a compelling reason not to build it there?

A clothes dryer duct can be flexible for the transition piece. That is the portion between the dryer and the permanent duct connection at the wall. It must remain exposed and less than 8' long. It is code allowed. The portion in or through the wall, however, must be solid and smooth. The kinds of ducts for the transition piece are as follows:   1. plastic flex which is the worst 2. rigid, don't use the aluminum thinwall duct in the dryer section of the big box store, move an aisle over to the sheetmetal in the HVAC section and pick the 25ga, 26ga, or 30ga duct whichever they carry on hand 3. foil flex which is also crapola 4. semi-rigid aluminum flex is the one if you choose flex If you plan to lower the vent wall cap, that means you'll have to patch the inside and outside walls, not to mention cutting a clean 4 1/8" dia hole. There are some clearances outside you have to meet, like min 36" from any other openings. You can certainly use rigid duct inside instead of the flex - I would suggest only if you can see the duct as you push in the dryer, and can shimmy down there to tighten the screw on the hose clamp. It you are toolless, it also means you'll have to buy some tin snips, and either HVAC tape (foil not duct or "duck") or sealant (no screws into ducts). They do make some fancy dancy kits of plastic magnet couplers and such to supposedly make it easier lining up the dryer, don't know the success of those.

@fisherpurdue - Houzz is not a neutral source for advice and you should take the advice you get here with a grain of salt.  You can do that with various other woodworking or cabinetry sources on the internet if you want, but you really should do that. One of the biases you will often see here is the belief that relatively small problems are catastrophic failures and anyone who spends less than $100,000 on cabinets can't expect any quality.  Neither of those things are true. Here is my 2 cents... There are certainly problems with the face frame construction, but a few problems with face frames are not sufficient to determine overall quality and certainly not a catastrophic failure in and of themselves.  Face frames are easy to make.  Give me a pocket hole jig, a jobsite table saw with a miter sled, and a couple of story sticks and I could easily site-build great face frames on installed cabinets in an afternoon.  Uninstall them and I could site-build face frames that are superior to the best cabinet brands.  Face frames are just not that hard to do and do well.  That also means that face frame problems are not that hard to correct and correct well. There are certainly problems but it is actually hard to determine why you are having those problems.   That is dubious fabrication.  That looks like a board they didn't even true the end of their stock.  They just grabbed something and used it. I don't quite understand this joint but that is not a quick joint done to save time.  You have a dadoed face frame and the extra trouble of the joining the base to the face frame when it is dadoed.  So the quality is a bit of a mystery and I would want to know more before I commented.   That is a popped glue joint and looking at that cabinet, I suspect your cabinetmaker is correct and someone handled these roughly, but it could also be bad manufacturing and it is difficult to ascertain which.  I suspect it is a combination of both things, the glue joints were weak and popped but wouldn't have popped if they were handled with care. You have posted a lot of problems with popped joints and if a lot of different cabinets have these then certainly that adds weight to the poor manufacturing theory, however, if this is one or two cabinets that would add weight to the idea that this is mishandling by someone. ---- If you want to throw money away, it is your money and feel free to do that.  However, in my informed opinion, you are not even approaching a reasonable basis to breach the contract.  The right to cure is in the UCC and you are unlikely to get your money back until you have given everyone involved a chance to cure the defect, which can be easily done. I suspect your best options is to stop asking who is at fault and start asking how it will be remedied.  Allow the cabinetmaker to build new face frames that you carefully inspect and document before they are coated and only if that fails do you have any chance at recovery. --- There is nothing wrong with inset cabinets, they avoid many of the problems with spacers that frameless cabinetry has and the wood movement thing is just not a real problem.  Your gaps between doors and face frame will grow or shrink less than 1 mm per year in a climate controlled home.  It just isn't that big a deal.

Regarding "cost"...The rangehood alone will be quite expensive -- decorative ones like that are not cheap.  You've designed a high-end Kitchen, not a mid-range Kitchen.  Wood species & finish, fixtures, counter materials (butcher block? Other?), decorative elements, etc., will all affect the cost.  Without more info, even those living in Seattle may not be able to give you a ballpark/guess as to whether it's enough. Is anything else included?  Kitchen flooring?  Changing/adding/removing windows, walls, or doors/doorways in the Kitchen? Regarding spice storage below the counter -- we did that and ended up moving all the spices to an upper cabinet b/c they were too low to be easily accessed.  Some people put them in drawers (in the top position) as well.  We're a tall family, so the upper cabinet (a middle shelf) works for us. For the corner upper, get an easy-reach with a pie-cut shape rather than a diagonal cabinet.  Those diagonal cabinets reduce the "face/head" space in the corner, an issue because you have very little space b/w the rangetop and sink, which is prime real estate/counterspace for prepping (b/w your only water source and the rangetop).  In addition, storage is too deep to be useful in a diagonal cabinet and will be difficult to keep tidy looking (glass doors). Your prime prep space is too small -- you need at least 36" of continuous counterspace b/w the sink and rangetop (either side of the corner).  Your ovens are taking up needed counterspace. Right now, most of your counterspace is in the island, which will not be particularly useful for prepping because of the lack of a water source in the island. If you put a sink in the island, then the lack of counterspace b/w the rangetop and sink will not be that big of an issue b/c that's not where you'll be prepping. Note that KEY components of a functional/successful Prep Zone are: Also important, but not as important as the above 3 items, is the trash pullout in the Prep Zone but easily accessible to the Cleanup Zone. For functionality...My recommendation is to either put a sink in your island or get a range instead of a rangetop + ovens and then move the range to the left to provide at least 36" b/w the range and right corner. For cost...go with a simple stainless steel range hood instead of the decorative one and eliminate the pot filler (not very useful in the long run -- no drain to empty pots or to catch leaks/drips and you still have to carry pots of water from the range to the sink for dumping). Question:  are you on a well or do you have "city water"?  If a well, a pot filler is more work than using the sink b/c you should run water for a couple of minutes to flush the pipes if water has been sitting in the pipes for more than a few hours.  You will need to run the water into a container and then dump it (or use it to water plants).

I do villages :) Not only Christmas, but also other builds through the year. For a glitter ice pond, lay down a sheet of plastic first. Trust me. I have a shelf I do as ice pod and creek with glitter. Lay down the plastic, place your mirrors. If you have lamps on wire, you can plan to lay it under your mirrors to hide the wires before you start pouring glitter- make sure your mirrors have a little bit of feet on them. Pour down some of the glitter for base snow, hill up around the mirror edges. Place in your stuff- trees, lanterns, houses, benches... Detail pour your glitter to fill in gaps, make piles, ect. If you take a small brush, you can drag glitter out a bit to blend in the edge of your pond. Place your smalls- people and pets. After the holiday remove pieces in reverse order, shaking/brushing off glitter as much as glitter can be. Then take your plastic sheet and pour your snow back into the jar for next year. I usually use snow blankets and a bag of white stuffing for most of my general snow detailing. The stuffing helps make drifts, fill the gap and smooths transitions between building bases and the blanket, and helps the uneveness of snow illusion better than just a flat blanket. Buffalo snow can be a fun add to help with snowdrifts and extra snow sparkle. I prefer the fine shred stuff. As a bonus, it can be dyed with food coloring. You can take some and dye it green for your Easter display if you want. There is also tiny snowflake glitter, but it's kind of pricy for a small jar of it. I use a lot of foliage. Village pine trees, some with snow. Regular foliage for regular decorating that in miniature use becomes holly bushes, sparkling trees with red fruits, white iced or metallic iced stuff in the back to snow and sparkle it up a bit. If you are into building more permanant and realistic edge around a mirror for a pond or to make snowdrifts, get Snow-Tex. It's fluffy in the jar, and dries solid. Snow-Tex

That doesn't look like a screw; that looks like the head of a pop rivet.  If you want to remove it, you'll have to drill it out with a bit that is just slightly larger than that hole. Pop rivets come in several sizes, but the drill bit for that one is probably 1/8". Carefully drill until the outer ring breaks loose and then you can push the rest of the rivet into the cavity in the frame. When you've done this for all the pop rivets, the screen should come free. If you want to remount it -- and you haven't damaged the holes -- you can get a pop rivet tool and fix it in place again. If you have messed up the holes and made them even slightly larger, pop rivets won't work and you'll need to screw it in place.

In general, weeds are weeds because they don't need as much fertilizer and water as garden plants. Fertilizer will benefit pretty much any plant, unless there's a significant mismatch in something like pH.  (as in sticking a fertilizer for acid-loving plants on a alkaline-lover).  There are far nastier weeds than plantains, so I'd pull them out and not worry about them.

"  Can fertilizers cause growth of such plants? " Short answer - no. Fertilizers may gave accelerated spring growth but they certainly didn't cause the plants' growth. That can only be attributed to by seeding or in some cases, the distribution (usually through tilling or digging) of roots or other plant parts that will regenerate plant growth.

"  Can [organic] fertilizers cause growth of such plants? " Short answer - ummm, it depends.  When you hang out in organic lawn care forums for 20 years recommending people to get their raw materials at the feed store, you see some things.  For example, don't use bird seed as a fertilizer.  Sure it has a lot of protein/nitrogen, but you'll have a yard full of weeds, because it is not a ground product.  Similarly, "cracked corn" will have some viable kernels of corn in it which are small enough to go through the screen before going into the bag.  You will get a few corn plants from that product, but one mowing takes care of it. So this brings up the question, what did you use for your organic fertilizer?  It sounds ridiculous but it looks like the stuff my wife grows as lettuce. So did you use lettuce seed in the fertilizer? That's a rhetorical question to get you thinking.  What else might have been tossed into that area that dropped seeds?

The misunderstanding by both HU's comments (BTW same guy) is that a 12/3 cable will have black, red, white, + ground. The black and red will be separate circuits with a shared neutral. This is allowed when both breakers are tied, so that shutting off one will shut off the other simultaneously. Assuming neither circuit is a SABC. In principle, the 3 wire plus ground cable could be fed by a simple 240 Vac breaker and would, in turn, feed a small breaker box at the island.  This breaker box would be populated with breakers tailored to the requirements of the particular circuits that they fed.  It would be desirable for the feed to have been heavier gauge because I am not sure that the load will never be greater than 80% of the feed cable's ampacity without seeing all the specified loads.  And since the island itself requires a receptacle (pile of relevant rules incorporated by reference) that could be loaded by a high current plug-in portable appliance. meeting code might be a challenge.

If that cable can be pulled from the conduit and there is conduit to boxes at each end, then the conduit could be repopulated by lower AWG number THWN to feed a suitable breaker box (perhaps as few as six breakers).  You want no limitations on what can run simultaneously, and also voltage drop minimized for all combinations of activity. Extra Info about Mohawk Mohawk Mohawk produces its own carpet but also lends its production capabilities to smaller brands. On the whole, Mohawk products are similarly well-reviewed, though it’s fair to say that their SmartStrand carpet line may be their most popular carpet. SmartStrand is made of DuPont’s hybrid-polyester fabric, triexta, which substitutes a significant amount of petroleum (the main ingredient in most synthetic carpets) with a corn byproduct. Triexta carpet is eco-friendlier than other synthetic carpets but performs better than everything except the most resilient nylon products—and Mohawk is the only carpet manufacturer to make it. Mohawk also sells triexta under several different brand names, like Karastan and Lees carpet.

The floor is an oil finish. Either select something else in the engineered category, spend more,  or do an LVP. This is going to be HIGH maintenance in a wet climate, coupled with dogs. For stubborn mineral stains Restoration Oil can be used on a board by board basis, following instructions for use of Restoration Oil (available on Hallmark Floors website). When we look at arctic treelines around the world, we find that they sometimes experience primarily clonal reproduction (where the treeline species are capable of it), and sometimes sexual reproduction. The null hypothesis would be that sexual reproduction is episodic over time, occurring during climatic warm intervals that favor complete cone and seed development, with reversions to clonal reproduction during less favorable periods. She wanted to contain the mess to the kitchen/family room and keep an eye on us.   The table took up a huge space in the family room and there was limited other seating.   She did keep big floor pillows and blankets next to the TV and at night the kids laid on the floor to watch TV.    We added a second table to the family room that changed over the years.  First just a little kids table, then a small table, then one with leaves that could expand.    By the time I was in high school and the older kids had spouses and kids we were up to 14 most nights at dinner.   If we had a few extra we would use TV trays and sit at the sofa.  Later mom added another table in the laundry room for the teenage grandkids. My mom continued to watch the grandkids that were local until my dad passed away when I was in my 30s.  She watched the little ones during the day and picked the older kids up from school.  Everyone came to her house after work and we had dinner as an extended family.  At times there were 20+ people. She also added a pool table and ping pong table to the basement by the time I was a teenager and some of the kids would go there when the family room got too crowded.   This may make more sense to people if they knew that my mom was raised in an Amish household and we lived in an Amish community.  I know that most people don't have the multigenerational dinner hours on a daily basis.   I do think that this daily interaction made our family much closer than most families and I am so thankful that in my 60s my siblings are still my best friends and we still count on each other and lean on one another and take care of one another and are there for our siblings kids and grandkids. Right now I am waiting on a call back from a vet to discuss the prognosis of my nieces cat so that I can help her make the best decision on whether to continue treatment or put him down.   I worked in the humane industry for 25 years and am better suited to help make this decision than anyone else.   My one sister is a retired pediatrician and helps all of us with medical decisions.   Susie was a business leader and helps the younger generation with career guidance.  I am planning a day to teach 3 of the age 30 something grandkids how to bake my mom's Christmas pastries, as the older generation is getting too old to do it.  Tom takes all the young ones fishing and teaches them about boats and fishing, Ron is the expert on wildlife, Reid knows everything about birds and trains, Len is the expert on gardening.  I help with color selection and sewing. Susie and Betty are amazing cooks and are the kitchen experts.  We share the burdens and knowledge based on our strengths.  The rough patches in life are made so much easier when you have this type of family support system and the good times are even better when shared with those you love. I hope that your family is able to build the same kind of multigenerational bonds and go through life with their siblings as their best friends.

If you feel do not warm air when the auxilliary heat is on, then the problem might be the back up electric heat strips. A competent HVAC tech should be able to figure that out.  Would not necessarily recommend investing in an expensive repair if you plan to live in this house for several more years. Some heat pumps perform better than others at low temperatures. But it comes down to the heat loss of your house. If the heat gain provided by the heat pump is less than the house's heat loss, then you will not be able to maintain the house at 70 degrees. The auxiliary heat on my old Washington, DC heat pump stopped working twice. In 2021 I replaced the heat pump after it started leaking and had other problems. I recommend a two-stage unit which, when equipped with heat strips and a supporting thermostat, will give you three levels of heating: stage 1, stage 2, and stage 2+Aux. Most of the time it runs in stage 1 which runs the compressor at about 70% capacity and allows a slower blower speed which makes the system virtually silent (i.e., no whooshing). Cool Breeze (coolbreezeplumbingheatac.com) in Gaithersburg installed my unit; I don't know if it services VA. Shop around! I was very specific with my specs and prices varied all over the place. My package heat pump is Carrier but with some exceptions Carrier, Bryant, and ICP products are all the same.

Looks like a combination of root girdling and sun scald. Clues to root girdling are the abnormal trunk flare and surface level roots. If you brush away the mulch, you might find the roots are encircling the tree, rather than growing laterally. It's usually a transplanting issue. Sun scald damage is preventable by wrapping trees over winter from the lowest branches downward. Tree guards can also prevent young trees from potential wildlife damage.

The biggest issue is air sealing your rim joist area. If you want to do a deep dive, google "rim joist air sealing." The current thinking is using rigid foam board cut to fit in each joist space with spray foam or caulk of gaps.

About trees planted in the landscape: First year they sleep. Second year they creep. Third year they leap. IOW, it takes some time for the tree to get its feet under it and established. I have a question re how you went about planting the trees and what was the condition of their roots at plant-out time. * Were the roots congested to the degree the entire root/soil mass could be lifted from the pot intact? * If yes to above, did you do anything to correct the congestion, or did you simply make a planting hole, set the plant, and back-fill. * Did you use native soil to back-fill the hole, or did you 'amend' the soil you used to back-fill with organic matter? The reason I ask is because root congestion has a profound effect on branch extension, and can slow extension growth to the point you would swear no extension is occurring. Also, planting holes not filled with native soil encourage roots to remain within the confines of what was the original planting hole. This (back-filling with native soil) is more a concern for the future, but the root congestion question and how it was handled at the time of planting-out is of immediate concern because congestion severely limits availability of resources essential to growth, including root growth. For plants in the landscape, no one without access to analysis of the soil your trees are in can tell you what is appropriate in terms of how much, how often, or with what product(s) you should fertilize. Any other contention is just a SWAG. How often you fertilize depends ion the type of fertilizer you use. A controlled release product might be appropriately applied once per year; whereas a soluble synthetic product might be appropriately applied as often as each fortnight. This assumes that the NPK % of the product are appropriate, and they won't be. A soil analysis with recommendations might have you applying things like elemental sulfur, magnesium sulfate, potash, urea, ..... almost never a commercially prepared multi-nutrient fertilizer product. If a soil test just isn't in the cards, and since nitrogen is the nutrient most deficient in the landscapes, go with a slow release (not controlled release - they are different) product high in N. Something like 30-10-10 or 27-0-3 is about the best you can do if you you have to guess. Choosing fertilizers for container grown plants is easier because you can discount the nutritive value of materials like pine bark and peat. Coconut products require work-arounds for best results because of it's higher pH and high K content. Al

I think you may be confused as to what constitutes a 'native' plant  :-)  A native is a species of plant that is indigenous to that area. The red cedars - junipers, Juniperus virginiana - are natives but not the crab. Like most of the ornamental crabapples sold, 'Donald Wyman' is a hybrid derived from Malus floribunda, or the Japanese flowering crab. It may well have some American crabapple species DNA in its make up as well but the hybridization has removed it from any "native" plant status. By definition, a manmade hybrid cannot be considered a native species.

I had very poor drainage at the back edge of my backyard, because the neighbor behind me was on a hill. My yard got all the rain that washed down that hill with no particular place to go. There was a professionally dug French drain going perpendicular to the back fence, along the side fence, exiting in the curb of the street. I had some laborers dig out the poison-ivy riddled scraggly hedge along the back edge of my backyard and then dig an 18" deep straight-sided trench for 25', ending into the original French drain. I then had them lay landscape cloth in the trench and straighten it out. Then had them add a couple of inches of 3/4" gravel. On the of the gravel, I had them lay 25' of perforated PVC pipe, with the holes downward. Then I had them swaddle the landscape cloth around the pipe tightly and pin it in place that way with landscape staples. We then filled the rest of the trench up with the soil that had been shoveled out. No more flooding!

" Broken glass panes, lost seals can allow cold, outside air to penetrate inside plus let warm air escape..."  from the link....As I read this, I see it as referring to window seal not glass seal, but it's hard to say for sure. In any case, a lost IG seal will not result in what you are seeing, while a lost window seal might. IG or dual pane glass packages are sealed for three reasons. In no particular order of priority, first to protect LowE coating, second to allow for gas (usually argon) fill, and third to allow the use of sufficient desiccant in the airspace to keep the space dry which lowers the dew point inside the space to a level that whatever tiny amount of moisture remains in the space will not condensate inside the space. Losing the seal does three things. First the argon gas will escape, second ambient air will enter the space resulting in corrosion of the LowE coating, and third because the desiccant becomes saturated, the dew point within the space will rise to a level where condensation can (and will) form inside the space. Worst case, a seal failure might raise the IG U factor by .05 or so, it will not result in the sort of surface condensation/ice that you are seeing. Whether or not you have a LowE coating, what spacer is used in the IG construction, and the material and design of the window frame will all affect the formation of condensation much more than will an IG seal failure, but why your glass is below freezing is the primary question, and IG seal failure would not cause that. There could be a problem in the seal between the glass and the sash or a weatherseal issue allowing cold outside air to penetrate that seal and cooling the inside glass way down. I would be very surprised if assuming that you warmed the glass enough to melt the ice and dry the glass, then removed the screen and left any curtains open and you still experienced ice formation like that, unless that window was in a bathroom which would explain moisture but not  that much ice. I finished cooking with the stovetop burners. The following day, I removed the burned out baking element to get a replacement from a local parts warehouse. When I got back with the new element, but before I installed it, I found the range's display panel would light up but nothing worked - not the clock, not the stove top burners, nothing. Installing the new baking element did not change that. Turned out the stove had come with a wiring connector defect for which GE had issued a recall notice. GE sent an authorized repair tech to replace the connector. Tech said that when the harness connector failed and shorted out, the failure had cascaded back to the range's main control board.  GE overruled him, saying the connector failure (for which it had issued the recall) may have contributed to or been caused by the baking element burn-out but claimed the control board failure was coincidental and out of warranty.

As you discovered, the more crevices the plant has, the harder it will be to dislodge those bamboo sheaths. So I'd look to either very large/coarse-leaved plants like Bird of Paradise (Strelitzia species) or even a large trunk-forming succulent like Euphorbia ammak 'Variegata', or very feathery ones like Mahonia 'Soft Caress' or Acacia cognata 'Cousin Itt' that don't have enough leaf surface to trap the sheaths. Make sure you choose species that can handle the sun exposure there, including the glare off the white wall and the urban setting. The bamboo won't stop raining debris no matter what you plant, so you or your gardener might invest in a shop vacuum (with the narrow crevice tool attachment) to suction out debris from the Agave and other plants — much more effective than trying to blow it out. Also, topping bamboo really isn't an effective way to control debris. Bamboo doesn't grow like shrubs or trees; bamboo canes (or culms) are genetically predetermined to grow to a certain height -- say, 20' -- and then stop growing. Topping them creates that dense "witch's broom" of branchlets visible just below the cuts, which creates even more leaves and therefore more debris. It would be much more effective to cut out the old, mature culms at the base of the plant as the new ones grow in, allowing the new culms to reach their full height before cutting them out the following season. Good luck! We'd love to see photos of what you decide to do.

Hi, ykindschi, Your geothermal heat pump shouldn't contribute to an indoor air quality problem any more than an air source heat pump or even a gas furnace would. Most homes operate at a slight negative pressure due to a combination of "stack effect" and a HVAC system that is starved for air flow on the return side.   Stack effect occurs when warm indoor air rises to the upper levels of a home, pulling in outside air on the lower levels, like a chimney, of sorts.  The driving force for stack effect is greatest in winter when the temperature differential is greatest.  You've experienced Wisconsin weather for the past 22 years, so stack effect by itself is not likely the cause of your problem. Given the change to your HVAC system, I think there's a good chance that the blower on your new air handler is a higher capacity than the old one.  If no modifications were made to the duct work system, a higher capacity blower would result in a system that's even more starved for air than the old one.  That increases the potential for back drafting--a condition where outside air is drawn into the home by backward flow through fireplace chimneys, hot water heater exhausts, range vent hoods, etc. bringing soot and contaminants into the home.  Lastly, let's not forget the addition of the RenewAire heat recovery ventilator.  While these are typically set up to exhaust air at the same rate as they introduce fresh air, the intake could be blocked by snow on the roof or a ductwork issue or a blower problem resulting in more exhaust air flow than make up flow and contributing to back drafting.

Hi, Ykindschi, You noted that you have a gas fireplace--which can be another potential source of back drafting.  Essentially, any connection between the interior of your home and the exterior--including bath vent fans (the backflow dampers don't seal well) and even gaps around windows and doors that allow for air exchange are potential routes for air to enter your home.  You can also pull air from your crawl space into your home either via leaks in the return duct work or through penetrations in the 1st floor.   Check also for critters in the crawl space.  They can be a source of sporadic "odiferous events." You noted an increase in air flow with the new system which suggests a larger capacity blower.  If no modifications were made to the duct work system, my bet is that the system is more air starved than before.   A higher capacity blower will increase the amount of air being pulled though any leaks in the return ductwork.  Fortunately, that's something that can be easily measured.  If you set up pressure monitoring, you'll be able to check how it varies over time, and hopefully correlate it with either atmospheric conditions or a set of HVAC operating conditions.

Another potential route for back drafting is the plumbing vent system.  If you have a bathroom that's not used frequently, the traps may have dried out enough to allow sewer gases to be pulled into the home.  I've seen this occur in homes where the guest bathrooms were not used for long periods of time.  Traps will dry out faster in winter than in more humid periods.

@ykindschi, It may be difficult to identify the source of the pollutants entering your home, but you can do a couple of things to address the negative pressure inside your home which is drawing them in.  In the end, if the problem goes away, the specific pollutant source is academic.  Start by measuring the differential (indoor vs. outdoor) pressure.  You can do that using a manometer and some tubing you can purchase for less than $100.  It will enable you measure the contribution of various exhaust equipment (e.g., bath vent fans, clothes dryer, fireplace, hot water heater, etc.) as well as each change you make.  Two changes I'd suggest are reducing the blower speed and sealing the ductwork.   Both should improve the operating efficiency of the system and mitigate the potential for drawing pollutants into your home.

Non magnetic results suggest the material is 300 series stainless steel, which should be very resistant to any staining that is actually bonded to the metal. That is, it should rinse off with soapy water or a de-greasing agent.  I did, however, receive my Wolf hood chimney extension with finger prints on it that wouldn't clean with solvents.  I had to use a phosphoric acid rinse to remove them.  (Such rinses are available from automotive parts distributors that support body shops.  Do not use without complying with all safety directions.) While I might be partial to taking the unit back, that might be difficult in many imaginable circumstances, so I would start with water spiked with dishwashing detergent or Simple Green, and if that didn't work go for more aggressive solutions.  Before sanding I would try Barkeepers Friend on a spot, always working with the grain.  If that worked, then I would try it on the entire surface.  If one gets to having to sand, a phosphoric acid rinse may be needed anyway to stabilize the surface. I fear that in the worst case, the coloration is due to the metal being very but not uniformly hot when rolled and it might not be possible to correct it even with sanding.

Hi, sblauv, Your expectations regarding energy savings from zoning may have been, well, over blown.   Zoning of residential HVAC systems is first and foremost about comfort.  Any energy savings is a bonus.  The amount of energy savings is affected by a lot of variables:  the area and specific arrangement of the rooms on each zone (e.g., large vs. small rooms, rooms with one exterior wall vs. rooms with two or three exterior sides, rooms with attic above vs. conditioned living space above,) the construction details of the home (e.g., windows, exterior doors, insulation) the heat gain/loss due to the orientation of the home (e.g., solar heat gain,) the design and leakage of the duct work system and the turndown capability of the system. Your system has five zones.  If the heating/cooling load of each zone is equal, your system would need to be capable of operating at 20% capacity.  I suspect your system's minimum air flow rate won't allow operation of some zones without bleeding off excess air into another zone.   Ask your installer to give you a thorough review of how to operate the system and ask about its limitations.  If they didn't perform a duct blaster test before installing your system, ask them to do one.  If you find the duct work system is leaky, improving the sealing will go a long way toward reducing your energy bill and improving comfort, too.

"I could never prove it, but I am 100% convinced that the landlord (who had a store next to mine) was using my electricity. Shoot, I was probably paying for 3 or 4 business's electric! " Whether intentional or by mistake it isn't uncommon due to wires sharing trays,conduit and raceways on exterior walls in strip centers.  It isn't a simple diy unless one has a considerable amount of electrical experience but an electrician can figure out whether neighbors are tapped into their meter IF WIRES INCOMING to meter are exposed (not in conduit).   Turn all lights out,hvac and other equipment off then look at spinner on meter.  More precise is to clamp an amp meter onto meter feed.  Electronics on some of your equipment might pull 1 or 2 amps combined for clocks and timers while in off mode but if feed shows more than 5amps make another sweep to make sure everything is off.  If wires from utility to meter and/or wires from meter to your breaker panel are in raceway or conduit,locating source of high amprage draw requires opening them which might require permit.  If both feeds are exposed,it's much simpler and no permit is required to trace from inside panel.  Once you are sure all equipment is off and high draw persists,  move clamp to each breaker and flip those off with draw.   If all your equipment still works,leave breakers off and seal or lock the panel.   Fire code in some jursidictions forbid panel being locked but I don't expect a week will land anyone in prison.   If some of your equipment doesn't work,look for double lugging on breakers that were turned off.   If it isn't critical having electric power when not in building AND wires are expose as in last scenario ,skip the above and simply tripping the main in panel when you leave will flush scofflaws out if there are any..

The easiest on you and the rose is to sever the roots at the pot holes, prune the top back in balance with the root ball then plant is as a normal canned plant. Trying to retain the roots grown into the ground and more of the top growth is going to be difficult on you and if you're unsuccessful in balancing the top and bottom growth, the top will die back to what the roots can support. If you want, you can literally bare root it so there is no soil ball and the only top growth remaining is what you had when it was a bare root. That way, the feeder roots as well as anchor roots will spread out into a larger area than they may have if you left the potted root ball intact. As long as you keep it hydrated and protected from any hot sun (presuming you're getting any of that right now - we aren't) and drying winds, it will resurrect and grow. Ideally, just after planting, you will receive rains to thoroughly water it in and push new growth quickly.

Appears to be a classic case of overwatering. Or at least, not providing adequate drainage. The pot is still sitting in its foil wrapping. This should be removed as soon as the plant is brought home, as it will collect and retain water and impede good drainage. There may also be an issue with the soil media being overly moisture retentive - most prebagged mixes are. Remove any dead or dying leaves, as they are not helping anything. I'd also unpot and examine the roots for rot or mushiness and then repot with a high quality, textural and fast draining potting soil.

Regardless, if either are the cause, there is nothing to be done about it other than removing the damaged leaves if they are too unsightly to tolerate, so reread Pam's advice about drainage and water retention. No one can hazard a guess. Interior designers structure their fees based on experience, and this could be years or decades  Also their markets, their costs of doing business . You could be near the center of Boston, or in the woods of Springfield. Personally, I know none who work on a flat "whole project " fee for anything residential. You will ask why. I will answer in one word. Emotion. Emotion is the word that defines residential work. It is why architects generally specialize in EITHER residential or commercial, and the same holds true for interior designers. Homes are simply more personal - the same owner who'd be speedily decisive/ fine with a pleasing, functional result in a corporate setting could spin and twist him or herself into knots regarding their own home! I can only tell you what you want. You want someone to work in tandem with your architect/ contractor/subs. The informed go between/ the guru between you and them. You want a built in? A mud cubbie area? He/she designs it - contractor executes. As it applies to your kitchen? A good interior designer generally has a pro KD on speed dial. I often "design" a kitchen/bath layout, spec all finishes, select appliances, lighting, tops, et al  with a client,  but no possible way am I writing a cabinet order- hours and hours FRAUGHT WITH MISTAKE POTENTIAL! You want the interior to flow. That means as it applies to all the elements in whatever your end desired style /flavor shall be. From trims, to flooring to you name it. All the permanent aspects and their colors, materials, finishes. You will need some furnishings.? Rugs, seating, tables, lighting , accessories.....the elements that make your home, yours. Some you undoubtedly own and want to keep. some will be new. What's your budget? How decisive are you? Do you need to see two options? Or will you need to see six? ( Not recommended btw ). Which is why you need a very clear idea of what you want or expect from any designer, and must understand that the more attention and service ? Hence follows the "price". You aren't just paying for a designers time. You are paying for the art, the science, the skill, the experience. As I say to clients? "This all sounds abstract, does it not? It is in fact abstract, UNTIL.....you arrive at a destination that thrills you. The result that you never imagined could be so lovely, functional, comfortable and y.o.u. You pay for that reality; that is the point and only purpose, any designer, anywhere" Bottom line? Find the "one" . Talk to friends who've done work. Talk to a few designers and clarify your expectations with regard to scope of work and your budget. Get a clear contract, make sure you fully understand it, before you sign it. Is there another way? No. Working with any designer is an ongoing relationship. It's a dialogue , ideas, and more. It is mutual trust as well. You have to find that fit.

"I had no idea it was a safety hazard." A window behind a cooktop is more of a safety hazard in a colder climate, which it looks like you are not in.  What happens in a colder climate is that the interior layer of glass of the window warms from the cooking, while the exterior layer of the window is cold - perhaps extremely cold if it is January in, say, Boston.  That differential will cause the window to break, though if it is tempered glass it would be less dangerous when it breaks, but still, who wants a window shattering while you are cooking. But there are other reasons not to have a window behind the cooktop.  One is that the window will show cooking splatter and be unsightly unless you are constantly cleaning it.  If you want the window for the view to the outside, who wants to look through grease splatter to see that view?  Also, to clean the window, you will have to reach across the cooktop to do so, which isn't that comfortable.  And also, a setup of an exhaust hood over a window can be difficult and costly in the way of ductwork and hanging the hood, it just depends on your home, but it is more trouble than it is worth.

Generally speaking, in contracts, reasonable errors (typos) become the actual contract.  In other words, if the drafter makes a typo and both parties sign then the typo becomes the agreed upon contract as long as it is reasonable (one party could reasonably believe that the typo was actually what was being agreed on). Contradicting errors in a contract generally go against the drafter of the contract. E.g. if your contract says insulation for all walls, but the calculated square footage is less than all walls.  Then it depends on who wrote the contract and made the mistake.  If you wrote the contract and did the calculation wrong then it would only be for the square footage you calculated, while if he wrote the contract and did the calculation wrong it would be for the all walls. However, there is a caveat.  Just because he does less doesn't mean you get a discount.  It just means he has to have been willing to do more.  If the same contractor from my above example shows up and I only ask him to do 70% of the walls in the home, I can't get a 30% discount because I didn't ask him to do all the work that was specified in the contract.  I can either ask for all work to be done, or can pay the full amount. --- Knowing all that above...here is my advice.  It is probably not worth the fight.  Being in the right is a far cry from being whole.  It is easy to know you are correct and a whole lot harder to get the contractor to agree you are correct.  Unless this is a significant amount of money or significantly different than what you wanted, I would see if I could get a small discount for the mistake and move on.
