From our Review Report on Delta  Faucets.  Some Delta faucet finishes are given a final coating to combat water spots and fingerprints. There are two types. Lumicoat™ and Spotshield®. Spotshield has the additional advantage of being anti-microbial, reducing bacteria and mold accumulation. According to the company:   "The finish technology allows users to easily wipe the surface clean  with only a soft cloth, eliminating the need for cleaners and  chemicals." These are what are known as  hydrophobic coatings.  They are formulated at the molecular level to shed water. Because water  does not stock, it does not dry on the faucet leaving what are called  water spots. Many are also  oleophobic. They repel oil such as the oil on your fingers which makes them fingerprint-resistant. Typically these coatings are very thin, as thin as 2-4  nanometers, so thin that they do not obscure the finish under the coating or change its appearance. Currently, there are two SpotShield finishes, SpotShield Brushed  Nickel and Spotshield Stainless. Lumicoat is available on a much wider  range of finishes. Faucets available in Lumicoat finishes are identified  on Delta's website. We have seen no data on the durability of Lumicoat or Spotshield.  Delta undoubtedly has such data, but has not seen fit to make it public. Whatever the finishing technology used, however, Del­ta guarantees all  faucet finishes for a lifetime, indicating a very high level of  confidence in the durability of its finishes. In a one-year old home was it working correctly at one time? Is this your first winter in the house? If so, with one loop warm and the other cold, are the bathroom loops on the same circulating pump? In the photo I see you have flow control or ON/OFF valves on the loops. They all look to be full open. With the T-stat set so the heat is ON and with water circulating, does each outflow loop feel warm to the touch? How about each return loop? Is the loop that is cold near an exterior wall? Or on cantilevered framing where that portion of the bathroom floor overhangs the exterior wall below? If you've had a cold snap and the underside of the floor is exposed to the cold air, and there's inadequate insulation in the joist bay(s)/framing, there is a chance the loop has frozen up. The impellers in circulating pumps can go bad, but typically not one year in. And if other loops sharing that circulator are warm you can likely rule out a bad circulator. A bathroom could be served by more than one loop. If one loop is on the bathroom t-stat and the other loop is on a bedroom t-stat for example, you could get a split demand for heat. I'd think that is an outlier through. Easiest troubleshooting it to create a demand for heat and then check the loop's supply and demand to see if both ends of the loop are warm.  Then work backwards. Check any zone valves to make sure they are operating. Any circulating pumps to make sure they are operating.

For plant health, I don't think it matters where the scion is placed. For grafters, it's often easier to graft higher on the trunk of the rootstock, especially when the scions have very short internode distances.  But most buyers prefer to buy plants with foliage as close to the ground as possible.  So most grafters make an effort to graft close to the ground.

For standards or lollipop conifers, they are almost always top grafted. That is because these are typically dwarf selections that grow slowly and never develop much of a trunk on their own. So the tall straight trunk you see is some other compatible conifer with the dwarf lollipop cultivar attached at the top. It is very much a personal taste thing but I find them to look very unnatural.

@Ron Jennings Pro-style gas ranges often do have burner spacing more in line with what you want.  My 30" wide NXR range is something of a knock-off of older Wolf (and DCS) designs, particularly in burner layout.  The front and back burners are about 10½" apart (center to center).  Side to side  the burners are about 17"  apart (center to center) and 6½" in from the sides.  My recollection is that the distances were similar when I measured a Blue Star range. If you want to more precise measurements, I believe Wolf, Blue Star, and other brands have downloadable CAD files on their websites.

Per NKBA guidelines: In a kitchen with three work centers the sum of the three traveled distances should total no more than 26′ with no single leg of the triangle measuring less than 4 feet nor more than 9 feet. The three main "work centers" to be concerned about are the fridge, the cooktop, and the main sink.

I share some of the preferences of others here as I actually prefer knobs and having a temperature control for each burner instead of one common control for all burners. And those are two things that the Bosch is lacking, at least for that model. However, I can think of 3 things to add here. Bosch has a reputation for being one of the most reliable in the induction category. I believe that LG also has an overall good reputation for reliability. And while I share your aesthetic love of the blue enamel, there are numerous anecdotal reports that blue coloured oven enamels are less robust than the other colours and are more prone to flake off than the others. This delamination can occur with any colour of enamel, of course, but blue enamel in LG, Wolf, Electrolux, and kitchenAid ovens have had issues with shards of enamel, which popped loose from the steel and end up, blown around inside the oven with the convection fans which can present a real health hazard. With the limited exception of Wolf, most brands refer to the failure of porcelain on steel as an “anesthetic issue“. Even Wolf, known for going the extra mile for many of its customers, now is limiting how well it reimburses for this issue. If you do a search here on the forums, you will find many appliance consumers with broken enamel and broken hearts over the issue. Mind you, this does not mean that it happens to every one of these blue enamelled appliances and those here who have enjoyed, any of the four brands that I mentioned may be doing just fine, but I would look at the pattern that has appeared over time with blue enamel. The issue has risen its head due to a combination of factors that include the use of pyrolytic self cleaning cycles, as well as the shift that appliance manufacturers made when they started putting bottom oven elements below the oven cavity versus the old way when the element was exposed and above the bottom of the oven. This change creates a lot more thermal stress on the oven cavity liner than the old element position did. I have no doubt there are exceptions, but I have not seen very many posts here on the forums of Bosch ovens having enamel issues. Lastly, I would call around and search online to perform a bit of an audit of appliance repair services in your geographic area to see how many options you have for Service for any brand you purchase. Service availability across various regions of North America can vary substantially with Samsung and LG having reputations for less convenient access to people who work on their appliances. Some say that LG has improved and this may be accurate but I would always check to be sure. This doesn’t let Bosch off the hook either because their service can be plentiful or spotty, depending on where you live. I know how much aesthetics matter to many of us and I personally had to pass on an exquisitely beautiful Italian brand of appliances that I really wanted and I passed on it largely because there was no service or parts availability where I live. At the end of the day, the food always has to be prepared and set to the table. Good luck with your selection whatever you decide.

The wick works better when the hole is through the bottom at the sidewall.        I honestly did not think a cast iron plant would be fussy in their choice of soil composition. Most plants commonly grown as houseplants (other than cacti and some succulents) do not vary much in what they want insofar as a grow medium and moisture levels. They almost ALL want a medium that is evenly damp or moist with plenty of air porosity to drive root function. Where they DO vary is where the limits to what they will tolerate lie. The most commonly grown houseplants all tolerate indoor conditions. Some are known to tolerate low light or dry soil conditions better than others, but very few will tolerate the watering cycle that includes a large fraction of roots completely inundated for such long periods. A well-made 5:1:1 mix will (structurally) last much longer than media based on peat/ coir/ compost/ composted forest products, and can generally be watered almost at will without serious consequences in the form or limited root function or poor root health. The reason a 5:1:1 mix with too much fine material can't offer the same benefits as a 5:1:1 mix with an appropriate fraction of fine material is exactly the same reason that adding a bit bark and perlite to a poorly made commercial mix doesn't work. It is essential the the volume of particles larger than about 1/8" make up somewhere around 80-85% of the mix. Examples: A) If you have a jar of peat and add an equal measure of pine bark thinking it will improve aeration, it will be a failure because there is more than enough peat to fill all pore space between bark particles. B) If you have a commercial grow medium you feel is holding too much water and try to amend it with pine bark and or perlite, thinking it will improve aeration, it will also be a failure unless you add so much bark and perlite that, combined, they make up a fraction of the medium by far larger than the original soil you started with. In fact, adding pine bark and or perlite to a water-retentive medium continually DECREASES o/a air porosity until reaching "threshold proportion", where there is no longer enough fine material to fill pores between the coarse material. From that point on, adding additional coarse material significantly increases o/a aeration. Al

When selecting counter tops, go into it with your eyes open.  Etching on marble is a fact of life, and it shows up less on honed finished than on polished.  I prefer honed because it's a more casual look than polished, but marble is marble and trying to make it behave like another material is a fool's errand.  Keep in mind that it's a work surface, not a work of art.  All it needs is to be cleaned, nothing else.  I've had my Danby marble for 8 years, and it shows etches and chips because I don't baby it.  If you don't like the look of well-used marble, then get something else. I also have honed Jet Mist granite, and it too shows marks.  But  so does my polished gray quartz.  Nothing is bullet-proof, so get what you like, and live your life.

White, silver, or light tan pavers are a clean look and can be used effectively in either classical or contemporary designs. Travertine is the traditional material for this application, but a ceramic paver such as the Rinox is much less likely to stain than natural stone. If there's any shrubbery around that makes berries (especially purple berries), expct birds to leave an abundance of purple splats on your paving in the fall and winter. More importantly, if you're in full sun (as most pools are), glare could be a real problem; the summer sun can reflect off of white or glossy surfaces just as brightly as it does off of water. The only other factor to consider is slip resistance, but an outdoor-rated paver such as the Rinox should be manufactured with that in mind (check the product specs if you're not sure).

Chitting can be done with indirect sunlight or in a bag. Or both. Some folks do it in the bag that they came in from the store while it's sitting on the counter- usually by accident rather than with the purpose of planting them. The point is, you provide the potato with some warm and light to wake the potato up. Normally potatoes should be stored cooler, darker to keep them in their dormant state that we eat them in. Putting them in a windowsill gives them the warm for chitting. Putting them in a paper bag can help control the light and make it mellower. Also can help maintain the moisture level of the potato better than leaving it out in the open. This can help trigger the eyes more than or quicker than the chlorophyll production in the skin. Also, greening in the skin indicates the development of solanine, the toxin of the family :) Once a potato is chitted, the new growth can be in the sun to grow while the tuber does it's thing under the dirt. Chitting a potato is a bit akin to sprouting a seed before transplanting into the garden. You are providing the conditions for the potato to start it's growth phase before planting it instead of direct seeding it. Chitting is not absolutely necessary. For many gardeners it helps ensure success much like starting seed indoors before transplanting out helps ensure success with those plants.

You may be making a mistake painting your husbands new pole barn.  I suggest you get the opinions of many others how horrible it looks, because it could just be you and your tastes. Let me tell you something about the paint on metal panels used for pole barns.  The very best quality panels will use Polyvinylidene Fluoride paint and is the very best paint one can put on steel panels.  It's also very expensive and will last many decades before any signs of fading and chalking.  Anything you paint over this paint will peel, fade and chalk in short order.  Trying to paint over polyvinylidene fluoride paint would be a huge mistake. The other paint used on quality panels is Silicone modified polyester paint which will carry warranties of 30+ years against fading and chalking.  The next runner up would be 100% acrylic enamel paint that will last 5 to 10 years before looking like something entirely different because of fading and chalking. It would be a good idea to find out which paint was used on your panels to determine what is the best paint to apply over the original paint.  NOW if the metal panels are bargain basement cheap panels painted with acrylic enamel or some other cheap paint then paint away.  The cheap paint will chalk and fade and look terrible anyway in 5+ years.

there is no such thing as Soft Quartzite.  it's either quartzite or it's not. Fantasy Brown?  marble/dolomite educate yourself on what you're buying. Sellers will change names of their slabs. Quartzite will NEVER etch.  why?  because it's made of quartz not calcite or dolomite, the latter two are the reason it etches. if they tell you "oh it's fine. some quartzite has marble (calcite in it)  NO. Hi Susan, Thanks for the additional information. As others have indicated, 1000mm wide (or occasionally 1200 wide) tend to be the maximum for singe unit, double door pantry units as an "off the shelf" configuration - this is due to the typical maximum door width being 600 wide, above which you can have structural issues. You can get wider - usually though only as top/bottom split pantries, and then with bifold doors on each side, but you are usually hitting another price point. DIY are generally amongst the most competitve on raw price - they are a "stack it high, sell it cheap" operation who do all they can to squeeze every ounce of cost out of their direct-to-customer operation. As a result, however, the onus is on you for everything - ensuring the design fits, is fit for purpose etc. You therefore take on all design, fit & installation risk, and if things go awry, then the remedial hassles (and costs) sit firmly with you. If you are comfortable managing all of this, then you can potentially grab a bargain - as long as you execute well! Their internal options do tend to be rather basic and as far as I can see, theil larder is plain shelves. Regarding your options - sometimes to build up to the sort of width you have to play with, you can opt either for 2x 800 wide pantries, or a 1000w plus another 500 or 600 - the image below   was an installation we did with a butler's pantry flanked by a fridge freezer (1000 & 600 wide respectively). Or a 1000w flanked on either side by a 400w unit - either in plain shelves (to keep costs down) or with internal drawers. It can still vary quite a bit - the more fancy internals you have (wicker baskets, solid oak door racks etc), the higher it would be. Do you already have a design you are looking to use? You could also consider installing a dimmer switch to control the brightness of the lights and create a more relaxing ambiance when desired. In terms of sconce lighting, it's understandable that you may feel it would be out of place with the small upper cabinet and painted wall. " I’d like to put in some noise-abating privacy trees (maybe evergreen). " As previously noted, plants are very poor at any noise abatement. I live with my property surrounded by a block wide greenbelt so heavily planted you can't walk through it.....but I can still hear the noise of outside activities from the bordering properties a block away. Sound waves pass right through all that vegetation! Only a solid wall - like those constructed alongside freeways - will work effectively to deflect noise. Even a berm or mound is not much help unless it is tall enough......and very few are :-) Instead, focus on how you wish to use the backyard and develop a landscape plan that will address those needs/wants. Including a water feature somewhere near where most of your outdoor living takes place will be far more effective at diminishing any road noise than a bunch of plants could hope to!! You have a big chunk of real estate to work with and it is well beyond the scope of any advice or suggestions you might generate from an online forum that attracts mostly hobby gardeners, not designers :-) The best advice you have received here so far is to hire an experienced designer to assists you in this project.

Why did you buy this home instead of any of the other homes you saw? What spoke to you when you walked through the home? With every renovation you plan think long and hard and determine realistically how much more you would have spent to buy the home if this renovation was done.  Then find out what the renovation will actually cost. Reality is that price is based on location, square footage and overall condition. You can't change the location. The old saying that the three most important things to look for in a home are location, location and location is because location has the largest impact on a homes price. In most cases changes to square footage costs far more than it adds to the value of the house.  Midrange additions have an average of 30% ROI.  Spend $150k and the price of your home will go up by $45k. Cosmetic changes is the only thing left, and other than minor cosmetic changes they usually cost more than they increase the sales price. https://www.remodeling.hw.net/cost-vs-value/2023/ Anything you spend that has a negative ROI means that in 5 years you will have less money to spend on your next home than if you hadn't renovated the last home. Bonap should have the states where Florida betony has spread to in purple, not green, but BONAP gets a lot of things wrong. BONAP lumps the invasive European Phragmites with our rarer native Phragmites and list them combined as native. The do the same exact thing with our native and invasive Typha species and also Urtica dioica and U. gracilis, and Achillea millifolium and A. gracillis. We know that Florida betony is on the move because botanists look at all the places the plant has been observed, and those observations go all the way back to the time of Linaeus. Botanists are more concerned with the geology and hydrology of a place, not the border lines. Borders help nail locations. Most botanists today use GPS. The seeds of  Florida betony can also cling to people, pets and cars which also spreads it.

If your intent to block more UV is to limit fading, then using laminated glass along with LoE 366 will block more UV than will the 452 using "ordinary" glass, but visible light also contributes to fading, so that while blocking UV will slow fading, it isn't the whole story. Showing the comparison between the three different Cardinal coatings and including laminated glass, you can see that while using laminated glass results in all three coatings pretty much eliminating UV, the ISO-CIE (predicts actual fading potential), doesn't significantly change the fading potential of one coating versus another. Again this is due the the amount of visible light allowed through the glass. Less visible light equals less fading.  Second thought....are you looking at blocking more UV as a means of blocking more solar heat gain through those west facing windows? If so, while a very common misconception, actually UV doesn't contribute to solar heat gain, that would be IR, so blocking UV really doesn't help in keeping heat out.

You are too focused on symmetry.  This happens naturally to people who have never worked with blueprints/drawings before.  They are seeing it on the 2D page, but not understanding that in real life, symmetry or not is rarely noticed.  The only exception is a sink in front of the window, and even then, it often does not matter. When you see things lining up on a drawing, your brain is imagining that you are standing in one static place with no depth or depth perception.  In real life, you just move a few feet one way or the other, or closer or farther, and the symmetry or not will change because your perspective and angle have changed. I want you to think about all your relatives' and friends' kitchens.  Go through them in your mind.  Ask yourself if you have ever said to yourself "look how symmetrical this kitchen is", or "look how asymmetrical this kitchen is".  So do not sacrifice good kitchen design for the goal of symmetry, it's a bad trade. A prep sink would be good in the island, in the corner. Also, not what you asked, but ixnay on the spice pull-outs on either side of the range.  Those are a holdover from the '90s, and people who put them in 20+ years ago opt not to have them in their next kitchens.  The spice pull-outs make you bend and peer to see the spices, the bottles jostle and fall over, and the spices or condiments are exposed to the range's heat.  Better to have a spice insert in a drawer - people love those.  Just remove the pull-outs, and make the drawers on either side of them wider - a top drawer in either one of those adjacent drawer stacks would be an ideal place for a spice drawer with a spice insert.

I have not read all the posts here so I may be repeating suggestions. I think the area to the right of your range (for adequate prepping) is too small, as is the prep sink. I have a set up somewhat similar only with much more space, and I am continually frustrated and feel squeezed in. Here is a photo to give you a feel for placement and dimensions. There is 38” between stove and prep sink (sink is actually 13” wide) and 43” from sink to wall. The prep spaces to the right and left of the sink are not ideal, but certainly doable, but your design has virtually no real prep space. For me, the main frustration in my set up is the ridiculously small dimensions of my prep sink. Tiny prep sinks are not very functional. At least not for the way I prepare foods in my kitchen. You really need to analyze how you will use your sink. Large leafy and long vegetables are awkward to clean in such a sink, and there is not much room for large bowls or other prep materials. If you’re washing veggies or other foods, where will you put them once they’re clean and ready for prepping/cooking?  You are squishing your proposed prep area into a really small space….. you need more elbow room. Also, for me, the fact that I neglected to add a dishwasher (even a small one) near my prep sink is a major annoyance EVERY SINGLE DAY. I am always putting knives, spoons and various utensils along with measuring cups etc. into that sink, and if I don’t want to hand wash them, I have to dribble them over to the dishwasher to put them in. I do have two dishwashers, but they are still not in close proximity to the prep sink. So….it’s really important to understand how YOU will function in your kitchen and how you will use that prep sink. So, I would say that your prep area with that small sink is not the best design and barely useful. I also wouldn’t want my coffee maker infringing into my prep area. so I think a better area for your coffee maker would be near your under counter fridge which would also put it near refrigeration for easy access to creamer/milk etc.  We actually use bottled water so it was not necessary for our coffee maker to be near a sink, and in a former home, we actually installed a pot filler next to the coffee maker for easy access to water for filling. In my kitchen, where I spend 90% of my time (and where all the magic happens) is right on the cutting board in between the range and prep sink and my biggest complaints are that the sink is way too small for prepping and there is no dishwasher nearby. Otherwise, its location is fantastic (close to stove/sink and fridge/freezer). At the very least, I would move the coffee maker and enlarge the prep sink to more functional dimensions and ABSOLUTELY find space for a small dishwasher or single dishwasher drawer wherever the prep sink happens to be. I truly wish someone with knowledge would have warned me about the frustrations I mentioned above.  The solutions would have been very simple, and I would have had a much better functioning kitchen. I agree with others who stated that symmetry is overrated. It‘s really not necessary for your range to be lined up with your fireplace (or even the island for that matter).  As one who made some blunders in my layout, and after living here for over 4 years now, I am painfully aware that functionality trumps pretty and symmetry by far.  Pretty is important to me for sure, but the way the kitchen functions is ultimately what you will be dealing with on a daily basis ….for good or bad. And although I am also big on symmetry, I would gladly give some of that up to alleviate the things that needle me daily.

When the brows are laminated, the final appearance is more apparent and the individual hairs of the brows can be seen pointing in the same direction. Even so, it looks a lot better and quite natural. On the other hand, microblading also results in larger, more realistic brows. The brow hair seems natural, although not as natural as it does in brow lamination. In addition, the brows are significantly better defined than in eyebrow lamination.

Brow lamination is a semi-permanent treatment that sets the brow hairs in place, giving them a fuller and more uniform look. The process involves applying a special solution to the brows, which is then dried and brushed through to give them a desired shape. Brow lamination can last up to 8 weeks, and is a great option for those who want to achieve a more polished look without the commitment of microblading. Microblading is a semi-permanent makeup technique that uses a special tool to create hair-like strokes in the brows. This technique is ideal for those who want to fill in sparse areas or reshape their brows. The results of microblading can last up to 18 months, and require regular touch-ups to maintain the desired look.

I don't have experience with blackberry cuttings; but what you have is a blackberry scion if I compare it to the fruit trees I do have experience with. Fruit wood cuttings are called scions. If I keep a scion in a plastic freezer bag with some damp newspaper or peat moss around the cut end of the cutting they will last out the winter if the cutting or scion is dormant. Some sources seem to just stuff some of the damp  paper or peat in the bag and the moisture seems to keep what's in the bag and not in contact with the cut end alive. You can keep the plastic bag in a refrigerator unless you have fruit like apples in there. So i keep mine in an unheated integral garage and last almost as well as in the frig.

Scions typically refer to grafting material only, not starting a plant from cuttings! For stem cuttings to take root, they generally require plant tissue that is also in active growth or well budded, not dormant. Holding over the cuttings until a suitable time to plant - refrigerated or not - is not going to work in this case.

The best houses orient the public rooms towards the south for the best passive solar heating and cooling The best houses are L, U, T, H, or I shaped. The best houses are only one to two rooms deep. And covered lanai, porches, garages, etc count as rooms in this case. The best houses make sure kitchens have natural light, meaning windows so one doesn't have to have lighting 24/7 to use the kitchen. (And no, dining areas with windows 10' or more from the kitchen will not allow for natural light.) (The covered porch means it won't get natural light) The best houses make sure all public rooms and bedrooms have windows on at least two walls. The best houses do not if possible put mechanical rooms, pantries or closets on outside walls The best houses do not have diagonal interior walls making for odd spaces. The best houses keep public and private spaces separate. (the bedroom right off the foyer so sound can travel to that bedroom?) The best houses do not have you walk through the work zone of the kitchen to bring laundry to the laundry room. The best houses do not have the mudroom go through any of the work zones of the kitchen. The best houses do not use the kitchen as a hallway to any other rooms. The best houses do not put toilets or toilet rooms up against bedroom walls or public areas. The best houses do not have walk in closets too small to stand inside. The best houses have separation, such as closets, between bedrooms and between bedrooms and public rooms. The best houses do not have roofs that are overly large, and dominate the exterior of the house. The best houses do not have stick on exterior materials only on the front façade. The best houses have an organizing “spine” so it’s easy to determine how to get from room to room in the house and what makes sense. Meaning they don’t have meandering circulation paths.

More about using a "tell": Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips in order to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions - which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma and creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Al

If the damage was done last Fall, that really hasn't been much time for much healing to occur. But even given more time and things go well, you'll only have healing of the inner and outer bark layers, the heartwood itself won't heal, so you're looking at a few to several years before the wound is fully encapsulated with enough new layers to bind things together again. It's hard to tell from the pictures provided but some of those branches look dead and will have to be removed. If it were mine, I'd wait a while (a season?) and if new branches start growing out from the sides of the trunk below the break and the damaged fork doesn't show good progress overall and the top doesn't fill out good, I might cut the trunk below the wounded fork and let the tree start up again from any of the new, lower branches, if that happens.

you will know by mid summer ... and then it will be a whole different batch of questions on how to deal with removing the dead part .. if in fact it is ... imo... you should have just properly pruned off the damage.. when it happened... instead of drilling holes thru the good part to try to save the bad part ... i understand why you had to try to save it.. been there.. done that... but it usually doenst work out .... so next time.. just properly prune it.. and let the tree grow itself into a new form ... and most importantly ... next time you buy a tree.. avoid all trees with that kind of bark-included V crotch.. they are inherently weak.. as you found out.. prevention stats at the point of sale ... books have been written on the topic ... https://duckduckgo.com/?t=ffab&q=bark-included+V+crotch&iax=images&ia=images ken

Garage doors tend to be the single largest architectural element in a facade.  As such they become an eye-magnet, overwhelming and dominating the facade.  It's why front facing garages are often problematic. To reduce this potential it's usually a good idea to reduce and eliminate the contrast that can be created by garage doors by making them match the existing adjacent siding.  If the garage doors are site built, use the same siding.  If the garage doors are pre-built paint them to match the existing adjacent siding.  Never make them a greater contrast and stronger eye-magnet. It's your front porch and entry which should be the eye-magnet. Good luck!

Susan, Yeah unfortunately that's the way it goes for mini splits, the other is if you start some sort clorox or vinegar treatment this may lead to other issues that tend to be more costly, not that those things won't eventually happen anyway, but these sorts of treatments tend to speed these wear issues up. (freon leaks) Most mini split models will drain via a gravity drain on an exterior wall of the structure. I would say it's important this drain is as short as possible has no loops or traps in it (mini split exterior drained unit only) AND a completely vertical drain or as vertical as possible. The idea is that when the system runs the condensate evacuates the entirety of the condensate drain. It will likely clog again, the idea is to minimize it. If for some reason the mini split head (indoor unit) was not placed on an exterior wall, your maintenance troubles will be harder to rectify. If water is allowed to sit in a horizontal drain run, it will start growth and or tiny dust particles that eventually fill the drain tube. Size of the drain tube (diameter) for these kinds of appliances are often times quite small so they are "designed" more or less to have these kinds of problems. The manufacturers cover their bases well within the confines of these arguments to include: We're not responsible for maintenance. Typically the mini splits are hung on an exterior wall the line set runs down that wall and to the exterior condensing unit. Some condenser models may have the ability to feed multiple heads (the indoor boxes that hang on the wall) while others may have a  condensing unit for each head. Each head will (should) have it's own separate gravity fed condensate tube (drain tube). Some models like cassettes that fit in ceiling space will come with condensate pumps that will pump the water out of the condensate reservoir these may also include some shut off device if the pump ever fails. Take a picture of the line set arrangement outside and you should be able to see where these condensate drains terminate (drain to). This may also give a few hints as to why you're having trouble so frequently.

(Yours probably won't fall off doing all the necessary searching, but to get you started, here are some salient rules that I suggest will be appropriate.) Hood functions include capture and containment.  Capture is enveloping the rising and expanding cooking effluent plumes so that they don't spread out into the room  Containment is transporting the partially filtered effluent to (usually) the outside. One might surmise that capture implies a hood larger than the cooking surface, and for wall hoods not over 36 inches above the cooktop this requirement can be met by a hood at least 3 inches wider than the cooktop each side, and extending at least 3 inches forward of the cooktop (depending on where the elements/burners/hobs are actually located).  Some forward size might be avoided if hot oil cooking occurs on back burners or the hood has side skirts or cabinets helping the flow field move forward a bit. For residential hoods, I recommend an actual 90 CFM per square foot of hood entry (capture) area.  This will require in CFM units a blower achieving the hood entry area (sq. ft.) times 90 ft/min air flow.  The rated (zero static pressure) blower flow rate should be about 1.5 times this CFM. Ducting should be sized to keep full-power actual flow velocity between 1000 and 2000 ft/min. No air leaves the kitchen that isn't replaced.  This replacement is called make-up air (MUA).  Code requires it, and avoiding various undesirable effects demands it.  MUA can be passively (no blower) or actively (with blower) supplied, depending on what pressure loss is safe for any combustion appliances (e.g., dryer, hot water heater) you have connected directly or indirectly to kitchen air instead of having their own MUA, or not having any (e.g., electric hot water heater).  Active MUA will be needed with sensitive combustion appliances, and also the fireplace if you intend to cook vigorously when operating it.  Else, passive may do. MUA should have means of heating it unless you would be willing to cook in winter with the windows open. For background, review the last decade's hood and MUA threads here.

It's nothing to worry about Dan.  Vernalization of onions can happen when they are actively growing in the vegetative or bulbing stage, or dormant and in storage, but other conditions must be met to change a onion's season to flower.Onions must pass a juvenile phase before they are receptive to chilling and is dependent on the cultivar which ranges from 4 to 14 leaves.  They also require temperatures below 50 degrees over a period of 60 days for complete Vernalization, and again depend on cultivar.  All these numbers are for long day onions but the same requirements stand for short day cultivars to force them to bolt and flower in the same year, but actual values will be different and I don't know what they are.Just like day light which is cumulative to cause bulbing, the same holds true for time required in the chilling process to cause total vernalization.  A few days of very cold temperatures will kill the plants before it will change their season and yours didn't die so all is good.  As far as leaf lose, there are some who think cutting half the leaves from the plants 1/2 way through the vegetative stage will give them bigger onions but I don't agree  and anyone who listened to the nonsense and tried claimed it was not true.  They believe it because they're parents told them this and a myth handed down generations.  You will lose size but not enough to be worried about at this early stage of growth.

author_name: daninthedirt (USDA 9a, HZ9, CentTX, Sunset z30, Cfa)
text: Well, this is interesting. I'll be harvesting my 1015s in a few weeks, and because we had a vicious freeze (10F) in January, and I lost ALL my onion leaves, I figured the bulbs wouldn't be as productive. Fortunately, the plants all resprouted, but I was expecting a penalty. That is, to the extent that one onion leaf is responsible for one onion ring, you'd think that losing leaves would cause loss of rings, and one would get smaller onions. Dixondale seemed to agree. Now, my plants are not quite as tall as they usually are, but the bulbs look large. I'll have a lot of 1lb onions. Maybe the loss of leaves happened early enough in their development (two months after setting the plants out) that the penalty wasn't as severe as it might have been. I'm not seeing any bolting either. (1015s usually don't bolt anyway.) I am pleased.

I'm no expert, just an amateur who grows several kinds of these South African plants. Your appears to be either Aloe ferox or Aloe merlothii. In my garden here in the Sonoran Desert that straddles the US/Mexican border, my several aloes are planted in the ground, so I don't have the option of moving them indoors when temperatures drop below freezing. (Yes, we do get frosts several times each winter; and routine June days of 110). If winter dawn temperatures drop below 29 F (about -1.6 C), I cover my aloes with cloths raised on stakes so the fabric doesn't touch the leaves. As with all succulents, if the plant is too plumped with water when frost comes, the plant is more vulnerable to damage as cells freeze and rupture. I water mine with a frequency based on temperatures, viz.:  90+ weekly; 80s alternate weeks; 70s every three weeks; 60 or below monthly or less. These tidy and easy-to-remember Farenheit numbers translate to Celcius at about 32.2+ weekly; 26.6+  alternate weeks; 21+ every three weeks; 15.5 monthly or less. If in doubt -- as when temperatures are variable, or there has been a lot of rain -- skip watering for a week. Getting to your question: I think the small grey ovoid thumb-print-sized spots are likely frost damage, which may turn blackish as they rot. Be very restrained with watering, to minimize expansion of rot spots. The bands of irregular green will probably even out. The tannish band across the base of that one leaf looks like it is preparing to die. Let it become brittle and rigid enough to snap off. From time to time, bend it gently; if it does not snap, leave it alone. If it will not snap off, do not cut if off, as that would expose living interior flesh to bacteria that will promote rot. Keep an eye on the spots; if they stay the same size, even if they blacken, the rest of the leaf should be okay. Eventually the leaf will age out as new ones grow out from the center, and when the old leaf becomes russet and brittle you can snap it off. In your photo, the soil looks both heavy and wet, and the pot plastic. If you can find a sack of cactus soil, re-pot the aloe in an unglazed terracotta pot, and raise the pot on clay feet or a bed of pebbles. Raising the pot allows the soil to drain rapidly when you water it, and the terracotta pot allows the soil to breath. These two types of aloe grow in the African wild in open grasslands, which is to say they can take as much sun as you can give them (other aloes prefer bright dappled shade). As another writer has suggested, you can always start with a new plant. If you pursue that, wait till weather warms a bit, and start out with the right soil and pot and watering schedule. Good luck with this, as everyone benefits from a bit of green in their lives. And happy New Year.

As I've written dozens of times here (scores?  hundreds?), depending on hood details but mainly relevant to residential style hoods, in my opinion you should strive to achieve an actual 90 CFM per square foot of hood entry aperture.  For reasons also repeated, you will have to chose a blower rated at about 1.5X this value.  This will ensure containment of plumes that are captured, but capture may or may not be satisfactory depending on cross drafts over the island. Most certainly, an exterior blower with an intermediate silencer will be quieter than the blower alone -- probably significantly quieter.  Blade tip turbulence noise is mostly high frequencies, and that is what the Fantech silencers are reasonably good at suppressing. Rumbly noises, if present, need to be dampened separately by loading the duct surfaces with some type of dampening material, such as used on car doors. Fantech silencers are 4 inches larger in diameter than the duct being used, so space for that has to be planned for. Actual MUA CFM has to be supplied for the actual hood CFM.  How it is controlled can vary, but depending on presence or not of combustion appliances, may need to be accurately controlled. You would find it helpful, I think, to read a portion of the myriad hood and MUA related threads here for better understanding.

Edgecomb Gray is actually more taupe (pink) than Revere Pewter which has more green tones. Lowering the level of light can often make greiges appear muddy, and next to taupe they often appear muddy. If Revere Pewter was appearing muddy in a room I would go warmer.   I would test Pashima and Stone Hearth. You always need to test the color in your own space to know for sure which is the perfect neutral. The color you currently have is very strong and may be influencing your view of the colors when testing.   If you have or even need to buy something large and white (A white paper table cloth, a white shower curtain liner, a white sheet)  it may help you see the colors better if you tape it over a portion of your current wall color. You also want to be looking at the colors next to the floor - floor color stays, wall color goes away, so your new color has to work with the floor and it doesn't matter how it looks next to the walls.

If you want more fat in your salmon, add butter.  If you are concerned about the thin edge, fold it over and tie it in place. I do not want sugar or anything sweet added to my salmon, and I generally sprinkle it with lemon juice after it is done. I prefer to cook salmon on the grill over wood and charcoal.  Because of the high fat content in salmon (including wild), it will absorb a lot of the smoke flavor, unlike a lean fish like swordfish, which tastes pretty much the same whether grilled over charcoal or not. I start with the skin side up and cook the fish until it will release from the grill, and this way I get good grill marks and smoke flavor.  Also, this allows the fat under the skin to "baste" into the fish instead of drip away.  If you cook it with the skin side down first, you lose a lot of flavor when the fat cooks out. For me, ATK is very hit or miss.  Most of their recipes use too much salt, and I omit sugar in a lot of them as well, but that is just my preference.  You might notice that they will say one thing one year and then a couple of years later say the opposite. I tend not to buy salmon out of season, but it is one of my favorite fish. Alaskan sockeye (netted) sometimes being an exception, we don't have a sockeye run here. Fat content varies greatly by time of year.  A late summer early fall coho is a very fat and flavorful moist fish, can hold its own alongside chinook on a plate at any table. I don't want to eat a fish artificially fed, and likely the same food day in day out.  Those penned Atlantic salmon sometimes have dye added to their feed to make the flesh more 'salmon like'....its not red without their natural varied diet. I do see the farmed Atlantic offered in stores here, I can't imagine why when we are 20 minutes from the Pacific.  Farming Atlantic has even been tried here with disastrous results of torn and damaged pens (storms and poor upkeep), escaped fish in huge numbers.  Our native American population was up in arms and horrified, and rightly so.  The companies with permits to farm lost their local licenses and aren't back in production.  But I don't eat farmed shrimp or prawns or any other farmed seafood other than oysters (they are not fed - the tides provide natural food). If I lived in the midwest I might view it differently.  Here, I don't have to.  Fish and almost any seafood is a simple cooking process.  Fresh, cooked hot and quickly, maybe a pat of butter and some salt and pepper but if a sauce is served, its along side and optional.

Ingredients 4 servings ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil ¼ cup harissa paste (our favorite is New York Shuk) 1 garlic clove, grated 1 lemon, halved 1 2-lb. skinless center-cut salmon fillet Kosher salt Mixed tender herbs (such as parsley, cilantro, dill, and/or chives; for serving) Preparation Step 1Preheat  oven to 275°. Whisk oil, harissa, and garlic in a medium bowl. Pour  half of harissa oil into a 2.5-qt. baking dish and swirl to coat. Thinly  slice a lemon half and remove any seeds; scatter slices in dish. Step 2 Season  salmon on all sides with salt and place in dish. Pour remaining harissa  oil over salmon, spreading evenly over flesh with a pastry brush or  spoon. Roast 15 minutes. Remove from oven and baste fish with harissa  oil pooled in dish. Return to oven and continue to roast until flesh  flakes apart easily with a spoon but is not quite cooked through, 10–20  minutes longer. Step 3 Use  spoon to break up salmon into irregular pieces. Arrange salmon and  lemon slices on a platter. Drizzle with any harissa oil left in dish,  squeeze remaining lemon half over, and scatter some herbs around.

But just to be more specific about the comment above from @User - the range needs to stay at 30” width unless you are also removing upper cabinets above the wider range.  The reason is that cabinets are made of combustible materials and finishes.  Therefore you cannot have cabinets directly over a range, or you’d create a serious fire hazard. If for example you replaced your 30” range with a 36” range, but made no changes to the uppers, that would mean 6” of upper cabinets are exposed to heat and flame of the 36” range.  That is against Building Codes.  I am being emphatic about this because 50% of house fires start in the kitchen.  And ranges or cooktops were involved in 61% of those fires, 87% of cooking fire deaths and 78% of cooking fire injuries. You also cannot have a 30” over-the-range microwave over a wider range.  Are you replacing the microwave with a hood?

Any deciduous tree can drop some leaves early if stressed for some reason....such as disease, drought or radical weather changes. But for an otherwise healthy and unstressed tree, it is of NO benefit to the tree to have an early leaf drop. It will affect the ability to photosynthesize successfully to store needed nutrients for winter and to stimulate spring growth. I would not expect many - if any - deciduous trees to demonstrate this trait under any "normal" circumstances. OTOH, broadleaved evergreen trees like magnolias, live oaks, arbutus, etc. will drop old leaves throughout the year but rarely in a one time, heavy quantity similar to a fall leaf drop with their deciduous cousins.

text: Standard spacing for bulb onions is 4", so you're good to go. Note that onions don't even begin to produce real bulbs until a month or so before harvest. At that time, the leaves should be 2-3 feet long. Hard to tell from your pictures, but your plants don't look that mature. Not quite sure what to expect if you're repurposing onion bulbs from the supermarket.

If they are supermarket bulbs that sprouted, you aren't likely to get bulb onions from those. Supermarket bulb onions are already done with their first year growing and are dormant. When they sprout, the are going into their second year of growing, which is their seed growing year. So energy production will go more into the greens and seed head formation than producing another big bulb. Some varieties of onions can divide and grow that way, but the varieties commercially grown for supermarkets tend not to do so since a single bulb is more desireable than dividing bulbs for the buyer. Sprouted bulbs are great for growing onion greens- I regularly have a pot or two in the kitchen window during the winter for them.

Those clusters look like what I get in the 2nd year, when I plant saved bulbs for seed. Those bulbs usually split into a cluster, typically 3-6 plants. If let go, they will send up seed stalks in the Spring (or whatever passes for Spring in your obviously warmer location lol) and eventually form a cluster of small, shallot-like bulbs. I never tried to re-plant those bulblets (DW just made soup from them) but suspect they would act like onion sets. " I believe pearl onions are just baby onions, and if you plant them from the supermarket, they should grow bulbs." True, if they were from the supermarket. But just an FYI, calling those small supermarket onions "pearl onions" is a misnomer, much like sweet potatoes being misnamed 'yams', or small pickled cucumbers being misnamed 'gherkins'. The real pearl onion, Allium sphaerocephalum, is an onion relative that looks like a miniature Elephant garlic... and forms clusters of genuinely pearl-sized bulblets under the main bulb. That main bulb seldom exceeds !" wide, but they can be planted densely.

I have never heard Allium spaerocephalum referred to as ’Pearl Onion’. It has many vernacular names, mostly referring to the flower head, for which it is usually grown, but not ime Pearl Onion. Pearl Onion usully denotes Allium ampeloprasum var. sectivum. I also would not say that calling small pickling cucumbers Gherkins is a misnomer. It's a culinary and usage term, not a botanical definition, denoting certain small cucumber cultivars grown specifically for pickling. There’s nothing wrong with that. It is a useful term imo.

Flushing the soil asap, getting the plant on a regular nutritional supplementation program so you're fertilizing about every 3rd or 4th time you water in summer and every 4th or 5th time in winter, establishing appropriate watering intervals, and providing a warm/bright setting for your plant should turn things around. A couple folks around here use huge inflatable swans in their ponds. They look like pool floats meant for a kid or maybe small adult? Put it on an anchor so it floats around "On patrol", but does not float away. They are fun :) And seem to work. We have live swans on our biggest pond, they for sure work. Once it gets up to small lake size, if the habitat can support both birds your mileage on a fake swan can go down if there are already live ones on the lake. I've heard of dead goose or gator decoys being used, but haven't seen them in action. How are you utilizing the edge of the pond? Geese prefer a gentle and open edge to a pond. Easy to walk on, see predators coming, and easy take-off space if needed. Messing with that can be a great way to keep them from wanting to stick around. Doing a bit of habitat modification can often do the trick. If you run a wire about 8 inches off the ground close to the waters edge that will stop them. It's their fence height, they are unlikely to duck under or hop over it. If you use flash tape on it, all the better. 12-18+ inches of fence, stacked rocks or wood, various planting and growths, and the like can block them. A solid line or fence is best, though you can break it up a bit into layering your stuff and creating switchback spots to walk through. Humans and dogs are fine with walking through switchbacks. Wild geese are not so fond of walking through what they can't see over- particularly if there are several geese together. They will do it, they just aren't fond of it and if there is easier beach access elsewhere on the lake, they will choose it first.  If you can put a stringer across the water a foot or so off from shore, they won't swim over it to walk up onto the shore. Stepping or walling your shore can be possible in some situations. It makes the waters edge not swim to walk accessable for birds. One of my smaller ponds is very deep with a natural step edge dropping in, it's surrounded by tall grasses. I've seen many places have retaining walls that come straight up out of the water- it's often for shoring or retaining, but also is very good at creating the step that geese don't want to use. If your geese are ealier spring stopovers. Letting your lawn get a bit shaggier in the fall and holding off a bit in the spring can make your lawn seem not so tasty or hospitable by comparison to neighbors lawns that get their last cuts later or start earlier. Spring geese love a fresh and verdant spring lawn. If your lawn is made up of sweeter or more tender grasses, growing more bitter and tougher grasses can help a bit. Especially if other lawns have tasty grass growing in them. If you are spring seeding your lawn, geese go after that too.

Although interest is expressed in APR it is only for the period outstanding.  So you are going to pay interest on $6,750 x rate/12 x months. Any realtor worth 20 cents is then going to demand the system be inspected by an HVAC professional who is probably going to advise replacement.  So you are going to be stuck replacing it anyway. Replacement after the purchase agreement is way more problematic as your house was likely already priced to sell with an older AC unit and you can't reprice it with a new unit.  It also gives the buyer input and approval over the repair and if you refuse the buyer's demands, you are going to have to disclose the reason the previous offer was terminated to any future sellers. Many buyers don't have the extra money to do the repairs outside the contract and so offering a discount often doesn't work as too many buyers can't replace it. --- I prefer to control the work completely outside the contract.  I would replace it and price the house accordingly.

I am going to give a more detailed explanation of why I typically replace old systems when I am getting ready to sell a home and the system has a problem. Houses with new units sell for more money than houses with old units.  According to the NAR, replacement of old heating and cooling systems has about an 85% return on investment when selling.  That seems a little high to me, but certainly buyers price in new units.  So let's make some assumptions and do a little math. Let's assume that the new unit only has just over a 50% return on investment and would increase the sales price by $3,500.  So, by not replacing your unit, you are paying some amount to repair it, let's say $500, and losing $3,500 in sales price, but are saving $6,750 in replacement.  So you are basically saving $2,750, by repairing your old unit rather than replacing it with a new unit. However, there is one additional complicating factor.  Most buyers are going to have an old unit inspected by an HVAC company and too many HVAC companies are just looking for an excuse for replacement.  So you have the added concern that the buyer is going to want an allowance or to have a new unit replaced.  So you could be spending the $6,750 anyway, except you are losing the advantage of pricing the home higher.  You are going to have to pay the $6,750 after spending on the repair and pricing the home $3,500 less. So in the above scenario you would be betting on a $2,750 savings against a $10,750 loss ($3,500 reduced price + $500 repair + $6,750 allowance or new unit).  I typically sell a home every year, sometimes two, I have been burned on that gamble too many times. --- Now in your area or at your price point the ROI when selling could be more or less than 50%, you might actually be at 85% which makes it a no brainer, or you might be at 25% which would make repair much more attractive. Good luck

All heat pumps have back up heating assistance. It is usually electrical heating strips installed inside the air handler. This is to provide a supplementary heat when the outdoor temperatures are low. It is possible you have not wired or configured your new thermostat to work with heat pump with back up heating. If you installed the thermostat, then review the installation procedure. If you did not do the installation then you will have to call a HVAC tech. Since you have crown identical to your existing, and the existing runs right into the adjacent wall, do a youtube search for "coping crown inside corners". Simplistically, you'll cut the crown at an inside 45 degree angle. Then use a coping saw to cut a slight back cut right right along the cut line made when you did the 45. The coped edge of the new crown will butt right into the profile of the existing crown as long as they have the same profile. If you're not familiar with the basics of cutting crown, do a search for "cutting crown upside down and backwards". You can miter the outside corners and miter or cope the inside corners. Coping inside corners works well if the inside corner angle is slightly off of a perfect 90 degrees. If your new crown has a different profile, you can scribe the end of the new crown to fit the profile of the existing crown. Enjoy!

Quartz has resin mixed in with ground stone. The percentage is important for quality. Some Chinese quartz has more resin. Quartz can scorch from a hot pan. Quartzite is often harder than granite. Taj Mahal varies in color depending on the slabs and some sources grade it for color. Take pictures of your slabs. Plan the layouts ahead of fabrication. Especially seams. Klem is correct. A T&P valve opens because of temperature or pressure.  Almost always a leak or drip is excessive pressure unless there's crud under the seat of the valve. But if you've replaced it, you've ruled out crud on the seat. Excessive pressure typically happens for two reasons: 1. The incoming water pressure is too high. If that's the case, you need a pressure reducing valve. Excessive water pressure can damage pipes, valves, appliances and the water heater. 2. There is already a pressure reducing valve on the main line (and it's working properly) but there's no expansion tank on the water heater. A PRV works as a backflow valve also, so when your water heater heats the water, there's no place for it to expand to if there's no expansion tank or the tank isn't working. This results in temporary excessive pressure. Both situations are very hard on your plumbing. The T&P valve is a safety... don't ignore the underlying issue.

I certainly understand the pleasure of a patio on the east side of the house. But our living areas faced SW, with bedroom in the NE and NW corners, and no windows on the NW side (not only a close neighbor on that side, but prevailing winter winds). It took full advantage of passive solar in the winter, and had minimal direct sunlight in the summer (thanks to well-placed trees in the front yard). We spent a lot more time indoors than outdoors, even in the summer. I completely agree with David Cary that orientation is paramount. You have very specific needs for your build, and meeting all those needs while optimizing orientation is quite the challenge. But I think I would prioritize the interior space, and if you have to use a screen or umbrellas to shade the deck in the afternoon, so be it.

The allelopathic properties of Schinus molle tend to be overstated. Male plants tend to be more adept at deterring competing weed seedling species but neither gender has a significant impact on more mature plantings. As long as you are not seeding in any new arrivals, you should be fine :-) Just follow the usual recommendations for plants that will tolerate dry shade. FWIW. most tree species will exhibit some degree of allelopathy but rarely to the extent of limiting or impeding other plantings.

" One of the main concerns with using pressure-treated lumber is that it contains chemicals that can be harmful to humans and pets." That is rather outdated information and has not been the case since 2004, when the EPA banned the old formulations (CCA - chromated copper arsenate) for pressure treated lumber. There certainly may be structures extant that contain old pressure treated wood but anything you can purchase now has been treated with chemicals considered safe for use in virtually any situation, including raised garden beds, lawn furniture, decks and fencing, kids' playground structures and dog houses or pet structures. Almost any wooden structure exposed to weather is recommended to be constructed from  pressure treated wood to ensure longevity and ALL current types of pressure treated wood or PT wood products are considered to be completely safe for any residential use. This is very easy to validate from virtually any online source.

IMO slate tiles can often be a mixed bag of thickness. Who chose the tiles ? If the tiles were gauged then this is on install issue but if just pallets of ungauged tile then who knows. I do understand the issue of the tiles coming off and the holoow sonds that has nothing to do with tile thickness but for sure with unguaged you might encounter these issues There is no uniform thickness to un-gauged slate, so getting a flat flooring surface can be difficult, requiring practices like back-buttering to get the tiles to lie flat. Typically, un-gauged slate is preferred for outside uses, and is great for things like garden stepping-stones. Gauged tile on the other hand is ideal for indoor applications, as the even thickness will make the floor flatter and more even.

What attracts pollinators most efficiently are exposed anthers and stamen. Nature favors single flowers because they possess the greatest concentration of stamen with anthers, therefore the most pollen. Pollinators are after the pollen and/or any nectar the bloom forms. If you want butterflies and bees, plant rose types which don't cover their stamen with too many petals, preferably single types which only really cover their stamen at night when the petals fold over to protect them from moisture. Yes, pollinators will visit less single types in efforts to access their anthers, but you'll have the most reliable activity with single to semi single blooms.

The types of hellebores artinnature is referring to with upward and outward facing flowers are intersectional hybrids with rather complex parentage. Although any hellebore is a great garden plant, these ones tend to be a bit limited in coloring as well as seldom featuring any double flowers. Unlike the vastly more common Helleborus x hybridus or "oriental hybrids" (with nodding, downward facing flowers in a vast array of colors), these intersectional varieties tend to have white, cream or pink/mauve flowers or a blend thereof.  These are not as common in nurseries and garden centers as the xhybridus but are easily available via mail order. They often have stunning patterned or marbled foliage as well FWIW, all hellebores are easy to grow. All they require is proper drainage and enough sun to promote flowering. While hellebores are shade tolerant, they grow beautifully in quite a lot of sun as long as protected from intense summer heat. Corsican hellebore, H. argutifolius, can be grown in full sun as that is its native condition. Not as hardy as some other varieties however.

There are so many experts on Maple staining here who have never actually touched a can of stain or finished Maple.  Including Creative Cabinets,  which is a fake business that Verbo created to lend credence to his posts. Unfortunately, I suspect your contractor is also someone who may not really understand the task at hand.  Soft Maple will get paper white after a single bleaching and hard Maple lightens almost as easily but will not usually get paper white.  The blotchiness of Maple is not as problematic with whitewashing stains, as whitewashing stains are often not penetrating stains. Here are some suggestions from someone who often whitens Maple.  What I use really depends on the piece  of wood I am using.  Maple can get “dirty” it can have lots of small pitch pockets that make it look like someone took a black marker and made dozens of small black marks on every door, or it can be really beautifully grained. Test the Minwax on some drawer backs and see what it looks like.  White stains are mostly going to sit on top of the wood like paint because wood doesn’t love to drink in titanium oxide.  It may look fine. If I was finishing cabinets I would just paint it.  One of the easiest and most common ways to whitewash cabinets is with a toner coat.   You literally just go buy a white coating and the same clear coating and mix one part white to ten parts clear and spray it (play with the ratio to get it right).  You can also use a clear base and colorant.  If you are happy with the look after a single coat, then switch to clear, if not add another coat.  Any experienced sprayer should be able to spray a toner coat. Maple bleaches easily and beautifully.  I use a lye etcher and a 35% hydrogen peroxide bleach, but with Maple you can honestly get away with household bleach.  Tamar over at 3x3 customs has a bleaching test video…I would argue that my results are slightly better than hers, but a bit more difficult.   There are plenty of videos on bleaching wood and it is not difficult. Finally, if you are concerned about your contractor’s ability to achieve good results, which may be a fair assessment given that he only uses Minwax products, investigate Rubio Monocoat hard wax oils.  The village idiot could apply Rubio Monocoat and get flawless results.  Hard wax oils are a strong and durable finish that are also infinitely repairable.   If you get a stain, just sand it out and apply the hard wax oil again, you will not be able to find the repair.   However, over time hard wax oils get pulled into the wood and so every five years or so you have to add a coat of renewer.  This is simply wiping the cabinets down with the renewal oil.  Hard wax oils are not quite as durable as conversion varnish or 2k polys, but again, they are repairable unlike those. If your Maple is pulling pink, which they sometimes do, add a mint white precolor to the Rubio.  If staining or painting add a small shot of green colorant to the coating (test results first).  On the color wheel greens are opposite of reds and so they neutralize red colors. Good luck -—

I've had peppers cross. Not such a biggie when it's something like two colors of a similar swet pepper or heat level of hot pepper. I've seen some color mutations or shape irregularities. Not so great if I want a pepper for particular qualities and they get lost. While peppers are self fertile, they also can be pollenated by outside influence like pollinators and weather. If a grower wants to ensure the purity of that pepper, they isolate some or all of it. I isolate by bagging a branch or cluster of buds before they start to bloom. Or I might grow one plant in isolation. I've seen local growers of produce isolate off a small section of plants out of their field. They cage in a few plants at the end of a row to save their seed for the next season.

Just saving the seeds from a diverse pepper patch won't guarantee you will grow a pepper plant true to the mother plant so not a good Idea if you care. No. 'Columnaris' and 'Fastigiata' are two separate cultivars of European hornbeam. 'Fastigiata' is the most commonly encountered of the two and it is a faster growing and taller and wider selection than 'Columnaris'. In fact, there is not much very fastigiate about 'Fastigiata', as over time it grows into a very plump, gumdrop shaped tree as much as 30' wide. If you want the tree to remain skinny, look for 'Frans Fontaine'. All of the positive aspects of Fastigiata but with a 12-15' spread at most. It should also be noted that it's not uncommon to have Columnaris and Fastigiata confused in the trade and therefore mistagged.

Columnaris will hit maybe 2/3 the height of Fastigiata and with a spread of 15-20'. Fastigiata will wind up about twice that width. Columnaris also develops at a slower rate than Fastigiata but no hornbeam grows very quickly anyway. I would Google images of both cultivars to see how they spread out with age and relative size differences. And I will point out again that neither of those two cultivars is very columnar, fastigiate or narrow despite their cultivar names.

Lucky bamboo is not a bamboo at all but a type of dracaena, Dracaena sanderiana. And like any other type of dracaena, it will grow just as well in container potting soil as it will in rocks and water. And a lot bigger and faster as well. And like any plant growing in an artificial medium, it does benefit from some nutrient supplementation. Without any, growth will ultimately stop. But it doesn't need much - a well diluted liquid whenever the water is refreshed will suffice. Rather than cutting them off, after removing the ties, I would carefully tease the two yellowed stalks and their roots out of the mess completely. There is no point to leaving them in place. Then repot in the media of your choice - water  and rocks or container potting soil. Keep out of direct sun and do fertilize lightly now and then :-))

At what point should I remove some leaves? Light levels are a key element in how much stored energy the plant is likely to have and how much food it can make (a plant's true food is sugar, glucose - which it makes during photosynthesis), both of which should be at peak levels around the summer solstice (21 June in the Northern Hemisphere, where we live). The idea is to care for the plant as best you can, try to move it outdoors for at least several weeks before the solstice (you should be able to do that around Memorial Day), and make sure you're watering/ fertilizing appropriately. Good nutrition is essential to good vitality (health). An under-nourished plant can never be healthy. Let it adapt to being  repotted first? I'm guessing you potted up as opposed to doing a full repot, which includes bare-rooting, root pruning, and a change of soil. If you potted up, there isn't any adjustment to be concerned about. As soon as you see new growth after repotting or potting up, your plant is "adjusted". You might need to be extra careful about your watering intervals because the plant is more vulnerable to over-watering in a larger soil mass. That "allow your plant to adjust to its surroundings" thing is way over rated and not grounded in science. When we bring a new plant home, it immediately adjusts to its surroundings. If unwanted symptoms are noticed, it's not because the plant is adjusting, it's because the plant doesn't like the cultural hand it's being dealt. Wait til spring? Yes and no. "Spring" lasts 3 months. Early spring (winter and late fall, too) is about the worst time to do heavy work like repotting, hard pruning, or defoliation on most houseplants. Those procedures should be done when stored energy and current ability to create energy/food is at peak, which is around the summer solstice. The reason is the plants metabolic processes are humming because energy availability is at peak. This means the plant recovers fastest from any heavy work you might do to it, and will be better able to defend itself against insects and disease pathogens. Doing hard work out of season makes the recovery period much longer, and that isn't necessary. Plants have natural rhythms. Learning to take advantage the plant's period of strength and making allowances for when it's weakest is much easier on the plant, and it will make us feel like we're better nurturers. Those of us who don't look at plants more like pets than decorations all have a nurturing bone that needs to be satisfied. Yes? It would be nice if I could induce branching too. You haven't said what the top is made of, but judging by the consistency of the white color and lack of particulates and movement, I'm guessing its engineered stone. Because it's 33% plastic, estone is much stronger than natural stone and therefore requires less support. You are allowed to cantilever 3cm estone up to 15" without additional support, however, I can promise that with any span over 6', as you have, you'll get a sag. A sag in a top with a cutout can be catastrophic for cracking. You also have adjacent cantilevers which adds to the support problem. You can't just plop a leg here and there and call it good. The support problem should have been addressed at the design stage. The best support would be removing the top and having a custom 1" square tube steel frame welded, painted and installed. I would be inconspicuous and avoid knee-knocking. An acceptable alternative would be legs with steel stretchers (wood if you install the middle leg) between them. Plywood is not a good support for any stone cantilever support, no matter what the estone manufacturers say.
