It's probably too late, but when you truncate succulents, you can wipe the sap off the wound with a paper towel or clean rag until it stops flowing, then carefully paint the wound with waterproof wood glue. It might not be rot that you're seeing. Wounds in very fleshy plants like Crassula an Aeonium tend to desiccate/ dry out for a considerable proximal distance from the cut. The propagule (or cutting) is usually nowhere near as susceptible to drying out as the rooted portion of the plant; this because the plant is still working to move water upward through the plant's plumbing/ vasculature. I typically save tag ends (the part you cut off after securing) of different size zip ties to use as sort of a spatula. I squeeze the waterproof wood glue onto the zip tie tail. then spread it over the wound carefully, so the wound itself is covered but clue isn't smeared all over the stem below the wound. Typically, that's where you want your back-budding to occur, instead of looking at a bunch of dead/ desiccated tissue. All of these plants are grown from single stems and all were treated with waterproof wood glue as a matter of course. I always treat Crassula and Portulacaria that way, too, along with all wounds larger than about 1/4" on my bonsai trees as well.    This one ^^^ has been reduced over time and is growing in a Chapstick cap  While I agree with the idea that treating wounds of most trees in the landscape more often than not exacerbates rot issues further down the road, creating problem/ hazardous trees, that doesn't apply to trees grown in containers because they are not subjected to the massive forces of strong wind and tons of weight. There is no question that this technique hastens production of callus tissue to cover the wound and prevent unsightly dieback. Al

HU: You have a 2cm engineered stone countertop. To drill the holes you want, you'll need a $62.74 diamond-tipped bit and a $210.65 angle grinder to chuck it onto. So you're almost $300.00 into tools that you'll unlikely ever use again. Maybe you could rent the grinder, or get someone with experience for the same or a little more money. You'll fire up the tool and holding it at a 45* angle, touch the bit to the top. As it digs in, raise the tool to perpendicular. You've either got a shop vac running adjacent, or a helper with a squirt bottle pumping as fast as possible.   There is some risk. You could buy the wrong bit, one for wet use, and the heat from drilling dry will melt the brazing holding the diamonds. Now you've buried an ugly black diamond ring into your top. When you get a larger bit to cut out the buried bit tip, it strikes the buried tip and kicks you out of the hole and your diamond bit skids acrosss the top as shown above.   Repairing your white particulate top inconspicuously would be much more difficult than this was. The sink would have to be dropped, the top cut to the splash, some splash sacrificed to get repair material, and you'd have a seam at each end of your rear sink rail and a splash problem to resolve. You'll want to verify that your new hole location doesn't interfere with any clips holding your sink in place and avoid drilling the sink flange too please. You have to drill far enough away from the clip that your nut doesn't get interference from it. While you're under there, I'd remove the faucet, lose the escutcheon plate if it's not covering holes, and reinstall it. Much nicer look. Yes Patricia, that is a replacement faucet and that escutcheon is designed to cover existing holes, however its use is optional. Good luck.

Sound sensitivity can be related to ADHD too. Sound sensitivity is a thing. Sometimes people don't realize how overload on human sound they are till they go camping and enjoy the "quiet". Nature really has a lot of noise. It's being called green noise currently. Most people are familiar with white noise, or static sound that has broad spectrum noise. Brown noise has more  low frequency, like roaring rivers and rumbling earth or sky. There is something to be said for the theraputic nature of sound frequencies. But it's the lack of human noise that can make green and other noise seem quiet. Having sound sensitivity issues can amp up short tolerance for human noises. There are people that a lack of human noise is just as much of a sound sensitive issue. They need the radio or TV on, or go nuts in the rural setting away from human noise for too long. It might be the lack of human noise, or it may be they have issues with other noise colors.

I'd like to report on how it went. The light wasn't very good and I realized that there were obstructions that prevented me from getting low enough to see the gap between the blade and the concrete. Unless we're using a fresh medium that comes with as starter charge of fertilizer or we're working with a newly acquired plant, we should assume our container media is devoid of nutrition. Regular applications of an appropriate fertilizer is an essential part of maximizing plant's opportunity to realize as much of their genetic potential as possible. My immediate first thought is that you should hire a landscape designer for at least an onsite consultation. There are literally scores of excellent designers in the greater Seattle area and I'd be happy to make a few referrals if needed. A good designer will help you to clarify the proposed new layout and make appropriate plant suggestions for a relatively modest hourly fee. I'd also suggest you review Great Plant Picks. This website is a PNW database of some of the most garden worthy and dependable plants for this area. They are broken down into various listings for various growing conditions, including drought tolerance. The Puget Sound region is considered to be a recurring summer drought area. We get almost no measurable precipitation from late June/early July through to the end of September and often into October. Selecting native species that are climate adapted and drought tolerant ornamentals makes a great deal of sense. They will need regular deep irrigation until established, however.

" How can a lawn in Seattle with all that rain look that bad. " All what rain? There is a mistaken presumption that it rains here all the time. It doesn't. Average annual rainfall is only 37" - much less than much of the country. And very little tends to fall between June/July and October, with this past summer being one of the driest on record with barely .5" measured over that period. Unirrigated lawns here in summer often look similar to the OP's. They are not dead, only dormant, and come back to life with cooler, wetter weather. But if that is the current state of the lawn, then there is more going on than a lack of irrigation. As what is there is going to be reduced and replaced, the issue is somewhat moot.

Most showers are limited by code (and just common sense) to 2-2.5 gpm. In Cal I believe it's 1.8 now. Yes, your GC should know local code... it's part of why he's getting paid. Forgiveness is definitely not easier than permission if you get flagged. This may be your first rodeo, but code inspectors have seen this a million times already and are looking for it. You start getting into water heater size and other issues when you go with multiple shower heads also. It gets expensive, and the novelty wears off pretty quick also. Be careful also about getting too far afield of what your contractors are familiar with.  If your GC is wise, he's giving you some supplier choices that he's familiar with and can support. You don't want to learn about "issues" with odd-ball faucets at finish. You want to stay in your role as "Owner" and not muddy the water by getting too much into GC territory. It's the GC who is responsible for it all coming together right. It's fine to say what you want the end product to be, but when you get into flow rates, psi, code,  etc... you are in the wrong lane. Most of the major US brands over a certain price point are going to give you long life, warranty, etc. It becomes about style and such after that. It's possible that the two finishes could complement each other and create a layered, eclectic look, or they could clash and create an awkward contrast. Without seeing the finishes in person, it's difficult to say for sure how they will look together. An air source heat pump is a great way to heat a high performance house, but you would need to do significant energy efficiency upgrading to a Victorian terrace to make it feasible - as in add a lot of insulation to walls, ceiling, ground floor, etc... This can be costly, even though it is definitely worth doing as it will make your home more comfortable and cost less to heat. However, an air source heat pump generally needs a pump room - it sounds like it's an easy swap from a little boiler on your wall to a similar sized unit that converts heat from air - but this isn't the case. It would still be worthwhile you adding more insulation to your home though and reducing heating needs that way. If you can reduce the amount you need to put heating on and stay comfortable then your home will be more eco and cost less to run, even if you stick with a gas boiler. Pruning is seldom needed except for removal of faded flowers (which is called deadheading), but if  you do prune, it is best to prune around March in the Pennsylvania area, understanding that they currently have dormant, spring 2023 flower buds so you may lose all or many spring blooms. Try to limit the number of branches cut to about 1/3 of branches with flower buds. This reduces the spring blooms but the remaining branches will provide some blooms. Typically, there is little need for pruning azaleas and rhododendrons if planted where they can attain their plant label's estimated size at maturity. If growth becomes excessive, reduce the size with light  pruning. Plant form can be improved by pinching out the soft, new shoots in spring. Each spring, after the flower buds start to swell and the smaller leaf  buds become different/obvious, use pinching on the top of the plant  to prevent it from getting taller. Prune out any dead, diseased, crossing, leafless (leafless after the spring leaf out!) or damaged branches, and if the plants have become scraggly, start cutting the oldest  branches back to encourage growth in younger branches. Review throughout the growing season if the sides are not getting much direct sunlight. Where to prune exactly: With larger leaf rhododendrons (elepidotes), only prune just above the growth joints. Each year as the plant starts to grow there is a visible growth joint that indicates where the branch started growth and that is where dormant growth buds are located. With your  azaleas and any small leaf rhododendrons (lepidotes), you can prune anywhere along the branch as the azalea branches have dormant growth buds nearly everywhere.

I have two Aero gardens - and I don't usually grow tomatoes or tomato seedlings in them. I'll use peat pots under strong grow lights to do tomatoes. Then when they are about 8" tall or so, I'll harden them off. 2 weeks later I'll plant outside in containers or huge grow bags. I'll sink the plant down so that 1/2 of it is buried along with roots. Then wait. I usually have rows of 12' tall, crazy prolific tomatoes and lots of fruit. Oh, and I ONLY grow cherry tomatoes. However, for the first time, I tried a micro cherry tomato called Tip Top (something like that). Stays very small and bushy, loads of small orange fruit. Supposedly for growing indoors on window sills or AG type gardens. I've found this actually works in the Aero Garden - but I've had to only grow one or at most, 2 plants (and nothing else) in the AGs. My AGs are all 6 or 7 pod, tall sized.) The tomatoes get sprawling and bushy, and take a good long time to grow. I actually added grow lights in addition to the light on the AG. (FYI, AG lights are replaceable, and you are supposed to replace the after so many hours.) I get a handful of ripe tomatoes about every 3 days or so now. Of course, I get BOWLS full from my outside cherry tomato plants right now... lol. Back to the original OP's questions: Worth saving? Likely. Tomatoes are super adaptable and forgiving. Stop trimming them tho. Up pot them into some 12-14" diameter and at least 12" deep pots while you wait for spring to plant them outside. Plant them deeply, sinking the stem at least a couple inches down. That will encourage the stem to grow more roots to support the plant better. In the larger pot, you can add a small cage or trellis to let them grow taller and bushier. They need more light for sure. Get some cheap 'stick in the pot' led grow lights, and add a few to each pot. You'll need to rig up an extension cord/power strip of course. I suggest to stop snipping them because when you do that, you truncate all the growth on that part of the plant for good. You can still have suckers that will overtake the world, but you've truncated the plants natural growth process by trimming them. You'll also need to feed them a bit more often but LESS to keep them happy while they wait. Choose a tomato version fertilizer, that you can dilute into the water to 1/2 strength. Key is to feed more often, but only at 1/2 strength while they are potted. As someone already said, 'shaking' the to induce pollination when there are no flowers is useless. Must have flowers first. Shaking stresses the plant too much, and tomato stalks are notoriously 'snappy'. #1: Don't plant seeds so early. You'll get plants way ahead of nature's timeline in your climate. Look up the info on the tomato variety and read about it's seed germination times. You can plan better next time with that info. #2: if you 'must' pollinate something - simply use a small, soft hair brush to swipe/wipe the flower parts in the order needed. (not foam, not stiff, not a paint brush). Try a makeup brush if you don't have a watercolor brush. You can Google how to do this for your plant (it is different for each type of plant). tldr: Yes. Repot to a much much bigger pot, plant seedling DEEP, set them on the floor, add lots of led grow lights, a trellis or tomato cage, feed 1/2 strength every 2 weeks. Stop pruning, only pinch off suckers in between joints. When spring comes 'harden them off': move them outside during the day, bring inside at night. Do this for at least a week. Then plant. Hope some of this helps you.

It is marginata and the margins are inconspicuous due to low light. The sudden change in stem diameters is an indication (likely) of the change from high light to low light. Low light causes elongation of cells (promotes a reduction in diameter) and reduces the necessity of the plant to make more cells to store excess photosynthate (sugars/starches), which also contributes to limiting of the diameter of stems/branches. You CAN propagate by cuttings, but success would be much more likely if you waited until June/early July (if you live in the Northern Hemisphere) because the plant should be in a higher state of vitality (more reserve energy) and days are longer/brighter, which means the (then) current ability to make food (plants make their own food during the process of photosynthesis) will be at peak levels; or, you could air layer the top off starting the layer at your leisure. Success is pretty much assured if you layer instead of propagate by cuttings. The already rooted stems will then back-bud and grow new branches. That response, back-budding, will also be more enthusiastic of you separate the layer in June/early July. The plant definitely wants more light. What have you been doing insofar as fertilizing? Al

First, check the manufacturer's installation instructions.  The length of most portable A/C exhausts is limited and it may not be sufficient to reach your attic.  Assuming it will, the concern about venting it into the attic is the potential to introduce moisture and the attendant problems (e.g., mold, mildew, etc.)   You might consider boosting the flow of conditioned air to the room either via changes to your existing duct work or using a transfer grill and fan as alternatives.  Either would enhance cooling without the need for an exhaust or the need to deal with condensate.

Provided your unit produces condensate, you'll be introducing some amount of moisture into your attic in the exhaust air stream.  Whether that causes a problem depends on the rate at which moisture is introduced, the attic volume, and the attic ventilation rate. You may be able to address your issue less expensively--and without any condensate or exhaust stream to deal with-- if you use a powered room-to-room transfer fan.  Here's an example: https://shop.tjernlund.com/products/as1

I agree it's not  good idea to exhaust anything into an attic and I think the objective can be better achieved without the added cost and complexity of a portable A/C unit.  That said, I don't believe that venting the OP's portable A/C into an attic is prohibited by code--at least not the 2018 IRC, but, it might be buried somewhere in the fine print.

Portable air conditioners are a poor way of cooling and in your case I believe it will be detrimental to overall cooling of building. Your portable obivously doen't have both intake and a discharge hoses or you would be discharging at same place the intake comes from outdoors.  Using room air to cool coils then discharging (to attic or outdoors) heated air does 2 negative things.  #1 Discharging air from inside a building will pull an equal quinity of air from outdoors.   You just took xx cubic feet of cool air and exchanged it for hot air which now has to be cooled.  #2 Not only did you trade cool air for hot air, the portable motors give off almost as much heat as the cooling coil takes from air.   So you actually add heat to inside building instead of cooling it.   You are 10x to 1 better off doing as Chas Ross suggested in moving air from adjoining room(s) to computor room.  Just for the record even though it is the least efficient means of cooling, a portable with intake and discharge hoses can cool a room better than a funeral fan if no other options are available.  Bottom line, a 120 volt window shaker is a far better option than a portable.

There are several factors to consider when choosing the best hardwired undercabinet LED lighting for a kitchen: Brightness: Look for lighting with a high lumen output to ensure that the countertop is well-lit and that food preparation tasks are visible. Color temperature: Choose a color temperature that is warm and inviting, such as 2700K to 3000K, to create a cozy atmosphere in the kitchen. Energy efficiency: Select LED lighting with a high efficiency rating to save energy and reduce electricity costs over time. Dimming capabilities: Consider installing dimmer switches to allow for adjustable lighting levels and create different moods in the kitchen. Color rendering index (CRI): Choose lighting with a high CRI, ideally 90 or above, to accurately render colors and allow for accurate food preparation. Durability: Look for lighting that is made from high-quality materials and is designed to withstand the heat and moisture present in a kitchen. In addition, consider integrating smart lighting technology into the kitchen. Smart lighting systems allow you to control the lighting with a smartphone app, voice commands, or even through home automation systems like Amazon Alexa or Google Assistant. This can provide greater convenience and flexibility in managing the lighting in your kitchen.

I believe I have the identical furnace but with the Bryant name on it instead of Carrier. Mine was installed in 2000, and I have had significant issues with the inducer fan and motor. The furnace brings this fan up to a higher speed when the furnace first starts to purge the firebox of any combustibles, and then it slows down to the requires speed of either the high or low fire. The first issue I have had with it was kind of a ticking noise that I could hear from outside the house where the furnace vent is (at sidewalk level). This turned out to be the inducer fan which is made out of plastic, but has a steel bushing in the center which goes over the motor shaft. The bushing had come loose from the plastic fan and was causing it to wobble and rub on the housing. I repaired it with epoxy but it was not in balance and the fan became noisy. In Canada they will not sell this fan as a separate item, but I was able to locate one in the US and replaced the fan with a new one. But, I have had other issues. The seal between the fan and the motor had gotten damaged and was not sealing well. I also neglected to annually clean the condensate trap, and water backed up into the fan housing and the motor. The motor bearings seem to have gotten water into them and were stiff. This was causing the fan to be slow in coming up to speed and generated the 42 code, so the furnace will not run. With some hesitation I decided to replace the motor bearings. It was not an easy job, and not for the faint of heart. This motor I believe is a permanent magnet variable frequency design, and the control board is soldered right on the end of the motor. With careful desoldering you can get it off and the bearings can be replaced ($16 for new ones at a bearing shop). It worked for a few years and I had to revisit the motor and seal issues. However this year it failed to start up again with the 42 code and I decided to bite the bullet and replace the unit. At least for the design of motor I have they do not sell the motor or fan, but the complete unit. It cost me $1520 CDN to replace it, with me doing the work. I had a really hard time finding the replacement unit. Carrier claimed that they were right out of stock right across North America, but I found a one man furnace repair guy that had one to sell me. I did it myself as I have had this thing out a few times now and know how to do it. He wanted $200 to do it. Here is a link to the kit instructions. I see your furnace model is listed as being suitable for it. https://www.shareddocs.com/hvac/docs/1009/Public/07/IIK-340793-762-01.pdf Bottom line is that if you have this unit you may want to address it sooner rather than later and get the complete replacement unit, and not be caught in a jam with cold weather and no parts. The other alternative is to buy a new furnace, but that will be a lot more. For what it is worth the new replacement unit has worked very well since I put it in. Perhaps there are many more years of life left in the furnace now, but the cost to repair it is not minor. The other issue I have had with this furnace is the two differential pressure switches. I had to replace them. And since the replacement fan motor is a different design you are supposed to replace these switches when you change to the later design motor. I have also replaced the original ignitor with a hot rod ignitor. Other than this, the furnace has been "prefect!" When it comes to replace it, I think I will look for a simpler design.

The furnace was installed in 2004 - at my last service I was told the heat exchanger was developing pinholes so I guess this will force the issue on replacement. D. Klees, If this furnace was registered I would think that heat exchanger should be under part warranty. Usually 20 years is the norm for heat exchangers of this 2004 time period. All other parts of the furnace are only under 10 parts typically if the unit is registered. It's not likely you will be able to do this work yourself thru a distributor, you'll need a licensed contractor in your area to handle warranty exchange of the heat exchanger. If you're not the original purchaser of the equipment then there may be a clause that limits warranty periods for second or more owners of a specific property.

There was a class action lawsuit raised on the heat exchanger issue. I have a file about an inch thick on this problem furnance. Somewhere in there, I recall that Carrier extended the warranty if one really wants to go down that rabbit hole. Keep in mind that the firebox in these furnaces operates under a negative pressure. Any leakage through pinholes, if they exist, will be fresh air into the exhaust stream which goes outside the house.

Thanks very much for all the replies! My son has a friend  who is in  HVAC  and these are his comments  FWIW! ===================================== That furnace has a variable speed ECM blower motor. There is no capacitor or belt like your dad mentioned. 1 of 2 things. 1) Either the bearings are failing on the motor. Nothing you can do about it. They're permanently sealed, lifetime lubricated. Would need to replace the motor. Or... 2) these motors can sometimes "hunt" at start up. They are looking for a reference point. Kinda like they have a built in tachometer to measure the rpm. Sometimes nothing can be done to stop it from happening. They always do this at start up, but it can become noisier and take longer as they age. If the blower wheel is dirty and causing an imbalance it may contribute to this. If it's dirty and you clean it, the noise may stop.  My theory is that the dust that accumulates inside the motor also contributes to it struggling to find the reference point, but that's just a guess. ===================================== Based on all the information, I’m reasonably confident this isnt a short-term crisis - I figure when the weather cooperates, I’ll pull the blower assembly and check/clean everything - but based on the age I’m fairly certain the wife will have me researching a new furnace for our golden years!

If you have the original motor in your furnace that I had in mine, which is 4 years older, there is another more remote possible cause. This motor is very heavy and has multiple steel balance plates on the end of it which I think is to try and keep it from vibrating at higher speeds. On top of the weights, there are fairly soft rubber mounts for the motor, that if worn can let it move enough to cause noise. I thought for a while that was the source of the noise. They can be replaced and it did it. But, it didn't really help. By just taking the cover off the bottom of the furnace you can reach the end of this motor. Jiggle it around and see if it could be hitting something to make the noise. You can also stick your fingers into the end of the motor cooling fan and see how hard it is to turn, or if there is any roughness to indicate the motor bearings have failed. Contrary to what your son's friend says, the bearings can be replaced, but it is a difficult job and the average furnace repair guy is likely not brave enough to try it, and you may not want to pay them for the time it takes. I don't recall the inducer wheel being dirty and that causing unbalance. It is quite doable to take out the whole motor and fan housing. Then you can reach in and check if the impeller wheel is loose on the shaft. That is probably the most likely cause.

How do I stop water from getting into the kitchen from the bathroom? Easy.  Cap off the shower and take tub baths. Looking at the very first picture.  See how the tub flange is exposed and the tile is sitting on top of it.  That is an indication that the original install was bad.  Typically, backer board sits just slightly above the tub deck and covers the flange.  This requires that the studs above tub height are firred out to insure a plumb install of the backer board. So, unless that tub has some unusual double flange design, this was a tear out/ redo from Day 1.

I am a homeowner, not a pro. Our primary bedroom shower failed when our house was only 10 years old. My then husband thought it was the grout that failed, which damaged the wall behind. He tore out the tile and backer board and replaced it all, regrouped and sealed. It failed again. My now husband demoed it all down to the studs and found dry rot, wet rot, mold like you’d never want to see. We moved out of our bedroom and into a guest room. To fix it required replacing all the damaged studs and rebuilding the entire area, not only the shower, but all affected areas. He rebuilt it using specialized backer board for showers and a membrane system specifically designed for waterproofing showers. He researched online, consulted with  a friend who is a general contractor, read about code requirements in our area. We also had a general contractor who specializes in bathrooms give us a quote. He learned a lot and ultimately felt that if he listened to professionals, adhered to product instructions and didn’t try to cut corners for a quick fix, he could handle the job. The most important thing he did was determine the source of the failure, which turned out to be a poorly designed and installed garden window that was allowing shower water to leak into the wall. All the regrouting in the world wouldn’t have stopped the problem and regrouting would not have been better than nothing. It would have simply given us a false sense of security and we’d have probably delayed the project longer, resulting in more damage and this more extensive and expensive repairs.Your water is almost certainly coming from somewhere behind the wall, wall behind the tile and grout. Anything you attempt with tile or grout is likely just a very temporary cover up. Meanwhile, whatever is happening behind your wall is continuing to happen. It’s important to understand that while you’re trying to remedy this from the outside, the damage continues inside. No one here is being deliberately obtuse, they are genuinely trying to help you. You are looking in the wrong direction, they’re trying to steer you back in the direction of a thorough and permanent solution to your problem. Your bathtub, shower and entire surround need to be removed and replaced using proper products and construction methods. If you don’t have the skills to do this, you will need to hire a professional contractor who remodels bathrooms. This is not a handyman job. The tiler/grouter is happy to do a quick shoddy “fix” and be down the road with your money in hand, and yes happy to tell you this will fix it. You want someone who can and will identify the source of the failure and rebuild your bathroom correctly.Best of luck to you, I hope you get a beautiful and functional new shower at the end.

Try it a few days and if you still get water in the kitchen you'll know there's a plumbing leak in the walls/floor.

You'll need to weigh the additional upfront and maintenance costs for two systems versus the cost of a single, higher-capacity system with zone controls.   Your HVAC contractor should be able to help you make an informed choice.   Either option should be able to maintain comfortable conditions inside your home.  Keep in mind that a single system with zoning will likely require more space for ductwork than systems where each is dedicated to a single level of your home.  While it's always a good idea to plan for duct work in the architectural design phase to avoid an unpleasant surprise during construction, its' even more so for a single system serving multiple floors.

I have a similar size house and basement with two furnaces. The two furnaces were an upgrade option when the house was purchased by the previous owner. I am always thankful the option was chosen 40 years ago when the house was built. This is money well spent in my opinion. Basements below ground have a small heat loss. The radiant floor heating in the basement is something you could do without if you need to balance HVAC budget if adding the second furnace. One option is to insulate the floor and add a zone off the first floor furnace. If you will be adding AC then the this added zone will help reduce the basement's humidity level.

"If you will be adding AC then the this added zone will help reduce the basement's humidity level."  As you noted, Mike, basements have small heat loss.  They also typically have small heat gain so they rarely call for air conditioning.  If they do, air conditioning supplied by a 1st floor system would require the system to have a high turndown capability.   We find that dehumidifying basements typically requires installation of a dehumidifier which is integrated into the HVAC.

Prior to installing the Carrier Infinity furnaces and AC in my house, I needed to run a dehumidifier in the basement to keep the humidity at an acceptable level. During the installation I had a return vent and one supply vent added to the finished area of the basement. The humidity level is not comfortable throughout the summer. The dehumidifier is collecting dust in the unfinished part of the basement. I agree if the basement has a high humidity level, a dehumidifier may still be required. In my case it was not needed. The extra money spent on a communicating variable speed furnace and 2-stage AC has been offset by not running a dehumidifier.

You have a lovely carnosa!  I like to refer to them as the "OG" carnosa or "heirloom" carnosa.  These have been around for a long time, shared by many, and will continue to give and give. Carnosas can be happy in many types of media.  They dislike having wet feet.  So whichever media you choose, just be sure to let it dry completely before watering again.  I like to grow my carnosas in a chunky mix.  But rest assured that many people have grown them potting soil for decades. Fertilizing is one of those other opinion type things.  I give mine DynaGro Foliage Pro.  But the woman I got one of my huge carnosas from used tomato fertilizer on hers and they were gorgeous.  You can also use foliar feed sprays like orchid spray.  Don't over think it.  Just give it some food but don't over feed. They like to climb or trail.  They will put out long vines that will initially be leafless and those will want to wrap around something.  They will literally wrap around themselves or anything in their path.  They wrap counter-clockwise.  So if you do give it something to climb and give it a headstart, be sure to remember that. If you want a bushier plant, you can chop some of those vines and root them in water, then stick them back in the same pot. Just to give you an idea of their potential, here's the one I inherited from a neighbor before I brought it home.  Yes, that's one pot.   this is the "tomato fertilizer" one too.

Why so sitngy with information? I can tell you that all loads must reach the foundations so the configuration of the dormer might spread those loads differently but the total loading won't change. I suspect the engineer's gable design created 2 point loads on the front wall (but without the engineer's drawing I'm only guessing).  There are many ways to frame any style of dormer. Basements below grade have small heat loads and almost zero cooling loads. Some of the heat loss from the current boiler and furance may be enough to keep the basement comfortable. Hi, Joe, Conditioning basements can be challenging because the heating and cooling loads tend to be small and outdoor air exchange tends to be less compared with above-grade living areas. You should also consider fresh air ventilation requirements for basement living areas.  A properly sized heat-recovery ventilator (HRV) or energy-recovery ventilator (ERV) would be good candidates.

What kind of flooring are you hoping to get installed? The builders who recommend to screed over the quarry tiles, what kind of flooring do they recommend putting on top of the concrete? Is that going to make the floor less cold? Without a DPC, isn't there going to be a risk of efflorescence? You'll still have to deal with vapour coming up through the floor, so you'll be limited in the kind of flooring you can use. I doubt you could put vinyl flooring without a vapour barrier, but I'm not sure. I'm not an expert, but (assuming your floor is original) unless you insulate the floor, it will continue to be cold. And to insulate the floor, you will have to dig it out unless you have enough head room to raise it. You could potentially install a wooden floor so it doesn't feel as cold, but it would need breathing room underneath to avoid damage from the ground moisture. You could also add vapour-permeable insulation underneath. As for DPC causing damp walls, what do the builders recommending it say about that? My understanding is that you could put a drainage system on the inside of the house, under the slab, (example: https://hammerandhand.com/best-practices/manual/7-basements/7-4-basement-retrofit/). It might still be a good idea to insulate the floor to avoid condensation issues. I would personally consider a proper DPC to decrease the humidity inside the house, especially in a humid climate, but it's an expensive intervention. As water turns into vapour, it uses up energy (heat) and cools down the air. Without a DPC, the more you heat your place, the more water from the ground turns into vapour and gets into your house, so it's not very energy efficient.

Another random piece of sartorial trivia. The Irish kilt is a fairly recent thing (19th c?), kilts are Scottish, the Irish thing was more of a shift, if it was a full garment or a skirt. Evil faeries would abduct children and they were more interested in boys, so you could trick the faeries into thinking a small boy was a girl by having him wear a skirt until he was older/big enough to fight off the abductor. (So the story of "why" goes.) My grandfather, who was 78 when I was born, so was born in the 19th c. was born in America, but lived in a mining village, wore a dress until he started public school. They are breaking dormancy early. Hydrangea Vanilla Strawberry (VS) is a mid-season hydrangea paniculata summer bloomer. Paniculatas like it begin to develop flower buds depending on their geographical location, weather, etc. but you could say the invisible buds start in late spring or early summer and blooms start soon afterwards so June-July. Here in Texas, VS leafs out in March and blooms in June (it should leaf out later up north though). Crape Myrtles are notoriously very late to leaf out here in Dallas, somewhere between April to May in some years. CMs are currently asleep. Roses here tend to stay evergreen in most years albeit with fewer old leaves by this time and with some leaf out in Feb-March. Spireas are quite hardy, almost impossible to winter kill here. Mine are still dormant in Texas. But sometimes a mild winter with a surprise cold ending is worse than a cold snowy winter. In Atlanta, this happened several decades ago and a large percentage of trees got killed. Periodically check the 10-15 days weather forecasts. Depending on exactly how warm things are, consider mulching, covering with sheets and deeply watering the early risers before any overnight crash in temperatures that might be followed with cold drying winds. Winter has been unusually warm here too; already hit 90F a week ago. Leafing out over here are roses, irises, salvias, azaleas, forsythias, some hydrangeas and a few trees. Blooming are some azaleas, camellia japonicas, winter honeysuckle, flowering quince and redbuds. If cold temperatures return with a vengeance, you may need to protect some plants and remove some dead wood afterwards. It should not impact Vanilla Strawberry's summer blooms. Good luck, Luis

I've been out of college for, well, a few years, but I'm brushing off my thermodynamics hat for this research For a metal, cast iron has a relatively poor thermal conductivity. That's part of why it's such a good cooking material - it holds the heat you apply. That said, compared to acrylic, it has a significantly higher thermal conductivity. Also, cooking and bathing are different, of course. When cooking, you have the skillet over a heat source. With a bathtub, you add the hot water, and then the heat begins to transfer through the tub and into the room. A cast iron tub has a high thermal mass vs acrylic, so it can hold a lot of heat. I found this website, where they actually did measure it (yay, quantitative data!) and found the cast iron bath water cooled faster than this company's "coreacryl" which is a bit more than just plain acrylic: https://www.bathsofdistinction.com/coreacryl-vs-cast-iron-bathtubs-s/82.htm @artemis78 - with your cast iron tub, do you fill it with really hot water? I'm thinking that if one runs the hot water say at 120F, that would give enough extra heat to get the tub up to temperature, while the water cools to a more comfortable bath temp of say 100-105F. I noticed that link above doesn't show continuous temperature drop. My guess is the cast iron starts to stabilize a bit once the tub temperature and water temperature get more into equilibrium.

@stm25rs good question--I'd never thought about that! I do usually draw baths by turning the water on as hot as it will go and then turning it down near the end to get it to the target temperature. Trust me on the thermodynamics: if you fill a cast iron tub  and an acrylic  tub with the same volume of water at the same initial temperature, the  cast iron tub will suck out more  heat from the water and radiate it away  than the acrylic,  and lower the overall water temperature faster. However,  the cast iron may give the illusion of being warmer because your body is in direct contact with  something that has higher thermal mass than acrylic so your senses tell you it's warmer. It's like if someone dropped a button and a penny in your hand and both were at the same high  temperature: the penny would feel a  lot hotter than the button  because of the  much greater  amount of  energy contained in the  metal.

artemis- Well, I should explain that your butt and back may feel a little warmer, but the overall temperature of the water will be a little lower in the cast iron tub because the tub will transfer heat out of the water faster and radiate it to the room faster. In the long run, it may not be a big enough difference to worry about.  I just have a problem with people claiming cast iron performs better at retaining heat when thermodynamics tell us just the opposite.

Suppliers - You should be able to find one or more Quartz/Granite suppliers in your area who carry one or more of the manufacturers Quartzpending on where you live. In the Austin, TX Metroplex area we have several a large suppliers with indoor warehouses of slabs to view as well as their websites to view material virtually. Fabricators / Installers - You can also look for smaller fabrication / installation companies who shoud have samples or full slabs for one or both of the sources listed above.  Make sure to get references prior to selecting a fabricator / installer. Feel free to look through some of my projects to view various quartz and granite countertop installations well as complimentary tile backsplashes. Just click on my logo to the upper left of this comment. Finally, a word of advice for installation of any solid surface on cabinets. I recently painted a bedroom set of furniture with a latex paint that was a combination of paint & primer.  It turned out well.  The main thing is to be sure that they are squeaky clean.  This is what I did.  First I used a deglosser on all surfaces.  Then I wiped it down with TSP cleaner.  Then 3 coats of the combo primer & paint in satin finish.  Be very sure that the paint is thinned , if it is too thick it will peal & dent really easily.  Thin coats with a good amount of drying time in between coats worked best.  I also added something to the paint that slowed down drying time so that I could catch runs if they occurred & they did.  Good luck if you decide to tackle them.  It is not for anyone in a hurry.

Undertones are just someone's subjective opinion of what a color looks like to them under a random light source and in a random context - which is why it's subjective. @HU-925329097 - I think you need to consult with an attorney before you do anything else.  Whoever produced the buildable plans had a duty to ensure that all measurements were correct, rarely would a builder have a duty to verify measurements on plans that they didn't produce.  If there were contradictory numbers you might argue that they should have sought clarification, but their counter is going to be they had no duty to verify and therefore it wasn't their job to catch the error. In my experience the builder is going to win this and your best bet is to try to negotiate a lower amount.  Of course, I am making a lot of assumptions on the details I don't have and your particular situation may have nuance that will change that. --- In every state it was always your property, even if you haven't paid the builder a single cent.  A builder may have a clause that doesn't allow the owner access to the home during construction, that still doesn't give them the right to keep you out, it just means that your entry on the property would be a breach of contract, I doubt that many courts would find that a material breach, but it is possible. However, the builder's biggest tool to encourage payment is a mechanic's lien.  Mechanic's liens are very easy to get, but harder to perfect.  In other words, there is a good chance that you are going to get a lien on your property even if you don't believe you owe the money.  The builder then has some period of time to perfect the lien.  Perfecting a mechanic's lien is not easy and it can be quite expensive, but if/when perfected your home is in foreclosure, which most people just pay rather than have their home foreclosed on. Again, consult with an attorney in your area, who has construction experience.  I suspect you might be better off paying the contractor and suing him for breach of contract for the driveway than allowing him to get a mechanic's lien.

Sure!  But be cautious about ”Universal Design.”  I have found that it compromises, trying to be good for all.  Instead, it is good for some and leaves others stranded in a handicapped bathroom on a toilet too far from any wall to get a grip on anything to help you get up!  (Yes, that is my own personal story and I ended up having to turn halfway round and use the plumbing pipes on a flush-o-matic to push off of for a lift, while the stadium usher who took me there was likely wondering if I had drowned!) Universal design works (most of the time) in public facilities, where people of various abilities will be using the bathrooms.  When designing a bathroom for an individual, though, you have the opportunity to meet their own current needs and plan for future changes.  So, your person uses a wheelchair.  Figure out some of their needs by assessing their abilities, need (and future need) for assistance, and the size and plumbing constraints of the room.  Explore technology that can help, like hoyer-type lifts to elaborate ceiling track systems that can pick someone out of their bed or chair into a sling system, then using ceiling tracks, transport them to a commode, bathtub bathtub, or shower in their bathroom.  I have seen a few houses for sale where such track systems were in place, presumably for long-term disabilities. If your person can transfer from their chair to the toilet unaided, you figure out what room they need from which angle, and where grab bars are needed. There are trombone slide like grab bars that mount onto the wall behind the toilet and hinge up agaist the wall or down next to the toilet as needed.  If a person needs somone on one side or other, or beside/behind the toilet to assist, you need to provide room for this.  One wheelchair universal design guideline for commercial spaces said that a handicapped toilet was to have 5 ft of open space on three sides, which is how I, a walker user with bad knees, almost got stranded.  So figure out what is needed now, and what is reasonably to be expected in the future.  If your person needs grab bars, figure where to attach them. Wheelchair accessible sinks are available that hang on a wall or sit on a floating counter that are deep enough to allow a person in a wheelchair pull up and reach the sink without hitting their legs on the wall behind.  Most major manufacturershave one or two.  There are even vanities available that have a bit of storage that will hold these sinks.  They are wall-hung, to allow footrests to swing under the counters without obstruction.  They cost a few thousand dollars, more than they look like they should, presumably due to low consumer need.  Then there are the white plastic pumbing covers that you often see in medical settings below the sinks.  These are installed so that if a user is pulled up under the sink and their leg makes contact with the plumbing, a hot tap water supply pipe or a hot drain won’t burn them. Wheelchair users sometimes use a specially designed shower chair that they transfer into outside the shower (or even in the bedroom) that can be wheeled into a shower and which allows access for reaching to wash most places.  Others, who have good sitting balance, may use a simpler shower stool that they transfer to from the wheelchair.  This would require a more open space and room for the wheelchair to sit in the room while the person is in the shower.  There are also swivel transfer benches that are great for people who can stand to transfer.  They are perhaps 3 ft long and have a chair that swivels and slides along a track.  We used one of these for my father in law before we remodeled our bathroom.  He would stand and pivot so that his back was to the tub, then sit onto the bench seat.  His caregiver would then push the seat backwards while lifting his legs, lock the slider, unlock the swivel, and turn the seat so he was facing the shower controls and lower his legs into the bathtub.  The seat had a back to it and optional arms. For an open showeer situation, where the bather may need assistance at times, there are short, 3 ft tall folding caregiver shower doors.  These keep the water confined into the shower better than a curtain, letting the caregiver stand outside the shower and keep their legs out of the spray.  You top these plastic or glass panel folding shower caregiver doors with a short shower curtain above them that is long enough to stay behid the caregiver doors when the person does not need assistance and is using the sprayer.  Generally, people find it easier to use a chair or stool that is mobile than a built-in shower bench.  It is a matter of being able to reach better to assist a person who is not up against two walls. Think also about whether the wheelchair user might sometimes use a scooter or a power chair.  These may limit how close a person can get to a sink to wash their hands, so a semi-recessed  sink like mine, which protrudes from the counter may be better for them.  These are not necessarily made for handicap use, but  may work better in some circumstances. For the shower itself, you can have a custom tiled shower made to your specifications.  Often, people will use a floor that slopes from the room floor to the back wall of the shower with a long linear drain or trench drain at the back wall.  You will need to consult with a builder or other professional to learn if this is an option for the home.  Constraints sometimes arise about how to fit in the slope needed.  I chose a premade solid surface shower instead.  My drain is at the front of the shower floor, a 4” square you can see in the center front.  It has a half-inch high dam that directs water to remain in the shower and head for the drain and a half-inch deep trough under the metal drain cover.  This is inadequate to hold the water in at times (I went through some hair loss in which I could slow the drain with hair before a single shower was through!) and I do overflow into the bathroom fairly often.  That is why my entire bathroom floor is waterproofed using a barrier method that my builder had trained in, and why there is an actual sloped Kerdi shower kit making up the majority of my bathroom floor.  I have a floor drain in front of my shower as back up, and it is the best design choice I made (with the help of the pros here at Garden Web/Houzz).  See the dark square in front of the vanity leg, by the reflection off the tile?  That is my floor drain.  I chose my shower because it is easy care Solid Surface and because it is 37.75” deep.  It gives me much more depth than the Swanstone Handicapped Shower at 34”.  Transolid made mine. Swanstone does have a much better guarantee, though.  My builder was able to make the shower level with the floor by removing the subfloor over the floor joists and replacing them with subfloor between the joists that is level with the top of the joists.  This gave us 3/4” and the shower floor under the room floor did the rest.  We did have to make the flooring slope upwards from the doorway  to meet the shower floor in the room floor.  It is noticeable, but no one has tripped yet walking into the room. Because my shower floor is level with the room floor, it does provide me with a 5 ft turning radius at the toilet and at the shower, which is recommended for wheelchair users.  Another space consideration I made was to  go to the local wheelchair store and get the turning radius for an electric wheelchair that fits me.  I then made my bathroom counter a mere 16” deep, to give me space enough there.  My builder made my walnut vanity  only 14” deep at the bottom.  He built it from my design.  I chose a 36” pocket door for maximum access.  This is the house’s only full bathroom.  We did move the shower wall out about 6 - 8” into the adjoining bedroom.  That made the bedroom‘s closet that much deeper, so I stole it back by having an 11” deep cupboard put in the lower half of the closet for the bathroom.  This is how we fit a handicapped bathroom, with storage, into a 8.5’ long basic bathroom.  I hope this gives you lots of key words to search on and an idea of how thought processes work when dealing with this kind of remodel.

Don't worry about the tree roots. Unless the rocks are piled around the tree trunk very deeply, they do not hinder water penetration and tree roots extend out a significant distance from the tree base anyway. Likely the rocks cover only a very small portion of the root system. Unless you wish to give them away again, I'd consider something like a dry stream bed if it fits into the garden design. While a dry stream bed may direct water/rain runoff during heavy weather, it is NOT a rain garden. Rain gardens are intended to slow runoff and allow it to be reabsorbed into the ground before hitting the storm drain system and that requires a special type of rain garden soil, not rocks.

Hi there, One thing to think about if you are wanting to alter this building to a habitable space is the ceiling height in the bedrooms and living space, which may need to be an average of 2.4m high. Check with the building code for your area. That might restrict you putting the bedrooms entirely in the pool end of the building. You will need to allow plenty of space for insulation in the ceiling to keep the summer heat out so this may affect the final ceiling height once you have battens and ceiling lining under the rafters. I've attached a sketch which puts the main bedroom opening onto the deck, which if you are the only occupant for the majority of the time, is a nice feature. You could install insect screens on the sliders and sleep with the door open in summer and leave it open for ventilation during the day. The kitchen living and dining run the length of the side with the view with the dog cleaning and laundry area at the pool end of that space. The living and dining space is simple and long for plenty of tables for the girls in the future and is easily observed from anywhere so will be easy to manage. The second bedroom/office would be on the south corner so it would get a bit of morning and afternoon sun. It is longer into the higher roof area to make sure it has a good average ceiling height. This room can double up as office and storage and you can make the robe/linen/storage cupboards as you like it. The bed may need to be pushed to the side when the puppies need the space or have a sleeper couch. I have shown only a two burner hobb to save some space as you would seldom use more than two at a time. I disagree with the above comment. I think you need to be very careful about using (cool) grey. To be clear, grey is just a rather meaningless word to describe potentially dozens of different colours. Blue/greys can feel extremely cold and can potentially clash with other pale warmer neutrals. Also, the cool grey 'trend' began to wane around 4 years ago and it has been replaced by warmer more 'classic' neutrals. This is apparent from a quick glance at any social media platform or any paint manufacturer posts such as Little Greene or Farrow and Ball. This matters as trends pass and can devalue a house. There is a large amount of grey tiles, flooring and vanities that have been manufactured and need to be sold. If you are using grey, be sure to question if the room is light enough not to feel too bleak and that there is wood or something warm to create a contrast. Greys that have a 'tinge' of colour are a good bet as they can provide a sophisticated neutral backdrop rather than 'battleship' grey which can feel a little too much like undercoat.

Choosing the right colour for a north-facing room can be a bit challenging as it tends to receive less natural light and can appear cooler than other rooms in the house. Warm colours can help counteract the coolness of a north-facing room and create a cosy inviting atmosphere. Dark colours can be cosy and dramatic, they tend to absorb light and can make a north-facing room feel even darker. So if you do want to use dark colours, you can absolutely consider using them as you are suggesting, as accents or on a feature wall rather than throughout the entire room. With reference to the other colours in the room/hallway next to it then perhaps you might want to think about an all over colour (wall and ceiling) in a tonal grey. Grey tones can work well in north-facing rooms, as they can complement the coolness of the light. Consider using warm grey with a pink undertone or even a beige undertone to to add warmth and depth to the space whilst being cohesive with the other rooms. Thanks

While integrated LED recessed lights have become more common in recent years, there are still plenty of options available for recessed lighting with replaceable bulbs. These types of fixtures are often called "retrofit" or "remodel" housings and are designed to be installed into an existing ceiling without the need for major modifications. Retrofit/remodel housings typically come with a standard screw base (E26) or a reflector (BR30) that can accept a range of different bulbs, including LED bulbs. These fixtures offer the flexibility to change the color temperature or brightness of the light as desired and make it easier to replace bulbs when they burn out or become outdated. If you're having trouble finding retrofit/remodel housings, try searching for "recessed lighting housings with replaceable bulbs" or "E26/BR30 compatible recessed lighting." You can also check with a local lighting supplier or electrician to see what options are available in your area. In addition, if you're interested in home automation, consider looking into smart LED bulbs that can be controlled through a smartphone app or voice assistant. These bulbs can often be dimmed and adjusted to different color temperatures, making them a versatile and convenient option for any home.

In 50 years of designing buildings I've learned the value of capturing the essence of a building in the early design phase in a simple drawing without all of the details, but with the ones that are important. Tall steep hipped roofs are traditionally French and contrary to the American vernacular you wish to emulate; covered porches should show the support beams; gable forms should be used sparingly for greater emphasis and, above all, use arbitrary colors rather than rendering the cladding materials and sketches instead of CAD in the early phase of design. There is a physiologic/anthropological reason for the tooth crowding that occurs in the lower anterior, and it is also related to the reason we often do not have room for our wisdom teeth. Prehistorically we ate a lot of abrasives with our food and our teeth wore down. If you think of teeth being shaped essentially like ice cream cones, as the teeth wear down they get narrower. They would shift forward and toward the middle to close the spaces so our gums did not get damaged. Then partway through live we would get another molar in back to help with grinding and then we would die. Now we eat much softer food, our lives are much longer and our mandibles are getting smaller, They still move toward the center but don't wear them down and the front teeth have small enough contact points that they can shift past each other and overlap.

If the grow medium deep in the pot is nearly dry and the plant is wilting, it's almost certainly due to under-watering. If the plant wilts while you can still easily detect moisture in the grow medium, it's almost certainly due to over-watering. Wilting occurs when a plant's internal water pressure drops to a point low enough that the plant can no longer maintain turgidity (keep its cells full of water under pressure). Less experienced growers very commonly think reflexively that because a plant or planting wilted, it must follow that the grow medium is too dry and the plant needs watering. Clearly, if there is not enough water in the soil, logic would lead one to that conclusion. What might seem counter-intuitive is the fact that too much water in the grow medium also can, and does, cause wilting; this, because roots need an adequate supply of oxygen in order to function efficiently/normally. An excessive amount of water displaces air in the grow medium and a fraction of that air contains oxygen required by the roots. If a planting wilts, first check to see if the soil is dry. Using a wooden tell inserted into the soil all the way to the pot bottom is probably the most reliable way of checking for soil moisture and determining if it's time to water if the tell comes out dry or nearly dry, it's time to water. Ask if you're unfamiliar with using a 'tell' or want more info. If you determine the soil is dry, of course you should water unless there is reason not to. E.g., perhaps the plant needs or you want it to have a dry rest. If a planting wilts while you can still easily detect moisture in the medium, odds are very high that over-watering is the cause of the wilting for the reason already described above. Often, growers will report they've been watering, but the plant is still wilted, but it does perk up at night. This is because there are many small holes (stomata) on leaves through which gasses from inside the plant are exchanged with gasses from the air surrounding the plant, one of the gasses that moves out of the leaves is water vapor. In preparation for the respiration or dark cycle, special cells surrounding stomata (guard cells) close the openings through which water escapes. This helps the plant rebuild all or more often some of it's internal pressure, which often conspicuously even if not entirely reduces the degree of wilting. When you see this, you can be quite sure over-watering is in play. Al

It's really not tricky. Plants vary more in what they will tolerate than in what the want. If you set cacti and about 2/3 of the succulents aside from the group of plants we commonly grow as houseplants, they pretty much all want a medium that drains well and provides plenty of air porosity in the soil, even at container capacity (when the soil is holding as much water as it can hold). Many erroneously believe that because PLs are found naturally at water's edge that they want or need or can tolerate a saturated soil. They can't, because growing in a container is not like growing at waters edge because the root structure of plants with their feet in water is very different than roots of the same plant in a pot. So, when it comes to watering a PL, the objective is to use a grow medium you can keep moist enough w/o it holding so much water after a thorough watering that it affects root function or root health. A "tell" allows you to monitor moisture levels deep in the pot, where it counts. There is no need to be concerned that the top inch or two of the soil is dry, but there is concern if the soil becomes dry all the way to the bottom and causes the plant to wilt. I'll leave something at the end of the post about using a tell. If you water correctly, so you're wetting the entire soil column and at least 20% of the water applied exits the drain hole with no pathway by which the waste water can make its way back into the grow medium, and are getting the watering intervals right, fertilizing is extremely easy. It's when you are forced (by an excessively water-retentive medium) to water in sips to avoid watering, salts from fertilizer solutions and tapwater builds up in the soil, which limits water and nutrient uptake. Flushing the soil as you water prevents that, and after a few waterings resets the medium's fertility level to near zero. Not flushing regularly not only allows salts to build in the soil, it also allows nutrient ratios, each to the others, to become skewed. When this occurs, an excess of one nutrient can cause a deficiency of one or more other nutrients. Case in point: If someone is using a bloom booster (high in phosphorous) fertilizer for containerized plants, they are supplying more P than the plant can use. Excess P causes deficiencies of calcium, potassium, copper, zinc, and especially iron. Ideally, the fertilizer you use would provide nutrients at a ratio as close to the ratio at which nutrients are taken up. The RATIO that does this best and can be used for an extremely high % of plants (95%+) is 3:1:2. A fertilizer's RATIO is far more important than it's NPK %s, but hobby growers seldom pay much attention to it. Commonly used examples of 3:1:2 ratio fertilizers include 24-8-16, 12-4-8, and 9-3-6. I use Foliage-Pro 9-3-6 for nearly everything I grow in pots. It contains all nutrients essential to normal growth (few products can make that claim), in the ratio at which the average plant actually uses the nutrients, and it derives >2/3 of its nitrogen from nitrate sources .... a big plus for plants grown indoors because it helps to keep plants full and compact.   It makes most sense to tie the frequency with which you fertilize to the number of times you water .... as long as you're watering correctly. In summer, you can fertilize about every 3rd-4th time you water, and in winter about every 4th-5th time. Keep track by dropping a marble, button, other object, in the pot when you water. If you're regimen has you watering every 4th watering, when you're about to drop in the 4th object, fertilize instead, retrieve the objects and start the cycle over. Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips in order to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions - which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma and creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell' (more reliable than a 'moisture meter'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) works better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half or in several pieces, depending on how deep your pots are. Sharpen both ends of each tell in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell's tip comes out nearly dry. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Al

You can have a radiator there. The Egress window is all about a net clear window opening to escape and emergency personnel to enter having full gear on and whatnot to rescue... the height from the basement floor is so you can climb out (the radiator can only assist in doing that). The height above the floor should not exceed 44" but lately some jurisdictions have been changing that to 42". The same goes for the window wells located outside the egress window they also must meet certain sizes and requirements. The code wants to make sure that the emergency exit can be opened from the inside without using a key or tools, in other words, or anything except your hands. The same goes for grills, bars, storm windows, or anything else installed over emergency exits, they also must open from the inside without using tools or keys, and also comply with the opening size and location requirements for an emergency exit.

^ and that description is exactly why a local inspector might not allow a radiator in front of an emergency escape and rescue opening (not "egress"). One could argue that the radiator, which you have to lean over to reach the window, can impede easily opening it. It is also not moveable or steppable, so may impede access vertically. It's up to your inspector and/or fire code marshal.

It is not recommended to choose paint colors before the lighting is installed, as the lighting can significantly affect the appearance of the colors on the walls. It's important to consider the type and location of the lighting in the room, as well as the natural light that enters the space. In your case, with minimal natural light and six can lights, it's important to choose colors that will look good under both natural and artificial light. Holding up color cards to the window can give you an idea of what the colors will look like in natural light, but it's not a complete representation of how they will look under artificial light. I would suggest considering smart dimmable RGBCW (Red, Green, Blue, Cool White, Warm White) recessed lighting. These lights have the ability to change color temperatures and adjust brightness levels, which can help to create a more balanced and natural-looking lighting scheme in your room. By choosing these types of lights, you can be more confident in your color choices, knowing that they will look great in any lighting condition. I would also recommend testing your paint colors in the actual space before making a final decision. You can purchase sample sizes of paint and apply them to a small section of the wall to see how the color appears in different lighting conditions. This will help you to make an informed decision and ensure that you're happy with the final result. Overall, it's important to consider the lighting in the space when choosing paint colors, and I encourage you to explore smart lighting options to create a more balanced and natural-looking lighting scheme.

I see evidence of water/moisture/condensation on your framing lumber. Assuming that water isn't leaking in from above, I assume that warm moist air is moving up from the living space below, finding a cold surface and causing condensation. The damp materials then host mold. That would be my theory. If that was my house I would buy a case of cans of spray foam, the $50 gun to apply it, and go to town filling every nook and crany where warm air can move from below into the attic.  If you start moving insulation around you may find wet or discolored insulation indicating where the big streams of air are coming through. If you have a door or hatch to the attic, those would be prime culprits but so would any opening in the sheetrock ceiling. I did this in my last two homes while they were being built which was a lot easier than after insulation was installed. Good luck.

I post this all the time. Anything in bold really needs to be relooked at and worked on. The best houses orient the public rooms towards the south for the best passive solar heating and cooling The best houses are L, U, T, H, or I shaped. The best houses are only one to two rooms deep. And covered lanai, porches, garages, etc count as rooms in this case. The best houses make sure kitchens have natural light, meaning windows so one doesn't have to have lighting 24/7 to use the kitchen. (And no, dining areas with windows 10' or more from the kitchen will not allow for natural light.) The best houses make sure all public rooms and bedrooms have windows on at least two walls. The best houses do not if possible put mechanical rooms, pantries or closets on outside walls The best houses do not have diagonal interior walls making for odd spaces. The best houses keep public and private spaces separate. The best houses do not have you walk through the work zone of the kitchen to bring laundry to the laundry room. The best houses do not have the mudroom go through any of the work zones of the kitchen. The best houses do not use the kitchen as a hallway to any other rooms. The best houses do not put toilets or toilet rooms up against bedroom walls or public areas. The best houses do not have walk in closets too small to stand inside. The best houses have separation, such as closets, between bedrooms and between bedrooms and public rooms. The best houses do not have roofs that are overly large, and dominate the exterior of the house. The best houses do not have stick on exterior materials only on the front façade. The best houses have an organizing “spine” so it’s easy to determine how to get from room to room in the house and what makes sense. Meaning they don’t have meandering circulation paths. Additionally the kitchen layout needs lots of help. How wide is the master closet?

It seems very common on here and perhaps in real life to put a standard "small lot" house on acreage. I know someone in real life who did the same - he is kind of a jerk so I haven't invited myself over to take a look but I heard what he was doing. Obviously, it is cheaper to put everything in a tight place from a land clearing standpoint so there may be some advantage to doing what this plan does. But the house would be a lot more sun filled if you spread it out a bit. Things like semi-detaching the garage will allow more sun in (or completely detaching but I understand that isn't everyone's desire). Your goal is really to have the most windows, particularly into public places where you spend waking hours in, to be on the south side. The south has the most sun in the winter which is when you need the light the most. That also helps heat the house - for free. Then as the sun gets higher in the sky, you get less sun during the summer. Sun that is easy to build overhangs to block out. I have a number of these and is great to have sun cascading into our kitchen in the winter and then perfectly blocked but visible all day in the summer. But, but the view. Yes - that is a consideration and with the right layout, you can have both. It sounds like you might be too far into things to change course. You appear to be working with someone who doesn't work the site/orientation into the plans which is really unfortunate. Cost isn't always a problem. Some draftsmen are very good. It isn't always about spending a lot of money on the plans but certainly any money you have already spent may be lost if you change courses.
